**Measure X Housing Fund (affordable housing development share)**
- Agency: Contra Costa County Department of Conservation and Development (75% share); Health, Housing and Homeless Services (H3) administers the 25% services share
- Type: loan
- Typical award: Measure X is a countywide half-cent sales tax (Nov 2020, 20 years, began April 1, 2021). The Board committed $10,000,000 in year one and about $12,000,000 a year after; the County's Measure X allocation table shows the Local Housing Trust Fund line at $12,600,000 (FY 2023-24), $12,902,400 (FY 2024-25), $13,156,577 (FY 2025-26) and $13,306,957 (FY 2026-27), with a 20-year total near $258,000,000. Capital share available through the housing NOFA: $9,707,500 in FY 2025/26 (including $2,000,000 recaptured from Anton San Ramon) and $7,880,690 in FY 2026/27. FY 2026/27 awards: $5,380,690 to 949 Moraga Road (SAHA and Sunflower Hill, Lafayette, 47 IDD units) and $2,500,000 to Rumrill Commons (Novin, San Pablo, 39 units). Earlier: $5,000,000 to El Cerrito Plaza Parcel A South (Related, 69 units), $4,968,158 to Choice in Aging Senior Housing (SAHA, Pleasant Hill, 82 units, matched with $2,963,384 state LHTF), $1,770,958 to Village of Hope Pittsburg (Hope Solutions, 15 PSH cottages). Minimums: $500,000 for capital projects, $250,000 for renovation and microhome projects, $25,000 to $500,000 for predevelopment with no more than $1,000,000 a year for predevelopment (Board, Sept 16, 2025).
- AMI requirement: Priority to households at or below 50% AMI (designated target population); up to 80% AMI eligible. Rental loans 55 years; homeownership 20 years or more (80% AMI, 81% to 120% allowed). Grants only for pilot, innovation and capacity-building projects.
- Cycle: annual NOFA (next: 2026-12-07 (FY 2027/28 NOFA with CDBG-Housing and HOME, applications due 5:00 PM). Loan agreement required within two years of contingent award; work must start within one year of loan execution; grants spent within two years.)
- Layering notes: County pages on www.contracosta.ca.gov refuse automated fetches (403); the same pages and DocumentCenter PDFs were opened on 2026-11-06 through the site's CivicPlus origin host (ca-contracostacounty3.civicplus.com), and Board reports were read through the contra-costa.legistar.com API. Largest discretionary local source in the 12 target counties. Same 3% simple, 55-year residual receipts terms as HOME, but no federal cross-cutting rules, so it is the preferred fill for projects inside cities without their own gap funds and for IDD, senior and farmworker deals. Predevelopment loans are not forgivable and must be repaid even if the project dies. The County used Measure X as the local match to win a $2,963,384 state Local Housing Trust Fund grant (FY 2024/25) and as match for Homekey awards (El Portal Place, $5,200,000). The 25% H3 share (about $4,068,983 in FY 2026/27) funds services, prevention and legal aid through a separate two-year RFP and is not capital. Awards are contingent on other commitments (Dec 31, 2027 for FY 2026/27 awards) and executed loans by June 30, 2028; the County recaptured $2,000,000 when Anton San Ramon stalled and pulled Harbor Pointe's Measure X request in May 2026. Local and state funds are public funds under Labor Code 1720(b), so state prevailing wage applies unless a 1720(c) exemption fits the deal, such as 1720(c)(5)(E) for below-market loans with at least 40 percent of units restricted 20 years at or below 80 percent AMI (see prevailing_wage_basis).
- Source: https://www.contracosta.ca.gov/8750/Measure-X-Housing-Fund
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-06)

**Multifamily Housing Revenue Bonds, County of Contra Costa conduit issuer**
- Agency: Contra Costa County Department of Conservation and Development, bond administration (Kristin Sherk, 925-655-2889)
- Type: bond
- Typical award: Active issuer. Board approvals: El Cerrito Plaza Parcel A South, up to $35,700,000 tax-exempt plus $10,000,000 taxable (Res. 2025-383, Nov 4, 2025, JPMorgan private placement, 6.824% TIC); Lakeside Apartments, Concord, up to $30,000,000 for RCD's 124-unit acquisition-rehab (Res. 2026-59, March 3, 2026; CDLAC allocation in hand, sale resolution expected May 2026); Res. 2026-196, up to $15,075,837 for a 124-unit acquisition-rehab (May 19, 2026); Res. 2025-362, $29,238,977 tax-exempt plus $8,000,000 taxable (Oct 21, 2025); Res. 2025-196, up to $40,000,000 for an 84-unit development (June 10, 2025); Res. 2025-117, up to $50,000,000 for 70 units (April 15, 2025). Fees per the 2018 Debt Policy appendix: $2,500 application fee, issuance fee at closing, annual fee of 0.125% of outstanding principal (minimum $5,000, may be subordinated) for the 55-year regulatory agreement term.
- AMI requirement: CDLAC and Section 142(d) minimums; County regulatory agreement typically runs 55 years. Recent deals are 100% affordable at 30% to 60% AMI. Projects must be in the unincorporated area or in a city that approves the County as issuer (cities often use CMFA or CSCDA instead).
- Cycle: rolling (next: Tied to CDLAC rounds. The program web page still says the County is not currently accepting applications, but the Board approved six bond resolutions between January 2025 and May 2026; the FY 2026/27 guidelines (section 9.4) direct any County-funded project seeking CDLAC bonds to contact DCD bond staff about the County acting as issuer. Allow for a TEFRA hearing and inducement resolution before the CDLAC deadline.)
- Layering notes: County pages on www.contracosta.ca.gov refuse automated fetches (403); the same pages and DocumentCenter PDFs were opened on 2026-11-06 through the site's CivicPlus origin host (ca-contracostacounty3.civicplus.com), and Board reports were read through the contra-costa.legistar.com API. The County issues for projects it also lends to (El Cerrito Plaza, Lakeside), which keeps one regulatory agreement and one monitor; bonds are payable solely from project revenue with no County pledge and the sponsor reimburses TEFRA and approval costs. The 0.125% annual issuer fee is in line with CMFA and CSCDA. Tax-exempt bonds alone do not trigger state prevailing wage, but County, HOME or Measure X loans in the same deal do, and Davis-Bacon follows HOME and CDBG. Program overview and 2018 policy appendix are on the County DocumentCenter.

**Permanent Local Housing Allocation (PLHA), Contra Costa Urban County entitlement**
- Agency: Contra Costa County Department of Conservation and Development (HCD entitlement grantee for the Urban County)
- Type: grant
- Typical award: HCD 2024-2028 Formula Allocation NOFA: Contra Costa County CY 2024 $1,523,318 and CY 2025 $1,631,698; 2024-2028 five-year estimate $9,520,738. The $13,021,068 figure in Resolution 2026-406 (Oct 20, 2026) is the five-year estimate for the earlier 2020-2023 allocation cycle, adopted to amend that Five-Year Plan for the owner-occupied workforce housing rule. FY 2025/26 allocation $1,860,477 with $1,767,453 to projects after 5% administration; FY 2024/25 award $1,876,423 to El Cerrito Plaza Parcel A South; FY 2022/23 award $1,000,000 to Choice in Aging Senior Housing and $1,650,000 to Rumrill Commons. Roughly $1,500,000 to $1,900,000 a year, now split with 40% to homeownership under the state's 2024 workforce housing rule, so the rental share is under $1,000,000 a year. Used as a companion to Measure X in El Cerrito Plaza (7 PLHA units of 69) and Choice in Aging. PLHA states no wage rule of its own; construction use is public funds under Labor Code 1720(b), subject to the 1720(c) exemptions (see prevailing_wage_basis). **Project-Based Vouchers, Housing Authority of the County of Contra Costa (HACCC)**
- Agency: Housing Authority of the County of Contra Costa, 3133 Estudillo Street, Martinez; Tony Ucciferri 925-957-8055 (PBV), Robert Moore, Director of Development, 925-957-8025
- Type: rental assistance
- Typical award: HACCC administers about 9,500 Housing Choice Voucher and CoC households and owns 963 public housing units plus two tax credit developments (2025 RFP). Most recent PBV invitation for proposals (REQ-12092025, released Dec 8, 2025, due Jan 8, 2026): up to 15 units for existing properties needing no more than $3,000 per unit of rehab, aimed at properties converting from CoC project-based rental assistance to PBVs. PBV waiting lists opened for partner properties in June to August 2025, Oct 27 to Nov 13, 2025 and March 2 to 19, 2026. Public housing repositioning underway (Las Deltas main campus developer RFQ due Feb 4, 2025; repositioning financial and legal consultant RFPs in 2025 and 2026).

HACCC is not a Moving to Work agency. Public housing repositioning (Las Deltas in North Richmond, El Pueblo, Bayo Vista) may produce RAD or Section 18 PBV units for partner developers. - Typical award: Full or partial exemption of property tax on units occupied by households at or below 80% AMI (Rev. and Tax. Code 214(g)); worth roughly 1.1% or more of assessed value a year depending on the tax rate area (1% base rate plus voter-approved debt). ### El Dorado County

**Affordable Housing Density Bonus (Zoning Ordinance Chapter 130.31) and the Affordable Housing Ordinance in development (inclusionary with in-lieu fee)**
- Agency: El Dorado County Planning and Building Department, Planning Division (530-621-5355), with the Affordable Housing Task Force (established April 2, 2024, Resolution 046-2024)
- Type: density bonus
- Typical award: State Density Bonus Law (Government Code 65915) as implemented in Chapter 130.31: up to 50% density bonus for the standard affordability tiers, up to 80% or unlimited density for 100% affordable projects, plus concessions, waivers and reduced parking. No local bonus beyond state law was found.
- AMI requirement: State tiers: 5% very low, 10% low, 10% moderate for-sale, or 100% affordable. The draft Affordable Housing Ordinance presented to the Task Force October 14, 2026 would require, for West Slope residential projects of 5 or more units or lots, 10% of rental units at 80% AMI for 55 years or 10% of for-sale units at 120% AMI for 45 years, with alternatives (in-lieu fee, off-site units, land dedication, conversion of market-rate units) and exemptions including deed-restricted affordable projects, mixed-use projects that are two-thirds or more residential, shelters and transitional housing, and projects where 51% or more of units are 1,600 square feet or less.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Density bonus is by right with the planning application. Resolution of Intention 163-2025 (November 4, 2025) started the Chapter 130.31 amendments; the Task Force's fee nexus study consultant was being selected in October 2026 and the ordinance and in-lieu fee will return to the Board after the study. No adoption date set.)
- Layering notes: Entitlement tools, not money. Diamond Village II (31 units) was approved under SB 35 by the Planning Commission in January 2025, which shows the ministerial path works in the unincorporated county. Watch the inclusionary ordinance: a 100% affordable project is exempt, but mixed-income workforce projects on the West Slope would pick up a 10% at 80% AMI obligation or an in-lieu fee once adopted, and the Task Force is also studying Community Facilities Districts and Enhanced Infrastructure Financing Districts as infrastructure tools. Staff flagged litigation risk around inclusionary exactions. The Tahoe Basin portion of the county is also subject to TRPA allocations and coverage rules, which this ordinance would not cover (West Slope only).
- Source: https://eldorado.legistar.com/LegislationDetail.aspx?ID=39161&GUID=DFA60236-9A16-41B1-9531-7361F8A62AB9&Options=&Search=&FullText=1
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-06)

**Affordable Housing Trust Fund and Affordable Housing Special Revenue Fund (no development NOFA)**
- Agency: El Dorado County Planning and Building Department, Affordable Housing Unit (program administration contracted to Housing Group LLC dba HousingINC through December 31, 2026); Housing@edcgov.us
- Type: loan
- Typical award: Small and discretionary. The Affordable Housing Special Revenue Fund held about $600,151 in April 2026, fed by building permit activity, and the Board committed $550,151 of it to the Caldor Fire Grizzly Flats Homeowner Rebuild Program (forgivable loans up to $73,318 for about 12 fire-displaced households, administered by HomeAid Sacramento). The separate Affordable Housing Trust Fund receives the County's share of CMFA bond issuance fees (for example $6,000 from the Diamond Village II issuance). No multifamily development award from either fund was found.
- AMI requirement: None codified. Staff describe the Special Revenue Fund as having no specific restrictions, with use at the Board's discretion for affordable housing purposes. The Trust Fund is designated for studies, program development or contributions toward creating housing.
- Cycle: rolling (next: No NOFA. A request would go through the Affordable Housing Unit and require Board action.)
- Layering notes: Reclassified from other to loan in the November 8, 2026 audit: the Affordable Housing Special Revenue Fund is deployable at Board discretion and its only recent use was forgivable loans (up to $73,318 per household) under the Caldor Fire Grizzly Flats Homeowner Rebuild Program (Resolution 064-2026, April 7, 2026). Do not underwrite County gap money in El Dorado. The county has no inclusionary fee revenue yet, no housing bond and no sales tax measure, so the Trust Fund is capitalized only by occasional conduit issuance fees and permit-related deposits. The planned Affordable Housing Ordinance (inclusionary with an in-lieu fee set by a fee nexus study now being procured) is intended to expand the Trust Fund, which is the only path to a real county gap source in the next few years. County housing staff capacity is thin: a single Administrative Analyst position was reinstated in April 2026 and HousingINC runs the program in the interim, so allow time for any County action (Board Policy A-6 resolutions, TIF offsets, TEFRA hearings).
- Source: https://eldorado.legistar.com/LegislationDetail.aspx?ID=40257&GUID=FB19D33E-5F00-40BD-BC9C-519FBDAA8C4D&Options=&Search=&FullText=1
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-06)

**Behavioral Health Services Act (BHSA) housing interventions, El Dorado County HHSA Behavioral Health**
- Agency: El Dorado County Health and Human Services Agency, Behavioral Health Division (Integrated Plan FY 2026-27 through 2028-29 adopted June 23, 2026)
- Type: grant
- Typical award: Housing Interventions budget about $4,050,000 per year (30% component). Capital Development Projects line $500,000 in FY 2026-27 and $500,000 in FY 2027-28 (about 12% of housing interventions, under the 25% cap), both for the Forni Road Housing Services Site (county-owned interim housing with temporary tiny homes and a congregate services building, partly funded from Capital Facilities and Technological Needs). Remaining housing dollars go to rental subsidies, operating subsidies (about 15 people), a Flexible Housing Subsidy Pool, transitional rent and outreach and engagement.
- AMI requirement: BHSA eligible population: adults with serious mental illness or substance use disorder who are chronically homeless, homeless or at risk of homelessness; at least 50% of housing interventions for chronically homeless people; no more than 25% of housing interventions for capital.
- Cycle: closed/inactive (next: Capital line is fully committed to the County's own Forni Road site for FY 2026-27 and 2027-28; no developer NOFA. The Integrated Plan can be revised annually (draft due to DHCS each March 31) and the next three-year plan starts FY 2029-30.)
- Layering notes: Unlike larger counties, El Dorado's BHSA capital is reserved for a county-owned interim housing campus, so a developer cannot expect BHSA gap funding for PSH before FY 2029-30. The operating subsidy and Flex Pool lines are the realistic ask: a PSH project with units set aside for BHSA clients could request a multi-year rental or operating subsidy agreement and services contract from Behavioral Health, which also strengthens an MHP or NPLH-style supportive housing application. BHSA capital is public funds under Labor Code 1720(b) but carries no wage rule of its own; coverage turns on the 1720(c) exemptions and project facts (see prevailing_wage_basis). Contact Behavioral Health early in the annual update cycle (fall) to be included in the following year's plan.
- Source: https://www.eldoradocounty.ca.gov/files/assets/county/v/1/documents/health-amp-wellbeing/mental-health/draft-eldoradocounty_2026-2029_integratedplan-web-version-1.pdf

**County development fee waivers and deferrals for affordable housing beyond the TIF offset (none found)**
- Agency: El Dorado County Planning and Building Department
- Type: negative finding
- Typical award: None. The County Developer Programs page lists only the Traffic Impact Fee (TIF) Offset and Collaborative Opportunities; no general affordable housing fee waiver or reimbursement program is offered to developers. The TIF offset (Policy B-14) is the only fee incentive. The separate Building Fee Deferral Program (listed under Homebuyers, page live on November 8, 2026) lets very low-income applicants defer building fees on new construction or health and safety repair permits until refinancing, resale or change in ownership; new guidelines are marked coming soon and it is aimed at individual homeowners, not multifamily developments. School, fire and other agency impact fees are not waived: Racquet Way Phase 2 (24 units) still owed about $87,360 to the Office of Education and $36,240 to the fire district after a 50% TIF offset was recommended.

Use the full 2025 TIF schedule less the B-14 offset on income-restricted units, plus full school, fire and County building and planning fees. The Building Fee Deferral Program is a homebuyer-side program for very low-income applicants; confirm with the Planning and Building Department (530-621-5824, Loans@edcgov.us) before assuming it covers a multifamily project.

- Agency: El Dorado County Health and Human Services Agency (HHSA), Community Services Division; hhsa-grants@edcgov.us
- Type: grant

- AMI requirement: HCV eligibility at 50% AMI or below (75% of admissions at 30% AMI); PBV HAP contracts up to 20 years with extensions. HCV waitlist has been closed since 2016.
- Cycle: rolling (next: No open PBV competition as of November 8, 2026. The 2026-2030 Five-Year PHA Plan (adopted September 29, 2026) reports a prior competitive PBV selection and PBVs committed to El Dorado Haven, and its section B.5 contains no statement of intent to make non-competitive PBV selections, so a non-competitive award would need a plan amendment first. Contact the PHA (530-621-6300) to ask about a future PBV RFP.)
- Layering notes: PBVs are the one County-controlled operating subsidy available for supportive housing in El Dorado, and with about 417 vouchers the pool is about 80 PBVs at most, several already committed to El Dorado Haven. A project with 10 to 20 PSH units should open the conversation with HHSA early and align with the EDOK Continuum of Care Coordinated Entry, which the PHA references. PBVs on a newly built or rehabilitated project with nine or more contract units trigger federal Davis-Bacon wages under 24 CFR 983.153(c); they do not by themselves trigger state prevailing wage, but state funding layered in usually does. The HCV program is federal; the PHA has no local rental assistance money. The Tahoe Basin is in the county PHA's jurisdiction but check overlap with the City of South Lake Tahoe programs.
- Source: https://www.eldoradocounty.ca.gov/Services/Assistance-Programs/Housing-Energy-Assistance/Housing-and-Homelessness/Public-Housing-Authority
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-06)

**State HOME and CDBG (non-entitlement county) and Affordable Housing County Participation Requests for HCD applications**
- Agency: El Dorado County Planning and Building Department, Affordable Housing Unit; Loans@edcgov.us; Board approval of resolutions under Board Policy A-6
- Type: loan
- Typical award: El Dorado County is a non-entitlement jurisdiction, so HOME and CDBG come through state HCD competitions and the County has used them for homeownership, not rental development: HOME $500,000 First-Time Homebuyer award (Resolutions 058-2026 and 080-2026) and a 2025 CDBG application for up to $1,500,000 for the First-Time Homebuyer Program (Resolution 180-2025). Developers seeking state funds that require a County co-applicant or resolution file an Affordable Housing County Participation Request Form at least 10 weeks before the HCD deadline.
- AMI requirement: HOME: at or below 80% AMI with HOME rents and affordability periods; CDBG: low and moderate income benefit. A developer-sponsored state HOME rental application through the County would carry HCD's 55-year regulatory agreement.
- Cycle: annual NOFA (next: Follows HCD's HOME and CDBG NOFA calendar (hcd.ca.gov/grants-and-funding/nofa-calendar). Submit the County Participation Request Form at least 10 weeks before the HCD deadline so the Board can adopt the resolution.)
- Layering notes: The County's HOME and CDBG dollars are committed to first-time homebuyer loans, so a rental project should not count on them. The practical value of the County here is as a resolution sponsor or co-applicant for state programs (HOME rental new construction, CDBG public infrastructure, Joe Serna farmworker, MHP) in a non-entitlement area where a local government signature is required. Build the 10-week lead time plus Board calendar into the HCD application schedule. State HOME in a project triggers Davis-Bacon on 12 or more HOME units and HOME cross-cutting requirements (environmental review, Section 3); state prevailing wage turns on other public funds and the Labor Code 1720(c) exemptions.
- Source: https://www.eldoradocounty.ca.gov/Services/HomebuyerRehab-Loans-Affordable-Housing-Development/Developers/Developer-Programs/Collaborative-Opportunities
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-06)

**Tax-exempt multifamily bonds: County TEFRA approvals for CMFA issuances (County not an issuer)**
- Agency: El Dorado County Board of Supervisors (TEFRA host approval, agenda through the Planning and Building Affordable Housing Unit); issuer California Municipal Finance Authority (CMFA), JPA member since October 2014; CSCDA also available
- Type: bond
- Typical award: Project-sized conduit issuances. CMFA TEFRA approved March 10, 2026 for up to $12,000,000 for Diamond Village Apartments II (31 units, 750 Black Rice Road, Placerville area, paired with $3,560,000 of HOME-ARP). CMFA closed $37,800,000 of bonds for SNO Foundation and Kingdom Development in El Dorado County in 2026. No County-issued multifamily bonds.
- AMI requirement: Federal 4% LIHTC and bond rules: at least 20% of units at 50% AMI or 40% at 60% AMI (or income averaging), 55-year CDLAC regulatory agreement.
- Cycle: rolling (next: TEFRA hearings are placed on regular Board agendas with published notice; allow 6 to 8 weeks from request to Board action and align with CDLAC rounds. County receives a share of the CMFA issuance fee for its Affordable Housing Trust Fund.)
- Layering notes: The County has no bond program of its own and does not take financial risk on conduit issues, so the TEFRA approval is procedural. Staff reports are prepared by the Affordable Housing Unit, which is stretched; submit the TEFRA request package early. Diamond Village II is the current template for an unincorporated El Dorado 4% deal: SB 35 ministerial approval, CMFA bonds, HOME-ARP from the state, TIF offset for the affordable units, and PBVs through the County PHA for the NPLH or homeless set-aside units. Private activity bonds alone do not trigger state prevailing wage, but tax credits plus state funds in the same deal usually do.
- Source: https://eldorado.legistar.com/LegislationDetail.aspx?ID=39922&GUID=053DC3F5-D26C-4E77-9729-7F71D94BADDA&Options=&Search=&FullText=1
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-06)

**Traffic Impact Fee (TIF) Offset Program for Developments with Affordable Housing Units (Board Policy B-14)**
- Agency: El Dorado County Planning and Building Department, Affordable Housing Unit, with the Department of Transportation and the Chief Administrative Office; Housing@edcgov.us; 330 Fair Lane, Placerville (Housing Unit moving to 768 Pleasant Valley Road, Diamond Springs)
- Type: fee waiver
- Typical award: Up to $1,000,000 of TIF offsets authorized each year from federal and state transportation revenues, with unused balances carried forward; Board may award more than the annual amount. Since December 2007 about $4.7 million of offsets have supported 344 affordable units. Recent awards: Diamond Village Apartments Phase II $436,632 for 30 units at 80% AMI (about 94% of the project TIF, May 12, 2026); Racquet Way Phase 2 recommended at 50% ($139,098 of $278,196) in February 2026 and denied by the Board. Staff reported about $13 million of offset capacity remaining in the program.
- AMI requirement: Developments of 5 or more units in the unincorporated county with a submitted planning application and at least 20% of units affordable to very low, low or moderate income households. Deed restriction through a TIF Offset Affordable Housing Agreement: 55 years for rental units, 45 years for ownership units (lengthened from 20 years in the September 29, 2026 revision). Must be able to pull permits within 2 years of award (extensions in 1-year increments, up to 3).
- Cycle: annual NOFA (next: No open round as of November 8, 2026. Round 37 applications were accepted January 1 to 15, 2026 with Board awards in spring 2026. Revised Board Policy B-14 (approved September 29, 2026) reviews offset requests twice a year in February and August; the County TIF Offset page still posts only the Round 37 notice, so watch for a new public notice ahead of the February 2027 review.)
- Layering notes: This is the County's only recurring development incentive and it is an offset, not cash, so it reduces the fee line of the sources and uses rather than adding a source. A 30-unit project at 80% AMI saved $436,632 in 2026. Scoring criteria: complete packet, site control, developer capacity, benefit to lower income households, Housing Element alignment, mixed income, services and infrastructure, likelihood of construction within 2 years. The Advisory Committee docked Racquet Way for a market-rate developer's limited affordable housing experience, so bring a compliance track record. The 2026 revisions also changed TIM to TIF, removed ADU language and asked the Affordable Housing Task Force to study eligibility up to 150% AMI, 100% offsets for low income units and CAO-delegated awards; none of those were adopted as of September 2026. Fee reductions under Labor Code 1720(b)(4) have an unsettled prevailing wage effect, but most projects using this offset also carry tax credits or state funds that trigger it anyway. Other impact fees (school, fire) still apply. Cities (Placerville, South Lake Tahoe) are outside the program.
- Source: https://www.eldoradocounty.ca.gov/Services/HomebuyerRehab-Loans-Affordable-Housing-Development/Traffic-Impact-Fee-TIF-Offset-Program-for-Affordable-Housing
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-06)

**Welfare Exemption (property tax), El Dorado County Assessor**
- Agency: El Dorado County Assessor, Jon DeVille, 360 Fair Lane, Placerville; 530-621-5719; with the California State Board of Equalization (Organizational Clearance Certificate)
- Type: tax abatement
- Typical award: Exemption of property taxes on the share of units restricted to lower income households (Revenue and Taxation Code 214(g)): full exemption for units at or below 80% AMI in LIHTC or publicly financed projects, partial exemption for the qualifying share in mixed projects. In El Dorado the 1% base rate plus voter-approved debt applies to the exempt value.
- AMI requirement: Nonprofit or limited partnership with a nonprofit managing general partner holding a BOE Organizational Clearance Certificate, recorded regulatory agreement (tax credits, bonds, HOME, PLHA, local agreement) restricting rents to lower income households.
- Cycle: annual NOFA (next: File BOE-267 (first year) or BOE-267-A (annual) with the Assessor by February 15 each year. Late claims filed by January 1 of the next year can cancel 90 percent of tax, penalty and interest, and later claims 85 percent, with the combined tax, penalty and interest capped at $250. Property acquired after the January 1 lien date must file within 90 days of the first of the month after acquisition or by February 15 of the following year, whichever is earlier. Supplemental forms BOE-267-L or BOE-267-L1 attach as applicable.)
- Layering notes: Standard underwriting item. The Racquet Way staff report noted the project does not currently qualify for a welfare tax exemption because it is developed by a market-rate developer rather than a nonprofit, which is a reminder that a for-profit TIF offset recipient without a nonprofit managing general partner pays full property tax; the developer can instead request a restricted assessed value under Revenue and Taxation Code 402.1 that reflects the rent restrictions. The County's 55-year TIF offset agreement counts as a recorded restriction for the 402.1 valuation but does not by itself qualify for 214(g).
- Source: https://www.boe.ca.gov/proptaxes/countycontacts.htm
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-06)


### Fresno County

**Affordable Housing Development NOFO (HOME, HOME-CHDO, HOME-ARP and PLHA combined annual round)**
- Agency: Fresno County Department of Public Works and Planning, Community Development Division (ComDev@fresnocountyca.gov, (559) 600-4292)
- Type: loan
- Typical award: The February 19, 2025 NOFO offered about $15,534,572 across PLHA, HOME, HOME-CHDO and HOME-ARP; all five applications were reserved: Cherry Crossing II, Sanger (64 units, Self-Help Enterprises), Reedley Elderly and Selma Elderly (Self-Help, $2,000,000 HOME-CHDO each for 11 assisted units, $181,818 per unit), Sanger Modular now Sendero Commons (UPholdings and RH Community Builders) and Park Kingsburg (Horizon ELOM, $2,000,000). The 2026-27 Action Plan reserves $5,018,870 of HOME for projects selected under the 2026 NOFO. Historic County awards were capped at $1,000,000; the 2025 NOFO raised the recommended maximum to $2,000,000 per project with justified requests above that considered.
- AMI requirement: HOME 20-year federal affordability (County loan terms typically 55 years; Reedley and Selma Heritage: 15-year HOME affordability on 11 units, loan repaid by March 31, 2083); PLHA 55 years with half the PLHA units at 60% AMI and half at 80% AMI; HOME-ARP qualifying populations.
- Cycle: annual NOFA (next: No open round as of November 8, 2026. The County page says the 2026 NOFO was not issued in time for CTCAC 9% Round 1 due to staff capacity and that staff anticipates opening an application period for the CTCAC Round 2 4% and 9% cycle (no date posted). Remaining HOME and HOME-CHDO funds are available first come, first served; PLHA is 100% reserved with new funds pending and HOME-ARP is 100% reserved. Contact ComDev@fresnocountyca.gov or (559) 600-4292 to confirm timing.)
- Layering notes: Fresno County splits housing work three ways: the Department of Public Works and Planning, Community Development Division (ComDev) runs the Urban County HUD programs, PLHA and the annual Affordable Housing Development NOFO; the County Administrative Office's new Office of Housing and Homelessness (OHH, created November 18, 2025) administers HHAP, the Continuum of Care and Transitional Rent and is absorbing housing programs from Behavioral Health and ComDev (Phase 2 approved November 3, 2026); and the Department of Behavioral Health co-applies for Homekey+ and NPLH and funds BHSA housing. Fresno Housing (the joint City and County Housing Authorities) is the dominant developer and voucher source. The City of Fresno and Clovis are separate entitlements with their own programs (Pass 3). fresnocountyca.gov and fresnohousing.org open normally; Board records are on fresnocounty.legistar.com and the Legistar web API client 'fresnocounty'. This is the County's only standing capital program and it is explicitly sized as gap money for 9% tax credit deals: 0% or 3% simple interest at the applicant's election, repayment deferred to maturity or as residual receipts (recent deals 50/50 split), non-recourse, subordinate to senior debt, loan term at least through the affordability period, and HOME may be converted to a grant by Board action. Eligible locations are the Urban County only: Fowler, Kerman, Kingsburg, Mendota, Orange Cove, Reedley, Sanger, Selma and unincorporated areas including County islands inside Fresno and Clovis; projects inside the cities of Fresno and Clovis are ineligible. Davis-Bacon applies at 12 or more HOME-assisted units; PLHA states no wage rule of its own; construction use is public funds under Labor Code 1720(b), subject to the 1720(c) exemptions (see prevailing_wage_basis). Reservation letters are written to support CTCAC applications; final agreements require NEPA, subsidy layering review and Board approval and typically land 8 to 12 months after reservation. Source is the NOFO page with the 2025 NOFO PDF and reservation letters; the Reedley and Selma Heritage agreements are at fresnocounty.legistar.com (files 26-0593 and 26-0069, June 30, 2026).
- Source: https://www.fresnocountyca.gov/Departments/Public-Works-and-Planning/divisions-of-public-works-and-planning/community-development-division/Affordable-Housing-Development-Program-%E2%80%93-Notice-of-Funding-Opportunity
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-07)

- Agency: Fresno County Department of Behavioral Health with the County Administrative Office; development partners UPholdings and RH Community Builders, and Fresno Housing
- Type: grant
- Typical award: Sendero Commons, Sanger (88 units, 87 PSH at 30% AMI, 45 veteran units; total development cost $54,007,788): Homekey+ $29,853,131 ($26,295,016 capital, $3,558,115 operating; award notice March 20, 2026, standard agreement approved October 20, 2026), NPLH Round 4 $18,147,660 ($10,000,038 capital, $8,147,660 operating, transferred from the failed Libre Commons project), HHIP $530,000, local contributions $5,476,959 (County HOME-ARP $2,500,000 and PLHA $2,364,219). County committed 20 years of supportive services ($10,241,756) and a 20-year rental subsidy on 42 units through Transitional Rent and BHSA ($15,314,934). The County also co-applied with Fresno Housing for Davu Village (former Parkside Inn, 1415 W. Olive Avenue, Fresno; total cost $22,362,000; resolution up to $35,000,000, April 3, 2025 application).
- AMI requirement: Homekey+ and NPLH: all assisted units for households with serious mental illness or behavioral health needs experiencing or at risk of homelessness, 30% AMI, Coordinated Entry referrals, 55-year regulatory agreement.
- Cycle: rolling (next: No fixed deadline as of November 8, 2026. HCD accepts Homekey+ applications over the counter until funds are exhausted (NOFA amended March 27, 2026, adding incentives for veteran units; HCD reported about $360 million requested for veteran units of about $1.033 billion available). The County approved the Sendero Commons Homekey+ and NPLH standard agreements on October 20, 2026. A developer seeking County co-application should approach Behavioral Health and the Office of Housing and Homelessness with a site and services plan.)
- Layering notes: Fresno County splits housing work three ways: the Department of Public Works and Planning, Community Development Division (ComDev) runs the Urban County HUD programs, PLHA and the annual Affordable Housing Development NOFO; the County Administrative Office's new Office of Housing and Homelessness (OHH, created November 18, 2025) administers HHAP, the Continuum of Care and Transitional Rent and is absorbing housing programs from Behavioral Health and ComDev (Phase 2 approved November 3, 2026); and the Department of Behavioral Health co-applies for Homekey+ and NPLH and funds BHSA housing. Fresno Housing (the joint City and County Housing Authorities) is the dominant developer and voucher source. The City of Fresno and Clovis are separate entitlements with their own programs (Pass 3). fresnocountyca.gov and fresnohousing.org open normally; Board records are on fresnocounty.legistar.com and the Legistar web API client 'fresnocounty'. The County's role is co-applicant, services provider and rental subsidy source rather than capital lender; the capital stack at Sendero Commons is state money (Homekey+ and NPLH, about 67% of cost) plus County HOME-ARP and PLHA. NPLH Round 4 money was reallocated once already, so timing of state agreements has run three to five years behind initial awards. Source is the October 20, 2026 Board item (file 26-0992).

**Public Facilities Impact Fees suspended countywide (unincorporated Fresno County)**
- Agency: Fresno County Department of Public Works and Planning, Development Services and Capital Projects Division
- Type: fee waiver
- Typical award: The County's Public Facilities Impact Fee ordinance has been suspended since 2017: the Board continued the suspension at hearings on October 31, 2017 and October 9, 2018 'until further notice', and the 2025 Housing Element Annual Progress Report (accepted March 17, 2026) states there has been no change. Unincorporated projects therefore pay no County public facilities impact fee; school district, water and sewer district and traffic mitigation fees still apply.
- AMI requirement: None; the suspension applies to all development regardless of affordability.
- Cycle: rolling (next: In effect until the Board acts to reinstate the fee. Confirm current status with Development Services before underwriting, and note that fees in the eight JPA cities are set by each city.)
- Layering notes: Fresno County splits housing work three ways: the Department of Public Works and Planning, Community Development Division (ComDev) runs the Urban County HUD programs, PLHA and the annual Affordable Housing Development NOFO; the County Administrative Office's new Office of Housing and Homelessness (OHH, created November 18, 2025) administers HHAP, the Continuum of Care and Transitional Rent and is absorbing housing programs from Behavioral Health and ComDev (Phase 2 approved November 3, 2026); and the Department of Behavioral Health co-applies for Homekey+ and NPLH and funds BHSA housing. Fresno Housing (the joint City and County Housing Authorities) is the dominant developer and voucher source. The City of Fresno and Clovis are separate entitlements with their own programs (Pass 3). fresnocountyca.gov and fresnohousing.org open normally; Board records are on fresnocounty.legistar.com and the Legistar web API client 'fresnocounty'. Fresno County has no affordable housing fee waiver program because it has no public facilities impact fee to waive; this is a cost advantage for unincorporated sites and County islands relative to the City of Fresno (which runs its own affordable housing fee deferral and infill waiver). The County also has no inclusionary ordinance, in-lieu fee, housing trust fund or Measure C housing component (Measure C is a transportation tax; its transit-oriented development program can fund infrastructure near affordable projects). Source is the 2025 Housing Element APR Board file (26-0110), Attachment B program implementation details.

No PBVs are currently awarded and no RFP has been issued.
- AMI requirement: HUD income limits; PBV program would follow 24 CFR 983 once adopted.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Approach HACM directly about a development partnership or a PBV commitment before a CTCAC application; the agency has no published selection process yet.)
- Layering notes: Madera County is a small non-entitlement county: the Community and Economic Development Department (planning, state CDBG and HOME applications) and Behavioral Health Services (BHSA, bridge housing) are the only County housing actors, the Housing Authority of the City of Madera (HACM) is the PHA for the county, and the Fresno Madera Continuum of Care (CA-514, led by Fresno County) handles HHAP and CoC funds. ### Marin County

**ADU and JADU development fee waiver, unincorporated Marin County (up to $10,000 for deed-restricted affordable ADUs; no countywide affordable multifamily fee waiver)**
- Agency: Marin County Community Development Agency
- Type: fee waiver
- Typical award: No fee waiver program exists for affordable multifamily housing. The only adopted County development fee waiver is the ADU and JADU program: a Board resolution of March 11, 2025 extends the Community Development Agency Director's delegated authority to waive or reduce building permit fees through December 31, 2026, up to $1,500 per JADU, $2,500 per ADU, $5,000 for an ADU deed restricted to a moderate-income household (81 to 100 percent AMI) and $10,000 for an ADU deed restricted to a low-income household (up to 80 percent AMI). In 2024 the County processed 27 ADU waivers (one affordable deed-restricted) and 1 JADU waiver totaling $78,000.
- AMI requirement: Base ADU and JADU waivers: owner affirms the unit will not be a short-term rental. Higher tiers: recorded deed restriction renting the ADU to a low-income (up to 80 percent AMI) or moderate-income (81 to 100 percent AMI) household.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Rolling until December 31, 2026, when the current delegation expires unless the Board extends it.)
- Layering notes: Corrected from a negative finding: Marin County has an adopted fee waiver, but only for ADUs and JADUs; there is still no countywide fee waiver or reduction for affordable multifamily projects. Development Code 22.24.020(C)(2) says nothing requires direct financial incentives such as fee waivers and leaves them to County discretion, so a multifamily developer would request fee relief case by case (Affordable Housing Fund or a density bonus concession). Separately, the County policies page describes reductions of the affordable housing impact fee or in-lieu fee for projects with affordable units beyond the minimum; that is an inclusionary compliance option under Chapter 22.22 (record 02b451fc33), not a development fee waiver. The ADU waiver stacks with the ADU Center technical assistance pilot.

- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-06)

Housing Interventions receive 30% of base allocations: $5,854,517 in year one, $5,733,901 in year two and $5,695,539 in year three (plus $125,000 of unspent MHSA moved to housing). Planned uses: rental and operating subsidies at four PSH programs, 16 to 22 local Behavioral Health vouchers, continuation of transitional rent and Bridge Housing programs after they end, a peer respite facility, and capital development for a new PSH project in year one. Known capital award: up to $1,931,918 in MHSA/BHSA capital match ($1,531,918 required match plus $400,000 contingency) for the nine-unit Carmelita House Homekey+ PSH conversion (April 14, 2026), with a BHSA-funded operating agreement and services contract to follow. Scattered-site housing and rental subsidy RFP HHS-2026-02 closed April 17, 2026.

**Inclusionary housing, affordable housing impact fee and commercial linkage fee (Development Code Chapter 22.22) with state density bonus (Chapter 22.24)**
- Agency: Marin County Community Development Agency, Planning Division (unincorporated area); fees deposited to the Affordable Housing Fund
- Type: density bonus
- Typical award: Chapter 22.22: 20% of units or lots in new residential projects must be affordable (projects of four or fewer units round up only above 0.70 of a unit), restricted in perpetuity unless shortened to match financing; income tiers very low (30% to 50% AMI), low (50% to 80%), moderate (80% to 120%) and middle (120% to 150%); alternatives in priority order are off-site units, land dedication and an in-lieu fee set at 125% of the requirement when a waiver is granted; single-family homes over 2,000 square feet pay an Affordable Housing Impact Fee (Ordinance 3500, 2008); non-residential projects pay a jobs-housing linkage fee by floor area and use (Ordinance 3798 and Resolution 2023-102 of Sept 19, 2023; Resolution 2016-122 for residential care and skilled nursing). Fees are indexed annually to the California Construction Cost Index; the June 23, 2026 adjustment was 3.9% and the FY 2026-27 in-lieu fee is $421,886.99 per required unit per the County fee page (2023-24 fee was $399,654). Chapter 22.24 implements Government Code 65915: base 20% bonus at 10% low or 5% very low income units, one to five concessions by affordability level, unlimited waivers of standards that physically preclude the project, height increases up to three stories near major transit for 80% lower income projects; the County may offer incentives to deed-restricted projects without a bonus but is not required to give fee waivers.
- AMI requirement: Inclusionary units restricted in perpetuity (or the maximum financing allows); density bonus rental units 30 years minimum under 22.24, moderate-income for-sale units in perpetuity. Rents capped at 50%, 65% and 100% of AMI levels for very low, low and moderate tiers.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Applies at entitlement (rolling); fees adjust annually by the CCCI, next adjustment expected effective July 1, 2027.)
- Layering notes: Marin's unincorporated inclusionary rule is one of the strictest in the state (20% in perpetuity, in-lieu fee only after off-site and land dedication are shown infeasible), and fee receipts flow to the Affordable Housing Fund that this database records separately. Fee revenue is modest because unincorporated development is small. A 100% affordable project satisfies the chapter automatically and uses the state density bonus. Density bonus alone does not trigger prevailing wage; Labor Code 1720(b)(4) would treat any fee waiver as public funds. Sources opened: Zoneomics mirror of Development Code Article III (Chapters 22.22 and 22.24) and the June 23, 2026 fee adjustment staff report on Granicus; the County fee calculator page was blocked.
- Source: https://marin.granicus.com/MetaViewer.php?view_id=33&clip_id=13163&meta_id=1442466
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-06)

**Marin County Affordable Housing Fund (Housing Trust Fund) and the annual federal and state housing NOFA**
- Agency: Marin County Community Development Agency, Housing and Federal Grants Division, 3501 Civic Center Drive, San Rafael; affordablehousing@marincounty.gov
- Type: loan
- Typical award: The Marin County Affordable Housing Fund (Housing Trust Fund, created 1988) is capitalized by inclusionary in-lieu fees, the single-family Affordable Housing Impact Fee, commercial linkage fees and County General Fund contributions (Guidelines 2023-2027, adopted Dec 12, 2023). It funds seed and catalyst costs, land acquisition, predevelopment, construction and gap financing; awards are generally $50,000 per unit, up to $100,000 per unit depending on funds, project type, location, bedrooms, affordability depth and restriction term, with higher amounts considered in high-resource areas. About 25% of funds are prioritized for preservation and rehab and 75% for new construction or conversion. Funds are generally loans (3 months to 55 years); the Board may award grants for smaller requests. The Fund also supplies the 1:1 local match for PLHA through the annual NOFA. The 2026-27 NOFA estimated about $3,100,000 total ($1,500,000 CDBG, $700,000 HOME, $900,000 PLHA inclusive of Trust Fund match). On June 23, 2026 the Board approved FY 2026-27 allocations: $676,641 HOME, $1,611,279 CDBG, and $476,762 estimated PLHA matched 1:1 by $476,762 from the Trust Fund (Oak Hill, Eden Housing, $553,524 combined; Bayfront Terrace, EAH, $400,000 combined); staff reported a Housing Fund balance of $14,032,062 after the match. Standalone Board actions recorded in earlier agendas include a $5,239,098 Trust Fund loan to Habitat for Humanity Greater San Francisco (April 15, 2025) and a $3,000,000 Golden Gate Village predevelopment loan restructured April 14, 2026.
- AMI requirement: Low, very low and extremely low income households; affordability restrictions in perpetuity unless the Board approves a shorter term required by a public financing source. Priorities: AFFH, leverage, high-resource areas, unincorporated Marin, RHNA, homeownership. Projects in cities and towns must waive all planning and building fees and, if the jurisdiction has a housing trust, provide a match from it.
- Cycle: annual NOFA (next: No open NOFA round as of November 8, 2026; the 2027-28 NOFA is expected to open early in calendar 2027 per the County funding page. Affordable Housing Fund requests are accepted year-round.)
- Layering notes: marincounty.gov, marincounty.org, assets.marincounty.gov, marinhhs.org and arcc.marincounty.gov sit behind Cloudflare and refused automated access on 2026-11-06, so County program pages could not be opened; Board agendas were read on marin.granicus.com and staff reports through its MetaViewer links where available. Marin's county money is small and project-specific: the Trust Fund mostly supplies PLHA match (about $500,000 a year) and five- to six-figure gap grants, with occasional larger loans for County-priority sites (Habitat in Novato, Oak Hill workforce housing next to San Quentin, Golden Gate Village). The County also weighed joining an Affordable Housing Guarantor Financing Program for Oak Hill in April 2025. Local and state funds are public funds under Labor Code 1720(b), so state prevailing wage applies unless a 1720(c) exemption fits the deal, such as 1720(c)(5)(E) for below-market loans with at least 40 percent of units restricted 20 years at or below 80 percent AMI (see prevailing_wage_basis). Sources opened: Board agendas for April 15, 2025, June 10, 2025, Dec 5 and 12, 2023, April 7 and 14, 2026 and June 23, 2026 on Granicus, the April 14, 2026 Golden Gate Village loan staff report, and the Local News Matters reports of April 6 and June 24, 2026. NOFA amounts and dates come from search engine excerpts of the County NOFA page, which is why this record is needs_confirmation.
- Source: https://www.marincounty.gov/departments/cda/housing-and-grants/funding-projects/affordable-housing-fund-guidelines
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-06)

**Measure W West Marin transient occupancy tax, community housing share**
- Agency: Marin County Community Development Agency (community housing share) with the Measure W West Marin TOT Oversight Committee and Working Group
- Type: grant
- Typical award: Measure W (2018) made West Marin a special transient occupancy tax area with an additional 4% tax on short-term rentals, funding long-term community housing and emergency services. Under the guidelines approved by the Board on August 18, 2026 (in effect July 1, 2026 to June 30, 2027), Direct Housing Assistance receives $100,000 a year and Housing Production receives the remainder of the community housing funds, covering predevelopment, acquisition, development and preservation of rental and ownership housing, septic upgrades for deed-restricted units, conversions, ADUs and JADUs, and transitional housing. HCD 2024-2028 Formula Allocation NOFA estimates: CY 2024 $509,302, CY 2025 $545,537, five-year $3,183,138. Example award: $605,062 to EAH Housing in 2024 ($302,531 PLHA plus $302,531 Trust Fund). FY 2026-27 round: estimated $476,762 PLHA available, $3,600,000 in PLHA requested; PSC recommended Eden Housing Oak Hill $553,524 and EAH Bayfront Terrace $400,000 (PLHA plus 1:1 match, $953,524 total), preliminary until the State confirms the 2026 allocation.

- Cycle: annual NOFA (next: No open round as of November 8, 2026. The FY 2026-27 NOFA (CDBG, HOME, PLHA with Housing Trust match) ran January 19 to February 19, 2026 and the Board approved PLHA recommendations in June 2026 pending the State award. The FY 2027-28 NOFA is not yet announced; in the prior cycle the Priority Setting Committee set the timeline in December, the NOFA was noticed in mid-December and applications opened in mid-January, so the next window is expected around January to February 2027.)
- Layering notes: Roughly $1,000,000 a year including County match, spread across two or three projects. Marin's housing element was certified in 2025, so PLHA flows without the compliance holds seen in San Mateo. PLHA states no wage rule of its own; construction use is public funds under Labor Code 1720(b), subject to the 1720(c) exemptions (see prevailing_wage_basis). Figures from the HCD 2024-2028 PLHA NOFA (opened), the Dec 5, 2024 PSC packet on GovDelivery (opened) and search excerpts of County pages. Audit Nov 8, 2026: June 23, 2026 Board staff report (FY 2026-27 CDBG, HOME, Housing Fund and PLHA recommendations) opened on marin.granicus.com; marincounty.gov NOFA pages return 403. The Nov 3, 2026 Housing Trust workshop report shows an $18,820,048 uncommitted Trust balance, $18,650,000 in pending requests and a Trust guidelines update planned for 2027, which may affect match availability.

**Project-Based Vouchers and public housing conversion, Marin Housing Authority (MHA)**
- Agency: Housing Authority of the County of Marin, 4020 Civic Center Drive, San Rafael, 415-491-2525; procurement on procurement.opengov.com/portal/marinhousing
- Type: rental assistance
- Typical award: MHA holds 496 public housing units and 2,541 Housing Choice Vouchers (3,037 combined, FY 2027 draft PHA Plan) and serves the whole county under cooperation agreements with every city. The FY 2027 plan begins converting the roughly 300-unit senior and disabled public housing portfolio (Mill Valley, San Rafael, Novato) to project-based vouchers through a RAD and Section 18 blend, and Golden Gate Village (296 units, Marin City) is converting under RAD with Burbank Housing: Phase 1 (93 units) reached a $97,600,000 financial close on Aug 19, 2026 (CMFA bonds, CDLAC allocation of $41,748,341 and about $3,985,091 in annual federal credits), RAD subsidy began Sep 1, 2026, management moved to Burbank Aug 14, 2026 and rehab runs through Feb 2028; Phase 2 (207 units) is planned as six sub-phases from 2027 to 2030; Phase 2 TEFRA for up to $160,000,000 of bonds was set for Oct 20, 2026; the full program is estimated at $266,600,000. MHA runs PBV waitlists for partner properties (Victory Village in Novato, Edgewater, Piper Court, Fireside, Toussin Senior, Vivalon Healthy Aging Campus, 1251 S. Eliseo PSH in Larkspur) but has issued no developer PBV RFP recently; 94 Emergency Housing Voucher households were told in Oct 2025 that funding ends in 2026. The County contributes $250,000 a year for MHA's resident services director and has committed more than $6,250,000 to Golden Gate Village since 2022.
- AMI requirement: Households at or below 50% AMI at admission (75% at or below 30% AMI); PBV waitlists per property; Shelter Plus Care and HOPWA administered by MHA for the CoC; HAP contracts up to 20 years.
- Cycle: rolling (next: No open round as of November 8, 2026. MHA has no project-based voucher solicitation posted on its website or procurement page, and its September 2026 Board report shows capacity committed to the Golden Gate Village and senior portfolio RAD conversions. Ask MHA directly about PBVs for specific supportive housing projects.)
- Layering notes: MHA's capacity is going into its own RAD conversions through 2029, so new PBV awards for third-party projects are scarce; Shelter Plus Care and County-funded subsidies (Binford Road temporary rental support, $744,432 contract Dec 16, 2025) fill the gap for PSH. A HAP contract is not a prevailing wage trigger; Davis-Bacon applies to PBV construction of nine or more contract units, and RAD and public housing work carry Davis-Bacon regardless. Sources opened: MHA website pages, the FY 2027 draft PHA Plan (HUD-50075-ST), the April 14, 2026 Golden Gate Village loan staff report, Board agendas on Granicus and Patch and Local News Matters coverage of the bond approvals. Audit Nov 8, 2026: MHA website (home, procurement and 2027 Annual Plan notice pages) and the Sep 29, 2026 MHA Board agenda and Executive Director presentation on marincounty.primegov.com opened; no PBV RFP or new PBV commitments found.

- Agency: Marin County Board of Supervisors (TEFRA hearings) with the County Executive and Community Development Agency; bonds issued by the California Municipal Finance Authority
- Type: bond
- Typical award: The County holds TEFRA hearings as the CMFA member jurisdiction but does not issue bonds or take on liability: Golden Gate Village Phase 1, up to $50,000,000 (hearing and resolution Oct 14, 2025; CDLAC allocation $41,748,341); Golden Gate Village Phase 2, up to $160,000,000 (hearing Oct 20, 2026). Other Marin deals through CMFA include Centertown II in San Rafael ($18,442,396) and a $30,075,000 acquisition issue; a 2023 Marin City bond approval drew a lawsuit against the County and CMFA. Marinwood Plaza (125 units, 124 restricted) used CalHFA's Mixed-Income Program (April 2026).

- Cycle: rolling (next: Schedule the TEFRA hearing on a Board agenda with 7-day newspaper notice before the CDLAC application; for projects inside cities the city council holds the hearing (Daly City-style). No County issuer fee.)
- Layering notes: Plan on CMFA or CSCDA as issuer in Marin. Bonds alone do not trigger state prevailing wage; County Trust Fund, HOME or MHA money in the deal does. Sources opened: Board agendas of Oct 14, 2025 and Oct 20, 2026 on Granicus (the Oct 2025 staff report is image-only), Patch and Local News Matters coverage, and the CalHFA Marinwood Plaza listing in search results.

**Welfare Exemption (property tax), Marin County Assessor-Recorder-County Clerk**
- Agency: Marin County Assessor-Recorder-County Clerk, Shelly Scott, Marin Civic Center, San Rafael; 415-473-7215
- Type: tax abatement
- Typical award: Full or partial exemption of property tax on units occupied by households at or below 80% AMI under Revenue and Taxation Code 214(g); worth roughly 1.1% or more of assessed value a year depending on the tax rate area. The Assessor-Recorder posts the BOE-267 series including BOE-267-L, L1 and L2 for low-income housing.

Code 270, and the County FAQ confirms partial relief for late filings).
- Cycle: rolling (next: 2027-02-15 (annual claim deadline for the 2027-28 roll). File the first claim on acquisition so the construction period is covered.)

- Typical award: CDC administers about 750 Housing Choice Vouchers, about 136 Permanent Supportive Housing vouchers (Coordinated Entry referrals), VASH, FUP and Mainstream vouchers, and project-based vouchers at Sun House, Ukiah (10 one-bedroom units for senior veterans via the VA), The Plateau, Fort Bragg (20 PSH units in a 69-unit Danco development, the most recent PBV award) and Orr Creek Commons, Ukiah (RCHDC). Administrative Plan Chapter XXI (adopted May 15, 2025) allows project-basing up to 20% of budget authority with selection by competitive RFP or without a new competition for projects already selected through LIHTC or HOME competitions within three years.
- AMI requirement: PBV households at or below 50% AMI (75% extremely low income); PSH units filled through Coordinated Entry.
- Cycle: rolling (next: No open RFP as of November 8, 2026 (CDC Project Bids and Awards: none at this time); a LIHTC or HOME project competitively selected within the prior three years can request PBVs without a new competition.)
- Layering notes: Mendocino County has no housing department: the Executive Office Grants Division administers state CDBG and HOME program income, Social Services is the administrative entity for the Mendocino County Homeless Services Continuum of Care (CA-509) and HHAP, Behavioral Health and Recovery Services holds BHSA, NPLH and bridge housing, Planning and Building Services handles density bonus and the Housing Element, and the Community Development Commission of Mendocino County (CDC, the housing authority) supplies vouchers and owns housing. The County repealed its inclusionary ordinance on September 10, 2024, has no housing trust fund money, no NOFA and no impact fee waiver; County capital help has come from state pass-through grants (CDBG-DR, Homekey) and small HOME program income balances. Ukiah and Fort Bragg run their own programs (Pass 3). mendocinocounty.gov, the Legistar web API client 'mendocino', mendocino.granicusideas.com and cdchousing.org all open normally. CDC PBVs underwrote The Plateau and Orr Creek Commons and are the only operating subsidy available for a Mendocino PSH project; the prior-competition exemption means a CTCAC award can be converted into a PBV request directly. Source is the CDC programs page; selection rules from Administrative Plan Chapter XXI on cdchousing.org.
- Source: https://cdchousing.org/programs

- Agency: Monterey County Board of Supervisors (Housing and Community Development or sponsoring department)
- Type: bond
- Typical award: The Board holds TEFRA hearings and adopts approving resolutions for conduit issuers at no County liability; the most recent example is the June 23, 2026 hearing and Resolution 26-104 approving up to $40,000,000 of California Statewide Communities Development Authority bonds for Montage Health facilities. Multifamily housing bonds for projects in unincorporated Monterey County follow the same process; recent affordable projects in the county (Greenfield Commons, Lightfighter Village) used city TEFRA approvals.
- AMI requirement: For housing bonds, at least 20% of units at 50% AMI or 40% at 60% AMI under the bond regulatory agreement.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Request a TEFRA hearing through HCD or the Clerk of the Board at least six weeks before the CDLAC application.)
- Layering notes: Monterey County's Housing and Community Development Department (HCD, Craig Spencer, Director; Darby Marshall, Housing Program Manager) runs the Inclusionary Housing Ordinance, the Monterey County Housing Trust Fund, PLHA, the Urban County CDBG and HOME programs and County land dispositions; the County Administrative Office Homelessness Strategies and Initiatives Division (CAO-HSI) runs HHAP and the SHARE Center; the Health Department Behavioral Health Bureau holds BHSA; the Coalition of Homeless Services Providers leads the CoC (CA-506, shared with San Benito); and the Housing Authority of the County of Monterey (HACM) and its Development Corporation supply vouchers and develop housing. Salinas, Monterey, Seaside and other entitlement cities run their own programs (Pass 3). countyofmonterey.gov blocks automated access (pages and documents), so records were built from the Legistar web API client 'monterey' and its Granicus attachments, hamonterey.org, chsp.org, zoneomics and HCD tables. The County is not an issuer; it hosts hearings for CSCDA, CMFA and CalPFA on request. Source is the June 23, 2026 TEFRA item (Legistar file RES 26-104).

**County land for affordable housing: 855 East Laurel Drive, Salinas (Eden Housing) and SHARE Center reconfiguration**
- Agency: Monterey County Housing and Community Development Department and County Administrative Office, Homelessness Strategies and Initiatives
- Type: land

The adjoining SHARE Center (845 East Laurel Drive, 128-bed navigation center) is being reconfigured with twelve non-congregate family cabins and a 30-bed recuperative care area using a Central California Alliance for Health Housing Fund award of $3,222,262 and Health Department match for a $6,444,524 budget (October 30, 2026, Resolution 26-194).

- Cycle: rolling (next: Eden Housing is assembling local funding (County trust fund and PLHA, City of Salinas) before CTCAC applications; no other County sites are currently offered. **Density bonus and incentives (Chapter 21.65) and Sixth Cycle Housing Element implementation (by-right approvals, objective design standards)**
- Agency: Monterey County Housing and Community Development Department, Planning Services
- Type: density bonus
- Typical award: Chapter 21.65 (Ordinance 5177, 2011) implements state density bonus law up to a 35% bonus (5% very low income units earn 20%, rising by 2.5 points per additional percent) with incentives, parking reductions, child care and land donation bonuses; Section 21.65.110 states the bonus does not satisfy the Inclusionary Housing Ordinance and inclusionary units are computed on base plus bonus units. The Sixth Cycle (2023-2031) Housing Element Update and implementation package went to the Board on October 23, 2026 (ORD 26-021) after the Planning Commission on October 7, 2026, adding Chapter 18.20 objective design standards, a coastal by-right approval chapter (20.59), rezoning of housing sites and amendments to Titles 18, 20 and 21; HCD had found the third submittal (April 2026) still needing revisions.
- AMI requirement: Government Code 65915 thresholds with recorded qualifying unit agreements (Section 21.65.120); inclusionary obligations remain.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Requested with the land use application; confirm Housing Element adoption and HCD certification status (late 2026) because HHAP second disbursements and state program eligibility depend on it.)

**Inclusionary Housing Ordinance (Chapter 18.40), in-lieu fees and the 2026 fee-based restructuring proposal**
- Agency: Monterey County Housing and Community Development Department; Housing Advisory Committee
- Type: regulatory requirement
- Typical award: Current ordinance (first adopted 1980, revised 2003): 20% of units in residential projects affordable, analyzed by Keyser Marston as 6% very low, 6% low and 8% moderate income plus a 5% Workforce I component, with in-lieu fees for fractional units and small projects; in-lieu fees collected at building permit 2021-2025 are tabulated in the September 2026 workshop packet. The 2026 KMA In-Lieu Fee Analysis found maximum supportable fees of $73.90 to $305.60 per square foot of saleable area by product type. Staff recommended (Housing Advisory Committee workshops September 2 and 11, 2026) converting to an entirely fee-based program for projects under 250 units, charging 33 to 35 percent of the maximum fee on habitable square footage above the first 1,500 square feet, exempting all multifamily (duplex to fourplex and ADUs under 1,200 square feet), encouraging land donation for 20% affordable units on projects of 250 or more units, indexing the fee annually and allowing fee revenue to be spent countywide.
- AMI requirement: Very low (50% AMI), low (80% AMI), moderate (120% AMI) and Workforce I (to 150% AMI) for-sale and rental units with long-term resale and rent restrictions; inclusionary units are calculated on base plus density bonus units.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Board action on the restructured ordinance and new fee schedule expected late 2026 or 2027 after Housing Advisory Committee recommendations; LeSar and KMA remain under contract (Amendment 10, April 2026) to complete the fee studies. Until adoption the 2003 ordinance and existing in-lieu fees apply.)
- Layering notes: Monterey County's Housing and Community Development Department (HCD, Craig Spencer, Director; Darby Marshall, Housing Program Manager) runs the Inclusionary Housing Ordinance, the Monterey County Housing Trust Fund, PLHA, the Urban County CDBG and HOME programs and County land dispositions; the County Administrative Office Homelessness Strategies and Initiatives Division (CAO-HSI) runs HHAP and the SHARE Center; the Health Department Behavioral Health Bureau holds BHSA; the Coalition of Homeless Services Providers leads the CoC (CA-506, shared with San Benito); and the Housing Authority of the County of Monterey (HACM) and its Development Corporation supply vouchers and develop housing. Salinas, Monterey, Seaside and other entitlement cities run their own programs (Pass 3). countyofmonterey.gov blocks automated access (pages and documents), so records were built from the Legistar web API client 'monterey' and its Granicus attachments, hamonterey.org, chsp.org, zoneomics and HCD tables. The County concluded the inclusionary mandate produces few units (about five per project) and wants a reliable fee stream for the Housing Trust Fund, land acquisition and leverage of state programs; a fee-based ordinance would make market-rate permits the County's main local revenue source for affordable housing. Source is the September 11, 2026 Housing Advisory Committee workshop item (Legistar file 26-799) with the staff report and KMA analysis attached.

### Napa County

**Affordable Housing Impact Fee and Inclusionary Requirements (County Code Chapter 18.107)**
- Agency: Napa County Housing and Community Services; Planning, Building and Environmental Services
- Type: regulatory requirement
- Typical award: Not a subsidy; it capitalizes the Affordable Housing Fund. Fees adopted Oct 21, 2025 (3-2 vote), effective Jan 16, 2026, phased 50% in 2026, 75% in 2027, 100% in 2028: residential per sq ft $0 up to 2,500 sq ft, $43 for 2,501-3,500 sq ft (was $10.75), $86 above 3,500 sq ft (was $12.25); ADUs under 751 sq ft exempt. Nonresidential per sq ft: hotel $100 (was $9), retail and restaurant $58.40 (was $7.50), office $14.68 (was $5.25), industrial $7.70 (was $4.50), warehouse $7.50 (was $3.60).
- AMI requirement: Ownership projects: 20% of single-family detached units or 17% of attached units for moderate income (120% AMI) households, 40-year restrictions. Rental projects pay housing fees or elect the alternative of 12% of units at low income rents under a rent regulatory agreement. Exempt: farmworker units of 1,200 sq ft or less, 100% affordable projects, certain multifamily and SRO projects, projects of four or fewer units may pay a per-unit fee. Equivalency proposals (off-site units, land dedication) allowed with Planning Commission approval.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Fees apply to applications filed after Jan 15, 2026 at 50% of the new schedule; 75% in 2027; full schedule in 2028. The Board also directed staff to create a fee deferral program for owners who rent units as affordable housing; terms not yet published.)
- Layering notes: Relevant to developers two ways: 100% affordable multifamily is exempt from the fee, and the fee stream funds the County Affordable Housing Fund. A fee exemption or waiver can count as public funds under Labor Code 1720(b)(4), so confirm prevailing wage exposure with counsel. Applies only in unincorporated Napa County; each city has its own inclusionary and linkage rules (Pass 3). Code text was read from the Zoneomics mirror (Ordinances 1334 of 2010, 1386 of 2013, 1491 of June 4, 2024 and 1495 of Sept 24, 2024); fee amounts come from Sonoma Index-Tribune and CBS Bay Area coverage of the Oct 21, 2025 vote. napacounty.gov pages and DocumentCenter PDFs sit behind Cloudflare and refused automated access on 2026-11-06, so the county's own page could not be opened; the official FAQ is https://www.napacounty.gov/3951/Affordable-Housing-Impact-Fee-Housing-Co.
- Source: https://www.zoneomics.com/code/napa-county-unincorporated-CA/chapter_36
- Confidence: needs_confirmation (researched 2026-11-06)

**Affordable Unit Permit Fee Waiver and Expedited Processing (County Code 18.107.120)**
- Agency: Napa County Planning, Building and Environmental Services
- Type: fee waiver
- Typical award: Under County Code 18.107.120 (as amended by Ordinance 1495, Sept 24, 2024), residential projects that build affordable units under 18.107.080, 18.107.100 or 18.107.110 get: building permit application fees waived for the affordable units, flexibility in unit size and interior features, attached affordable units allowed in single-family projects, and expedited permit processing. If a state density bonus is requested, these incentives count only when each is requested as a state incentive. The Zoneomics mirror also shows housing impact fees refundable if a project does not proceed and a refund is requested within 90 days; that provision was not in the official text read.
- AMI requirement: Units must satisfy Chapter 18.107 affordability (40-year minimum; 55 years for density bonus rentals).
- Cycle: rolling (next: The Oct 21, 2025 fee action also directed staff to design a fee deferral program for owners renting units as affordable housing; watch for the ordinance in 2026.)
- Layering notes: Modest value for multifamily since the chapter is written around inclusionary units in small unincorporated projects. Waived fees count as public funds under Labor Code 1720(b)(4) and can trigger state prevailing wage, so confirm with counsel. Code text read from the Zoneomics mirror; napacounty.gov pages and DocumentCenter PDFs sit behind Cloudflare and refused automated access on 2026-11-06, so the county's own page could not be opened; confirm with the County.

**HOME and CDBG, Napa County (state non-entitlement status)**
- Agency: California HCD state HOME and CDBG programs; Napa County Housing and Community Services as applicant
- Type: grant
- Typical award: None directly. Napa County is not a HUD CDBG entitlement urban county or a HOME participating jurisdiction. The City of Napa is the only CDBG entitlement in the county (FY 2024-25 entitlement $583,519) and draws HOME and ESG through State HCD grants. No County of Napa state HOME or CDBG award for 2024 or 2025 surfaced in HCD award lists.
- AMI requirement: State HOME: 20% of HOME units at 50% AMI, rest at 60% AMI, 55-year HCD covenant. State CDBG: 51% of units for households at or below 80% AMI.
- Cycle: annual NOFA (next: Follow HCD state HOME and CDBG NOFAs (state records). A developer in unincorporated Napa or the four small cities needs the County or city to apply as the state HOME or CDBG grantee.)
- Layering notes: There is no county-level HOME or CDBG pipeline to layer in Napa; this is a negative finding. The City of Napa CDBG and HOME programs are Pass 3. Napa County received $207,965 of State ESG for CA-517 in the 2024 NOFA, usable for shelter and rapid rehousing, not capital. Davis-Bacon applies at 12 or more HOME-assisted units or 8 or more CDBG-assisted units; state prevailing wage turns on the local or state funds in the deal and the Labor Code 1720(c) exemptions (see prevailing_wage_basis). Status inferred from the City of Napa 2025-2030 Consolidated Plan, the City FY 2024-25 CAPER and HCD award lists; confirm with the County.
- Source: https://www.cityofnapa.org/DocumentCenter/View/14570/DRAFT-City-of-Napa-2025-2030-Consolidated-Plan
- Confidence: needs_confirmation (researched 2026-11-06)

**Napa City and County Continuum of Care (CA-517) and HHAP homelessness funding**
- Agency: Napa County Housing and Community Services (CoC collaborative applicant and HHAP administrative entity) with the Napa City and County CoC board
- Type: grant
- Typical award: HHAP Round 7 preliminary allocations (HCD, 2026): Napa City & County CoC $511,466.08 and Napa County $477,368.34, delivered as third and fourth disbursements of HHAP 6 under the Amended HHAP 6 NOFA dated August 7, 2026 ($829,350,000 statewide). HHAP Round 5: Napa County $698,089.89 and Napa City & County CoC $727,623.09 (regional total $1,425,712.98, awarded individually). HHAP Round 6: nearly $1,000,000 awarded March 2, 2026 for rapid rehousing and rental subsidies, permanent housing services, coordination and the City of Napa prevention and diversion program. HHAP Round 2: County $160,645 plus CoC redirect $250,000. State dashboard: $4,900,000 HHAP rounds 1-5 to the Napa area 2019-2025 ($3,000,000 direct to the County) and $15,000,000 Encampment Resolution Funding rounds 1-3. HUD FY 2025 CoC awards to CA-517 were small: $21,564 coordinated assessment, $40,874 HMIS, $50,000 planning; the 2026 local priority listing (July 23, 2026) ranks about $300,000 County engagement and housing navigation, $400,000 City of Napa outreach, $214,000 HACN Shelter Plus Care PSH renewal, $108,000 DV bonus and $500,000 CoC bonus. State ESG via CA-517: $207,965 (2024 NOFA).
- AMI requirement: HUD CoC and HHAP target people experiencing homelessness; HHAP permanent housing uses include operating subsidies, rental assistance and capital for PSH. Homekey Round 2 funded Burbank Housing's Wine Valley Lodge conversion (54 PSH units, $18,113,600 with the City of Napa).
- Cycle: annual NOFA (next: No open round as of November 8, 2026. HUD FY 2026 CoC applications were due August 26, 2026 under the modified NOFO; HHAP 7 needs no new application.)
- Layering notes: For PSH underwriting the usable pieces are HHAP operating or rental subsidy commitments and HACN Shelter Plus Care or PBVs, not capital; the CoC is small (Point-in-Time 2024 found 494 people). Napa County has no Measure-type housing sales tax and no NPLH balance surfaced. HHAP capital is public funds under Labor Code 1720(b) but carries no wage rule of its own; coverage turns on the 1720(c) exemptions and project facts (see prevailing_wage_basis). Sources opened: HCD HHAP Round 5 awardee list, HCD HHAP Round 6 award release, HUD FY 2025 CoC award report, HCD 2024 ESG award list, the County's HHAP Round 2 application and the state accountability dashboard. napacounty.gov pages and DocumentCenter PDFs sit behind Cloudflare and refused automated access on 2026-11-06, so the county's own page could not be opened; the CoC page is https://www.napacounty.gov/1036/Napa-Continuum-of-Care and the 2026 priority listing figures come from search excerpts of a County PDF that could not be opened.

**Napa County Affordable ADU Forgivable Loan Program (single-unit, recorded for completeness)**
- Agency: Napa County Housing and Community Services
- Type: loan
- Typical award: Under the updated underwriting guidelines (V2) adopted by the Board on March 10, 2026: base forgivable loan $60,000 for a 1-bedroom or $85,000 for a 2-bedroom ADU plus up to $20,000 in rebates, for a total maximum of $80,000 or $105,000 (lesser of that amount or actual development cost). 5.0% simple deferred interest, forgiven monthly (1/60) over the 5-year affordability term; opt-out by repaying the unforgiven balance. Launched March 2023 (2023 range was $45,000 to $105,000). Funded from the Affordable Housing Fund.
- AMI requirement: Owner-occupant of a single-family home in Napa County rents the ADU to a household at or below 80% AMI at HCD 80% AMI rents (2026 examples $2,563 for 1-bedroom, $2,884 for 2-bedroom) under a 5-year covenant; loan forgiven on compliance.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Open until funds are exhausted; applications through the County.)
- Layering notes: Not a multifamily source; recorded so the Affordable Housing Fund's competing uses are visible (ADU loans, farmworker centers, homeless services and fair housing all draw on the same fee revenue). Terms from the Napa Valley Community Foundation launch notice (March 17, 2023) and County news releases quoted in search results; napacounty.gov pages and DocumentCenter PDFs sit behind Cloudflare and refused automated access on 2026-11-06, so the county's own page could not be opened; the 2026 notice is https://www.napacounty.gov/CivicAlerts.aspx?AID=858.
