**Napa County Affordable Housing Fund**
- Agency: Napa County Housing and Community Services (County Executive Office)
- Type: loan
- Typical award: Gap loans historically $500,000 to $2,000,000 per project: $2,000,000 requested for Burbank Housing Stoddard West (51 units, 2017), $650,000 plus $148,000 for Turley Flats in St. Helena (8 units, 2017-2018), $500,000 for SAHA Manzanita Family Apartments (51 units, 2019, with $750,000 HEAP), $200,000 for 963 Pope Street in St. Helena (5 units, 2025). The 2010 NOFA offered $5,000,000 plus $2,000,000 reserved for farmworker housing. By 2017 the fund had loaned $22,000,000 for more than 1,000 units since 1992; fee revenue runs about $2,000,000 a year and the fund also pays for farmworker centers, homeless services and fair housing.
- AMI requirement: 55-year affordability covenant for rental projects (40 years for County-assisted ownership). County preference for projects in the unincorporated area, deeper affordability, permanent affordability and local workers where allowed by law. Loans may be forgiven after 40 to 55 years by Board action.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Rolling since the 2010 NOFA; the County accepts applications year-round under the 2010 application and the 2020 joint underwriting guidelines. Requests go to the Napa County Housing Commission and then the Board of Supervisors; time them to the CTCAC round.)
- Layering notes: Capitalized by residential inclusionary in-lieu and impact fees and nonresidential housing impact fees under County Code Chapter 18.107 (Ordinance 1026, 1992); the October 21, 2025 fee overhaul (phased in from Jan 16, 2026) should raise annual revenue. Terms per the joint guidelines: 3.0% simple interest (lower if needed for feasibility), 55-year term from permanent loan conversion, 50/50 split of residual receipts between the City/County and developer, balance due at maturity, subordinate to senior debt, 90% maximum LTV on senior debt, monitoring fee $100 per unit for the first 40 units. Deferred developer fee may be repaid from cash flow within 15 years before residual receipts split. Most funded projects are inside the cities; the County obtains RHNA transfer credits in exchange (80% of County RHNA goes to the City of Napa under the Napa Pipe agreement through 2058), which limits funds for other jurisdictions. County loan is public money, so state prevailing wage applies under Labor Code 1720 unless an exemption fits. napacounty.gov pages and DocumentCenter PDFs sit behind Cloudflare and refused automated access on 2026-11-06, so the county's own page could not be opened; the program page is https://www.napacounty.gov/443/Affordable-Housing-Projects and the source given is the joint underwriting guidelines hosted by the City of Napa.
- Source: https://www.cityofnapa.org/DocumentCenter/View/8030/2020-Napa-City-County-UW-Guidelines-PDF
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-06)

**Napa County Behavioral Health Services Act (BHSA) housing interventions**
- Agency: Napa County Health and Human Services Agency, Behavioral Health Division
- Type: grant
- Typical award: No developer awards. Napa's BHSA Integrated Plan FY 2026-27 through 2028-29 (provisionally approved by DHCS, approved by the Board of Supervisors) allocates 45% BHSS, 38% FSP and 17% Housing Interventions; DHCS approved Napa's request to use 17% instead of the 30% Housing Interventions target. Housing Interventions fund tenant-based rental assistance through Abode Services (18 units a year), possibly one 17-unit shared-housing PBRA project, interim housing operating subsidies (27 people a year), and two small capital repair projects at existing properties: Carolina Room Repairs (5 units, about $75,000 per unit) and the Skyline Apartment staircase renovation (19-unit HUD 811 property on state land leased by the County, about $400,000 per unit). No capital NOFA for new PSH.
- AMI requirement: Housing Interventions serve BHSA-eligible people with serious mental illness or substance use disorder who are homeless or at risk. Napa requested an exemption from the requirement to spend 50% of Housing Interventions on chronically homeless individuals.
- Cycle: rolling (next: No open round as of November 8, 2026. No developer solicitation; funds are committed through the FY 2026-29 Integrated Plan, with annual updates.)
- Layering notes: funding_type stays grant: the Plan funds housing capital (two repair projects) and rental subsidies. For a PSH sponsor the realistic ask is referral of BHSA-eligible tenants with Abode-administered TBRA or a small operating subsidy, paired with Homekey+, HHAP or HUD CoC; Napa shifted part of its 30% housing target to FSP (3 points) and BHSS (10 points). BHSA capital is public funds under Labor Code 1720(b) but carries no wage rule of its own; coverage turns on the 1720(c) exemptions and project facts (see prevailing_wage_basis). napacounty.gov is Cloudflare-blocked; the Plan and staff report were read on the County's Legistar (matter 14224).

**Napa County Density Bonus and Incentives (County Code 18.107.170-18.107.190)**
- Agency: Napa County Planning, Building and Environmental Services
- Type: density bonus
- Typical award: Density bonus, incentives and concessions, parking reductions and development standard waivers per Government Code 65915; the chapter defers to state law where they conflict.
- AMI requirement: State density bonus thresholds (County Code 18.107.170 implements Gov. Code 65915 for housing developments as defined in state law). Affordable housing agreement required for any bonus, incentive, parking reduction or waiver: rental target units affordable at least 55 years (or longer if financing requires), for-sale units 45 years with sale to a qualified nonprofit if no income-qualified buyer within 180 days (18.107.180(E)-(G)). Requests are filed with the first discretionary permit with detailed submittals; incentives and waivers may be denied only on specified written findings (18.107.180(B)-(C)). On-site inclusionary units can count toward the bonus; paying in-lieu fees does not (18.107.170(D)(3)).
- Cycle: rolling
- Layering notes: Unincorporated Napa County is mostly Agricultural Preserve and Agricultural Watershed zoning, so multifamily sites are scarce; the 2023-2031 Housing Element (adopted Dec 19, 2023, HCD compliance letter Feb 22, 2024) relies on a 106-unit RHNA and RHNA transfers to the City of Napa. Inclusionary units count toward the state bonus (Latinos Unidos del Valle de Napa y Solano v. County of Napa, 2013). Ordinance 1495 (Sept 24, 2024) updated the incentives and density bonus sections. Code text read from the Zoneomics mirror; napacounty.gov pages and DocumentCenter PDFs sit behind Cloudflare and refused automated access on 2026-11-06, so the county's own page could not be opened; confirm against the official code at library.municode.com or the County.

**Napa County Housing Authority Farmworker Centers (CSA No. 4 assessment and HCD matching funds)**
- Agency: Napa County Housing Authority (Board of Supervisors sitting as the Authority)
- Type: negative finding
- Typical award: Operating support for three county-owned dormitory centers (180 beds, about 400 farmworkers a year): County Service Area No. 4 vineyard assessment at $14 per planted acre raises about $650,000 a year (about 30% of operating cost); HCD Napa County Farmworker Centers Account match up to $250,000 a year (Health and Safety Code 50711.5, funded by SB 2); AB 1890 (Chapter 905, Statutes of 2026, signed Sept 30, 2026) raises the match to $500,000 a year once the Legislature appropriates it; AB 317 (2017) $200,000 General Fund support expires FY 2028-29. The County Affordable Housing Fund also subsidizes operations.
- AMI requirement: Centers serve migrant and seasonal farmworkers; AB 1890 bars use of the state funds to house H-2A workers.
- Cycle: closed/inactive (next: Not available to outside developers; funds flow only to the County-owned centers. CSA 4 assessment is reauthorized by growers every five years.)
- Layering notes: Reclassified from other to negative finding in the 5_audit pass: the HCD Napa County Farmworker Centers Account (Health and Safety Code 50711.5) is an annual state match of up to $250,000 paid only to the Napa County Housing Authority for operating its own three farmworker centers, funded from the SB 2 Building Homes and Jobs Trust Fund, with an equal local match required; nothing is deployable to outside developers. Napa's only county housing authority is a farmworker-center operator with no Housing Choice Vouchers or development lending; the public housing agency for the county is the Housing Authority of the City of Napa. Farmworker rental projects in Napa instead layer the state Joe Serna Jr. Farmworker Housing Grant, the State Farmworker Housing Tax Credit (Pass 1) and the County Affordable Housing Fund, which once reserved $2,000,000 for farmworker projects and whose fees exempt farmworker units of 1,200 sq ft or less. The 2024 Napa County Farmworker Housing Needs and Impacts Assessment found 16% of year-round and 26% of seasonal workers in overcrowded housing. napacounty.gov is Cloudflare-blocked; the Authority page is https://www.napacounty.gov/467/Housing-Authority (707-253-4112). AB 1890 figures were not re-checked in this audit.
- Source: https://california.public.law/codes/health_and_safety_code_section_50711.5
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-06)

**Permanent Local Housing Allocation (PLHA), Napa County non-entitlement formula share**
- Agency: Napa County Housing and Community Services (HCD formula grantee)
- Type: grant
- Typical award: HCD CY 2024-2028 Formula Allocation NOFA: Napa County CY 2024 $219,600 and CY 2025 $241,967; five-year estimate 2024-2028 $1,372,500. By comparison the City of Napa (entitlement) is $223,362 and $239,253 for the same years. Earlier rounds: 2020 formula awards to the City of Napa only; the City also administers PLHA for American Canyon, Calistoga, St. Helena and Yountville under delegation agreements, not for the County.
- AMI requirement: PLHA statute: rental assistance at or below 60% AMI unless the plan targets up to 120% AMI (150% in high-cost areas); 55-year covenant for rental development; County five-year plan governs local uses.
- Cycle: annual NOFA (next: HCD releases the annual formula allocation each year; the County must hold a resolution and five-year plan for 2024-2028. No County NOFA to developers was found; the County's plan and uses could not be read because its site blocks automated access.)
- Layering notes: Small dollars (about $220,000 to $240,000 a year) better suited to ADU loans, predevelopment or operating subsidy than to a construction gap. PLHA states no wage rule of its own; construction use is public funds under Labor Code 1720(b), subject to the 1720(c) exemptions (see prevailing_wage_basis). Confirm with Housing and Community Services (707-253-4112) whether the County's five-year plan directs PLHA to multifamily or to its ADU forgivable loan program ($105,000 maximum per ADU as of April 2026).

**Project-Based Vouchers, Housing Authority of the City of Napa (countywide HCV administrator)**
- Agency: Housing Authority of the City of Napa (HACN, HUD CA073), a City of Napa agency that administers Section 8 for all of Napa County
- Type: rental assistance
- Typical award: About 1,455 active vouchers as of early 2024 (City Consolidated Plan); the 2021 Administrative Plan allows up to 20% of budget authority to be project-based, with a 45-PBV limited preference for Napa Continuum of Care coordinated entry referrals and 15 tenant-based vouchers. Recent allocations: 8 PBVs for Stoddard West (City of Napa, 2017), 38 PBVs for Heritage House (3700 Valle Verde Drive), 8 PBVs for Napa Cove (66 units, American Canyon). Shelter Plus Care PSH renewal about $214,000 in the 2026 CoC listing.
- AMI requirement: Households at or below 50% AMI (75% at 30% AMI on admission); PBV units limited to 25% of units in a building unless serving elderly, disabled or supportive services households.
- Cycle: rolling (next: No open PBV RFP as of November 8, 2026. HACN selects PBV owner proposals by advertised RFP under 24 CFR 983.51(b)(1) or without competition under 983.51(b)(2) for projects selected through a competitive public funding process within the prior three years; developers request PBVs after a CTCAC, HCD or HOME award.)
- Layering notes: Recorded at county level because HACN is the only public housing agency in Napa County and attaches PBVs to projects in American Canyon and other cities; the Napa County Housing Authority runs farmworker centers only and holds no vouchers. Developers normally request PBVs after a CTCAC or HCD award, which lets HACN use the non-competitive path. PBV HAP contracts run up to 20 years with extensions. Federal Davis-Bacon applies to PBV new construction or rehab of 9 or more contract units; state prevailing wage is not triggered by PBVs alone. City of Napa records in Pass 3 will cover HACN's city-only programs.
- Source: https://www.cityofnapa.org/DocumentCenter/View/7814/2021-Section-8-Administrative-Plan-PDF
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-06)

**Welfare Exemption processing, Napa County Assessor**
- Agency: Napa County Assessor-Recorder-County Clerk (John Tuteur)
- Type: tax abatement
- Typical award: Full exemption of property tax on qualifying low-income rental units under Revenue and Taxation Code 214(g) once the BOE issues an Organizational Clearance Certificate; the Assessor rules on the property-use side of the claim.

Assessor valuation line 707-259-8740, main office 707-253-4467, 1127 First Street, Suite A, Napa. Contact is from the BOE county assessor directory; napacounty.gov pages and DocumentCenter PDFs sit behind Cloudflare and refused automated access on 2026-11-06, so the county's own page could not be opened; the Assessor's exemptions page is https://www.napacounty.gov/1081/Exemptions-From-Property-Taxes.

### Nevada County

**7th Cycle Housing Element (2027-2035) RH rezone program and lower income site inventory**
- Agency: Nevada County Community Development Agency, Planning Department
- Type: zoning incentive
- Typical award: Draft 7th Cycle Housing Element released for 30-day review October 5, 2026 and directed to HCD on October 20, 2026. RHNA 3,712 units (1,703 lower, 730 moderate, 1,279 above moderate). Site inventory shows a 677-unit lower income shortfall, so the County must rezone about 42 acres to the RH (Residential High) zone at a minimum 16 units per acre by May 15, 2030 (if adopted and certified within 120 days of the May 15, 2027 deadline). Candidate sites are near community regions and rural centers with services.
- AMI requirement: Rezoned sites must accommodate lower income units; state law requires by-right approval for projects with at least 20% lower income units on shortfall rezone sites.
- Cycle: rolling (next: HCD review November 2026 to early 2027; adoption hearings spring 2027; certification deadline May 15, 2027; rezoning complete by May 15, 2030.)
- Layering notes: Nevada County's Housing and Community Services Department (HCS, Tyler Barrington, Director, 950 Maidu Ave, Nevada City, 530-265-1645, Housing@nevadacountyca.gov) sits inside the Health and Human Services Agency and administers the Western Nevada County Regional Housing Trust Fund, PLHA (as delegated applicant for Grass Valley and Nevada City), state HOME and CDBG awards, the MORE mobile home program and the new Down Payment Assistance Program; the Behavioral Health and Homelessness Department (Cari Yardley, Director) holds Homekey+, BHSA and the Truckee Navigation Center; HHAP is administered by the Homeless Resource Council of the Sierras as the CoC CA-531 lead; and the Regional Housing Authority (Sutter, Nevada, Yuba, Colusa and Lake counties, Yuba City) supplies vouchers. Grass Valley, Nevada City and Truckee run their own programs (Pass 3). The County has no inclusionary ordinance, no housing impact fee and no affordable housing fee waiver program; the only land use incentive is the state density bonus ordinance. nevadacountyca.gov opens directly and the Legistar web API client 'nevco' exposes staff reports and attachments at legistar.granicus.com/nevco/attachments/. The rezone list is the pipeline of multifamily sites in unincorporated Nevada County for the next decade. Developers should comment on candidate sites now and pair a rezone site with the Prohousing Designation, density bonus and PLHA Round 4 and 5 funds. The 2025 Housing Element Annual Progress Report was accepted January 27, 2026.

- Agency: Nevada County Behavioral Health Department

**Residential Density Bonus and Incentives for Affordable and Senior Housing (Land Use and Development Code Section 12.03.160)**
- Agency: Nevada County Community Development Agency, Planning Department
- Type: density bonus
- Typical award: Implements Government Code 65915 for projects of five or more units: 10% lower income, 5% very low income, 10% moderate income (for-sale), 50% senior, 50% workforce housing (60% to 150% AMI, a local category with a 20% bonus, at least 50% of adult tenants working in the county and 25% of units at 60% to 80% AMI), 10% transitional foster youth, disabled veteran or homeless units (35% bonus), or 100% affordable projects. Bonus and incentive tables track state law; 100% lower income projects (up to 20% moderate) get an 80% bonus and four incentives, and within one-half mile of a major transit stop get no maximum density plus up to three additional stories or 33 feet. Senior developments get 20%, with a separate local senior amenity table. Parking ratios reduced per state law. Additional bonus and incentive provisions for transitional and supportive housing are in the Section governing those uses.
- AMI requirement: 55-year covenants for rental very low and lower income bonus units; moderate income for-sale units per state law.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Not applicable; applied with the land use entitlement. The 7th Cycle Housing Element (2027-2035) will rezone at least 42 acres to the RH zone at 16 units per acre to cover a 677-unit lower income shortfall, with rezoning due by May 15, 2030.)

### Orange County

**Apartment Development Revenue Bond Program, County of Orange conduit issuer**
- Agency: County Executive Office, Public Finance (Louis McClure, 714-834-5999, Luis.McClure@ocgov.com) with the Public Financing Advisory Committee (PFAC) and Board of Supervisors
- Type: bond
- Typical award: Tax-exempt multifamily bonds for new construction or acquisition-rehab anywhere in Orange County; a typical bond loan is $7,000,000 or more with issuance costs of about $300,000, 30-year amortization, credit enhanced (Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac, bank letter of credit) or privately placed at County discretion. Borrower pays all issuance and finance team costs. No recent County issuances were located; most Orange County deals use CMFA or CSCDA (for example Valencia Garden in Orange, CMFA $18,499,022).
- AMI requirement: At least 20% of units for very low income households, or 10% very low plus 30% at 60% AMI, for the longer of 15 years or the life of the bonds (about 30 years); County loans may be added for deeper affordability.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Apply after site control and a lender commitment: PFAC approves the financing concept and team, the Board holds the TEFRA hearing and adopts the inducement resolution, then the County applies to CDLAC; bonds must close within 90 days of the CDLAC award. Call the CEO public finance contact before preparing an application.)
- Layering notes: The County keeps a conduit program on paper (Attachment H to the 2026 Supportive Housing NOFA, opened) but the pipeline shows cities and developers using CMFA and CSCDA instead; expect PFAC review to add six to eight weeks versus a JPA issuer. Bonds alone do not trigger state prevailing wage; County loans in the same deal do. Confirm current issuer fees with the CEO, as none are published.
- Source: https://housing.oc.gov/sites/hcd/files/2026-03/Attachment%20H%20-%20Apartment%20Development%20Revenue%20Bond%20Program.pdf
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-06)

**Development fee waiver for affordable housing (no countywide program)**
- Agency: OC Public Works, OC Development Services
- Type: fee waiver
- Typical award: None adopted. The County has no impact fee waiver or deferral program for affordable housing in the unincorporated area. The 2026 Supportive Housing NOFA treats city waivers of impact, school, sanitation and mitigation fees as eligible local match, and County loans may pay building permit fees as an eligible cost.
- AMI requirement: Not applicable.
- Cycle: closed/inactive (next: Not applicable. Ask the host city for fee waivers to satisfy the County NOFA match requirement.)

**HOME, CDBG and ESG, Orange County Urban County program**
- Agency: OC Housing and Community Development, Community Development Division; Craig Fee, Community Development Manager, 714-480-2996
- Type: grant
- Typical award: FY 2026-27 Annual Action Plan: CDBG $3,467,220 annual allocation plus $20,000 program income and $806,834 prior-year resources ($4,294,054 available); HOME $1,244,582.84 plus $135,000 program income; ESG $302,608. Five-year ConPlan FY 2025-29 expects about $12,900,000 CDBG and $4,100,000 HOME over the remaining years. HOME housing development dollars are awarded only through the Supportive Housing NOFA; CDBG goes mainly to public facilities, public services and housing rehabilitation through the annual Request for Applications (generally due in November under the Funding Allocation Policy and Process).
- AMI requirement: HUD income limits (80% AMI, HOME rents); the County's NOFA restricts HOME-assisted PSH units to 30% AMI for 55 years. CDBG new construction only by a CBDO.
- Cycle: annual NOFA (next: FY 2027-28 Funding Allocation Policy and Process posted Oct 2026; the RFA for CDBG, ESG and HOME public service and facility projects is generally due in November with the Action Plan draft out for 30-day comment in March and Board adoption in spring. Housing development applicants should use the Supportive Housing NOFA instead.)
- Layering notes: Small program for a county of 3.2 million because most cities are their own entitlements. Urban County members: unincorporated area plus Brea, Cypress, Dana Point, Laguna Beach, Laguna Hills, Laguna Woods, La Palma, Los Alamitos, San Juan Capistrano, Seal Beach, Stanton, Villa Park and the metro cities Placentia and Yorba Linda; Anaheim, Santa Ana, Irvine, Garden Grove, Huntington Beach and 15 other cities run their own CDBG and HOME (Pass 3). The County is not the HOPWA grantee. The County's HOME-ARP allocation was folded into the Supportive Housing NOFA rather than offered separately. Davis-Bacon and state prevailing wage apply. Pages and the FY 2026-27 Action Plan PDF opened on housing.oc.gov.
- Source: https://housing.oc.gov/community-development
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-06)

**Housing Opportunities Overlay (Zoning Code 7-9-44), Affordable Housing Permit (7-9-124.3) and density bonus (7-9-87)**
- Agency: OC Public Works, OC Development Services, Planning Division (Deysi Munoz, 714-667-8815, Deysi.munoz@ocpw.ocgov.com)
- Type: density bonus
- Typical award: The 2024 Housing Opportunities Overlay Manual allows 100% affordable rental or ownership projects, emergency shelters, multi-service centers and low-barrier navigation centers by right in the C1, C2, CN, MX, M1, R2, R3 and R4 districts of unincorporated Orange County, approved through an administrative Affordable Housing Permit with no public hearing (the permit process also applies to projects at least 20% affordable in those districts). Qualified projects must be 100% affordable to low and very low income households (at or below 80% AMI), with 70% low income and at least 30% very low income units, a minimum density of 30 units per acre and generally at least 16 units. Density bonus follows Government Code 65915; on-menu incentives include side, front and rear setback reductions, up to 10 feet and one additional story of height, and a lot consolidation density incentive up to 45% total. The County NOFA's Attachment J lists eligible sites. No county inclusionary housing ordinance or in-lieu fee.
- AMI requirement: Overlay projects: 100% affordable, 70% low income and 30% very low income, with recorded covenants; density bonus units per state law (55 years for rental).
- Cycle: rolling (next: Not applicable; ministerial. Unincorporated communities include Midway City, Rossmoor, North Tustin, Ladera Ranch, Rancho Mission Viejo, Silverado and El Modena. Confirm site eligibility with OC Development Services; processing fee deposit applies.)
- Layering notes: The overlay matters because most of the County's own land-use authority covers small pockets; the 2026 NOFA gives unincorporated overlay sites the first 60-day application window and the higher $137,500 per unit subsidy. Density bonus and by-right approval do not trigger prevailing wage. Manual PDF opened on ocds.ocpublicworks.com; zoning code mirror on Zoneomics shows section headings and overlay affordability terms.
- Source: https://pwds.oc.gov/sites/ocpwocds/files/2024-08/Orange%20County%20Housing%20Opportunties%20Overlay%20Manual%202024%20.pdf
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-06)

**Housing Successor Low and Moderate Income Housing Asset Fund (Orange County Housing Authority as Housing Successor to the Orange County Development Agency)**
- Agency: Orange County Housing Authority as Housing Successor, administered by OC Housing and Community Development
- Type: loan
- Typical award: Housing Asset Fund balance $29,240,000 at June 30, 2024 (FY 2023-24 SB 341 report). Funds are offered only through the County's Supportive Housing NOFAs: $4,000,000 added to the 2016 PSH NOFA in April 2018; 2020 NOFA awards of $2,400,000 to Clara Vista (former Tahiti Motel, Stanton, 60 PSH units, completed Dec 2023) and $453,600 each to Mountain View (Lake Forest, 71 units) and Orchard View Gardens (Buena Park, 66 units); no Housing Successor funds were in the 2023 NOFA, but they are a named source in the 2026 NOFA.
- AMI requirement: Health and Safety Code 34176.1: households at or below 80% AMI, at least 30% of spending over five years for extremely low income households, 55-year covenants; excess surplus rules force spending when the unencumbered balance exceeds the greater of $1,000,000 or four years of deposits.
- Cycle: rolling (next: No separate round; request Housing Successor funds through the open 2026 Supportive Housing NOFA (first come, first served, no fixed deadline as of November 8, 2026).)
- Layering notes: A large idle balance (about $29,000,000) that the County must spend to avoid excess surplus findings, so it is the most flexible local money in the NOFA pool: no federal strings, 30% AMI target through the NOFA. Use it for sites outside HOME geography or where Davis-Bacon is a problem. Housing successor funds are public funds under Labor Code 1720(b), but 1720(c)(4) excludes affordable units paid for solely from Low and Moderate Income Housing Fund money; other funds in the deal decide coverage (see prevailing_wage_basis). Housing successor page and FY 2023-24 report PDF opened on housing.oc.gov.
- Source: https://housing.oc.gov/housing-development/orange-county-housing-authority-housing-successor
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-06)

**MHSA/BHSA permanent supportive housing capital and Capitalized Operating Subsidy Reserve (Orange County Health Care Agency through OC Community Resources)**
- Agency: OC Health Care Agency, Behavioral Health Services (MHSA/BHSA Housing Program), with OC Housing and Community Development administering loans
- Type: loan
- Typical award: BHSA Integrated Plan FY 2026-29 (Board May 19, 2026): Housing Interventions component $73,500,000 a year; planned capital development $18,375,000 a year (the 25% statutory maximum) plus about $990,508 from other sources; rental subsidies $14,000,000 a year; operating subsidies $6,787,829 a year; $36,750,000 a year reserved for chronically homeless people. Named capital pipeline: Mercury Senior Apartments (Brea), Lampson Workforce Housing (Los Alamitos) and projects to be determined in San Juan Capistrano, Anaheim Hills, Buena Park and Fountain Valley, 56 BHSA units of 416 at about $208,000 per BHSA unit. Since June 2018 the County has completed 476 MHSA units with 196 in the pipeline toward a goal of 2,396 PSH units by 2029; each MHSA dollar leveraged about $5.50. HCA also granted $20,500,000 of MHSA and General Fund to the Orange County Housing Finance Trust. Loan limit $207,235 per regulated unit for capital and another $207,235 for COSR under the 2026 NOFA.
- AMI requirement: Extremely low income (30% AMI) adults experiencing homelessness with a serious mental disorder (WIC 5600.3(b), BHSA eligibility under WIC 5830(a)), certified by HCA and referred through CES; rents at 30% of the 30% AMI limit or 30% of SSI; no minimum income where PBVs or COSR are provided; MHSA/BHSA units at most 49% of the project; units at least 450 square feet with full kitchens and furnishings; 55-year covenant.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Apply through the 2026 Supportive Housing NOFA (open since March 6, 2026) with an HCA review meeting before submission. The three-year plan runs July 1, 2026 to June 30, 2029 with annual updates; HCA moves money to OCCR under a three-year spending plan, so NOFA amounts rise when new BHSA allocations post.)
- Layering notes: Orange County's BHSA program is the deepest county PSH source in the 13 counties researched: $18,400,000 a year in planned capital plus a COSR that replaces PBVs when none are available (zero interest, forgivable over 15 to 20 years, sized to cover MHSA unit operating deficits). Pair the capital with 4% credits and OCHA or city PBVs; use COSR when PBVs are refused. MHSA/BHSA capital alone may avoid Davis-Bacon; the NOFA says state prevailing wage may apply under Labor Code 1720 and is decided per project with counsel input, while HOME (12+ units) or PBVs (9+ units) trigger Davis-Bacon. Terms are in Attachment D of the 2026 NOFA (opened); budget figures from the Integrated Plan PDF on ochealthinfo.com (opened). HCA does not run its own developer NOFA.
- Source: https://housing.oc.gov/sites/hcd/files/2026-03/Attachment%20D%20-%20MHSA%20BHSA%20Term%20Sheet.pdf
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-06)

**Orange County 2026 Supportive Housing NOFA (HOME, HOME-ARP, MHSA/BHSA, 15G Reserves, Housing Successor funds)**
- Agency: OC Housing and Community Development (OC Community Resources), 1501 E. St. Andrew Place, Santa Ana; Michelle Zdeba, Housing Development Manager, 714-480-2994; Sherluna Vien 714-480-2936; OCHCD.NOFA@occr.ocgov.com
- Type: loan
- Typical award: Up to $20,900,000 in loans authorized by the Board Feb 10, 2026 and released March 6, 2026 (OpenGov NOFA 2026-01), plus up to 100 Housing Choice, Mainstream or VASH project-based vouchers. Replaces the 2025 NOFA ($12,050,000 and up to 150 PBVs) and the 2023 NOFA ($67,100,000 authorized, $32,700,000 and 218 PBVs in Amendment 1). Maximum County subsidy per assisted unit: $137,500 (any bedroom size) in the unincorporated area and Urban County participating cities; $95,000 (0BR), $100,000 (1BR), $105,000 (2BR+) in all other cities. MHSA/BHSA capital limit $207,235 per regulated unit plus up to $207,235 per unit for a capitalized operating subsidy reserve. Minimum five assisted units; total development cost above TCAC's $650,000 per unit threshold needs justification.
- AMI requirement: All County-assisted units restricted to households at or below 30% AMI who are experiencing homelessness, filled through the Coordinated Entry System, with a 55-year regulatory agreement from the qualified project period. MHSA/BHSA units serve adults with serious mental illness and may not exceed 49% of project units. Projects outside the unincorporated area must show host-city financial support at least equal to the County request (land, fee waivers and infrastructure count) and accept a RHNA transfer or credit to the County.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Open on a first come, first served basis as of November 8, 2026 until funds are committed by Board action, the NOFA is replaced, or HCD suspends intake; no fixed deadline. All geographic tiers are now open (any eligible location since the third tier began in June 2026). Allow at least eight months from a complete application to Board approval. PBVs only for sites in OCHA jurisdiction.)
- Layering notes: The County's only capital program and it is PSH only: every assisted unit must be 30% AMI and CES-referred, so it fits a 4% or 9% deal with a PSH set-aside, not a general affordable project. Terms: 3% simple interest, 55 years, residual receipts split 50% to public lenders pro rata and 50% to the developer, monitoring fees of $500 setup plus $3,795 a year plus $22 per unit, replacement reserves $250 to $500 per unit, partnership management fee up to $25,000. Davis-Bacon applies at 12 or more HOME-assisted units or nine or more PBV units; projects using only MHSA/BHSA or Housing Successor money may avoid Davis-Bacon but state prevailing wage applies to public funds. HOME-ARP, 15G Reserves and Housing Successor dollars are pooled here rather than offered separately. OCHA PBVs can be requested with no capital. Homekey+ projects vetted through the County RFI skip the geographic tiers. NOFA, exhibits and sample loan documents are posted on the NOFA page (opened 2026-11-06).
- Source: https://housing.oc.gov/housing-development/developer/notice-funding-availability
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-06)

**Orange County Housing Finance Trust (OCHFT) permanent supportive and affordable housing loans**
- Agency: Orange County Housing Finance Trust, joint powers authority of the County of Orange and 27 cities (9-member board, 4 County and 5 city seats), administered by County staff
- Type: loan
- Typical award: 2024 NOFA (due March 15, 2024, availability extended by Addendum 2 through July 2026, now fully committed): $25,700,502 from County MHSA ($12,371,809), County General Fund ($1,000,000) and state Local Housing Trust Fund matching grants ($12,328,693), split in thirds across North, Central and South service planning areas, project cap $3,500,000. Awards 2020 to 2024: $55,035,131 to 32 project awards funding 441 Trust-restricted units in 2,477 total units (2024 round $22,143,076 for 152 units across 10 projects including Cypress Village Irvine $3,500,000 and Aspan Court Lake Forest $3,490,000). June 30, 2025 audit: notes receivable $25,013,554, net position $54,579,510; FY 2024-25 deposits $4,000,000 MHSA, $1,200,000 County, $3,000,000 CalOptima, $402,747 LHTF. $250,000 federal community project funding presented April 2026. Goal 2,396 PSH units by 2029.

Terms mirror the County NOFA: 3% simple, 55 years from conversion, 50% residual receipts, TCAC developer fee limits, $25,000 partnership management fee cap. Awards are small ($500,000 to $3,500,000) and used as last-in gap money on 4% and 9% deals, often alongside County MHSA loans and OCHA PBVs. Member cities: Aliso Viejo, Anaheim, Buena Park, Costa Mesa, Dana Point, Fountain Valley, Fullerton, Garden Grove, Huntington Beach, Irvine, La Habra, Laguna Beach, Laguna Hills, Laguna Niguel, Lake Forest, Los Alamitos, Mission Viejo, Newport Beach, Orange, Placentia, San Juan Capistrano, Santa Ana, Seal Beach, Stanton, Tustin, Westminster and Yorba Linda. OCHFT NOFA Section 3.12 makes LHTF-funded projects subject to state prevailing wage unless a Labor Code 1720(c) exception applies (see prevailing_wage_basis). NOFA page, developments page, member list and 2025 audit opened; the 2024 NOFA PDF is hosted on Squarespace.

**Permanent Local Housing Allocation (PLHA), Orange County Urban County entitlement**
- Agency: OC Housing and Community Development (HCD entitlement grantee for the Urban County)
- Type: grant
- Typical award: HCD 2024-2028 Formula Allocation NOFA: Orange County CY 2024 $892,973, CY 2025 $956,505, five-year estimate $5,581,081. The County's amended PLHA Five-Year Plan (Attachment A-C-E, December 2023 NOFA) uses only Sections 301(a)(6) and 301(a)(7): about 88% for homelessness activities (45% Buena Park and Placentia navigation centers via the North SPA collaborative, 32% regional emergency shelters such as the Yale Transitional Center for the unincorporated area and Laguna Hills, 4% Laguna Beach case management and supportive services, 7% Dana Point outreach and rapid rehousing), 7% for accessibility modifications in low-income senior owner-occupied homes in Laguna Woods (3%) and Seal Beach (4%), and 5% administration. Ask OCHCD whether the plan was amended for the state's 2024 requirement that 40% of new PLHA fund owner-occupied workforce housing, and whether the 11.45% development share is folded into the Supportive Housing NOFA.)

- Agency: Orange County Housing Authority (OC Community Resources), 1501 E. St. Andrew Place, Santa Ana, 714-480-2700; PBV requests through OC Housing and Community Development NOFA staff
- Type: rental assistance
- Typical award: 26 PBV projects listed on the OCHA site total 693 PBV units (for example Stanton Inn 71, Oasis Huntington Beach 62, Tahiti 59, Ascent 57, Avon River 48, Casa Paloma 48, Crossroads at Washington 43, Salida Del Sol 40). The 2026 Supportive Housing NOFA offers up to 100 Housing Choice, Mainstream or VASH PBVs (150 under the 2025 NOFA; 218 under the 2023 NOFA Amendment 1). ### Placer County

**Affordable Housing and Employee Accommodation Ordinance (County Code Chapter 15.65): 10% inclusionary requirement, in-lieu fee and employee accommodation fee**
- Agency: Placer County Community Development Resource Agency (entitlement review) and Economic Development and Housing Division (fee collection and use); nexus study update by BAE Urban Economics under a February 4, 2025 contract
- Type: regulatory requirement
- Typical award: Regulatory requirement and the County's only local housing revenue. Ordinance 6050-B (October 27, 2020), effective January 1, 2021: new private residential projects of more than 100 units must make 10% of units affordable; projects of 8 to 100 units may instead pay an in-lieu fee per habitable square foot of each market-rate unit. The fee was $2.00 initially and is indexed; the Board's April 7, 2026 annual impact fee adjustment raised it from $2.73 to $2.84 per square foot effective July 1, 2026. An Employee Accommodation Fee of $2.84 per net building square foot applies to new non-residential development in the Sierra Nevada and Lake Tahoe area (Tahoe Truckee Unified School District boundary). Exempt: projects of 7 or fewer units or where most units are under 1,600 square feet, deed-restricted affordable housing, ADUs, infill sites, transit priority areas, mixed-use projects at least 70% residential, and others in Section 15.65.050. Fee revenue funds construction of affordable housing, preservation, acquisition-rehab of multifamily projects and first-time homebuyer assistance.
- AMI requirement: 10% of units affordable for projects over 100 units, with the in-lieu fee option for 8 to 100 units; compliance terms set in a development agreement or affordable housing agreement. A BAE Urban Economics nexus study update (draft, not approved) and ordinance amendments are scheduled on the County's project page for a Board update in fall or winter 2026 to 2027 and final Board adoption in spring or summer 2027.
- Cycle: rolling (next: No application deadline; applies at entitlement with fee paid before building permit issuance. Nexus study and ordinance amendments are scheduled for final Board adoption in spring or summer 2027 per the County project page as of November 8, 2026.)
- Layering notes: For a 100% affordable or deed-restricted project the ordinance is not a cost (exempt). For a mixed-income project over 100 units it is a 10% set-aside; between 8 and 100 units the fee is $2.84 per square foot (about $2,840 on a 1,000 square foot unit), low relative to Bay Area counties. The fee revenue is the pool behind the County's gap loans, so a higher fee from the 2027 nexus update would expand the only local source. The infill and transit priority area exemptions remove many western Placer multifamily sites from the requirement. Density bonus and inclusionary agreements do not trigger prevailing wage. placer.ca.gov program pages opened directly on November 8, 2026.
- Source: https://www.placer.ca.gov/6954/Affordable-Employee-Housing-Ordinance-Fe
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-06)

**Behavioral Health Services Act (BHSA) Integrated Plan FY 2026-29: housing interventions, rental and operating subsidies and capital development (Carriage Court Studios)**
- Agency: Placer County Health and Human Services, Behavioral Health (Adult System of Care; Amy Ellis, Director of Behavioral Health; Primary Housing Interventions Contact Jamie Gallagher, 530-889-7283); 11434 B Avenue, Auburn
- Type: grant
- Typical award: Housing Interventions is 30 percent of the BHSA base allocation (no exemption or transfer): $6,810,046 (FY 2026-27), $7,745,005 (FY 2027-28) and $8,270,067 (FY 2028-29), plus $1,000,000 a year of unspent MHSA carryover, for $7,810,046, $8,745,005 and $9,270,067 ($25,825,118 over three years). Total BHSA allocations are $22,700,154, $25,816,683 and $27,566,891. Planned BHSA and MHSA housing spending by year: capital development $1,952,000, $1,750,000 and $2,317,000 ($6,019,000 total; 25%, 20% and 25% of the component); permanent-setting rental subsidies $949,000, $1,110,218 and $1,383,768; permanent-setting operating subsidies $1,603,378, $1,770,912 and $1,185,232; interim rental subsidies $144,473 to $156,473; interim operating subsidies $2,357,780, $2,569,541 and $2,817,758; outreach and engagement $546,703 to $648,705 (7%); landlord outreach and mitigation $0, $354,000 and $300,000; participant assistance $50,000 to $200,000; housing navigation and tenancy sustaining $50,000 to $75,000; admin $156,200 to $185,413. Half of the component is dedicated to the chronically homeless. The one named capital project is Carriage Court Studios (Homekey): 55 total units, 10 funded with Housing Interventions, capacity 54, expected cost per unit $284,855, units available April 1, 2027. Plan targets 285 people a year on rental subsidies (367 units) and 463 people on operating subsidies (280 units).
- AMI requirement: BHSA eligible adults and families with serious mental illness or substance use disorder who are homeless or at risk of homelessness, prioritized through the CA-515 Coordinated Entry System; at least 50 percent of component funds for chronically homeless people. BHSA is payer of last resort and cannot pay for housing services covered by Medi-Cal managed care plans.
- Cycle: rolling (next: No NOFA. Capital in this plan period is committed to one project (Carriage Court Studios). Developers or operators of PSH serving BHSA clients should contact Placer County Behavioral Health housing staff (Jamie Gallagher, 530-889-7283) about rental or operating subsidies; new capital projects would need to be added in an annual update.)
- Layering notes: Classified grant: the plan funds housing capital (Carriage Court Studios) and rental and operating subsidies for housing. Placer County Behavioral Health has run its own housing team for about 20 years and braids BHSA with Homekey (Sun Rose Apartments, Carriage Court Studios, Brown Bear Studios), BHCIP, BHBH, HHAP, CDBG, County general fund, ARPA, opioid settlement funds, IGT revenue, Transitional Rent and Housing Trio Community Supports, HUD CoC and HCV/VASH vouchers. BHSA operating subsidies support CoC-funded PSH sites such as Timberline and Placer Street. Partners are AMI Housing (AMIH) and The Gathering Inn. The plan expects a 40 percent cut in HUD PSH renewals and BHSA to backfill about 100 households. For a developer, BHSA here is mostly an operating or rental subsidy source for PSH units serving BHSA clients, not open gap capital; the County Executive Office Economic Development and Housing Division runs the in-lieu fee gap loans and PLHA, and the Placer County Housing Authority (HHS) supplies project-based vouchers. Capital share (20 to 25 percent of the component) is higher than Nevada (0) and similar to Fresno.

**Launchpad workforce housing incentive, eastern Placer County (Transient Occupancy Tax through the TOT-TBID Dollars at Work program)**
- Agency: Placer County Executive Office, Economic Development and Housing (Timothy Cussen, Housing Specialist); Tahoe City office 775 North Lake Boulevard; funding recommended by the North Tahoe Community Alliance (NTCA) TOT-TBID Dollars at Work program
- Type: grant
- Typical award: $200,000 per unit for category one (condos, townhomes, multifamily units and conversions of non-residential or non-code-compliant space; single-family homes are not eligible), $125,000 per ADU and $50,000 per SRO unit, paid at completion once the 55-year workforce Use Deed Restriction is recorded. Funding: $1,000,000 inaugural NOFA LP-001 (released April 16, 2025; 8 applications) reserved $725,000 for two Kings Beach projects (Steelhead Avenue Cottage Court, 3 tiny homes, $600,000; accessible ADU, $125,000). NOFA LP-002, posted February 6, 2026, offered $3,275,000 ($3,000,000 of new TOT approved February 3, 2026 plus $275,000 carryover), drew 12 applications (55 units, $10,550,000 requested) and reserved $3,250,000 for four projects: Lake Forest Multifamily (12 studios, Tahoe City, $2,400,000), Dollar Hill Tiny Homes (3 units, $600,000) and two tiny home ADUs in Lake Forest and Cedar Flat ($125,000 each).
- AMI requirement: Units must be in unincorporated eastern Placer County within the Tahoe Truckee Unified School District boundary, outside avalanche hazard areas, with entitlements in place or allowed by right. A 55-year Use Deed Restriction (restarting on each transfer) requires occupancy as a primary residence by a qualified household with a local worker employed within the TTUSD area; no income limit or sales price cap. Units used to meet the Affordable Housing and Employee Accommodation Ordinance are ineligible.
- Cycle: annual NOFA (next: No open round as of November 10, 2026. The February 2026 NOFA LP-002 (applications February 25 to March 18, 2026) is fully reserved. The May 11, 2026 Board memo says staff will bring revised guidelines to the Board later in 2026, and the County opened a community survey in August 2026; a future NOFA depends on new TOT funding recommended through the NTCA TOT-TBID Dollars at Work program.)
- Layering notes: placer.ca.gov sits behind Cloudflare; the same County pages and DocumentCenter files open on the placerair.org host, and Board memos are on content.govdelivery.com/attachments/CAPLACER. Launchpad is a per-unit grant rather than a loan and is sized for small infill projects in Kings Beach, Tahoe City and the North Shore; a 10-unit workforce project could draw $2 million, which is meaningful against TRPA coverage and construction costs in the Basin. It pays only at completion, so it is bridge-financed. Guidelines Section III.f bars combining Launchpad with any other County program or subsidy unless the Board approves. The workforce (not income) restriction means it does not fit LIHTC deals directly but can fund unrestricted middle-income units in a mixed-income project. North Lake Tahoe TOT also funds the Workforce Housing Preservation Program and the Dollar Creek Crossing effort.

**Development impact fee waiver for affordable housing (Ordinance 659) and density bonus (Ordinance 348)**
- Agency: Riverside County Transportation and Land Management Agency, Planning and Building and Safety
- Type: fee waiver

Density bonus: Ordinance 348 was amended in March 2021 to adopt state density bonus law (Government Code 65915 and 65917.2) with incentives, concessions and waivers; the R-6 Residential Incentive Zone offers case-by-case density above the General Plan for projects with 15% of units at 80% AMI or 25% at 120% AMI. - AMI requirement: Affordable housing as defined by the DIF ordinance and the Housing Element; density bonus tiers per state law.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Claimed at building permit (DIF waiver) and at entitlement (density bonus). School, regional transportation (TUMF and WRCOG) and special district fees are not County DIFs and are not waived.)
- Layering notes: Riverside County's Housing and Workforce Solutions (HWS) department runs the Urban County HUD programs, PLHA, HHAP, Homekey+ sponsorships and project loans, while the Housing Authority of the County of Riverside (HACR, same Board sitting as Commissioners) supplies project-based vouchers, housing successor funds and land; rivcohws.org and harivco.org block automated access, so records were built from Board of Supervisors files on riversidecountyca.iqm2.com and media.rivcocob.org, RUHS Behavioral Health, the Assessor and the County Housing Element. Prevailing wage is marked unclear because waived fees can be read as public funds under Labor Code 1720(b)(4). Source is the County 2021-2029 Housing Element HCD submittal (Programs 1.1d and 1.2b and the constraints chapter).
