### Sacramento County

**Community Development Block Grant (CDBG), Urban County of Sacramento**
- Agency: SHRA for the County of Sacramento
- Type: grant
- Typical award: 2027 Action Plan: $6,151,763 allocation plus $2,025,000 prior-year resources ($8.18M); about $3.63M targeted to the housing development, preservation and homeownership goal (27 rental units rehabilitated, 10 constructed, 100 owner rehabs), the rest to infrastructure and public services. June 2025 notice listed $0 County CDBG for multifamily; June 2026 notice did not list CDBG.
- AMI requirement: At least 51% of assisted units for households at or below 80% AMI.
- Cycle: annual NOFA (next: Through SHRA rounds when offered (rehabilitation projects only); 2027 program year begins January 2027.)
- Layering notes: Limited developer value: CDBG cannot fund new construction unless carried out by a Community Based Development Organization, and SHRA offers it only for rehabilitation. Davis-Bacon applies at 8 or more units. Useful for acquisition-rehab or preservation deals paired with 4% credits and CalHFA or SHRA bonds. CDBG-CV balances are committed to the Mather Community Campus shelter.
- Source: https://www.shra.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/2027-County-AP-Narrative_Final.pdf
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-06)

**HOME Investment Partnerships Program, Sacramento County HOME Consortium**
- Agency: SHRA for the County of Sacramento (lead entity) and consortium cities Citrus Heights, Folsom, Rancho Cordova, Galt and Isleton
- Type: loan
- Typical award: 2027 Action Plan: $2,825,253 annual allocation plus $900,000 program income ($3.73M total). 2024 entitlement $2,965,817; year-end 2024 balance $15.7M ($9.1M uncommitted). $2,500,000 posted as available June 1, 2026. Recent project loans $1.5M to $8.9M (Arden Star $8.9M for 48 HOME units; Madison Square $4.45M; San Juan Phase II $4.2M).
- AMI requirement: 20% of HOME-assisted units at 50% AMI (Low HOME rents), remainder at or below 60% AMI with rents at 65% AMI; federal affordability period 5 to 20 years but SHRA records 55-year restrictions. 15% CHDO set-aside.
- Cycle: annual NOFA (next: Through SHRA multifamily pre-application rounds (next expected January 2027); HUD program year is the calendar year, 2027 Action Plan drafted August 2026.)
- Layering notes: Applies to the unincorporated county and the five consortium cities (Elk Grove and the City of Sacramento are separate HUD entitlements). HOME on 12 or more units triggers Davis-Bacon, and SHRA policy requires the higher of state or federal wage by trade when both apply; applicants must flag wage assumptions in the SHRA narrative. HOME units stack with CTCAC units but the HOME rent and income rules are the binding constraint on those units. SHRA may assign HOME rather than local fee funds to a request, so underwrite wages conservatively. Environmental review (NEPA) deadline falls two months after SHRA's application deadline. SB 802 (Chapter 417, Statutes of 2026) requires the County and cities to form the Sacramento Area Housing and Homelessness Agency, a regional JPA that absorbs SHRA, by January 1, 2028; expect program administration, fee funds and NOFA calendars to migrate to that agency during 2027-2028.
- Source: https://www.shra.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/2027-County-AP-Narrative_Final.pdf
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-06)

**Permanent Local Housing Allocation (PLHA), County of Sacramento**
- Agency: County of Sacramento (HCD entitlement recipient); SHRA administers the multifamily share
- Type: loan
- Typical award: 2024 PLHA income $6,666,613; year-end 2024 uncommitted multifamily balance $2,245,525 and single-family (down payment assistance) balance $2,804,135. Recent multifamily commitments: Arden Star $2.42M (13 units), San Juan $1.7M (7 units), San Juan Phase II $2.7M then increased to $4.7M (70 units). $0 posted as available for County projects June 1, 2026.
- AMI requirement: Multifamily share for households at or below 60% AMI (with workforce flexibility under the County's PLHA plan); 55-year restriction. At least 25% of each allocation is reserved for down payment assistance below 50% AMI.
- Cycle: annual NOFA (next: Through SHRA multifamily rounds as annual HCD PLHA disbursements arrive (SB 2 recording-fee revenue, variable). Next SHRA round expected January 2027; check the funds-available notice for a PLHA line.)
- Layering notes: State formula money without federal strings, so it is the preferred SHRA source when Davis-Bacon must be avoided (state prevailing wage still applies unless the below-market-loan exemption is met). Often paired with HOME in the same SHRA award (San Juan Phase II). The separate HCD Local Housing Trust Fund match program is no longer funding; the County's last LHTF award was 2024. SB 802 negotiations included language keeping PLHA flowing to all jurisdictions once the regional agency forms. SB 802 (Chapter 417, Statutes of 2026) requires the County and cities to form the Sacramento Area Housing and Homelessness Agency, a regional JPA that absorbs SHRA, by January 1, 2028; expect program administration, fee funds and NOFA calendars to migrate to that agency during 2027-2028.
- Source: https://www.shra.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/ATT-4-PLHA-Annual-Report.pdf
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-06)

**Project-Based Vouchers, Housing Authority of the County of Sacramento**
- Agency: SHRA (the County housing authority administers all vouchers for both the City and County)
- Type: rental assistance
- Typical award: Competitive RFP awards from the tenant-based HCV allocation or HUD-VASH; no RFP anticipated in 2026. Cap of 25 units or 25% of a building, whichever is greater, with exceptions for elderly or disabled households and units with qualifying supportive services (common for PSH). HAP contract up to 20 years with extensions to 40 years total.
- AMI requirement: HCV income limits (very low income, 75% of admissions at or below 30% AMI); PBV units leased through the Coordinated Access System for homeless set-aside units under a Housing First model.
- Cycle: closed/inactive (next: SHRA states it does not anticipate a Project-Based Voucher RFP in 2026; updates come through the SHRA listserv. HUD's 2026 budget guidance also asked PHAs to pause new PBV commitments except for public housing repositioning, so a 2027 RFP is uncertain. Non-competitive PBV remains possible for SHRA-controlled sites and for adding units to existing HAP contracts.)
- Layering notes: PBV HAP contracts underwrite debt on PSH units (rents at the payment standard, up to 120% of FMR with approval) and were the operating engine for Homekey, NPLH and MHP supportive units in Sacramento. With no 2026 RFP, new PSH deals should plan on Homekey+ operating grants, BHSA rental subsidies or the County Flexible Housing Pool instead. Referral mechanics for PBV PSH run through Sacramento Steps Forward (see Continuum of Care record). SB 802 (Chapter 417, Statutes of 2026) requires the County and cities to form the Sacramento Area Housing and Homelessness Agency, a regional JPA that absorbs SHRA, by January 1, 2028; expect program administration, fee funds and NOFA calendars to migrate to that agency during 2027-2028.
- Source: https://www.shra.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/SHRA-HCV-2027-Admin-Plan-Draft.pdf
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-06)

**SHRA Multifamily Lending Program (County gap financing)**
- Agency: Sacramento Housing and Redevelopment Agency (SHRA) on behalf of the County of Sacramento and the Housing Authority of the County of Sacramento
- Type: loan
- Typical award: Gap loans sized to the financing gap after all other sources; no stated per-project cap. County funds posted June 1, 2026: HOME $2,500,000, Housing Trust Fund $900,000, Affordable Housing Ordinance fund $6,000,000, PLHA $0 (total about $9.4M). Recent County commitments: San Juan Phase II $11.7M (HOME $7.0M plus PLHA $4.7M, 70 units), Shiloh Arms $2.12M HOME, South Sacramento Homekey $1.9M. Projects must have 12 or more units.
- AMI requirement: 55-year regulatory agreement. Minimum per source: HOME 20% of HOME units at 50% AMI and the rest at or below 60% AMI; AHO fund 20% at 50% AMI and 80% at 60% AMI; Housing Trust Fund 50% to 80% AMI workforce households. Priorities: preservation at risk, then new construction (PSH and homeless, veterans, workforce 30% to 60% AMI, other), then rehab. Deeper affordability preferred.
- Cycle: annual NOFA (next: No open round as of November 8, 2026. SHRA states it is not currently accepting pre-applications; the 2027 schedule has not been posted. Based on the 2026 pattern, expect a January 2027 pre-application deadline for the spring TCAC/CDLAC round.)
- Layering notes: This is the primary local soft source for 9% and 4% deals in the unincorporated county (City of Sacramento projects use the parallel City pool, Pass 3). Terms: up to 4% simple interest, term up to 40 years from conversion or 55 years when senior public lenders require, 1.10x to 1.20x combined DSCR, 90% combined LTV, payments deferred during construction and deferred developer fee then amortized, residual receipts only when state or federal lenders require it. Nonprofit managing general partner required; applicants need prior affordable housing ownership experience. $12,500 good-faith deposit at full application; annual administration fee 12.5 bps of loan (max $15,000) or 5 bps of bonds (min $15,000). SHRA issues the CTCAC local needs letter and conduit bonds (see separate bond record). Applicants request gap funds without specifying a source; SHRA picks the source, so Davis-Bacon exposure depends on whether HOME (12+ units) or CDBG (8+ units) is assigned, and state prevailing wage applies unless the below-market-loan exemption (40% of units at 80% AMI for 20 years) fits. Pre-applications are timed so SHRA commitments are in hand before CTCAC and CDLAC deadlines, satisfying CDLAC readiness and the CTCAC tiebreaker. SB 802 (Chapter 417, Statutes of 2026) requires the County and cities to form the Sacramento Area Housing and Homelessness Agency, a regional JPA that absorbs SHRA, by January 1, 2028; expect program administration, fee funds and NOFA calendars to migrate to that agency during 2027-2028.
- Source: https://www.shra.org/multi-family-housing-financing-lending-resources/
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-06)

**SHRA Multifamily Mortgage Revenue Bonds (Housing Authority of the County of Sacramento conduit issuance)**
- Agency: Housing Authority of the County of Sacramento, staffed by SHRA
- Type: bond
- Typical award: No minimum or maximum bond amount; sized to the senior lender's loan. Issuance fee 25 bps of the bond amount at closing; annual administration fee 5 bps of outstanding bonds (minimum $15,000) plus $100 per SHRA-regulated non-bond unit per year; when another issuer is used SHRA still charges up to 0.25% for TEFRA review. CDLAC fees and 0.5% performance deposit pass through.
- AMI requirement: Federal and state minimum: 20% of units at 50% AMI, or 30% at 60% AMI plus 10% at 50% AMI (H&S Code 34312.3); non-competitive CTCAC projects targeting above 60% AMI must average no more than 59% AMI. Rents capped at 30% of 50% or 60% AMI. Bond regulatory agreement for the qualified project period or 55 years from 50% occupancy, incorporating the CDLAC resolution.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Pre-application and full application on the SHRA schedule tied to CDLAC rounds (2026: applications March 2 and Sept 1 for the July/Sept and March/May 2027 CDLAC rounds). Inducement resolution and TEFRA hearing go to the Board of Supervisors or City Council before the CDLAC filing.)
- Layering notes: Local alternative to CalHFA, CSCDA and CMFA for 4% deals in the City and unincorporated county (other cities by cooperation agreement). SHRA requires projects using other issuers to meet SHRA affordability and due diligence standards and pays for TEFRA review. Nonprofit owners seeking the welfare exemption must show ongoing day-to-day involvement (services, management or maintenance) under SHRA policy 9.1.11. Bonds alone are generally not treated as public funds for state prevailing wage, but SHRA gap loans or HOME in the same deal usually are. Private placements waive the investment-grade rating requirement. SB 802 (Chapter 417, Statutes of 2026) requires the County and cities to form the Sacramento Area Housing and Homelessness Agency, a regional JPA that absorbs SHRA, by January 1, 2028; expect program administration, fee funds and NOFA calendars to migrate to that agency during 2027-2028.
- Source: https://www.shra.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/2026-SHRA-Multifamily-Lending-Policies-County-final.pdf
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-06)

**Sacramento Continuum of Care (CA-503) funding and PBV PSH referral system**
- Agency: Sacramento Steps Forward (CoC lead agency and HMIS lead) for the City and County of Sacramento
- Type: rental assistance
- Typical award: HUD CoC Program awards described as tens of millions per round across more than 30 renewal projects; competition now runs every other year. 2026 competition: local letters of intent for new projects due July 2, 2026, local applications July 14, 2026, consolidated application to HUD Sept 30, 2026. Youth Homelessness Demonstration Program total $8,082,381 across seven projects (as of 2025).
- AMI requirement: CoC PSH serves households experiencing homelessness (chronic homelessness priority) through the Coordinated Access System; rental assistance and leasing, not capital.
- Cycle: biennial (next: 2026 round closed (HUD submission Sept 30, 2026). Next local competition expected 2028 under the every-other-year cycle, with renewals in between.)
- Layering notes: CoC dollars rarely fund capital, but CoC PSH rental assistance or leasing can replace PBV as the operating subsidy on a share of units, and CoC participation is required for Homekey+ and HHAP coordination. For PBV PSH buildings, SSF runs the lease-up: referrals begin 120 days before the temporary certificate of occupancy, are over-referred by 20%, and target full occupancy within 60 days of TCO, with SHRA paying the subsidy within 30 days of move-in. The 2023 City-County Affordable Housing Plan (SHRA, SSF, City, County) tracks a 649-unit PSH pipeline and a proposed joint PSH fund.
- Source: https://www.sacramentostepsforward.org/sacramento-continuum-of-care/2026-coc-program-competition-notice-of-funding-opportunity/
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-06)

**Sacramento County Affordable Housing Fee Deferral and Waiver Program (county impact fees and SacSewer impact fees)**
- Agency: County of Sacramento Department of Finance with SHRA certification; Sacramento Area Sewer District (SacSewer, formerly SASD and Regional San) for sewer impact fee waivers
- Type: fee waiver
- Typical award: Deferral or waiver of county development impact fees (Antelope, North Vineyard Station, Vineyard and Florin Vineyard plan area fees, library facilities fees, county transportation development fees) and SASD/Regional San sewer impact fees. Waivers are proportional to the share of very low-income units. Annual cap on waivers: greater of 200 dwelling units or 5% of prior-year new residential permits in the unincorporated county. SacSewer reported over $900,000 waived across five projects as of October 2025. $1,000 application fee; deferrals require a 10% fee deposit.
- AMI requirement: Deferral: at least 10% of units affordable to very low income (50% AMI) or 49% affordable to low income (80% AMI). Waiver: at least 10% of units at or below 50% AMI. Fees become due with interest penalties if the units are not delivered within 24 months.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Rolling, before building permit issuance; requires an SHRA Certification Letter, preliminary title report, and a recorded agreement, note and deed of trust (subordinable to construction financing). Deferred fees are due at close of escrow or 24 months after the agreement, whichever is first.)
- Layering notes: County impact fee relief applies to unincorporated projects; SASD and Regional San sewer impact fee waivers are available in all cities in the county and the unincorporated area. Sewer impact fees in Sacramento run several thousand dollars per unit, so the waiver is worth roughly $5,000 to $10,000 per very-low-income unit; it reduces basis and improves the CTCAC cost-containment score. Labor Code 1720(b)(4) treats fees waived or forgiven by a public agency as public funds, so a waiver can itself trigger state prevailing wage unless the project is otherwise exempt; confirm with counsel. City of Sacramento has its own fee deferral and fee reduction program (Pass 3).
- Source: https://feedeferral.saccounty.gov/us/en/affordable-housing.html
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-06)

**Sacramento County Affordable Housing Incentive Program (density bonus, Zoning Code Section 6.5.4)**
- Agency: Sacramento County Planning and Environmental Review
- Type: density bonus
- Typical award: State Density Bonus Law as implemented in the County Zoning Code Section 6.5.4 (Table 6.4): 20% bonus for 5% very low income rising to 50% at 15%; 20% for 10% low income rising to 35% at 20% and 50% at 24%; 5% for 10% moderate income for-sale rising to 50% at 44%; 80% bonus for 100% affordable projects (up to 20% moderate) with no maximum density within a half mile of a major transit stop, plus a three-story or 33-foot height increase there; separate schedules for senior, special needs, low income college student and land donation. Up to five concessions (Table 6.5: VLI 1 at 5%, 2 at 10%, 3 at 15%, 4 at 16% to 99%; LI 1 at 10%, 2 at 17%, 3 at 24%; five for 100% affordable; one more for child care). Table 6.4.1 (added June 11, 2026) adds a further bonus for projects restricting no more than 50% of units that provide at least 15% very low, 24% lower or 44% moderate income units.
- AMI requirement: Minimum five units with 5% very low, 10% low, 10% moderate (for-sale), or special population set-asides; rental target units restricted 55 years with professional management; units built concurrently and dispersed on site.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Rolling; filed with the entitlement application together with an Affordable Housing Strategies Memorandum; the County does not charge a processing fee for eligible applications (Housing Element page). Affordable Housing Agreement must be recorded before grading and building permits.)
- Layering notes: Parking maximums: 1 space studio and 1-bedroom, 1.5 for 2- and 3-bedroom, 2.5 for 4-bedroom; within a half mile of major transit 0.5 per bedroom, 0.5 per unit for 100% lower-income rental, none for special needs housing. Waivers of standards that physically preclude the project are unlimited but do not count as concessions. Land donation (one acre or 40 units, zoned 30+ units per acre) earns bonus and can satisfy the AHO. Combine with the AHO fee exemption (20% affordable at 17+ du/ac) and the Countywide Rezone Program sites for by-right or streamlined approval. 100% affordable LIHTC projects typically use the 80% bonus and parking reductions to cut costs rather than add units.
- Source: https://landuse.saccounty.gov/szc/ch6/
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-06)

**Sacramento County Affordable Housing Ordinance Fund (AHO affordability fee)**
- Agency: County of Sacramento (Planning and Environmental Review collects fee); SHRA administers the fund and lends it through the Multifamily Lending Program
- Type: loan
- Typical award: $6,000,000 available for new County projects as of June 1, 2026. 2024 fee revenue $5,128,243; year-end 2024 balance $11.1M ($6.3M uncommitted). 2014 to 2024 cumulative $32.8M, funding eight projects (650 units); AHO money averaged about 9% of total development cost and reached 61% of new affordable units built in the unincorporated area. Typical commitments $400,000 to $6.4M per project (Cornerstone South $6.43M for 29 AHO units; San Juan $5.2M for 21 units; Beech Hill $2.47M for 11 units).
- AMI requirement: Fund-assisted units: 20% at 50% AMI and 80% at 60% AMI, workforce (labor force) households, 55 years. At least 10% of fees must buy down units to extremely low income (30% AMI); at least 50% of fees must produce housing within large (750+ unit) development projects, which steers money to the Vineyard, North Vineyard Station, Florin Vineyard and similar growth areas.
- Cycle: annual NOFA (next: No open round as of November 8, 2026. AHO funds are awarded only through SHRA multifamily pre-application rounds; SHRA is not accepting pre-applications and has not posted a 2027 schedule (2026 pattern suggests a January 2027 pre-application deadline).)
- Layering notes: Unincorporated-county-only money (fee is charged only on unincorporated residential permits). Normally paired with 4% credits plus bonds or 9% credits, SHRA HOME, PLHA and the County Housing Trust Fund in one SHRA award. Developer side of the ordinance: market-rate projects may instead dedicate land, build units, enter a development agreement with an Affordable Housing Strategy, or buy banked unit credits from SHRA; multifamily projects with at least 20% affordable units at 17 or more units per acre are exempt from the fee, which is itself a meaningful incentive for mixed-income rental. AHO is a local below-market loan, so the Labor Code 1720(c)(5)(E) exemption may apply if no HOME or CDBG is in the stack; confirm with counsel. The County is mid-way through an AHO amendment study (Housing Element Program E3): KMA found 2% to 14% affordable production versus the 10% target; Board workshop Oct 6, 2026, nexus study through spring 2027, ordinance hearings expected winter 2027, possibly adding an inclusionary option and resource-area targeting. SB 802 (Chapter 417, Statutes of 2026) requires the County and cities to form the Sacramento Area Housing and Homelessness Agency, a regional JPA that absorbs SHRA, by January 1, 2028; expect program administration, fee funds and NOFA calendars to migrate to that agency during 2027-2028.
- Source: https://planning.saccounty.gov/us/en/planning-environmental-review/projects/long-range/aho.html
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-06)

**Sacramento County Behavioral Health (MHSA/BHSA) housing capital for permanent supportive housing**
- Agency: Sacramento County Department of Health Services, Behavioral Health Services, with SHRA screening projects through its multifamily rounds
- Type: loan
- Typical award: Not published as a NOFA amount. The FY2026-29 BHSA Integrated Plan budgets about $200,000 per BHSA unit for its planned capital project (30 BHSA units of 120, about $6M) and states 2 capital projects. Prior MHSA practice: SHRA's June 2025 funds notice said projects could be considered for County MHSA housing financing for PSH units; example $2.5M MHSA to Auburn Oaks PSH. BHSA requires 30% of county funds for housing interventions, up to 25% of that for capital.
- AMI requirement: PSH units restricted to persons with serious mental illness or substance use disorder who are homeless or at risk, referred through County Behavioral Health; typically 30% AMI or below with rental or operating subsidy.
- Cycle: rolling (next: No open round as of November 8, 2026. No stand-alone BHSA capital NOFA or solicitation is posted; housing requests ride on SHRA multifamily pre-applications (2027 schedule not yet posted, likely January 2027).)
- Layering notes: BHSA classification: the Integrated Plan funds housing capital and rental subsidies, so this is a deployable capital source (kept as loan, consistent with prior MHSA capital practice through SHRA). Successor to the CalHFA Special Needs Housing Program and county NPLH allocations (NPLH is closed; Sacramento County ran its last Request to Partner in 2020). BHSA capital and operating subsidies can underwrite PSH units in 4% and 9% deals and support CTCAC homeless priority and the CDLAC Homeless set-aside. Pair with Homekey+ and HHAP. County funds are public funds for prevailing wage. Amounts and process should be confirmed with Behavioral Health Services and SHRA before underwriting.
- Source: https://dhs.saccounty.gov/us/en/behavioral-health/about/bhsa.html
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-06)

**Sacramento County Housing Trust Fund (commercial linkage fee)**
- Agency: County of Sacramento (Chapter 16.89, fee collected at building permit); SHRA administers and lends the fund
- Type: loan
- Typical award: $900,000 available as of June 1, 2026 (was $0 in June 2025). 2024 fee revenue $1,605,084; year-end 2024 balance $6.36M ($1.2M uncommitted). Since 1991: $33.1M in fees, 29 developments, 3,037 total units. Recent loans $816,000 to $5.25M per project (San Juan $5.25M for 21 HTF units; Terracina at Wildhawk $4.6M for 18 units).
- AMI requirement: Households at 50% to 80% of county AMI who are in the labor force (jobs-housing linkage); 55-year regulatory agreement.
- Cycle: annual NOFA (next: Through SHRA multifamily pre-application rounds (next expected January 2027). Current fee schedule (2024 report): office and hotel $3.26, research and development and commercial $2.17, manufacturing and warehouse $1.08 per gross square foot, adjusted annually.)
- Layering notes: Oldest local source (1990). Revenue tracks commercial construction and is volatile, so the balance is usually smaller than the AHO fund. Used mainly for new construction workforce units at 50% to 80% AMI, which complements deeper-targeted HOME or MHP units in the same project. Local below-market loan; state prevailing wage exemption may be available absent federal funds. The companion City of Sacramento Housing Trust Fund (City Code 18.56) is a separate pool covered in Pass 3. SB 802 (Chapter 417, Statutes of 2026) requires the County and cities to form the Sacramento Area Housing and Homelessness Agency, a regional JPA that absorbs SHRA, by January 1, 2028; expect program administration, fee funds and NOFA calendars to migrate to that agency during 2027-2028.
- Source: https://www.shra.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/ATT-1-Housing-Trust-Fund-Annual-Report-for-2024.pdf
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-06)

**Welfare Exemption processing, Sacramento County Assessor**
- Agency: Sacramento County Assessor, Institutional Exemptions Section (BOE issues the Organizational Clearance Certificate)
- Type: tax abatement
- Typical award: Exemption of the qualifying low-income share of assessed value from the roughly 1.1% to 1.2% total property tax rate in Sacramento County (plus any direct levies that remain). Annual filing with the Assessor.
- AMI requirement: Per state law: lower-income units (80% AMI, 140% continuation rule) under LIHTC or a recorded regulatory agreement; limited partnerships need a nonprofit or eligible LLC managing general partner with an OCC and a Supplemental Clearance Certificate.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Annual claims due February 15 (next Feb 15, 2027; postmark next business day if a weekend or holiday). First-time filers submit BOE-267 with the BOE-277 OCC and the low-income supplemental affidavit (BOE-267-L or 267-L1 for partnerships). Contact (916) 875-0720 or ASR-InstitutionalExemptions@saccounty.gov.)
- Layering notes: Sacramento assessor applies the statewide rules (see Pass 1 BOE record); no county-specific abatement JPA exists. SHRA bond policy 9.1.11 additionally requires the nonprofit owner to have material day-to-day involvement (services, management or maintenance) for bond-financed projects claiming the exemption, which aligns with BOE managing-GP scrutiny. File the construction-period claim as soon as the OCC is issued and the site is under development to avoid a year of taxes.
- Source: https://assessor.saccounty.gov/us/en/exemptions/nonprofit-exemptions.html
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-06)


### San Benito County

**Affordable housing in-lieu fee fund and impact fee waivers for 100% affordable developments**
- Agency: San Benito County Resource Management Agency, Planning and Building; County Executive Office (impact fee program)
- Type: fee waiver
- Typical award: Chapter 21.03 (as amended by Ordinances 1052 and 1059, 2023; code text dated January 29, 2025 attached to the February 11, 2025 Board item) requires projects of 6 to 10 units to pay an inclusionary housing fee, lets larger projects pay in-lieu fees for fractional units under 0.7 or where site conditions qualify, and sets the fee by Board resolution in the Master Fee Schedule, updated annually by the Residential Construction Cost Index. The December 13, 2022 Board item proposed $30 per square foot based on the Vernazza Wolfe in-lieu fee study. Section 21.03.012(A) lets in-lieu fee monies fund construction, acquisition, rehabilitation, low-interest or equity participation loans, grants, rent subsidies, housing trusts and down payment assistance, and provide reasonable reimbursement to the County for infrastructure costs of impact fee waivers granted to 100% affordable developments. Fund balance and any waiver approvals are not published. Before 2023, developers voluntarily paid $4,500 per unit under development agreements.
- AMI requirement: Fund uses limited to extremely low, very low, low and moderate income housing (up to 120% AMI); impact fee waiver reimbursement applies only to 100% affordable developments.
- Cycle: rolling (next: No County in-lieu fund notice of funding availability was found as of November 10, 2026. Request an impact fee waiver with the entitlement application and confirm the in-lieu fund balance with Planning and Building.)
- Layering notes: San Benito County is a small non-entitlement county with no housing department: the Resource Management Agency (Planning and Building, Abraham Prado, (831) 637-5313) administers the inclusionary ordinance, in-lieu fees, density bonus and TEFRA hearings; the Health and Human Services Agency (Community Services and Workforce Development) runs HHAP, the shelter and the Migrant Center; Behavioral Health holds BHSA; and the Housing Authority of the County of Santa Cruz administers vouchers and PBVs for Hollister and San Juan Bautista. The County has no HOME or CDBG entitlement, no housing trust fund NOFA and no County loan program; Hollister runs its own PLHA and CDBG programs (Pass 3). sanbenitocountyca.gov and the amlegal code library block automated access, so records were built from Board of Supervisors packets on cosb.granicus.com (attachments on d2kbkoa27fdvtw.cloudfront.net), HCD allocation tables and hacosantacruz.org. Confirmation needed: the ordinance language creating the waiver reimbursement was read in the 2022 Board packet, but the current code text, the fund balance and any adopted waiver procedure could not be opened (sanbenitocountyca.gov and amlegal 403). Treat as a negotiable cost reduction for a 100% affordable project rather than a funded program.
- Source: https://cosb.granicus.com/services/legistar/download/pdf/3119505/Attachment_3._Chapter_21.03_Affordable_Housing_Regulations_of_the_San_Benito_County_Code.pdf
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-07)

**Behavioral Health Services Act Integrated Plan FY 2026-29 (Housing Interventions component)**
- Agency: San Benito County Behavioral Health Department (Rachel White, Director)
- Type: grant
- Typical award: Integrated Plan FY 2026-29 approved by the Board June 23, 2026 (4-0) after DHCS approval May 28, 2026 and a public hearing May 21, 2026. Statutory split is 30% Housing Interventions, 35% Full Service Partnerships and 35% Behavioral Health Services and Supports, but the County transferred 7% each from FSP and Housing Interventions into BHSS (about 23% Housing Interventions). The State approved spending up to 35% of the Housing Interventions component on capital development (above the standard 25%) for a housing development project with the Health and Human Services Agency to house HHSA and Behavioral Health clients experiencing homelessness. Dollar amounts are in the plan and budget attachments, not the staff report.
- AMI requirement: BHSA eligible adults and youth with serious mental illness or substance use disorder; at least 50% of housing funds for chronically homeless people under state law unless exempted.

**Inclusionary Housing Ordinance (Chapter 21.03 Affordable Housing Regulations) and in-lieu fee**
- Agency: San Benito County Resource Management Agency, Planning and Building (sbcplan@sanbenitocountyca.gov, (831) 637-5313)
- Type: regulatory requirement
- Typical award: Requirement rather than a subsidy: 15% of units affordable on site (for-sale and rental) or 20% off site under Sections 21.03.006 and 21.03.007; developments of 1 to 5 units exempt, 6 to 10 units pay the in-lieu fee automatically, 11 or more units build on or off site and pay the fee on fractions below 0.7 unit. In-lieu fee adopted December 13, 2022 (Ordinance 1052, Resolution 2022-149): $30 per square foot for for-sale homes based on the 15% requirement (Vernazza Wolfe affordability gap study). Example compliance: Lands of Lee subdivision affordable housing plan approved September 15, 2026 under Resolution 2024-146 (about 30 affordable units, 21% of the project).

- Cycle: rolling (next: Applies with each land use entitlement; no application deadline.)

### San Diego County

**Affordable housing on County-owned excess land (ground leases through Disposition and Development Agreements)**
- Agency: County of San Diego Department of General Services, Real Estate Services (RFP issuance and DDA), with HCDS (regulatory agreement and IHTF capital); Board of Supervisors approval
- Type: land
- Typical award: 12 County-owned surplus sites are in the pipeline for 100% affordable housing totaling about 1,762 homes (595 completed, 126 under construction, 1,043 upcoming), with $51.8 million of County capital committed to the sites. Nine sites are in the City of San Diego, plus Fallbrook, Ramona and Escondido. Terms are long-term ground leases (99 years at 620 E. Valley Parkway, Escondido, 134 senior units; 3177 Ocean View Boulevard, San Diego, 122 units with BRIDGE Housing and a San Ysidro Health clinic, about $500,000 initial rent then $300 a year escalating 3.5%). Next starts: 6255 Mission Gorge Road (337 units) and 5001 73rd Street (120 units) in early 2027, 4588 Market Street (138) in 2027, Ramona 12th and Main (100) and 5202 University Avenue (90, via SDHC) in 2028.
- AMI requirement: 100% affordable at or below 80% AMI under a County regulatory agreement (55 years or longer); specific populations (seniors, families, PSH) set in each RFP. Developer must comply with the County Working Families Ordinance (prevailing wage, skilled and trained workforce, paid sick leave) on County property.
- Cycle: rolling (next: No open round as of November 8, 2026; the County General Services Development Opportunities page lists only an RFP for a Behavioral Health Wellness Campus. Housing site RFPs are issued site by site after the Board declares a property surplus; expected next solicitations are the ground lease and renovation of the four Chula Vista public housing sites after HUD RAD/Section 18 approval and the Fallbrook North Orange and East Ivy site (program TBD).)
- Layering notes: County land deals come packaged: nominal ground lease, IHTF or other County capital (County sites had their own $12 million IHTF NOFA in July 2026 and get a location preference in every HCDS NOFA), PBVs where HACSD has jurisdiction, and Board support for state applications. In exchange the County requires 100% affordability, Working Families Ordinance labor terms (prevailing wage plus skilled and trained workforce on work over $1 million), ground lease payments to the IHTF, and a County regulatory agreement senior to other restrictions. Mission Gorge (337 units) and Ramona are the largest unincorporated or near-term opportunities; Ramona and Fallbrook sites test rural feasibility. Faith-based land partnerships (three developments, 220 units) are a parallel track.
- Source: https://sdcounty.legistar.com/LegislationDetail.aspx?ID=8704&GUID=2E56B0B2-5171-4711-9A3B-0DAF1260AC97&Options=&Search=&FullText=1
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-06)

**Behavioral Health Services Act (BHSA) housing interventions and Flexible Housing Pool, County of San Diego Behavioral Health Services**
- Agency: County of San Diego HHSA, Behavioral Health Services (Integrated Plan FY 2026-2029 approved June 9, 2026); Flexible Housing Pool Pilot administered by Brilliant Corners under a single-source contract approved November 18, 2025
- Type: grant
- Typical award: BHSA budget about $329.5 million in FY 2026-27, with the housing component at 27% of the local allocation (roughly $89 million a year by that percentage; the plan does not publish a single housing dollar total). Rental subsidies for about 2,672 people a year: 290 permanent slots (250 Flexible Housing Pool subsidies for ACT clients plus 40 operating subsidies at Starling Place, a Homekey+ site in the City of San Diego) and about 2,382 interim placements from a $23.6 million interim housing budget; 4,305 units a year funded in total. Flex Pool Pilot costs $3.45 to $5.35 million in FY 2026-27 (Behavioral Health Bridge Housing and BHSA). Capital development: none in FY 2026-27.
- AMI requirement: Medi-Cal eligible adults with serious mental illness or substance use disorder who are chronically homeless, homeless or at risk; at least half of housing funds for chronically homeless people; permanent settings include supportive housing, master-leased apartments, shared housing, board and care and recovery residences; Transitional Rent (six months, Medi-Cal managed care) feeds into BHSA subsidies.
- Cycle: rolling (next: No developer NOFA. The plan states the County will not fund capital development with BHSA in year one (to sustain treatment services) and will reassess in future years; operating subsidies are limited to the 40 Homekey+ units. Annual plan updates start FY 2027-28 (draft due to DHCS each March 31), and BHSA will absorb Behavioral Health Bridge Housing programs when that grant ends in FY 2028-29.)
- Layering notes: Unlike Orange or Contra Costa, San Diego County is spending its BHSA housing money on subsidies and a Flex Pool rather than capital, so do not underwrite County BHSA capital for PSH in 2026-27. The realistic asks are: Flex Pool tenant-based subsidies for units set aside for ACT clients (Brilliant Corners master-leasing or direct placements), a Homekey+ style operating subsidy agreement if the County co-applies (it has co-applied with Wakeland in Chula Vista and Casa de Amparo in Vista), and Medi-Cal Transitional Rent through the managed care plans for move-in. Community input asked the County to dedicate the full 25% to capital, so the FY 2027-28 update is the moment to request a capital line. BHSA capital, if used, would be public funds under Labor Code 1720(b); the County is not using BHSA Housing Interventions for capital development in the first plan year (see prevailing_wage_basis).

- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-06)

**CDBG acquisition and rehabilitation NOFA (NOFA 2026-01) and HOME Consortium entitlement, San Diego Urban County**
- Agency: County of San Diego HHSA, Housing and Community Development Services (HCDS), Community Development; community.development@sdcounty.ca.gov
- Type: loan
- Typical award: NOFA 2026-01 (released June 1, 2026, due July 10, 2026, awards November 2026) offered $1.7 million of CDBG for acquisition and/or rehabilitation of existing affordable multifamily units or land acquisition for affordable housing; new construction is not eligible. FY 2027-28 CDBG applications for public facilities, infrastructure and services ran September 21 to October 30, 2026. HOME and HOME-ARP ($11.9 million HOME-ARP allocation) flow through the capital NOFA; the County's loan portfolio holds about $82 million of federal funds across 123 developments.
- AMI requirement: CDBG: households at or below 80% AMI, HUD minimum 5 years but HCDS imposes 55 years. HOME: at or below 60% AMI with 20% Low HOME units, 20-year HUD minimum, 55 years enforced by HCDS. Eligible areas: Urban County (unincorporated plus Coronado, Del Mar, Imperial Beach, Lemon Grove, Poway, Solana Beach) for CDBG and PLHA; HOME Consortium adds Carlsbad, Encinitas, La Mesa, San Marcos, Santee and Vista.
- Cycle: annual NOFA (next: Next acquisition-rehab CDBG NOFA expected around June 2027 if HCDS repeats the 2026 schedule; HOME and HOME-ARP are in NOFA 2026-03 (due November 19, 2026). CDBG public facilities applications open each September for the following fiscal year.)
- Layering notes: Terms match the capital NOFA: 3% simple, 55 years, 50% residual receipts, $720 per unit replacement reserve for rehab, 12-month reservation with no extensions, $4,000 compliance fee. Federal money brings Davis-Bacon, Uniform Relocation Act, NEPA release of funds before any choice-limiting action, lead-based paint and Section 3. Useful for preservation buys of small existing properties in the Urban County cities where IHTF is the only other County option. The larger cities (San Diego, Chula Vista, Oceanside, Escondido, El Cajon, Carlsbad for CDBG) are their own entitlements for Pass 3.
- Source: https://www.sandiegocounty.gov/content/dam/sdc/sdhcd/new-docs/CD/01.NOFA_2026-01_CDBG-FINAL.pdf

**HCDS Affordable Housing NOFA (NOFA 2026-03): IHTF, HOME, HOME-ARP, CDBG and PLHA capital loans**
- Agency: County of San Diego Health and Human Services Agency, Housing and Community Development Services (HCDS), Community Development; 3989 Ruffin Road, San Diego 92123; community.development@sdcounty.ca.gov; (858) 694-4885; NOFA contact Felipe Murillo (858) 694-4807
- Type: loan
- Typical award: NOFA 2026-03 (released October 1, 2026, due November 19, 2026 at 2:00 pm, awards March 2027) offers about $16.0 million: $9.0M Innovative Housing Trust Fund, $2.5M HOME, $1.5M HOME-ARP, $1.8M CDBG, $1.2M PLHA. HCDS allocates sources at its discretion across awarded projects. Recent IHTF loans have ranged from $400,000 to $7.25 million per project (median about $3.5 million); HCDS's portfolio averages about $1.4 million of County-administered money per development. The prior round (NOFA 2024-01, due December 20, 2024) offered $6.5M HOME/HOME-ARP/CHDO, $3.5M IHTF, $1.5M PLHA plus 100 PBVs and 25 VASH PBVs.
- AMI requirement: 55-year minimum affordability for every award regardless of source. IHTF at or below 80% AMI regionwide; HOME and PLHA at or below 60% AMI (20% of HOME units at Low HOME rents); HOME-ARP at or below 30% AMI for people experiencing or at risk of homelessness; CDBG at or below 80% AMI for acquisition or rehabilitation only. Preferences: unincorporated area or County-owned land, projects applying to the 2027 second CDLAC/TCAC round, green building (LEED Silver, 50% onsite renewable), homeless units with secured services funding (HOME-ARP).
- Cycle: annual NOFA (next: NOFA 2026-03 applications due November 19, 2026 at 2:00 pm (USB plus electronic copy); virtual industry day was October 15, 2026; awards March 2027. HCDS has run at least one capital NOFA each year since 2018 and plans to award its newest $22 million IHTF allocation through NOFAs in FY 2026-27, so expect another round in 2027.)
- Layering notes: This is the main county gap source for the whole San Diego region, including the City of San Diego for IHTF money (HOME, HOME-ARP, CDBG and PLHA are limited to the Urban County and HOME Consortium cities listed in the NOFA). Loan terms: 3% simple interest, 55-year term, 50% residual receipts shared proportionally with other public lenders, GP loans may not be repaid ahead of the County, TCAC developer fee limits, replacement reserves $375 per unit (new construction), $500 per PSH unit, $720 per unit (rehab), $4,000 initial compliance monitoring fee. All other local funds must be committed before applying and senior lenders must subordinate to the regulatory agreement. Funds are reserved for 24 months and the County will not split or combine awards if a deal converts between 9% and 4%. Scoring (165 points) weights geographic location 30, financing gap 20, experience 20, target population 15, services 15, overall 15. Federal sources carry Davis-Bacon, NEPA, Section 3, BABA (HOME) and relocation rules; state prevailing wage on County loans turns on the Labor Code 1720(c) exemptions. PSH or PBV projects must fund a one-year transition reserve. No Place Like Home was offered through earlier County NOFAs and is exhausted.

**Inclusionary Housing Ordinance, In-Lieu Fee and expanded density bonus, unincorporated San Diego County (Zoning Ordinance Sections 6341 and 7430)**
- Agency: County of San Diego Planning and Development Services (ordinance and affordable housing plans) with HCDS (in-lieu fee trust fund and affordable housing agreements)
- Type: density bonus
- Typical award: Adopted June 24, 2026 (Ordinance 11009), effective October 22, 2026; projects with a complete or SB 330 preliminary application submitted by October 21, 2026 are exempt. Applies to residential and mixed-use projects of 10 or more primary units in the unincorporated area. Incentives: density bonus doubled relative to state law up to a 50% maximum (10% low income units earns 40% instead of 20%) plus two extra concessions, and 30-day priority discretionary review for projects providing 50% more low income units than required. In-lieu fees: $18.69 per interior square foot (rental, 95% market share assumed, effective $17.76), $21.37 (for-sale, effective $19.23), $41.82 (General Plan Amendment projects, effective $33.46), paid at building permit and deposited to an HCDS trust fund for affordable housing anywhere in the county including cities. Staff estimate 15 to 60 deed-restricted units a year.
- AMI requirement: For-rent: 5% extremely low (30% AMI) or 5% very low (50% AMI) or 10% low (80% AMI). For-sale: 5% very low or 10% low or 15% moderate (120% AMI). General Plan Amendment projects: 20% low. Units calculated on base density before bonus, rounded up at 0.5. Alternative compliance in Board priority order: land donation, affordable for-sale ADUs (up to 50% of requirement or 5 units), in-lieu fee for 50%, in-lieu fee for 100%, off-site units in the same community plan area, a village, a TCAC High or Highest Resource area or a VMT-efficient area (cities allowed). 100% affordable projects are exempt but record an affordable housing agreement. Market-rate permits are held until affordable units are permitted (50% rule) and finaled (75% rule).
- Cycle: rolling (next: In effect for applications submitted on or after October 22, 2026. Senior Housing and Small Lot zoning updates and Housing Unlocked zoning amendments are scheduled for the Board in fall 2026 and 2027; a programmatic EIR for low-VMT housing streamlining comes in 2027.)
- Layering notes: For a 100% affordable deal the ordinance is a zero-cost exemption plus access to the doubled density bonus if the project also meets a set-aside; for mixed-income workforce deals in the unincorporated area it adds a 5% to 10% affordable obligation or roughly $18 to $19 per square foot in fees. The in-lieu fee revenue becomes new County gap money administered by HCDS (the Board asked staff for a dedicated IHTF revenue source and this is the first one). Land donation sites must be suitable for multifamily at the displaced density with utilities, outside slopes, floodplains, farmland and habitat; donations over $1 million go to the Board. Density bonus and inclusionary agreements do not trigger prevailing wage; the Working Families Ordinance applies only on County-owned land. 2026 San Diego County AMI is $130,900.
- Source: https://www.sandiegocounty.gov/content/dam/sdc/pds/advance/HousingStudy/San%20Diego%20County%20Inclusionary%20Housing%20Ordinance%20Applicant%20Guide_10_22_26.pdf
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-06)

**Innovative Housing Trust Fund (IHTF), County of San Diego**
- Agency: County of San Diego HHSA, Housing and Community Development Services (HCDS); established by the Board of Supervisors October 10, 2017 (Administrative Code Article XV, Sections 230.8 and 232.5)
- Type: loan
- Typical award: Board allocations total over $129 million through seven allocations since 2017 (General Fund one-time money, plus redirected grant balances such as $2 million of Capital ESG in June 2025). $112 million has been awarded to 36 developments with 3,054 units in 22 communities, leveraging $1.6 billion. The newest $22 million allocation is being awarded through NOFAs in FY 2026-27: a $12 million IHTF NOFA for County-owned sites ran July 6 to August 10, 2026, and $9 million is in NOFA 2026-03 (due November 19, 2026). Loans to date range from $200,000 (Vista Lane) to $7.25 million (Terrasini, 95 units); most are $3 million to $7 million.
- AMI requirement: Households at or below 80% AMI (extremely low, very low and low income). NOFA 2024-01 required 99-year affordability for IHTF-funded units; NOFA 2026-03 states a 55-year minimum for all sources. Eligible anywhere in San Diego County, including all 18 cities.
- Cycle: annual NOFA (next: Through NOFA 2026-03, due November 19, 2026. The Board's October 7, 2026 five-year report directs staff to identify a dedicated ongoing revenue source for the IHTF; no ballot measure or fee is adopted yet, so future rounds depend on one-time Board allocations.)
- Layering notes: IHTF is the only County money usable inside the City of San Diego and the larger cities, which makes it the typical County piece of a City of San Diego deal alongside SDHC funds and Housing Authority of the City of San Diego bonds. It is a 3% simple, 55-year residual receipts loan under HCDS standard terms. HCDS also deposits ground lease revenue from County land deals (for example about $500,000 of initial rent from 3177 Ocean View Boulevard) and will deposit inclusionary in-lieu fees from the unincorporated ordinance into HCDS trust funds, so the fund will grow modestly from those streams. County-owned sites get a scoring preference and had their own $12 million round in summer 2026. Expect state prevailing wage on any IHTF-funded construction.
- Source: https://sdcounty.legistar.com/LegislationDetail.aspx?ID=8806&GUID=5FC31D6F-DC1F-407F-A2D9-2AA8C5F0F812&Options=&Search=&FullText=1

**Permanent Local Housing Allocation (PLHA), County of San Diego formula allocation**
- Agency: County of San Diego HHSA, Housing and Community Development Services (HCDS)
- Type: grant
- Typical award: HCD's 2024-2028 formula NOFA lists San Diego County at $1,389,802 (2024), $1,488,682 (2025) and an estimated $8,686,263 over five years (the City of San Diego is separate at about $4.1 to $4.4 million a year). HCDS puts PLHA into its capital NOFAs ($1.2 million in NOFA 2026-03, $1.5 million in NOFA 2024-01) and into a moderate-income down payment assistance program.

- Layering notes: Small relative to the IHTF but it is the one County source that can be used for moderate-income ownership. For rental projects it rides along with IHTF and HOME in the same application, same 3% 55-year loan terms. NOFA 2026-03 treats all funded developments as Labor Code 1720 public works (see prevailing_wage_basis). Cities with their own PLHA (San Diego, Chula Vista, Oceanside, Escondido and others) are Pass 3.

**Project-Based Vouchers and HUD-VASH PBVs, Housing Authority of the County of San Diego (HACSD)**
- Agency: Housing Authority of the County of San Diego, administered by HCDS Rental Assistance Division (Board of Supervisors sits as the Board of Commissioners); 3989 Ruffin Road, San Diego
- Type: rental assistance
- Typical award: Since the Board's September 1, 2021 direction to expand PBVs, HACSD has awarded 768 PBVs (HCV PBVs plus VASH PBVs); 479 PBV units are operating and 327 more open within one to four years. The FY 2026 Agency Plan lists 387 PBV units in 13 developments operating, 119 units in four developments opening in 2026 (Union Tower 24 VASH, Villa Serena II 15, Alvarado Senior Village 53, Palomar Point 27) and 333 units in eight developments opening 2027 or later. PBVs are awarded through HCDS NOFAs (NOFA 2024-01 offered 100 PBVs and 25 VASH PBVs; 65 additional VASH vouchers were secured in 2025). HACSD assists over 11,000 households and pays about $21 million a month to about 4,000 landlords.
- AMI requirement: PBV units at or below 50% AMI (30% to 50% AMI homeless or special needs populations in recent awards); VASH PBVs for veterans up to 80% AMI. Initial HAP contract of 20 years renewable for up to 20 more at HACSD's discretion. HACSD jurisdiction: unincorporated area plus Chula Vista, Coronado, Del Mar, El Cajon, Escondido, Imperial Beach, La Mesa, Lemon Grove, Poway, San Marcos, Santee, Solana Beach and Vista (not the cities of San Diego, Carlsbad, Encinitas, National City or Oceanside).
- Cycle: annual NOFA (next: No PBVs are offered in NOFA 2026-03 (due November 19, 2026). The HCV program closed to new applicants February 20, 2026 because of federal funding levels, so a PBV round depends on HUD appropriations; HACSD's 121 public housing units in Chula Vista are converting to PBVs through RAD/Section 18 with a developer RFP for ground lease and renovation expected after HUD approval (18-month process started November 2025).)
- Layering notes: PBVs are the County's operating subsidy for PSH and are usually requested in the same HCDS NOFA as the capital loan, with Coordinated Entry referrals through the Regional Task Force on Homelessness. HCDS requires a transition reserve sufficient to hold rents for one year if PBV assistance is not renewed. Nine or more PBVs in a project trigger Davis-Bacon under HCDS rules; PBVs alone do not trigger state prevailing wage. Projects inside the City of San Diego use San Diego Housing Commission vouchers instead (Pass 3). Watch the Chula Vista public housing repositioning: four sites (Dorothy Street, L Street, Melrose, Town Center Manor, 121 units) will be offered to an affordable developer under a ground lease with PBVs attached.

- Agency: Regional Task Force on Homelessness (RTFH, CoC lead and HMIS lead); County of San Diego HHSA, HCDS Office of Homeless Solutions (County HHAP administrative entity); City of San Diego (large city allocation)
- Type: grant
- Typical award: HHAP Round 6 (FY 2026-27 through 2028-29): County $12.1 million (accepted December 9, 2025), RTFH CoC $12.9 million, City of San Diego $25.8 million, from a joint regional application filed August 29, 2025. County HHAP rounds 1 to 6 total about $64 million ($9.99M, $4.57M, $12.79M, $10.5M, $14.1M, $12.1M); the region received $220.6 million in rounds 1 to 5 plus $46.2 million of Encampment Resolution Funds. County HHAP pays for Housing Our Youth, the Local Rental Subsidy Program ($6.6 million in Round 5), shallow rent subsidies, housing stability case management and harm reduction contracts, not capital. 2025 point-in-time count: 9,905 people, 5,714 unsheltered.

**Tax-exempt multifamily bonds: County TEFRA approvals for CMFA, CSCDA and other JPA issuances (County not an issuer)**
- Agency: County of San Diego Board of Supervisors (TEFRA host approval through the Finance and General Government Group, Debt Advisory Committee concurrence); issuers California Municipal Finance Authority, California Statewide Communities Development Authority, California Public Finance Authority, California Enterprise Development Authority
- Type: bond
- Typical award: Project-sized conduit issuances approved as consent items roughly monthly. 2026 approvals include CMFA bonds for 2581 Commercial Street Apartments (70 units, up to $13 million, March 24 and August 18, 2026), four CMFA issuances on March 24, 2026 (up to $20M, $13M, $40M and $72M), Island Family Housing (CSCDA, August 18, 2026), Fallbrook Trails, Promenade and Seaward Affordable Apartments (CMFA, September 2026), Vista Lane Family Apartments reissuance (165 units, up to $55 million, December 9, 2025) and Fallbrook Senior Apartments (up to $26 million, November 4, 2025). The County collects about $991 per approval to recover staff costs and takes on no debt.

Bonds alone do not trigger state prevailing wage, but County IHTF, HOME or PLHA in the same deal does. Pair the TEFRA timeline with the HCDS NOFA award (March 2027) and the 2027 second CDLAC/TCAC round that the NOFA rewards.

**Welfare Exemption (property tax), San Diego County Assessor**
- Agency: San Diego County Assessor/Recorder/County Clerk, Jordan Z. Marks; Institutional Exemptions unit, 1600 Pacific Highway, Suite 103, San Diego, CA 92101; (619) 531-5772; with the State Board of Equalization (Organizational Clearance Certificate)
- Type: tax abatement
- Typical award: Exemption of property taxes on units restricted to lower income households under Revenue and Taxation Code 214(g): full exemption for qualifying units in LIHTC or publicly financed projects and partial exemption for the qualifying share in mixed projects. In San Diego County the 1% base rate plus voter-approved debt applies to the exempt value, typically worth 1.1% to 1.25% of assessed value a year.
- AMI requirement: Nonprofit owner or limited partnership with a nonprofit managing general partner holding a BOE Organizational Clearance Certificate; recorded regulatory agreement (tax credits, bonds, HOME, PLHA, IHTF or County regulatory agreement) restricting rents to lower income households; BOE-267-L2 tenant data for projects without government financing or tax credits.
- Cycle: annual NOFA (next: Next annual filing due February 15, 2027 (claims for fiscal year 2027-2028); the Assessor form states claims must be filed each year by 5:00 p.m. on February 15. Claims filed February 16 through January 1 of the following year receive 90 percent of the exemption.)
- Layering notes: Standard underwriting item for every LIHTC or County-financed deal in the region. The County's 55-year regulatory agreement and the inclusionary affordable housing agreements qualify as recorded restrictions. File the Organizational Clearance Certificate copy with the first claim and use the San Diego forms posted at sdarcc.gov. Mixed-income inclusionary projects owned by for-profits do not qualify and should instead seek a restricted assessed value under Revenue and Taxation Code 402.1.
- Source: https://www.sdarcc.gov/content/dam/arcc/assessor/forms/property-tax-exemption-and-exclusion-forms/267WELFIRST.pdf
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-06)


### San Joaquin County

**Affordable Housing Density Bonus, Development Title Chapter 9-401 (unincorporated county)**
- Agency: San Joaquin County Community Development Department
- Type: density bonus
- Typical award: State-law density bonus codified in Chapter 9-401 (2026-10 code edition): 20% base bonus for 10% low-income, 5% very low-income or senior projects; 5% for 10% moderate-income for-sale units; 20% for 10% very low-income units for veterans, transition-age youth or homeless households; 35% for qualifying student housing; sliding scale up to 50% (2.5% per 1% very low-income above 5%, 1.5% per 1% low-income above 10%); land donation bonus 15% to 35%; floor area ratio bonus in the R-H zone for infill near transit with 20% of units at or below 50% AMI; 100% lower-income projects per Government Code 65915. One to four incentives or concessions by affordability tier plus parking reductions; the County may exceed these amounts (9-401.060).
- AMI requirement: 55-year rental affordability (longer if required by financing); for-sale units sold to qualifying buyers with equity sharing; affordable units integrated with and indistinguishable from market-rate units; replacement of existing affordable units required.
- Cycle: rolling (next: By application; pre-application response within 90 days; streamlined ministerial approval under 9-401.120 for eligible infill projects with at least 10% of units at or below 80% AMI (60 or 90 day review, deemed approved if missed).)
- Layering notes: San Joaquin County has no county housing trust fund, no county housing bond and no inclusionary ordinance; the County's own capital for multifamily is limited to HUD pass-through funds administered by the Human Services Agency Neighborhood Preservation Division (sjchsa.org), while the regional gap lender is the SJCOG-sponsored San Joaquin Regional Housing Fund and the main voucher and development partner is the Housing Authority of the County of San Joaquin (HACSJ). The unincorporated county has no inclusionary ordinance and no in-lieu fee, so the density bonus and concessions are the only land-use subsidy; the 2023-2031 Housing Element (HCD submittal revised January 2025, adopted and revised June 30, 2026 to transfer RHNA to the new City of Mountain House, 8,808 to 5,113 units) sets a quantified objective of 100 lower-income units through the bonus and commits to fee deferrals for affordable subdivisions. The ministerial pathway in 9-401.120 carries state prevailing wage and skilled workforce requirements for larger projects under Government Code 65913.4, so model labor costs before electing it. Most multifamily sites in the unincorporated county (French Camp, Garden Acres, Lodi and Stockton fringe) are constrained by water and sewer service, which the Housing Element names as the largest constraint. Source is the published Development Title chapter on gocodebook.com (County code host); confirm current text with Community Development at (209) 468-3144.

**Behavioral Health Services Act (BHSA) Integrated Plan FY 2026-29, housing interventions**
- Agency: San Joaquin County Behavioral Health Services (Health Care Services Agency)
- Type: grant
- Typical award: Three-year plan totaling $295,750,706 approved June 2, 2026 (5-0). The County requested a transfer of 7% from the housing component to Behavioral Health Services and Supports, leaving housing interventions at 23% of BHSA funds. Estimated housing intervention expenditures: $18,790,266 in year one and $42,013,536 in year two; the continuum table shows housing services of $37.0 million, $41.6 million and $37.8 million across the three years. Planned uses: project-based rental subsidies for about 150 people a year (64 permanent, 86 interim; 350 units), operating subsidies for about 116 people (228 units, property management staffing for SRO and transitional-to-permanent apartments), landlord outreach and mitigation for about 100, and two capital projects (a 50-unit tiny home project and the 33-unit Edison House, both braided with other funds, unit availability June 30, 2027, BHSA share capped at $450,000 per unit).
- AMI requirement: Individuals with serious behavioral health conditions who are homeless or at risk; at least 50% of housing intervention funds for chronically homeless households; PSH setting types and Housing First.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Plan effective July 1, 2026 through June 30, 2029 with annual updates each June. Behavioral Health Services completed a request for qualifications for housing developers in 2025-26 (RFQ 25107) and will work with the pre-qualified pool: Central Valley Low Income Housing Corporation, Delta Community Developers Corporation, Domus Development LLC, Mahogany and Oak Real Estate, Mutual Housing California, RHCB Development LP, Self-Help Enterprises and Visionary Home Builders of California.)
- Layering notes: San Joaquin County has no county housing trust fund, no county housing bond and no inclusionary ordinance; the County's own capital for multifamily is limited to HUD pass-through funds administered by the Human Services Agency Neighborhood Preservation Division (sjchsa.org), while the regional gap lender is the SJCOG-sponsored San Joaquin Regional Housing Fund and the main voucher and development partner is the Housing Authority of the County of San Joaquin (HACSJ). Classified as grant because the BHSA Integrated Plan funds housing capital (two capital development projects, the Tiny Homes project and Edison House, BHSA share at or below $450,000 per unit) and project-based rental and operating subsidies for housing. BHSA is the County's largest discretionary housing stream and the realistic source of project-based operating subsidy for PSH units in the unincorporated county and Stockton; capital is limited to the two named projects, so new deals should pitch rental or operating subsidies for behavioral health set-aside units rather than construction money. Behavioral Health Services also carries Homekey+ (Bridge to Home, $15,900,896 agreement with CVLIHC approved January 13, 2026) and Behavioral Health Bridge Housing Round 3 contracts, and is building the SJ BeWell campus with a $38.2 million BHCIP Round 2 award (March 2026). Pre-qualification through the BHS RFQ is the entry point for developers. The Board file (source) links the board order, the 490-page DHCS Integrated Plan submission (FileOpen.aspx?Type=4&ID=45761) and the June 2, 2026 presentation.

**CDBG and HOME, San Joaquin Urban County (Neighborhood Preservation Division NOFA)**
- Agency: San Joaquin County Human Services Agency, Neighborhood Preservation Division
- Type: grant
- Typical award: FY 2026-27 Urban County entitlements requested by jurisdiction: CDBG $2,948,080 (County share $1,740,858; Escalon $75,000; Lathrop $97,358; Manteca $420,911; Ripon $92,270; Tracy $521,683), HOME $973,290 (County share $663,627) and ESG $258,552, plus about $500,000 CDBG and $500,000 HOME program income. County HOME rental awards in 2026-27: DCDC Senior Housing at Salas Park (Lodi Commons) $230,024 entitlement plus $500,000 program income; STAND solar for permanent supportive shared housing $190,281; CHDO set-aside $145,993. Historic averages per the division: CDBG about $2.4 million a year, HOME about $700,000 a year, ESG about $200,000 a year.
- AMI requirement: HUD CDBG national objective (51% low and moderate income benefit) and HOME rent and income limits with HOME affordability periods; at least 15% of HOME to CHDOs. Lodi Commons (54 restricted senior units plus manager) is the current HOME-assisted rental example.
- Cycle: annual NOFA (next: No open round as of November 8, 2026. The 2027-28 Urban County CDBG, HOME and ESG NOFA has not been posted on the Neighborhood Preservation page; based on prior cycles (December posting, late January deadline) the next NOFA is expected around December 2026. Confirm with Neighborhood Preservation at (209) 468-3175 or neighborhood@sjgov.org.)
- Layering notes: San Joaquin County has no county housing trust fund, no county housing bond and no inclusionary ordinance; the County's own capital for multifamily is limited to HUD pass-through funds administered by the Human Services Agency Neighborhood Preservation Division (sjchsa.org), while the regional gap lender is the SJCOG-sponsored San Joaquin Regional Housing Fund and the main voucher and development partner is the Housing Authority of the County of San Joaquin (HACSJ). The Urban County covers unincorporated San Joaquin County plus Escalon, Lathrop, Manteca, Ripon and Tracy (qualification package for FY 2027-28 through 2029-30 authorized August 4, 2026); Stockton and Lodi are separate HUD entitlements with their own NOFAs (Pass 3). Roughly half of CDBG and HOME passes through to the five cities, so County HOME available for rental development is typically under $1 million a year including program income; the 2026-27 draft Action Plan says requests far exceeded funds. HOME is used as a small soft loan behind 4% and 9% tax credit deals. Lodi Commons (Housing Authority, 55 units, TDC $28,463,882) stacks $3,031,559 of County HOME from three fiscal years, $2,000,000 County HOME-ARP, $1,000,000 County HHAP, $5,400,000 HACSJ funds, $665,000 City of Lodi CDBG, $2,000,000 Health Net, $3,000,000 San Joaquin Regional Housing Fund, $500,000 HUD CPF and about $10.7 million LIHTC equity, with 32 PBVs and 22 ACC units (FONSI dated November 4, 2026). Davis-Bacon applies at 12 or more HOME-assisted units or 8 or more CDBG-assisted units; state prevailing wage turns on the local or state funds in the deal and the Labor Code 1720(c) exemptions (see prevailing_wage_basis). The Neighborhood Preservation pages moved from sjgov.org to sjchsa.org in 2026; the 2025-2029 Consolidated Plan and 2026-2027 Annual Action Plan are posted there.

**County General Fund one-time affordable housing contributions (no standing County housing trust fund)**
- Agency: San Joaquin County Board of Supervisors
- Type: grant

- Layering notes: San Joaquin County has no county housing trust fund, no county housing bond and no inclusionary ordinance; the County's own capital for multifamily is limited to HUD pass-through funds administered by the Human Services Agency Neighborhood Preservation Division (sjchsa.org), while the regional gap lender is the SJCOG-sponsored San Joaquin Regional Housing Fund and the main voucher and development partner is the Housing Authority of the County of San Joaquin (HACSJ). Recorded so the gap is explicit: County General Fund money for multifamily has been rare and discretionary, and the County's 2026 posture is to route capital through the SJCOG Regional Housing Fund (which the County helped capitalize through Measure K) and operating dollars through BHSA, HHAP and PLHA. Mountain House, incorporated in 2024, holds an $8.19 million affordable housing fund from its community services district era (Housing Element), now a city program for Pass 3.

**County-owned and surplus land for affordable housing**
- Agency: San Joaquin County General Services (real property), with Behavioral Health Services and Veterans Services for sponsored projects
- Type: negative finding
- Typical award: No standing County land program. Known actions: (1) Gianone Park remnant, APN 143-110-05, about four undeveloped acres at the north end of the 15.02-acre County parcel at 2885 E. Harding Way, Stockton (appraised September 8, 2023 at $930,000 assuming R-H zoning; currently zoned P-F). The Board declared it exempt surplus on November 12, 2024 (R-24-207) for the sole purpose of affordable housing, with no minimum bid and an as-is sale; the January 14, 2025 bid opening was continued to a date uncertain (B-25-28) after the Board signaled a desire to prioritize park funding, and County Counsel restated that the property was declared surplus for affordable housing. Sale proceeds would go to the Parks Development Fund. A follow-up Surplus Land Act notice of availability (sale or long-term ground lease, offers due January 30, 2026) appears only on procurement aggregators. (2) Victory Gardens, 49 HACSJ units for homeless veterans built on 2.5 acres of County-owned land in French Camp under a County ground lease, completed fall 2022. (3) The French Camp Veterans Village (about 150 tiny homes, WellNest Group with the Veterans Services Office, $38.5 million Homekey+ request authorized July 29, 2025) is not on County land: WellNest secured 16.5 acres near the VA clinic and Homekey+ funds would buy the land.
- AMI requirement: Gianone Park: the Board declared the site surplus solely for affordable housing. Surplus Land Act priority for developers with at least 25% of units at or below 80% AMI (Government Code 54222.5) or deeper restrictions negotiated with the County. Victory Gardens: HUD-VASH and Housing Choice Voucher households.
- Cycle: rolling (next: No open round as of November 10, 2026. The Gianone Park bid opening was continued to a date uncertain on January 14, 2025 and the later notice of availability closed January 30, 2026; no Board award of the site appears on 2025 or 2026 Board agendas. Watch Board agendas (sanjoaquincountyca.iqm2.com) and the HCD surplus land notices map.)
- Layering notes: San Joaquin County has no county housing trust fund, no county housing bond and no inclusionary ordinance; the County's own capital for multifamily is limited to HUD pass-through funds administered by the Human Services Agency Neighborhood Preservation Division (sjchsa.org), while the regional gap lender is the SJCOG-sponsored San Joaquin Regional Housing Fund and the main voucher and development partner is the Housing Authority of the County of San Joaquin (HACSJ). County land is the most likely form of County contribution to a new deal: Victory Gardens combined a County ground lease with VHHP ($6.8 million), tax credits ($19.6 million), County HOME, CESH and CDBG. The Gianone Park site is zoned P-F and would need a rezone; Board members have shown interest in park use of proceeds, so confirm Board direction with General Services before pursuing it.

**Development impact fee deferral for affordable housing (Housing Element program, unincorporated county)**
- Agency: San Joaquin County Community Development Department and Public Works
- Type: fee waiver
- Typical award: Typical planning and development impact fees for a multifamily unit in the unincorporated county were about $20,000 to $20,500 per unit in 2023 (County fees of roughly $9,200 to $9,650 plus County facilities $1,564, regional transportation $2,664, habitat mitigation $1,929, school $4,041 and fire $620). The 2023-2031 Housing Element commits the County to process fee deferrals for projects affordable to lower-income households and to study fee waivers or reductions for affordable projects; no fee waiver fund or standing deferral ordinance was found.
- AMI requirement: Projects affordable to lower-income households as defined in the Housing Element programs; terms set case by case.
- Cycle: rolling (next: No adopted deferral or waiver policy found as of November 8, 2026. Request deferral with the entitlement application. The Housing Element committed the County to evaluate by December 2025 waiving public facilities and County facilities fees for 100 percent affordable projects and to implement within three months if feasible; no Board action implementing it was found.)
- Layering notes: San Joaquin County has no county housing trust fund, no county housing bond and no inclusionary ordinance; the County's own capital for multifamily is limited to HUD pass-through funds administered by the Human Services Agency Neighborhood Preservation Division (sjchsa.org), while the regional gap lender is the SJCOG-sponsored San Joaquin Regional Housing Fund and the main voucher and development partner is the Housing Authority of the County of San Joaquin (HACSJ). Impact fees in the unincorporated county are low compared with Bay Area counties, so deferral is worth less than $20,000 per unit of carry; the larger cost issue is extending water and sewer to sites. Habitat mitigation (SJMSCP) and regional transportation fees are set by other agencies and are not waived by the County. Marked needs_confirmation because the Housing Element (opened) describes the policy as a commitment to study and implement, and no adopted deferral ordinance or fee schedule page was opened this pass; confirm with Community Development.

**HACSJ public housing repositioning and co-development (Delta Community Developers Corp.)**
- Agency: Housing Authority of the County of San Joaquin and Delta Community Developers Corp. (DCDC), its nonprofit instrumentality
- Type: land
- Typical award: HACSJ is repositioning its 910-unit public housing portfolio through RAD, Section 18 and mixed-finance deals and is itself the county's most active supportive housing developer. Pipeline from the FY 2026-27 Annual Plan and development page: Tracy Apartments Phases I and II (55 units each, replacing 17 demolished Tracy Homes units; sources include Health Plan of San Joaquin, HOME, Capital Fund loan, Freddie Mac permanent loan, U.S. Bank, LIHTC); Lodi Commons and Danny Drive (110 senior units each in two phases); Edison House (33 PSH units, Homekey+, Stockton PIP, HHAP); Grant Street Apartments (24 behavioral health units, MHSA, HHAP, ARPA); Sierra Vista Phase III (106 units, Section 18 disposition of 26 units in process, up to 80 approved vacancies); Conway Homes phased redevelopment. Sierra Vista Phase I was co-developed with CCHC, and HACSJ has sought a development partner for Sonora Square.
- AMI requirement: Public housing and PBV income limits with long-term use restrictions under RAD or Section 18 conversion; LIHTC restrictions on mixed-finance phases.

- Layering notes: San Joaquin County has no county housing trust fund, no county housing bond and no inclusionary ordinance; the County's own capital for multifamily is limited to HUD pass-through funds administered by the Human Services Agency Neighborhood Preservation Division (sjchsa.org), while the regional gap lender is the SJCOG-sponsored San Joaquin Regional Housing Fund and the main voucher and development partner is the Housing Authority of the County of San Joaquin (HACSJ). For outside developers HACSJ matters in three ways: as a PBV source, as a co-developer or ground lessor on repositioned public housing sites in Stockton, Tracy and Lodi, and as a competitor for the same County HOME, HHAP, Health Net and Regional Housing Fund dollars (Lodi Commons took $3 million of the $11.85 million Round 1 fund). Davis-Bacon and state prevailing wage apply to mixed-finance public housing work. HACSJ also operates farm labor housing in Lodi, French Camp and Thornton.
