### Sonoma County

**Affordable Housing Program fees (residential in-lieu fee and non-residential Workforce Housing fee)**
- Agency: Permit Sonoma (collection and compliance); fees deposited to the County Fund for Housing administered by the CDC
- Type: regulatory requirement
- Typical award: Residential: every unit in unincorporated Sonoma County must build affordable units or pay an in-lieu fee graduated by size; 2026 schedule $3,108 for units of 1,000 sq ft or less rising roughly $155 per 10 sq ft (about $19,000 at 2,000 sq ft, about $29,000 at 2,750 sq ft), paid before building permit final. Non-residential (Workforce Housing Program) 2026: office, commercial and hotel $3.69 per sq ft; industrial, warehousing and agricultural processing $3.80; retail and services $6.38; first 2,000 sq ft exempt. Both adjust each January 1 by the ENR Bay Area construction cost index.
- AMI requirement: On-site alternative for rental projects: at least 15% of units affordable to low and very low income, or 10% to very low and extremely low income; ownership projects 20% split between low and moderate income. Exemptions include ADUs, farmworker and agricultural employee housing, replacement of fire-destroyed homes within 10 years, and projects complying through other approved means (Code 26-89-045).
- Cycle: rolling (next: Compliance method must be selected with the first permit application; fee schedules reset every January 1 (2027 schedule due January 2027).)
- Layering notes: This is the revenue engine for CFH and the inclusionary rule that mixed-income rental developers in the unincorporated county must satisfy; a 100% affordable LIHTC project satisfies the requirement outright and pays no fee. Developers of market-rate or mixed projects can also meet it by land dedication or restricting existing units. The fee is separate from the traffic and parks impact fees that the Board waived for affordable projects in 2025-2026.
- Source: https://permitsonoma.org/regulationsandlongrangeplans/regulationsandinitiatives/housing/housinginitiatives/residentialprogram
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-06)

**Community Development Block Grant (CDBG), Sonoma Urban County**
- Agency: Sonoma County Community Development Commission (CDC) for the Urban County
- Type: grant
- Typical award: FY 2026-27 estimate: $3,145,583 for affordable housing projects, non-housing capital projects and microenterprise assistance, plus $247,872 for fair housing public services (the FY 2026-27 figure includes reprogrammed prior-year funds; the Consolidated Plan expects about $1.66M annual allocation). FY 2025-26: $1.88M total, with $941,605 to the countywide housing rehabilitation program and the rest to infrastructure and child care.
- AMI requirement: Units for households at or below 80% AMI (51% of units in assisted rental projects); affordable housing projects ready to proceed to construction preferred.
- Cycle: annual NOFA (next: No open round as of November 8, 2026. The FY 2027-28 combined CDC NOFA (CDBG, HOME, ESG, CFH, LMIHAF) has not been posted. Based on the FY 2026-27 schedule, expect a late February 2027 release with an early April 2027 application deadline; the agency has not announced dates.)
- Layering notes: Urban County entitlement area = unincorporated county plus Cloverdale, Cotati, Healdsburg, Rohnert Park, Sebastopol, Sonoma and Windsor; Santa Rosa and Petaluma are separate HUD entitlements (Pass 3). CDC lists affordable housing projects as a CDBG eligible use, but new construction remains limited by federal rules (CBDO carve-out) and most housing CDBG goes to the CDC's rehabilitation program and off-site infrastructure. Davis-Bacon applies at 8 or more units. Useful for site infrastructure or acquisition-rehab tied to a 4% deal.
- Source: https://sonomacounty.gov/notice-of-funding-availability-(nofa)-fiscal-year-(fy)-2026-2027
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-06)

**County Fund for Housing (CFH)**
- Agency: Sonoma County Community Development Commission (CDC)
- Type: loan
- Typical award: FY 2026-27 NOFA: $8,000,000 available (up from $1,500,000 in FY 2025-26 and $1.5M in FY 2024-25). FY 2025-26 awards: Freebird Development, Healdsburg, 42 units, $1,340,417; Burbank Housing, Guerneville, 21 units, $159,583. Minimum loan $100,000; maximum limited to one program year's funds unless the Board commits future years. Since 2003 the fund has invested over $24M in more than 550 homes.
- AMI requirement: Rental: all assisted units affordable 55 years, initially to very low income (50% AMI), may float up to low income (80% AMI) on turnover. Priorities: most units at lowest incomes, geographic distribution across cities and unincorporated area, Housing Opportunity Sites, integration with health and human services, PSH and special needs. Homeownership: first-time buyers at or below 120% AMI with 20% of units at 80% AMI.
- Cycle: annual NOFA (next: No open round as of November 8, 2026. The FY 2027-28 combined CDC NOFA (CDBG, HOME, ESG, CFH, LMIHAF) has not been posted. Based on the FY 2026-27 schedule, expect a late February 2027 release with an early April 2027 application deadline; the agency has not announced dates.)
- Layering notes: Sonoma's main local gap source, capitalized by County General Fund, Reinvestment and Revitalization Funds (former RDA), developer in-lieu fees from the residential Affordable Housing Program, non-residential Workforce Housing fees, countywide transient occupancy tax, and loan repayments. Residual receipts loans structured to be compatible with LIHTC investor requirements; interest set by the Commission. Awarded in one annual NOFA together with HOME, CDBG, ESG and LMIHAF so applicants file once. Funds may go to projects inside cities only where the city has a RHNA Sharing Agreement with the County (shelters and congregate facilities exempt). Sponsors must comply with the County Living Wage Ordinance; the policy is silent on prevailing wage, so the Labor Code 1720(c)(5)(E) below-market-loan exemption may apply unless HOME or CDBG is also used. The County does not act as a conduit bond issuer; recent Sonoma deals used CMFA (Burbank Housing $8.12M) and CalHFA. CFH awards are typically $1M to $3M and are counted as local leverage for CTCAC tiebreaker and CDLAC readiness.
- Source: https://sonomacounty.gov/development-services/community-development-commission/divisions/community-development/funding-opportunities/county-fund-for-housing
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-06)

**HOME Investment Partnerships Program, Sonoma Urban County**
- Agency: Sonoma County Community Development Commission (CDC) for the Urban County
- Type: loan
- Typical award: FY 2026-27 estimate: HOME $743,322 plus CHDO set-aside $99,090 (Consolidated Plan expects about $660,693 per year plus $60,000 program income). FY 2025-26: $495,519 HOME (George's Hideaway, Burbank Housing, $185,519; tenant-based rental assistance $310,000) plus $99,103 CHDO to George's Hideaway.
- AMI requirement: HOME rules: 20% of HOME units at 50% AMI (Low HOME rent), remainder at or below 60% AMI; affordability period 5 to 20 years by subsidy, CDC loan policies extend to 55 years. Ready-to-proceed projects preferred.
- Cycle: annual NOFA (next: No open round as of November 8, 2026. The FY 2027-28 combined CDC NOFA (CDBG, HOME, ESG, CFH, LMIHAF) has not been posted. Based on the FY 2026-27 schedule, expect a late February 2027 release with an early April 2027 application deadline; the agency has not announced dates. NEPA review, Section 3 and Build America Buy America compliance required before agreement.)
- Layering notes: Urban County entitlement area = unincorporated county plus Cloverdale, Cotati, Healdsburg, Rohnert Park, Sebastopol, Sonoma and Windsor; Santa Rosa and Petaluma are separate HUD entitlements (Pass 3). Small allocation (well under $1M a year), so HOME is usually a minor layer on one project per year alongside CFH and PLHA. Davis-Bacon applies at 12 or more HOME-assisted units. The County routinely uses HOME for TBRA, leaving even less for development. Programs are awarded in the single CDC NOFA with CFH and CDBG.
- Source: https://sonomacounty.gov/notice-of-funding-availability-(nofa)-fiscal-year-(fy)-2026-2027
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-06)

**Low and Moderate Income Housing Asset Fund (LMIHAF), Sonoma County Housing Successor**
- Agency: Sonoma County Community Development Commission as housing successor to the former County redevelopment agency
- Type: grant
- Typical award: Services: up to $250,000 per year for homeless prevention and rapid rehousing (FY 2025-26 and FY 2026-27 CDC NOFAs). Development: LMIHAF housing development spending was $3,837,187 in FY 2024-25 and $1,316,702 in FY 2023-24; the annual reports do not break this out by project or award size. Balance available for all other uses $2,509,338 at June 30, 2025 (down from $7,248,573 at June 30, 2024), of which $1,509,338 is excess surplus; loans and grants receivable $31,242,980.
- AMI requirement: Community Redevelopment Law housing provisions as applied by HSC 34176.1 (very low and low income). For development spending, at least 30 percent must go to rental housing for households at or below 30% AMI (FY 2024-25 report, Note 9); the report states Casa Roseland, under construction, has 32 percent of units at or below 30% AMI. Current NOFA awards are homeless services.
- Cycle: annual NOFA (next: No open round as of November 8, 2026. LMIHAF is offered only for homeless prevention and rapid rehousing services in the combined CDC NOFA; the FY 2027-28 NOFA has not been posted (expected about late February 2027 based on the prior cycle). No capital round is offered.)
- Layering notes: The Sonoma County Community Development Commission, parent entity of the Sonoma County Housing Authority, is the housing successor. The fund pays for services through the annual CDC NOFA and also finances development directly: $3,837,187 of housing development spending in FY 2024-25 and $1,316,702 in FY 2023-24. The FY 2024-25 report lists Roseland Village (665 Sebastopol Road, Santa Rosa, a former RDA property) and Casa Roseland as under construction but does not tie the development spending to a named project. Its plan for the $1,509,338 excess surplus (held more than 6 years) is reinvestment in affordable homeownership loans and/or new construction or preservation of affordable rental developments, so capital money is possible but is not offered through a posted competitive round. Former RDA Reinvestment and Revitalization money flows into CFH instead. Loan repayments ($31.2M receivable) replenish the fund. The FY 2025-26 report was not posted as of November 10, 2026.
- Source: https://sonomacounty.gov/Main%20County%20Site/Development%20Services/CDC/Documents/Successor%20Agency/Housing%20Successor%20Agency%20Annual%20Reports/Remediated_FY%2024-25%20Housing%20Successor%20Agency%20Annual%20Report.pdf
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-06)

**Measure O Behavioral Health and Homelessness sales tax, housing category**
- Agency: Sonoma County Department of Health Services
- Type: grant
- Typical award: Quarter-cent countywide sales tax (approved 2020, 10-year term) generating about $30M to $33M a year across five categories, one of which is Transitional and Permanent Supportive Housing. Pathways to Sustainability NOFA (released Aug 14, 2025) awarded $10M in Measure O plus $2.4M HHAP to 26 projects on Feb 10, 2026; PSH awards went to Committee on the Shelterless ($392,034 Measure O and $196,017 HHAP) alongside city, shelter and services grants.
- AMI requirement: Transitional and permanent supportive housing for people with behavioral health conditions experiencing homelessness; awards to date are predominantly operating and services, not capital.
- Cycle: annual NOFA (next: 2025-26 round awarded Feb 10, 2026. The County says it hopes applicants 'continue to submit proposals for future projects' but has not announced a 2026-27 NOFA; the February 2026 release noted doubts about future funding levels. Measure sunsets around 2030-2031.)
- Layering notes: Best viewed as an operating and services subsidy for PSH units rather than a capital source; pair with HCD Homekey+, MHP supportive units and PBVs. Sonoma's BHSA (Prop 1) housing interventions requirement (30% of BHSA funds, half for chronically homeless) begins July 2026 and is administered by the same department; no BHSA capital NOFA was found. County funds are public funds for prevailing wage purposes if used for construction.

**Multi-Family Development Fee Deferral Program**
- Agency: Permit Sonoma
- Type: fee waiver
- Typical award: Deferral of County development fees (traffic impact and parkland dedication fees; not school, water agency or sanitation district fees) from building permit final until permanent financing closes, under a recorded Fee Deferral Agreement.
- AMI requirement: Affordable rental or ownership housing for low- or very low-income households, or special needs housing (elderly or disabled) with at least 20% of units for low-income households.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Rolling; request by letter with the permit application. Approval requires a Director finding that the fees are not needed for near-term programmed improvements; agreement signed before building or grading permit.)
- Layering notes: Bridges construction-period cash flow so impact fees are paid from permanent sources at conversion, a common pairing with CalHFA or bond-financed 4% deals. Deferral terms (interest, security) are not published; a deferred fee charged at less than market terms may be treated as public funds under Labor Code 1720(b)(4). Separate single-family ADU affordable-fee deferral exists for restricted ADUs.

**Permanent Local Housing Allocation (PLHA), County of Sonoma**
- Agency: Sonoma County Community Development Commission (CDC) for the County of Sonoma
- Type: loan
- Typical award: FY 2025-26 distribution $979,795 (Burbank Housing Guerneville 21 units $555,795; Habitat for Humanity Sebastopol 4 ownership units $424,000). Separate NOFAs: Sept 10, 2025 for rental or ownership projects (due Oct 30, 2025); Sept 17, 2026 for affordable owner-occupied workforce housing only, $674,360 over the counter. Residual receipts loans.

Geography excludes the City of Santa Rosa and City of Petaluma, which receive their own PLHA.)

Mandatory technical assistance workshop before applying. Nonprofit and government applicants only. Below-market residual receipts loan, so the Labor Code 1720(c)(5)(E) prevailing wage exemption may apply absent other public funds that carry their own requirement.

**Project-Based Vouchers for Permanent Supportive Housing, Sonoma County Housing Authority**
- Agency: Sonoma County Housing Authority (division of the CDC); jurisdiction is all of Sonoma County except the City of Santa Rosa
- Type: rental assistance
- Typical award: 2025 PSH RFP: up to 100 project-based vouchers for studio, one- and two-bedroom PSH units in new construction or substantial rehab; applications were due June 24, 2025; 20-year HAP contract with automatic 20-year renewal; one-time $500 per voucher administrative fee plus billed-back environmental and legal review. Board of Commissioners committed 150 future PBVs to PSH (Nov 20, 2024) to support Homekey+ applicants. The authority administers about 2,988 vouchers and roughly $45M a year.
- AMI requirement: PSH for chronically homeless households referred through the Sonoma County Coordinated Entry System under its PSH prioritization policy; HCV income limits.
- Cycle: annual NOFA (next: No open round as of November 8, 2026. No new PBV RFP is posted on the CDC Doing Business page; the Housing Authority has not announced timing for an RFP for the 150 vouchers committed to PSH.)
- Layering notes: PBV HAP revenue is the operating subsidy that makes Homekey+, MHP supportive units and CFH-funded PSH underwritable in Sonoma; the 150-voucher commitment was adopted specifically to strengthen Homekey+ applications. Santa Rosa projects must use the Santa Rosa Housing Authority (Pass 3). Prior RFPs: 2018 and 2023 general rounds (up to 100 vouchers, $1,000 fee), 2022 existing-housing round (110 vouchers to 8 projects).
- Source: https://sonomacounty.gov/Main%20County%20Site/Development%20Services/CDC/Documents/2025%20RFP%20for%20PSH%20PBV.pdf
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-06)

**RED Housing Fund (Renewal Enterprise District, PG&E wildfire settlement capital)**
- Agency: RED Housing Fund, a nonprofit capitalized with $10M each from the County of Sonoma and the City of Santa Rosa (PG&E 2017 fire settlement), affiliated with the Renewal Enterprise District JPA
- Type: loan
- Typical award: Round 2 (NOFA issued March 4, 2026, due April 1, 2026): up to $5,000,000 in loans. Loan size up to 10% of project cost. Affordable projects: subordinate or senior loan at 3% interest, interest only during construction and up to 36 months after conversion, then amortizing, up to 18-year combined term, sized at minimum 1.05 combined DSC. Market rate or middle income: construction loan at senior rate plus 1% (4% floor), up to 3 years; permanent loan at first-position rate plus 1% (4% floor), up to 10 years. 1% origination fee ($10,000 minimum); commitments expire 18 months after Board approval. Round 1 (December 21, 2021 NOFA) awards: Acme Family Apartments $800,000, Aviara $2,400,000, Casa Roseland $4,200,000, 420 Mendocino Avenue $7,000,000, Pullman Lofts $2,300,000 (reduced to $1,300,000), South Park Commons $4,000,000.
- AMI requirement: Infill, mid- to high-density residential or mixed-use projects in transit-rich or planned areas meeting RED criteria; income mix may be affordable (up to 80% AMI), middle income (80% to 120% AMI), market rate, or mixed.
- Cycle: annual NOFA (next: No open round as of November 8, 2026. The NOFA page still shows the 2026 round; no future round has been announced. Email apply@redhousingfund.org for an upload link when a NOFA is open.)
- Layering notes: Lender of last resort (recycling repaid settlement capital) for projects the County and Santa Rosa want built in downtown Santa Rosa and other priority development areas; it accepts market-rate and middle-income deals that cannot use CFH or LIHTC. Capital is public settlement money, so prevailing wage exposure depends on loan terms. The separate private Sonoma County Housing Fund ($10M, Housing Trust Silicon Valley with the Santa Rosa Metro Chamber, predevelopment and acquisition loans up to five years) belongs in Pass 4.
- Source: https://redhousingfund.org/notice-of-funding-availability/
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-06)

**Sonoma County Density Bonus Program (Code Chapter 26, Sections 26-89-050 and 26-89-060)**
- Agency: Permit Sonoma
- Type: density bonus
- Typical award: State Density Bonus Law (Gov. Code 65915 to 65917) applied directly: the County acknowledges its Chapter 26 provisions are out of date and states it will comply with current state law until Housing Element Program 15 amendments are adopted (adding lower-income student housing, 100% affordable bonuses, and updated bonus and incentive calculations). Affordable Housing Incentives under Section 26-89-060 also available to projects building inclusionary units on site.
- AMI requirement: State thresholds (5% very low, 10% low, 10% moderate for-sale, 100% affordable, senior, special populations); county inclusionary units may be counted toward the bonus.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Rolling with the entitlement application; code update timing not published (Housing Element 2023-2031 Program 15). Contact Permit Sonoma Housing at (707) 565-1391.)
- Layering notes: Because the local code lags the statute, rely on Gov. Code 65915 as amended (up to 80% bonus and unlimited waivers for 100% affordable projects, 3-story height bonus near major transit, reduced parking) and expect staff to process requests case by case. Pair with the inclusionary on-site option so the same units earn the bonus and satisfy the Affordable Housing Program with no in-lieu fee. Permit Sonoma also maintains Streamlined Housing Developments (SB 35 and AB 2011 style) and Rezoning Sites for Housing pages for by-right sites.
- Source: https://permitsonoma.org/regulationsandlongrangeplans/regulationsandinitiatives/housing/housinginitiatives/densitybonusprogram
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-06)

**Sonoma County Homeless Coalition (CoC CA-504) funding: HUD CoC competition and Homeless Services Consolidated NOFA (HHAP, ESG, HHIP)**
- Agency: Sonoma County Department of Health Services, Homelessness Services Division, as CoC collaborative applicant
- Type: rental assistance
- Typical award: 2026 HUD CoC competition: about $4.9M in renewal funding; HUD had not announced CoC Bonus or DV Bonus amounts; local applications due July 21, 2026. Annual Homeless Services Consolidated NOFA (state ESG, one-time HHAP, DHCS HHIP and local sources): about $5.5M expected in the 2025-26 cycle (applications due Feb 7, 2025). HHAP rounds 1 to 5 brought $32.2M to the Sonoma area; HHAP Round 5 allowed one CoC Builds PSH construction project.
- AMI requirement: Homeless households via Coordinated Entry; CoC PSH rental assistance and services; HHAP permits permanent housing capital as an eligible use.
- Cycle: annual NOFA (next: No open round as of November 8, 2026. The FY 2026 CoC collaborative application and final priority listing have been submitted; the FY 2027 HUD CoC competition and the next Homeless Services Consolidated NOFA are not yet announced (the prior Consolidated NOFA cycle had a February deadline).)
- Layering notes: Operating-side partner for PSH: CoC rental assistance or HHAP operating subsidy can replace or supplement PBVs on supportive units. HHAP capital for permanent housing is allowed but Sonoma has directed most HHAP to shelter, outreach and rehousing. Developers should engage the Homelessness Services Division early so a PSH project appears in the CoC's regional action plan and Coordinated Entry referral agreements.
- Source: https://sonomacounty.gov/2026-notice-of-funding-opportunity-coc-program-competition-and-sonoma-county-coc-request-for-proposals-(rfp)
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-06)

**Traffic and Parks Impact Fee Waiver for Affordable Housing (2025-2026)**
- Agency: Sonoma County Board of Supervisors; administered through Permit Sonoma
- Type: fee waiver
- Typical award: Waiver of County traffic mitigation and parks impact fees for affordable projects in the unincorporated area that received building permits from Feb 1, 2025 through Dec 31, 2026; staff estimated up to $19.5M in fees waived across 15 eligible projects (over 1,900 affordable units) with a $1.5M General Fund backfill.
- AMI requirement: Units reserved for moderate-, low- and very low-income renters or buyers; recorded deed restriction of at least 55 years for rental and 45 years for ownership units. Minimum affordable percentage not stated in the County release; confirm with Permit Sonoma.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Expires Dec 31, 2026 unless extended; the County is studying its fee structure and may adopt a permanent program. Permits must be issued before the sunset.)
- Layering notes: Worth several thousand dollars per unit in the unincorporated county and reduces basis for the CTCAC cost containment score. Labor Code 1720(b)(4) counts fees waived or forgiven by a public agency as public funds, so a waiver can itself trigger state prevailing wage unless the project is otherwise exempt; most LIHTC projects taking HCD money already pay prevailing wage. Does not cover the affordable housing in-lieu fee, school, water agency or sanitation district fees. Multi-family fee deferral (separate record) remains available after the waiver sunsets.
- Source: https://sonomacounty.gov/sonoma-county-board-of-supervisors-reduces-fees-for-affordable-housing-projects
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-06)

**Welfare Exemption processing, Sonoma County Assessor**
- Agency: Sonoma County Clerk-Recorder-Assessor, Exemption Unit
- Type: tax abatement
- Typical award: Exemption of the qualifying low-income share of assessed value from the roughly 1.1% to 1.2% property tax rate plus voter-approved debt in Sonoma County.
- AMI requirement: Per state law: nonprofit or eligible LLC owner, or limited partnership with a qualifying managing general partner holding an Organizational Clearance Certificate; recorded regulatory agreement or deed restriction; tax savings must maintain affordability or reduce rents; plus government financing, LIHTC, or at least 90% lower-income occupancy.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Annual claims Jan 1 to Feb 15 (next Feb 15, 2027). First filing on newly acquired property due within 90 days after the first day of the month following acquisition or by Feb 15 of the following year, whichever is first; property must be in exempt use or under construction within 180 days of acquisition. File BOE-267 with the OCC, regulatory agreement and the low-income supplemental affidavit. Exemption Unit (707) 565-1881, assessor@sonomacounty.gov.)
- Layering notes: Standard statewide rules (see Pass 1 BOE record). Sonoma's assessor page is unusually explicit about the 180-day use requirement and first-filing deadline, which matters for construction-period exemptions on land acquired mid-year. No county property tax abatement JPA exists.
- Source: https://sonomacounty.gov/administrative-support-and-fiscal-services/clerk-recorder-assessor/assessor/real-property/tax-savings-(exemptions-prop-19-and-more)/exemptions/welfare-exemption
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-06)


### Ventura County

**Behavioral Health Services Act Integrated Plan FY 2026-29 (Housing Interventions component)**
- Agency: Ventura County Health Care Agency, Behavioral Health Department
- Type: grant
- Typical award: DHCS-approved BHSA Integrated Plan FY 2026-29 (May 2026) funds Housing Interventions: rental subsidies (706 people per year, 620 units, project-based and tenant-based), operating subsidies for PSH and interim settings (355 units per year), landlord mitigation and participant assistance funds, and capital development (up to 25% of Housing Interventions). Named capital projects with BHSA cost per unit: Santa Paula Motel Project (20 BHSA units of 21, $150,712 per unit, leasing 2028), Santa Clara Apartments (10 BHSA units, $213,538 per unit, leasing summer 2029), Fillmore Terrace (4 BHSA units, $200,000 per unit, leasing early 2029). Annual dollar totals are in a separate budget template not posted as an accessible file.
- AMI requirement: BHSA-eligible adults and youth with serious mental illness or substance use disorder, including chronically homeless individuals; referrals through Coordinated Entry and HMIS.
- Cycle: rolling (next: No open capital solicitation as of November 8, 2026; the Plan states VCBH will work with County Community Development to issue a NOFA to identify developers serving the BHSA population.)
- Layering notes: BHSA classified as grant because the Integrated Plan funds housing capital development, operating subsidies and rental subsidies for PSH. Capital projects braid BHSA with LIHTC, NPLH, HHAP and other sources. The Plan says VCBH is not participating in a Flex Pool at this time, so the earlier note about RFP 226001 for a Flexible Housing Subsidy Pool operator was not confirmed. Behavioral Health Bridge Housing capacity will be partly sustained with BHSA funds. Ventura County housing funding otherwise runs through CEO Community Development (CDBG, HOME Consortium, PLHA), the Area Housing Authority and the Housing Trust Fund Ventura County.

**CDBG and HOME, Ventura Urban County Entitlement Area and Ventura County HOME Consortium (FY 2026-27 Annual Action Plan)**
- Agency: Ventura County Executive Office, Community Development
- Type: grant

HOME development award: Many Mansions Mountain View II, Fillmore (49 units, five HOME-assisted) $1,092,580 including the CHDO set-aside; CDBG $120,000 to My Way Home for homebuyer assistance, $100,000 homeowner rehabilitation, up to $337,500 rental rehabilitation (10 units), $1,130,963 public facilities. HOME is a $1 million soft loan on a CHDO or tax credit deal, usually paired with County PLHA, General Fund NOFA money and an HTFVC loan. Davis-Bacon applies at 12 or more HOME units. ### Yolo County

**Behavioral Health Services Act (BHSA) housing interventions and capital set-aside, Yolo County HHSA Behavioral Health**
- Agency: Yolo County Health and Human Services Agency, Behavioral Health (Director Tony Kildare); Integrated Plan FY 2026-2029 approved by the Board of Supervisors June 23, 2026
- Type: grant
- Typical award: Projected BHSA funding $19.4 million in FY 2026-27 with Housing Interventions at 30% ($5,834,453); the Board's March 3, 2026 budget approach (Scenario 3) transfers 7% of housing interventions to Behavioral Health Services and Supports, leaving about $4.4 million for housing in FY 2026-27. The adopted plan commits to a procurement to allocate 25% of Housing Interventions funds (roughly $1.1 to $1.5 million a year) to capital development: property acquisition, new construction, and rehabilitation or renovation of existing units. Remaining funds pay rental subsidies after Transitional Rent ends, landlord damage mitigation, participant assistance and a new Housing Interventions Team. The Board also added 8 behavioral health case managers ($1 million a year) for permanent supportive housing sites.
- AMI requirement: Medi-Cal eligible adults with serious mental illness or substance use disorder who are chronically homeless, homeless or at risk; at least half of housing funds for chronically homeless people. BHSA housing interventions are available only after CalAIM Community Supports and the six-month Medi-Cal Transitional Rent benefit (provider Turning Point Community Programs) are exhausted.
- Cycle: rolling (next: The capital procurement (25% of housing interventions) has not been released as of November 6, 2026; the plan says it will be conducted during FY 2026-27. Behavioral Health Bridge Housing funding expires June 30, 2027, after which BHSA absorbs those costs. Annual plan updates begin FY 2027-28 (draft due to DHCS March 31).)
- Layering notes: Yolo is one of the few small counties committing the full 25% capital share, but at about $1.1 to $1.5 million a year it buys a handful of units: realistic uses are acquisition of small existing properties, a capital contribution to a PSH project with a BHSA referral agreement, or rehab of existing supportive housing (the Board asked staff whether capital can go to existing facility needs). Pair with YCH PBVs and the County's PSH case management staffing (8 FTE) to make a small PSH deal pencil. BHSA capital is public funds under Labor Code 1720(b) but carries no wage rule of its own; coverage turns on the 1720(c) exemptions and project facts (see prevailing_wage_basis). Behavioral Health is also the County's lead on Homekey+ interest and on the Encampment Resolution Fund application.

- Agency: Yolo County Health and Human Services Agency (County HHAP administrative entity and HPAC staff; HMIS lead) with the Homeless and Poverty Action Coalition (CoC board) and the City of Davis
- Type: grant
- Typical award: HHAP Round 6 allocations (HCD, based on the 2024 count): Yolo County $1,074,906.92 and the Davis, Woodland/Yolo County CoC $1,148,019.07. HHAP Round 7 preliminary allocations (FY 2026-27, disbursed as third and fourth disbursements of HHAP 6 under the NOFA amended August 7, 2026): Yolo County $1,231,712.43 and the Davis, Woodland/Yolo County CoC $1,319,691.89. HHAP rounds 1 to 5 brought $8.1 million to the Yolo area, $3.9 million of it to the County ($2.6 million spent). Round 5 County subawards approved March 3, 2026 include $135,000 to the City of West Sacramento for interim housing operating subsidies and $15,000 for rapid rehousing, both through February 2028. 2024 point-in-time count: 942 people, 633 unsheltered, 983 year-round beds.

HCD's HHAP application window is closed; HHAP 7 is a formula allocation to existing HHAP 6 grantees (County and CoC), not a competitive developer NOFA. For a PSH project the value is Coordinated Entry referrals through HPAC, possible HHAP or CoC operating subsidies for a handful of units, and the County's Behavioral Health Bridge Housing and Transitional Rent pipeline for tenants. **Development fee incentives for affordable units: 50% application and processing fee waiver (Sec. 8-8.118) and Housing Density Bonus (Chapter 8-12), unincorporated Yolo County**
- Agency: Yolo County Community Services Department, Planning Division; fee waivers subject to Board of Supervisors approval
- Type: fee waiver
- Typical award: Section 8-8.118(a) allows a fifty percent waiver of development-related application and processing fees for affordable units, subject to Board approval, plus modified standards for road widths, parking, lot coverage and lot size, priority processing and a density bonus. Chapter 8-12 (Ordinance 1445, August 14, 2014) codifies state density bonus law as of 2014: 20% base bonus for 10% low or 5% very low income units, rising to a 35% maximum, one to three concessions, parking caps of 1 space (studio and 1 bedroom), 2 spaces (2 to 3 bedrooms) and 2.5 spaces (4 or more bedrooms). No impact fee waiver program exists; County development impact fees are not waived for affordable housing.
- AMI requirement: Fee waiver applies to the affordable units in an inclusionary or 100% affordable project. Density bonus tiers per Government Code 65915 (the County code's 35% cap is superseded by current state law allowing 50% and unlimited density for 100% affordable projects).
- Cycle: rolling (next: Request with the planning application; the fee waiver needs a Board action. Chapter 8-12 has not been updated since 2014 and state law controls where more generous.)
- Layering notes: The waiver covers planning application and processing fees only, not the County's development impact fees, school fees or the cities' fees, so the dollar value is modest (tens of thousands on a typical project). Waived fees are public funds under Labor Code 1720(b)(4), which is why the prevailing wage flag is unclear; most projects using the waiver also carry state funds that trigger it anyway. Use state density bonus law directly rather than the 2014 County chapter, and expect staff to process it under Government Code 65915 as amended.
- Source: https://gocodebook.com/library/us/ca/yolo-county/title-8-land-development-and-zoning/chapter-12-housing-density-bonuses
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-06)

**Inclusionary Housing Ordinance (County Code Chapter 8-8), in-lieu fee and the Affordable Housing Program account, unincorporated Yolo County**
- Agency: Yolo County Community Services Department, Planning Division (ordinance and affordable housing agreements); in-lieu fees held by the County in the Affordable Housing Program account
- Type: regulatory requirement
- Typical award: Regulatory requirement, not a funding source. Ordinance 1451 (effective January 1, 2015) requires on-site affordable units: for-sale projects of 10 or more units set aside 20% (half low income, half moderate income); rental projects of 20 or more units set aside 25% very low income plus 10% low income; rental projects of 7 to 19 units set aside 15% very low plus 10% low. Smaller projects (9 or fewer single-family, 7 or fewer multifamily) pay an in-lieu fee assessed on a unit percentage basis. The in-lieu fee equals a percentage of the estimated cost to construct the required units, is set in the County Master Fee Schedule (last adopted June 24, 2025) and may be reduced up to 50% based on available subsidy; the current per-unit amount was not published in the opened documents (the 2009 schedule was $12,920 for-sale and $17,610 rental per required unit).
- AMI requirement: Rental inclusionary units must be permanently affordable (Sec. 8-8.108(b)); for-sale units carry a 20-year covenant that resets at each resale to a qualified buyer. Alternatives, only if on-site is shown infeasible: off-site units in the unincorporated county, land dedication (2 acres minimum), in-lieu fee, or housing credits transferable within 3 miles and 5 years. Density bonus units do not generate an inclusionary obligation.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Applies at discretionary approval; fee estimate given at approval and paid before final map, first building permit or certificate of occupancy. In-lieu fees must be spent or encumbered within five years of receipt unless the Board extends.)
- Layering notes: The Affordable Housing Program account (Sec. 8-8.116) is the County's only local housing fund and it is fed solely by in-lieu fees from small unincorporated projects, so expect a balance in the low hundreds of thousands at most; no NOFA or award from it was found. For a 100% affordable project the ordinance imposes no obligation and offers the incentives in Sec. 8-8.118 (fee waiver, standards modifications, streamlining, density bonus). For a mixed-income rental project of 20 or more units the 35% combined set-aside (25% very low plus 10% low) is one of the steepest in the region and is a real feasibility constraint in Esparto, Madison and Dunnigan; the ordinance predates current state density bonus law and the Latinos Unidos v. Napa decision, so confirm how the County applies it today. Davis, Woodland and West Sacramento have their own inclusionary programs (Davis in-lieu fee about $215,000 per unit) covered in Pass 3.
- Source: https://www.zoneomics.com/code/yolo-county-unincorporated-CA/chapter_8
- Confidence: needs_confirmation (researched 2026-11-06)

**Project-Based Vouchers and HUD-VASH PBVs, Yolo County Housing (YCH)**
- Agency: Yolo County Housing (Housing Authority of the County of Yolo, CA044), 147 West Main Street, Woodland; (530) 662-5428; Executive Director Ian Evans; Housing Program Manager Anisa Vallejo
- Type: rental assistance
- Typical award: YCH leases about 1,500 to 1,600 Housing Choice Vouchers countywide and owns 431 public housing units. It awarded 155 PBVs over the three years to January 2026 (84 to new construction) through RFPs, most recently a December 2023 pair of RFPs (existing housing, and new construction or rehabilitation) offering up to 40 PBVs with up to 3 HUD-VASH vouchers. The FY 2026 Agency Plan commits to allocating additional PBVs to new and existing projects until YCH reaches HUD's PBV cap (about 30% of vouchers) by the end of 2029, and to project-basing about 36 tenant protection vouchers from a 2026 Section 18 disposition at its Tupelo development in Woodland.
- AMI requirement: Very low and extremely low income households (at or below 50% AMI); PBV HAP contracts up to 20 years with extensions. The PBV waiting list has been closed since February 2023 and the HCV program has had intermittent voucher shortfalls since 2023 while Emergency Housing Voucher households are moved onto HCV.
- Cycle: annual NOFA (next: No open round as of November 8, 2026. YCH's Doing Business page lists only RFP P26-011 (landscape maintenance) and IFB B26-04 (exterior painting), no PBV RFP. YCH issues PBV RFPs as voucher budget allows and its FY 2026 Agency Plan targets reaching the 30% PBV cap by Q4 2029; contact Anisa Vallejo (avallejo@ych.ca.gov) to be notified.)
- Layering notes: PBVs are the one countywide operating subsidy for PSH in Yolo and YCH is unusually willing to project-base (goal of reaching the HUD cap by 2029), but federal HCV funding shortfalls since 2023 limit new awards; the County's BHSA plan calls voucher capacity 'extremely limited.' Nine or more PBV units in a project trigger Davis-Bacon under HUD rules; PBVs alone do not trigger state prevailing wage. Coordinated Entry through the Homeless and Poverty Action Coalition (HPAC, CoC CA-521) supplies referrals for homeless set-aside units. YCH is also converting or disposing of public housing (Vista Montecito, Yolito, Ridgecut in 2026; Yolano Village and Donnelly Circle in 2027 or later), which will generate more PBVs tied to its own redevelopment.

**State CDBG and HOME (non-entitlement county) and County housing programs, Yolo County Administrator's Office**
- Agency: Yolo County Administrator's Office (Mark Bryan, housing programs; housingprograms@yolocounty.gov) with grant administration contracted to Thurmond Consulting LLC through November 30, 2026; Yolo County Housing formerly administered the County CDBG program
- Type: loan
- Typical award: Small. Yolo County is a non-entitlement jurisdiction and applies to HCD's state CDBG and HOME competitions. The Board held the required housing public hearing on March 24, 2026 and authorized a $300,000 application for the 2025 state CDBG funding year (Resolution 26-34). Current CDBG use is an owner-occupied housing rehabilitation program with loans up to $100,000 for low and moderate income homeowners in the unincorporated area. Earlier HOME and CDBG awards funded first-time homebuyer assistance. No County loan to a multifamily development was found.
- AMI requirement: CDBG at or below 80% AMI (low and moderate income benefit) in the unincorporated area only (not Davis, Woodland, West Sacramento or Winters). HOME at or below 80% AMI with HCD's affordability covenants.
- Cycle: annual NOFA (next: No open round as of November 8, 2026. HCD's 2025 state CDBG NOFA portal closed April 3, 2026 and the next CDBG NOFA has not been posted; HCD's HOME Program Activities draft guidelines finished public comment September 9, 2026 with no new HOME NOFA open. A developer wanting the County as applicant or co-applicant should contact the County Administrator's Office before the next HCD NOFA opens.)
- Layering notes: Yolo County has no county gap loan program for rental housing and no development NOFA. Its state CDBG and HOME capacity is small and committed to homeowner rehab and homebuyer programs, and the County issued an RFP in September 2026 for housing program consulting (loan management, grant writing) to run these programs. The practical County role for a developer is the resolution or co-applicant for state programs (HOME rental, Joe Serna farmworker housing, MHP) in the unincorporated communities (Esparto, Madison, Knights Landing, Dunnigan, Clarksburg). The Board created a Farmworker Housing Ad Hoc Subcommittee in May 2025 and the March 2026 Board calendar listed hearings on a farmworker housing planning grant application. The three cities (Davis, Woodland, West Sacramento) run their own programs and are Pass 3. HOME and CDBG carry Davis-Bacon at their unit thresholds and federal cross-cutting rules; state prevailing wage turns on state or local funds and the Labor Code 1720(c) exemptions (see prevailing_wage_basis).
- Source: https://public.destinyhosted.com/yolocdocs/2026/BOS/20260324_3929/16187_Template_CDBG_meeting_presentation___SPANISH_DRAFT.pdf
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-06)

**Tax-exempt multifamily bonds: no County or YCH conduit program; CMFA and CSCDA issuances with local TEFRA approval**
- Agency: Issuers California Municipal Finance Authority and California Statewide Communities Development Authority; TEFRA approval by the host city council or, in the unincorporated area, the Yolo County Board of Supervisors
- Type: bond
- Typical award: Project-sized conduit issuances. Example: CMFA issued $6,668,698 of tax-exempt financing for Esperanza Crossing Apartments (Mercy Housing, a 40-unit new construction project on Woodland Avenue in Yolo County, 39 units restricted at or below 55% AMI for 55 years). No County of Yolo or Yolo County Housing bond issuance and no County TEFRA resolution appeared in the 2026 Board minutes reviewed in Pass 2 (January 27, March 3 and March 24, 2026).
- AMI requirement: Federal bond and 4% LIHTC rules: at least 20% of units at 50% AMI or 40% at 60% AMI (or income averaging), 55-year CDLAC regulatory agreement.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Request the TEFRA hearing through the issuer; allow six to eight weeks before the CDLAC application. For unincorporated sites the hearing goes on a Board of Supervisors consent agenda; for Davis, Woodland and West Sacramento sites the city council holds it (Pass 3).)
- Layering notes: Neither the County nor YCH runs a bond program, so budget issuer fees for CMFA or CSCDA. Bonds alone do not trigger state prevailing wage, but tax credits plus state or County funds in the same deal usually do. The County's TEFRA practice in the unincorporated area could not be confirmed from opened documents because no recent unincorporated bond-financed project was found.
- Source: https://www.cmfa-ca.com/mercy-housing-preserves-affordable-housing-using-tax-exempt-financing-issued-cmfa/
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-06)

**Welfare Exemption (property tax), Yolo County Assessor**
- Agency: Yolo County Assessor/Clerk-Recorder/Elections (ACE), Jesse Salinas, 625 Court Street, Woodland, CA 95695; (530) 666-8135; ace.yolocounty.gov; with the State Board of Equalization (Organizational Clearance Certificate)
- Type: tax abatement
- Typical award: Exemption of property taxes on units restricted to lower income households under Revenue and Taxation Code 214(g): full exemption for qualifying units in LIHTC or publicly financed projects and partial exemption for the qualifying share in mixed projects. In Yolo County the 1% base rate plus voter-approved debt applies to the exempt value.
- AMI requirement: Nonprofit owner or limited partnership with a nonprofit managing general partner holding a BOE Organizational Clearance Certificate; recorded regulatory agreement (tax credits, bonds, HOME, PLHA, housing authority or County agreement) restricting rents to lower income households; BOE-267-L2 tenant data where there is no government financing or tax credits.
- Cycle: rolling (next: File BOE-267 (first year) or BOE-267-A (annual) with the Assessor by February 15 each year (next: February 15, 2027) with BOE-267-L, L1, L2 and worksheets as applicable. Late claims: 90% of tax canceled if filed by January 1 of the next calendar year, 85% after (BOE Publication 149). The Yolo ACE website does not post exemption instructions; call the Assessor's office.)
- Layering notes: Standard underwriting item. Yolo County Housing is actively using the exemption as a financing tool: its FY 2026 plan commits to working with private investors to build affordable workforce housing 'utilizing the benefits of the welfare exemption,' and the December 2025 KIND West Sacramento deal deed-restricted 30 units for moderate income households with a YCH operating loan structured to meet exemption requirements. Check carefully that moderate income (above 80% AMI) units qualify only within the AB 84 over-income allowance; the core exemption is for lower income units.
- Source: https://www.boe.ca.gov/proptaxes/pdf/pub149.pdf
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-06)

**Yolo County Housing and New Hope CDC development partnerships, surplus land and farmworker housing sites**
- Agency: Yolo County Housing (YCH) with its nonprofit affiliate New Hope Community Development Corporation; Executive Director Ian Evans, ievans@ych.ca.gov, (530) 669-2219
- Type: land
- Typical award: YCH acts as co-developer, land owner and partner rather than lender. Current pipeline: Tupelo, 73 units in Woodland (one to three bedrooms, 30% to 60% AMI) with a $27,999,100 AHSC award announced December 10, 2025 (City of Woodland $1.5 million loan commitment, Sutter Health $1.5 million, Brinshore Development and Operative Office as partners, construction as early as 2027, about 36 project-based TPVs); 641 5th Street, West Sacramento, 37 units (New Hope CDC, groundbreaking planned 2026, completion target 2027); Yolano and Donnelly redevelopment in Woodland (HUD Choice Neighborhoods Planning Grant, September 2024, over 240 mixed-income units planned, three phases by 2029); El Rio Villa Phase I by 2029. YCH posted a Surplus Land Act Notice of Availability for its Dunnigan property on September 10, 2026 (60-day response window, priority to proposals with at least 25% affordable units) and is seeking developers for its vacant Esparto lots for farmworker homeownership by 2027. In December 2025 YCH partnered with Fulcrum Property and Pacific Housing to deed-restrict 30 existing West Sacramento units for moderate income households for 35 years using the welfare exemption.
- AMI requirement: Set deal by deal: 30% to 60% AMI at Tupelo (AHSC and tax credit rules); moderate income (80% to 120% AMI) in the acquisition and deed-restriction model; farmworker households at the Esparto lots. YCH's strategic plan targets a 15% increase (about 390 units) in affordable units it owns, manages or supports by 2029.
- Cycle: rolling (next: No open solicitation confirmed as of November 9, 2026. The Dunnigan Surplus Land Act response window closes about now and could not be re-confirmed on ych.ca.gov. Next expected openings: developer partnerships for the Esparto vacant lots (farmworker homeownership target Q4 2027) and Section 18 redevelopment of Yolano Village and Donnelly Circle (2027 or later).)
- Layering notes: In Yolo the housing authority, not the County, is the development partner that brings land, PBVs, migrant center operating experience and public housing repositioning capital. A developer can join as YCH's co-developer (Brinshore model at Tupelo), buy or ground lease YCH surplus land under the Surplus Land Act, or use YCH or New Hope CDC as the nonprofit managing general partner to qualify existing buildings for the welfare exemption (the KIND West Sacramento structure, where YCH provided a $25,000 operating loan and the deed restriction). Tax credits do not trigger state prevailing wage (DIR PW 2006-001); state prevailing wage turns on the local and state funds in these deals and the Labor Code 1720(c) exemptions, and HOME or CDBG add Davis-Bacon at their unit thresholds. YCH also operates the Davis, Madison and Dixon migrant centers for the state Office of Migrant Services, so it is the natural partner for Joe Serna farmworker housing applications in the unincorporated area.
- Source: https://www.ych.ca.gov/yolo-county-housing-celebrates-75-years/
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-06)


## City-Level Programs


### City of American Canyon

**American Canyon Affordable Housing Nexus Fee (ACMC 19.28.090) and Affordable Housing In-Lieu Fee Fund (Fund 340)**
- Agency: City of American Canyon Community Development Department and Finance Department
- Type: regulatory requirement
- Typical award: Requirement, not a subsidy. 2026 fee per gross square foot (Resolution 2025-94, adopted December 2, 2025, effective January 31, 2026, CPI adjusted each year, capped at 2% under Resolution 2016-15): single family and townhouse $3.64, stacked flats and apartments $4.22, ADU $0.00, office, hotel, retail and other nonresidential $0.93, warehouse and industrial $0.60. Fund 340 unaudited balance at June 30, 2023 was $400,075 after FY 2022-23 collections of $217,698 and a $70,492 transfer for the 189 Theresa demolition; the FY 2024-25 AB 1600 report was accepted December 16, 2025 but could not be opened this pass.
- AMI requirement: ADUs and affordable housing (deed restricted to lower income households) are exempt. Fee revenue is restricted to housing affordable to very low and low income households.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Paid at building permit issuance. Next CPI adjustment resolution expected on a December 2026 Council consent agenda for January 2027 effectiveness.)
- Layering notes: The fund is small and the City spends it on services (landlord tenant assistance, Section 8 support, farmworker housing contribution, maintenance of City owned housing, rent stabilization administration) rather than development loans, so there is no American Canyon trust fund NOFA to layer; a developer asking for a City contribution should request a Council action on a case by case basis. Exemption of affordable projects means 100% affordable deals pay no City housing fee. Fee resolution read on the City's Legistar download host (source_url); code sections and the AB 1600 FY 2022-23 report (americancanyon.gov PDF, retrieved via WebFetch because the site blocks scripts) were also opened. Fee revenue sits on top of the Pass 2 County fee structure only for unincorporated parcels; inside city limits only the City fee applies.
- Source: https://americancanyon.granicus.com/services/legistar/download/pdf/3766172/RESOLUTION_2025-94_-_FEE_UPDATE_2026.pdf

**American Canyon Density Bonus Ordinance (ACMC Chapter 19.27, repealed and replaced by Ordinance 2026-04)**
- Agency: City of American Canyon Community Development Department, Planning Division
- Type: density bonus
- Typical award: Requirement and entitlement incentive, not a subsidy. Restates Government Code 65915 as of 2026: base bonuses up to 50%, the 65915(v) additional bonus for projects that first reach 50%, 80% bonus (or unlimited density plus three stories or 33 feet within one half mile of a major transit stop) for 100% affordable projects, one to five concessions by affordability tier (four for 16% very low or 45% moderate for sale), land donation bonus of 15% up to a combined 35%, child care facility bonus, and parking maximums with zero parking for qualifying transit adjacent or 100% affordable projects. Equity sharing required on for sale moderate income units. The chapter states it does not require direct financial incentives or fee waivers.
- AMI requirement: State thresholds: 10% lower income, 5% very low, 10% moderate for sale, senior, student, or special needs units with 55-year restrictions.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Applies at entitlement; Ordinance 2026-04 adopted September 15, 2026 and effective 30 days later. The 2025 Housing Element APR (Planning Commission February 26, 2026, Council March 17, 2026) reports Crawford Way used a 15% state bonus (87 to 100 units).)
- Layering notes: No local enhancement beyond state law, so American Canyon offers nothing more than Government Code 65915; the chapter is recorded to show that the City's density bonus and inclusionary rules were brought current in 2026. Inclusionary units count toward the bonus thresholds. The City has no local housing trust fund NOFA, no HOME or CDBG entitlement (it is in the state non-entitlement pool, see Pass 2 record), and its PLHA share is programmed to ADUs through the City of Napa, so the local layer for an American Canyon deal is the state density bonus, HACN project based vouchers, CMFA bonds and state programs. Sun Square (30 units, 100% affordable revision pending) and Domaine (291 market rate units) are the active multifamily projects. Ordinance text read on the City law library (source_url) and the Planning Commission staff reports on the City's agenda host.

**American Canyon Inclusionary Housing Requirements (ACMC Chapter 19.28, repealed and replaced by Ordinance 2026-04)**
- Agency: City of American Canyon Community Development Department (Brent Cooper, Director)
- Type: regulatory requirement
- Typical award: Requirement, not a subsidy. Rental projects of five or more units: 5% very low, 5% low and 5% moderate income units (15% total), rental only, 55-year covenants. Ownership projects of five or more units: 10% of units affordable to lower income households (rental or ownership), 55 years. Fractions of 0.3 or more round up. Alternatives with findings of infeasibility: off site units, land dedication, acquisition and rehab of existing rentals (affordability extended 55 years), deeper affordability with fewer units, and as a last resort payment of the Affordable Housing Nexus Fee in lieu, deposited in the City housing fund for very low and low income housing. Inclusionary credits may be transferred to another project with Council approval.
- AMI requirement: Lower income means 80% AMI or below for Napa County; moderate up to 120% AMI. New residential development deed restricted to lower income households and tax exempt nonresidential development are exempt from the chapter.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Applies at entitlement with a recorded housing agreement. Ordinance 2026-04 was introduced September 1, 2026 and adopted September 15, 2026 (effective 30 days later) after Planning Commission hearings on April 23, June 25 and July 30, 2026. Crawford Way (100 townhomes, 2026 construction) is subject to the chapter.)
- Layering notes: American Canyon is the only Napa County city that still requires on site inclusionary units in market rate rental projects (Napa converted to a fee in 2012; Calistoga allows a moderate income option; St. Helena requires 20%). The 15% rental requirement, 5% at very low, can be paired with the state density bonus (5% very low earns the base bonus) and with HACN project based vouchers. City assistance under 19.28.060 includes density increases, reduced parking, reduced setbacks and waived, reduced or deferred planning, plan check, building permit and impact fees when on site units are infeasible. 100% affordable projects are exempt from the chapter and from the nexus fee. Code text read on the City's own law library (source_url) and in Ordinance 2026-04.
- Source: https://law.cityofamericancanyon.org/us/ca/cities/american-canyon/code/19.28.040
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)

- Agency: City of Napa Housing Division as delegated administrator for the City of American Canyon
- Type: loan
- Typical award: 95% of American Canyon's 2019-2023 PLHA formula allocation funds a Junior ADU and ADU loan program modeled on Napa's Junior Unit Initiative (forgivable loans and technical assistance to homeowners), 5% administration. Projected 4 households a year, 20 over five years. Allocation size is a small non-entitlement formula share (low six figures over five years).

### City of Anaheim

**Affordable Housing chapter: density bonus, by-right review of Housing Element sites, replacement housing and affordable parking ratios (Anaheim Municipal Code Chapter 18.52, Ord. 6627, August 11, 2026)**
- Agency: City of Anaheim Planning and Building Department, Planning Services Division
- Type: density bonus
- Typical award: Requirement and entitlement, not a subsidy. Sec. 18.52.020.010 adopts Government Code 65915 density bonuses and incentives by reference; Sec. 18.52.020.020 requires affordable housing to be provided under Chapter 17.40 (Inclusionary Housing); Sec. 18.52.020.030 makes review by right (Gov. Code 65583.2(h) and (i)) on Sixth Cycle Housing Element candidate sites for low and very low income units when at least 20% of units are restricted to lower income households; Sec. 18.52.020.040 allows affordable housing on institution-owned property per Sec. 18.38.023. Sec. 18.52.030 implements Housing Crisis Act replacement housing (55-year rental and 45-year ownership restrictions, relocation and right of first refusal; the right of first refusal does not apply to 100% lower income projects). Chapter 17.40 (Ord. 6593, October 29, 2024) requires rental projects of 35 or more units to set aside at least 10% of units onsite (at least 7% low income and 3% very low income) for 55 years, with in-lieu fee, offsite and land dedication alternatives; ownership projects are exempt.
- AMI requirement: State density bonus thresholds (5% very low, 10% low, 10% moderate for-sale, 100% affordable) with 55-year rental covenants; by-right review requires 20% lower income units on inventory sites; Chapter 17.40 inclusionary requires 10% of units in rental projects of 35 or more units (7% at 80% AMI low income, 3% at 50% AMI very low income), 55 years, or an in-lieu fee paid to the A-LHTF.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Applies at project application; no deadline.)
- Layering notes: Anaheim does have a citywide inclusionary ordinance for rental projects: Chapter 17.40 (Ord. 6593, October 29, 2024), cross-referenced in Sec. 18.52.020.020, requires 10% onsite affordable units (7% low, 3% very low income) in rental projects of 35 or more units, with in-lieu fees deposited in the A-LHTF; ownership projects are exempt. No affordable housing fee waiver ordinance was located. The Platinum Triangle and Beach Boulevard specific plans offer density, not money. Density bonus and by-right approval do not by themselves provide public funds. Chapter 18.52 read on the zoneomics mirror; Chapter 17.40 read on the gocodebook mirror (amlegal returns 403).
- Source: https://www.zoneomics.com/code/anaheim-CA/chapter_25

**Anaheim Local Housing Trust Fund (A-LHTF), Ordinance No. 6588; Program Guidelines and Funding Allocation Plan (adopted May 29, 2025, revised June 9, 2026)**
- Agency: City of Anaheim Housing and Community Development Department, with transfers to the Anaheim Housing Authority by cooperation agreement; 201 S. Anaheim Blvd., Suite 201
- Type: loan
- Typical award: Initial Funding Allocation Plan of $16,000,000: Build More Homes Initiative $5,000,000 (includes $1,000,000 from a federal grant restricted to housing production), First-Time Homebuyer programs $5,000,000 ($50,000 downpayment loans), Housing Stability Program $1,000,000, administration $500,000 (3.12%), reserve $4,500,000. Build More Homes funds pay for site acquisition, site preparation (environmental, demolition, relocation) and gap financing, structured as loans at 4% simple interest repaid from a residual receipts split; A-LHTF money may not exceed 50% of total City investment in a project. Eligible deposits include General Fund, federal PRO Housing grant, state Local Housing Trust Fund matching grants, REAP 2.0 (gap financing for infill with at least 65% residential floor area in mixed-use), Development Agreement community benefit payments, philanthropy and in-lieu fees paid under the City's Affordable Housing Ordinance.
- AMI requirement: Affordability follows the leveraged source (LIHTC, HOME, PLHA); where none applies the City sets project-specific requirements, generally 55-year covenants. Target beneficiaries: workforce households, households experiencing homelessness, active older adults 55 and over, special needs (transition-age youth, persons with disabilities, persons with AIDS). Shelters, transitional housing and group homes are ineligible.
- Cycle: rolling (next: No NOFA. Each expenditure requires a separate Council action; the Funding Allocation Plan is updated in the annual budget cycle (next spring 2027). Approach Housing and Community Development with a site or gap request.)
- Layering notes: Anaheim's answer to losing $15,000,000 to $17,000,000 a year of redevelopment set-aside: the trust consolidates HOME (FY 2024 $1,314,088), PLHA (about $3,000,000 a year), REAP 2.0 and General Fund into one locally controlled pool, with City gap financing averaging about $6,000,000 per recent project (Finamore Place, Miraflores) before land. The 50% leverage rule means A-LHTF is a secondary layer behind HOME, PLHA, County MHSA/BHSA loans, OCHFT and Anaheim Housing Authority PBVs. The Guidelines are also the City's vehicle for state LHTF matching grants, so expect future rounds to be tied to HCD LHTF deadlines. Local and state funds are public funds under Labor Code 1720(b), so state prevailing wage applies unless a 1720(c) exemption fits the deal, such as 1720(c)(5)(E) for below-market loans with at least 40 percent of units restricted 20 years at or below 80 percent AMI (see prevailing_wage_basis).0 funds carry infill and reporting rules. Guidelines PDF opened via anaheim.gov DocumentCenter (anaheim.net links return 403).
- Source: https://www.anaheim.gov/DocumentCenter/View/66427
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)

Beach Blvd (Silvermoon) and State College at Lincoln (about 0.51 acre) sought developers for lower income and special needs housing. **HOME, PLHA and CDBG entitlement funds used as affordable housing gap financing (Build More Homes Initiative)**
- Agency: City of Anaheim Housing and Community Development Department (HUD Programs division) and Anaheim Housing Authority
- Type: grant
- Typical award: HOME allocation FY 2024 $1,314,087.60 (down from $2,240,380 in FY 2010 and $1,067,408 in FY 2016); PLHA about $3,000,000 a year since 2019; together about $4,600,000 a year of recurring production money. City cash gap financing has averaged $6,000,000 per project on the last two developments (Finamore Place, completed February 2022, and Miraflores Apartments). The A-LHTF Build More Homes Initiative adds $5,000,000 of the initial $16,000,000 trust fund allocation. Anaheim also administers CDBG, ESG and HOPWA for the region.
- AMI requirement: HOME rents and 80% AMI limits with 20% of HOME units at 50% AMI; PLHA rental production at or below 60% AMI; City deals have typically been 100% affordable family, senior or supportive housing with 55-year covenants.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Annual Action Plan adopted each spring; developer solicitations are issued per site (recent Housing Authority RFPs covered 212 S. Beach Blvd and State College at Lincoln). Verify the FY 2026-27 HOME and PLHA figures with the department; the City documents page lists only the FY 2022-23 Action Plan.)
- Layering notes: Anaheim does not run a competitive NOFA; it assembles sites (Beach Boulevard corridor, former motels) and selects developers by RFP, then layers HOME, PLHA, A-LHTF and Housing Authority PBVs. The City is an HHAP direct recipient and a HOPWA grantee for Orange County, so operating subsidies for PSH can come from the same department. Stack order seen in practice: City land lease plus HOME or PLHA loan, Housing Authority PBVs, County MHSA/BHSA or OCHFT loan, 4% credits with CMFA or CSCDA bonds. Davis-Bacon on HOME projects of 12 or more assisted units; state prevailing wage on all City funds. Figures from the A-LHTF Guidelines (amended June 9, 2026), reopened Nov 10, 2026 on anaheim.net with a Chrome user agent. Project details from Pass 3 not reopened in the audit: Miraflores (85 PSH family units, 2024, 60-year ground lease, $3,000,000 HOME loan, 8 vouchers) and Center of Hope (72 PSH units, 2023, $2,000,000 City construction loan, 50 vouchers). anaheim.net HTML pages, Action Plan PDFs and CivicAlerts return 403.
- Source: https://www.anaheim.net/DocumentCenter/View/66427
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)

**Inclusionary Housing Ordinance (Anaheim Municipal Code Chapter 17.40, Ord. 6593, October 29, 2024) and In-Lieu Fee Schedule (Resolution No. 2024-126)**
- Agency: City of Anaheim Housing and Community Development Department (Affordable Housing Development Division), with the Planning and Building Department, Planning Services Division
- Type: regulatory requirement
- Typical award: Requirement, not a subsidy. Rental residential or mixed-use projects of 35 or more units must provide at least 10% of units onsite as affordable rentals: at least 7% at or below low income (80% AMI) and at least 3% at or below very low income (50% AMI) (Sec. 17.40.050.0201). Alternatives (Sec. 17.40.060): in-lieu fee, offsite construction (only if the Director finds onsite production economically infeasible; within Anaheim, reasonably close, built before or with the market-rate project), or land dedication in Anaheim zoned for the required units with value comparable to the in-lieu fee. In-lieu fee per Resolution No. 2024-126 (adopted November 19, 2024, effective 60 days after adoption): $10.00 per square foot of total habitable/leasable space in the entire project. City example: 240 units x 875 sq ft = 210,000 sq ft x $10.00 = $2,100,000, or $87,500 per required inclusionary unit (24 units). Fractional units: round up, or pay a fractional fee of $20 to $100 per square foot of one unit (0.2 to 1.0 of a unit; example 0.7 of a unit x 875 sq ft at $70.00 = $61,250). Fees are paid before the first building permit (pro rata by phase allowed) and deposited in the Anaheim Local Housing Trust Fund.
- AMI requirement: 10% of units in rental projects of 35 or more units: at least 7% at or below 80% AMI (low income) and at least 3% at or below 50% AMI (very low income), Orange County AMI per HCD; affordable rent is 30% of the applicable AMI percentage adjusted for household size (H&SC 50052.5) minus mandatory tenant-paid housing costs. Covenant of at least 55 years for rental units; after 55 years the covenant may be removed only if the property is redeveloped to a non-residential use. Affordable units must be built concurrently with or before market-rate units, match market-rate unit size (up to 15% smaller with approval), with proportional bedroom mix, comparable finishes and amenity access, dispersed, and no separate entrances. Ownership projects are exempt, so there are no for-sale set-asides.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Applies at project application; no deadline. In-lieu fees are due before issuance of the first building permit.)
- Layering notes: Rental only: Anaheim exempts ownership projects of every size, unlike the Santa Ana (587c1bf887) and Huntington Beach (adbbe8ef1b) ordinances in this database, which also reach for-sale housing. The $10 per square foot fee (about $87,500 per required unit in the City example) is the main alternative most market-rate developers will price against onsite units. Under Sec. 17.40.090, units provided for a state density bonus (Chapter 18.52, record 2db1a1727f) count toward this requirement if they also meet Chapter 17.40 standards, so a project with 10% low and very low units can satisfy both. Projects under a development agreement with comparable affordable obligations are exempt, which matters in the Platinum Triangle and other DA areas. In-lieu fees go to the Anaheim Local Housing Trust Fund (record ec67d2dea0), which redeploys them as gap loans through the Build More Homes Initiative; this is the City's own fund, not a County of Orange program, and no County inclusionary requirement applies inside Anaheim. Ord. 6593 recitals note it replaced a voluntary Housing Ambassador approach that had raised $561,000. Ordinance and fee resolution read in the City Clerk Laserfiche portal (records.anaheim.net); code text cross-checked on the gocodebook mirror because amlegal returns 403.
- Source: https://www.anaheim.gov/5190/Affordable-Housing
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-09)

**Low and Moderate Income Housing Asset Fund (Anaheim Housing Authority as Housing Successor to the Anaheim Redevelopment Agency)**
- Agency: Anaheim Housing Authority as Housing Successor, administered by Housing and Community Development
- Type: loan
- Typical award: FY 2024-25 Housing Successor Annual Report (dated December 16, 2025): $23,453,030 deposited into the LMIHAF ($13,794 from ROPS items), $22,615,135 spent ($21,423,871 on housing development: $12,312,921 extremely low income units, $2,423,602 very low, $5,205,580 low, $1,481,768 projects pending; $1,191,264 administration), ending balance $16,794,545, all unencumbered, no excess surplus. Housing assets: real property $74,016,700 (statutory value) and loans and grants receivable $49,680,717, total $123,697,417. Prior year-end balances: $38,146,030 (FY 2020-21), $30,063,646, $18,112,239 and $15,956,650 (FY 2023-24). Attachments A and B list many Authority-owned sites (for example 554 S. West Ave., 309 W. Midway, 212 S. Beach Blvd. (Silver Moon), 428 S. Melrose, 883 S. Anaheim Blvd.) marked RFP pending or pending RFP process. Senior test 17% (231 of 1,382 assisted rental units, 2015-2024). Before dissolution the Agency's housing set-aside was $15,000,000 to $17,000,000 a year.
- AMI requirement: Health and Safety Code 34176.1: low and moderate income households (up to 120% AMI), at least 30% of five-year expenditures for households at or below 30% AMI, senior cap of 50% over 10 years.
- Cycle: rolling (next: No open round as of November 9, 2026. The FY 2024-25 Housing Successor report lists multiple Authority-owned sites with an RFP pending but gives no release date; watch Anaheim Housing Authority agendas and contact Housing and Community Development.)
- Layering notes: Anaheim's LMIHAF is active: FY 2024-25 deposits of $23.5 million and housing development spending of $21.4 million, mostly on extremely low income units, with $16.8 million unencumbered at June 30, 2025, plus a large land inventory with RFPs pending. The A-LHTF Guidelines say Trust funds may be transferred to the Housing Authority to combine with other sources for site acquisition. Housing successor funds are public funds under Labor Code 1720(b), but 1720(c)(4) excludes affordable units paid for solely from Low and Moderate Income Housing Fund money; other funds in the deal decide coverage (see prevailing_wage_basis). Housing Successor Agency page opened on anaheim.gov; FY 2024-25 report opened on anaheim.net.

### City of Antioch

**Antioch Community Grants: CDBG, Housing Successor (LMIHAF) and PLHA funds (FY 2027/28 to 2029/30 cycle via the Contra Costa Consortium NOFA)**
- Agency: City of Antioch Community Services Department, Housing and Homelessness Division (housing@antiochca.gov, cdbg@antiochca.gov, 925-779-7082, 4703 Lone Tree Way)
- Type: grant
- Typical award: Antioch anticipates about $850,000 CDBG, $350,000 PLHA and $500,000 Housing Successor funds per year for the FY 2027-2030 cycle (about 30 programs funded annually; the City notes that funding for affordable housing development is limited and directs developers to County HOME). 2025-2030 Consolidated Plan anticipated resources: CDBG $911,040 annual allocation plus $272,888 program income and $1,174,496 prior-year resources in year 1 (prior-year includes $1,257,347 returned by Hope Solutions after a project did not proceed); PLHA $509,164 year 1 and $1,416,898 remainder; Housing Successor $600,000 year 1 and $1,750,000 remainder, of which $350,000 per year funds homeless shelter, services and prevention. Five-year goals include PLHA $150,000 for 10 new rental units, CDBG $850,000 for 65 homeless housing units, CDBG $1,367,157 plus PLHA $609,164 for 50 owner rehabs, and Housing Successor and PLHA loans for ADUs (25 ADUs). - Cycle: annual NOFA (next: Applications due Monday, December 7, 2026 at 5:00 PM through City Data Services (one joint application for Antioch, Concord, Pittsburg, Walnut Creek and the County); the Antioch CDBG Grant Committee (two councilmembers) hears presentations February to March 2027; Council adopts the FY 2027/28 Action Plan April to May 2027; funds effective July 1, 2027.)
- Layering notes: Antioch's local layer is thin (about $500,000 per year of Housing Successor money, much of it committed to homeless services) and there is no inclusionary trust fund, so Antioch deals depend on County HOME, CDBG-Housing and Measure X (county records), HACCC project-based vouchers, the County conduit bond program and State programs; the $2 million Housing Successor goal for 30 permanent supportive housing units in the prior Consolidated Plan went unspent after the Hope Solutions project fell through, so staff are motivated to place successor funds in a viable PSH or ELI project. **Antioch Housing Element incentives for lower-income housing (Programs 2.1.6, 2.1.7 and 4.1.3: fee support, land write-downs, expedited processing, density bonus ordinance)**
- Agency: City of Antioch Community Development Department, Planning Division, with CDBG and Housing Programs staff
- Type: density bonus
- Typical award: Regulatory and discretionary incentives, not a funded program. The certified 2023-2031 Housing Element (HCD certification October 12, 2023) commits the City to encourage extremely low income housing through targeted developer outreach, financial or in-kind technical assistance, fee support, land write-downs and expedited or priority processing, and to offer incentives supplementing state density bonus law (quantified objective: 175 ELI units); to meet at least three nonprofit developers annually and support funding applications; and to keep the density bonus ordinance consistent with state law (Program 4.1.3). Rezoning under the Housing Element raises many sites to 35 units per acre, and the Commercial Infill Housing (CIH) Overlay allows housing on commercial sites. No adopted fee waiver schedule exists; the proposed inclusionary ordinance expressly excluded fee waivers.
- AMI requirement: Case by case; state density bonus thresholds apply; City incentives target extremely low, very low and low income and special needs housing.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Applies at entitlement; no deadline. Housing Element program review occurs with each Annual Progress Report (April).)
- Layering notes: Antioch has no local fee waiver ordinance, housing trust fund or in-lieu fund, so these Housing Element commitments are the only local incentives beyond state density bonus law; developers should negotiate fee deferrals, land contributions from the City's surplus list (largest parcel about 5 acres, per the Consolidated Plan) and Housing Successor or PLHA gap loans as part of entitlement. Density bonus and incentives stack with County HOME, Measure X and HACCC PBVs (county records). Programs read from the certified Housing Element Goals, Policies and Programs chapter on the civicplus mirror (source_url) because antiochca.gov returns 403.

**Antioch Inclusionary Housing Ordinance (proposed AMC Title 9, Chapter 5, Article 43) and Inclusionary Housing Trust Fund (not adopted; continued into the General Plan Update on March 10, 2026)**
- Agency: City of Antioch Community Development Department, Planning Division (Zoe Merideth, Planning Manager, 925-779-6159)
- Type: regulatory requirement
- Typical award: Requirement, not a subsidy, and not in effect. Proposed terms: all residential projects of 5 or more units citywide; 15% of units affordable (10% very low income, 5% low income) in perpetuity; in-lieu fee $202,500 per required unit not built (PlaceWorks financing-gap method: $440,000 Antioch development cost per unit times a 46.02% countywide gap), adjusted each July 1 by CPI and due at building permit; an Inclusionary Housing Trust Fund with administrative guidelines (new construction, preservation, acquisition-rehab, ADUs, predevelopment loans, land purchase, homebuyer assistance) and an annual compliance monitoring fee. The Planning Commission recommended adoption 4-0 on February 4, 2026 (Resolution 2026-02, asking for Antioch resident priority, union preference and ELI priority). On March 10, 2026 the City Council voted 4-1 to continue the IHO into the broader General Plan Update instead of adopting it.
- AMI requirement: Proposed: 15% of units at very low (10%) and low (5%) income, affordable in perpetuity, with units at least 90% of market-rate unit size and the same bedroom mix.
- Cycle: closed/inactive (next: No adoption date. Track the Antioch General Plan Update (antioch.generalplan.org) for the inclusionary and trust fund components; a review every two years after adoption was proposed and would set the first in-lieu fee review.)
- Layering notes: Antioch currently has no inclusionary requirement, no in-lieu fee and no local housing trust fund, so market-rate developers face no affordable obligation and affordable developers have no City trust fund to apply to; the only City money is Housing Successor and PLHA (separate record). If adopted later, the $202,500 per unit fee would be the highest flat fee in the county (Pleasant Hill charges $271,350; Concord $15.10 to $20.13 per square foot; Walnut Creek $26.04 per square foot; San Ramon $15.16 per square foot for small projects). The County's Chapter 822-4 ordinance does not apply inside Antioch. antiochca.gov returns 403 to automated access; the ca-antioch.civicplus.com mirror serves the same pages, and the full March 10, 2026 council packet (399 pages, including Attachment G countywide fee comparison) was read at source_url.
