### City of Arroyo Grande

**Density Bonuses (Municipal Code Chapter 16.82; Ord. 596, 2007)**
- Agency: City of Arroyo Grande Community Development Department
- Type: density bonus
- Typical award: Requirement-based entitlement, not a subsidy. Local codification of state density bonus law. Ordinance 732 (adopted August 27, 2024; first reading August 13, 2024, to implement AB 1397 and update state density bonus provisions) amended Chapter 16.82 and added Section 16.82.015, which makes the density bonuses and incentives required by Gov. Code 65915 et seq. available on the terms and conditions in state law. Older 2007 sections on qualifying categories, incentives, waivers, parking, land donation and child care remain in the chapter, and Section 16.82.130 defers to state law amendments.
- AMI requirement: Per state density bonus law (55-year rental affordability governs); older chapter text still references 30-year affordability for low and very low income bonus units and equity sharing for moderate income for-sale units.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Not applicable; requested with the planning application.)
- Layering notes: Chapter 16.82 was amended by Ordinance 732 in 2024 to track state law; there is no local enhancement beyond state law. Inclusionary units under Chapter 16.80 can be used to qualify for the bonus (Section 16.80.110), which is the main local layering point. Arroyo Grande has no fee waiver ordinance, RDA successor housing fund or NOFA; its tools are the inclusionary trust fund and this chapter, plus County and HASLO resources. **Inclusionary Affordable Housing Requirements (Municipal Code Chapter 16.80; Ord. 595, 2007) and in-lieu fee**
- Agency: City of Arroyo Grande Community Development Department (City Council decides units, fee or land on each project)
- Type: regulatory requirement
- Typical award: Requirement, not a subsidy. Applies to new residential projects of two or more units, substantial rehabilitation of two or more units and condo conversions. Options: 5% very low income units, or 10% lower income units, or 15% moderate income units (rental or non-common-interest projects), or an equivalent combination; or an in-lieu fee set by Council resolution (the Housing Element reports the fee was raised from 1% to 5%, applied to construction valuation); or land dedication. Projects of two to four units may always pay the fee. Fees go to the Inclusionary Affordable Housing Trust Fund (Sections 16.80.070 and 16.80.080). Through 2020 only two very low income units had been entitled; nearly all applicants paid the fee.
- AMI requirement: Rental units restricted at least 55 years, ownership units at least 45 years, at affordable housing cost per Health and Safety Code 50052.5 and 50053; units dispersed and comparable to market-rate units; affordable housing agreement required before map approval or building permit.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Not applicable; fee paid before the first ministerial permit (grading, demolition or building). The FY 2026-27 Comprehensive Fee Schedule (effective July 1, 2026) lists the Affordable Housing in lieu fee at 0.05 for both FY 2025-26 and FY 2026-27, consistent with 5% of construction valuation. Housing Element Program E.1-1 called for amending the requirements and fee; no amendment to Chapter 16.80 appears in the code mirror.)
- Layering notes: Low threshold (two units) means almost every multifamily project pays into the trust fund, which is the City's only local gap source (separate record). Chapter 16.80.110 coordinates with the density bonus chapter; inclusionary units can count toward density bonus thresholds. Incentives listed in the Housing Element for inclusionary projects include density bonuses, fee waivers or reductions and modified development standards, but no standing fee waiver ordinance was found. County inclusionary ordinance was repealed in 2022, so this is one of only two active inclusionary programs in the county (with the City of SLO). Read on the zoneomics mirror; arroyogrande.org opens but its housing pages are thin and the eScribe agenda host renders in JavaScript.

### City of Atascadero

**Affordable Housing Impact Fee Deferral Program (Municipal Code Section 3-14.070 as amended by Ord. 666, September 26, 2023, and Council deferral resolution)**
- Agency: City of Atascadero Community Development Department and Administrative Services
- Type: fee waiver
- Typical award: Development impact fees and wastewater capacity charges, normally due at final inspection, may be deferred under a Council-approved agreement for residential units affordable to low, very low or extremely low income households. Staff reports and local coverage describe the program as a 17-year interest-bearing deferral loan for projects with five or more affordable rental units, with up to about $3 million in fees eligible; the City cites multifamily impact fees of roughly $12,000 to $15,000 per unit. Intended to improve TCAC competitiveness by lowering upfront cost.

- Cycle: rolling (next: Not applicable; request with the entitlement or before building permit issuance. Contact Community Development at (805) 461-5000.)
- Layering notes: Deferral, not forgiveness: fees are a City loan repaid over the term, so underwrite as soft debt. Implements Housing Element Program 2.E. EPS advised the City against outright impact fee waivers for fiscal reasons, so a waiver is unlikely. Stacks with state density bonus (Article 30), the inclusionary in-lieu fund, County Title 29 or Regional Housing Fund, HASLO vouchers and Urban County HOME. The ordinance text was read on the ecode360 code mirror (atascadero.org links to the September 26, 2023 resolution on records.atascadero.org, which returned a scanned PDF with no extractable text).

- Type: density bonus
- Typical award: Requirement-based entitlement, not a subsidy. No local enhancement beyond state minimums. Market-rate senior projects get the bonus but no other concessions. Projects that use the density bonus are exempt from the City's Interim Inclusionary Housing Policy.

The density bonus exempts a project from inclusionary units, so for mixed-income deals the bonus is usually the better path; 100% affordable deals use it for up to 80% bonus and unlimited density near transit under state law. **Interim Inclusionary Housing Policy (Council policy adopted June 24, 2003, amended November 25, 2003) and inclusionary in-lieu housing fund**
- Agency: City of Atascadero Community Development Department (fund and resale administration by Administrative Services, affordablehousing@atascadero.org)
- Type: regulatory requirement
- Typical award: Requirement, not a subsidy. Applies only to residential projects needing legislative approval (planned developments, subdivisions, rezones). 20% of units affordable; in multifamily and mixed-use areas split 20% very low, 37% low, 43% moderate (single-family areas 100% moderate). Projects of 1 to 10 units may pay the in-lieu fee or build; 11 or more units must build unless Council approves fees. In-lieu fee equals 5% of the construction valuation of the market-rate units; fractional units up to 0.499 pay fees. Collected fees sit in the City's inclusionary (in-lieu) housing fund, which has helped Peoples' Self-Help Housing (Atalaya Street 24 homes, Triangle parcel 11 units) and Corporation for Better Housing (60 very low and low income units). Housing Element Program 2.C commits the City to adopt a policy for using the in-lieu funds.
- AMI requirement: Deed restriction of 30 years under the policy (County Affordable Housing Standards used for income limits, rents and prices); inclusionary units are treated as density bonus units not counted against maximum density. Projects using the state density bonus and second units are exempt.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Not applicable. The 2022 EPS nexus study recommended replacing the policy with a citywide affordable housing impact fee (nexus-justified maximum $38.71 to $75 per sq ft, adopted fee to be set well below) and lowering inclusionary to 10% to 15% for large discretionary projects; no ordinance had been adopted as of the pages read.)
- Layering notes: Still an interim policy more than 20 years on; it only reaches discretionary legislative projects, so most by-right multifamily pays nothing. A 100% affordable LIHTC project is effectively exempt and can request the in-lieu fund as gap money; the fund balance is not published and should be requested from Administrative Services at (805) 470-3428. **Auburn 2021-2029 Housing Element Program A and Program I: case-by-case fee reductions or deferrals, alternative development standards and state CDBG and HOME applications for affordable housing (adopted May 24, 2021)**
- Agency: City of Auburn Planning and Public Works Department, with participating nonprofit and for-profit housing providers
- Type: fee waiver

- Agency: City of Auburn Planning and Public Works Department (1225 Lincoln Way, Auburn)
- Type: density bonus
- Typical award: Regulatory incentive, not a subsidy. Implements Government Code 65915 to 65918 through a ministerial density bonus permit processed with other entitlements: bonuses per state tables for very low, lower and moderate income units, 20% for senior, foster youth, disabled veteran and homeless housing, 80% for 100% affordable projects (no density limit within one half mile of a major transit stop), incentives and concessions by threshold with a three-story or 33-foot height increase when four concessions apply near transit, unlimited waivers of standards that physically preclude the project, land donation bonus, parking ratios per state law, and a recorded density bonus housing agreement. The Director must determine completeness and the eligible bonus within 30 days. Filing fee set by Council resolution.
- AMI requirement: State thresholds; affordable units governed by Section 159.340 (affordable rent and housing cost per Health and Safety Code 50053 and 50052.5) with 55-year rental covenants.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Processed with entitlements; no deadline.)
- Layering notes: Auburn (population about 14,000) has no local housing trust fund, inclusionary ordinance, in-lieu fee fund, housing successor fund or city NOFA; this chapter and the negotiated fee reductions in the Housing Element (next record) are the City's only tools. The Housing Element credits past density bonuses (one project received a 400% bonus with apartments in an R-1 zone and a 50% parking reduction) and Placer County land donation and Housing Trust Placer money for a 79-unit project. Gap funding for Auburn projects comes from Placer County in-lieu fee loans, County PLHA, Housing Trust Placer and PCHA PBVs. Chapter read on the zoneomics mirror (Auburn's code publisher is blocked); auburn.ca.gov DocumentCenter PDFs open directly.
- Source: https://www.zoneomics.com/code/auburn-CA/chapter_18
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)


### City of Berkeley

**Berkeley Housing Trust Fund (HTF) development, acquisition and predevelopment loans (BMC 21.28; 2021 HTF Guidelines; 2024 HTF RFP)**
- Agency: City of Berkeley Health, Housing and Community Services Department, Housing and Community Services Division, 2180 Milvia Street; housingdevelopment@berkeleyca.gov, (510) 981-5400
- Type: loan
- Typical award: Single application pools Measure O bond, inclusionary in-lieu and Affordable Housing Mitigation Fee revenue, Measure U1 general funds, HOME, PLHA and state pass-throughs. Current reservations: new construction $26,500,000 BUSD educator housing (110 units, Measure O), $11,996,669 1740 San Pablo (54 units), $11,996,669 St Paul Terrace (50), $14,531,301 Ephesian Legacy Court (80), $14,359,593 People's Park supportive housing (119), North Berkeley BART Lot B $11,563,636 plus EBALDC $5,926,364 plus Insight PSH $9,010,000 ($21,500,000 reserved); renovation $500,000 to $8,500,000. 2024 rehab RFP: about $5,800,000 available (including $1,200,000 HOME), $11,500,000 requested, awards $2,990,000 Adeline Street Apartments and $2,868,571 Ashby Lofts (June 2025). Standard terms: 55 years at 3% simple interest, annual payments from residual receipts; predevelopment loans 5 years at 3%. Fees: 1% origination, $600 subordination or assumption, $3,000 modification, $130 per hour project management.
- AMI requirement: At least 60% of units restricted to households at or below 30% and 60% AMI (BUSD educator housing up to 120% AMI by waiver); 55-year minimum regulatory agreement; portion of units to Section 8 and Shelter Plus Care voucher holders; Berkeley housing preference policy applies to lottery units.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Predevelopment requests may be submitted any time; development funds released by RFP when Council allocates money (last new construction RFP 2019-2021 Measure O rounds, rehab RFP November 2024). No development RFP open as of 2026-11-08; Ashby BART East Lot developer selection underway (October 2026). Funding reservations expire after 24 months and were extended to January 2028 for SHiPP, Ephesian and NBB in late 2025.)
- Layering notes: Berkeley's HTF is the second largest city pool in the county and the gateway to Measure O, U1 and in-lieu revenue. Reservations above show how the City layers Measure O (capital only), AHMF or in-lieu fees and U1 (operating reserves and predevelopment, which Measure O cannot fund). Stacks with Alameda County Measure A1 Berkeley base allocation and regional pool, Measure W (Ephesian Legacy Court and People's Park won Measure W in March 2026), Berkeley Housing Authority project-based vouchers, and state LHTF match (City applied for NBB projects). HTF Guidelines require state prevailing wage on all City-funded construction and a First Source hiring agreement (BMC 13.26). FY 2026 budget deficit left no U1 available for unfunded rehab requests, so near-term capacity depends on in-lieu fee collections (about $9,000,000 a year average).
- Source: https://berkeleyca.gov/community-recreation/affordable-housing-berkeley/housing-trust-fund
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)

**Density Bonus, BMC Chapter 23.330 (Ordinance 7787-NS, 2021; 7853-NS, 2023)**
- Agency: City of Berkeley Planning and Development Department, Zoning Officer and Zoning Adjustments Board
- Type: density bonus
- Typical award: Requirement and entitlement, not a subsidy. Incorporates Government Code 65915 and 65917.2 by reference with administrative regulations; incentives and concessions counted per dimensional or quantitative standard; City bears the burden of proof to deny; waivers negotiated through Use Permit and Design Review; regulatory agreement required before certificate of occupancy; qualifying units must meet Chapter 23.328 standards.
- AMI requirement: State thresholds; bonus units count toward the base for the 20% inclusionary requirement only as provided in 23.328.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Concurrent with the housing development permit application; no deadline.)
- Layering notes: No local enhancement beyond state law; Berkeley's leverage for affordable projects is instead the Southside and transit-corridor rezonings and the Housing Element Program upzonings. Inclusionary in-lieu fee applies to the base project only, which modestly favors bonus projects. Code read on the zoneomics mirror because berkeley.municipal.codes is script-blocked.
- Source: https://www.zoneomics.com/code/berkeley-CA/chapter_3
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)

**Inclusionary Housing Ordinance, BMC Chapter 23.328, and Affordable Housing In-Lieu Fee (Resolution 71,674-N.S.; successor to the Affordable Housing Mitigation Fee, BMC 22.20.065)**
- Agency: City of Berkeley Planning and Development Department (compliance plans) and HHCS (BMR program and HTF)
- Type: regulatory requirement
- Typical award: Requirement, not a subsidy. Projects over 5,000 sq ft of residential unit floor area must provide 20% of units as BMR (rental: half at 50% AMI, half low income, with Section 8 and Shelter Plus Care set-asides; ownership: all at 80% AMI) or pay an in-lieu fee of $62.83 per sq ft of residential unit floor area effective July 1, 2025 (up from $56.25; biennial California Construction Cost Index adjustment, next July 1, 2027), or a prorated mix. Full-fee payers deduct 5,000 sq ft (2,500 for single family); density bonus projects pay on the base project area. Fee due before certificate of occupancy. Revenue to the HTF: AHMF collections $3,112,000 (FY 2021), $16,208,000 (FY 2022), $14,224,000 (FY 2023), $10,716,000 (FY 2024), $831,000 (FY 2025); FY 2025 pipeline of 22 projects, 2,482 units, 214 BMR units and $22,600,000 projected fees. BMR portfolio 605 units in 61 properties.
- AMI requirement: 20% BMR for life of project (rental half at 50% AMI, half at 80% AMI; ownership at 80% AMI); projects with building permit or preliminary application before April 1, 2023 remain under the AHMF ordinance.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Applies at entitlement (preliminary Affordable Housing Compliance Plan) and building permit (final AHCP); fee indexed July 1, 2027.)
- Layering notes: This fee is Berkeley's primary dedicated affordable housing revenue (about $9,000,000 a year average) and funds the HTF record above, so BMR unit production and fee collections move inversely. Revenue is lagging while the IHO pipeline moves from AHMF to IHO entitlements, which matters for near-term HTF capacity. Developers using the state density bonus must still meet the 20% inclusionary requirement; 23.330.070 ties qualifying bonus units to 23.328 standards. Compare Oakland's per-square-foot AHIF ($19.73 to $36.17) and Fremont's $44 per sq ft for-sale in-lieu fee.
- Source: https://berkeleyca.gov/construction-development/permits-design-parameters/design-parameters/affordable-housing
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)

**Measure O Affordable Housing General Obligation Bond (November 2018, $135,000,000)**
- Agency: City of Berkeley HHCS with the Measure O Bond Oversight Committee and Housing Advisory Commission
- Type: bond
- Typical award: Voter-approved $135,000,000 GO bond (November 2018) for development, rehabilitation and preservation of affordable housing for extremely low through middle income households. The City has completed three of four planned issuances. First issuance about $30,000,000 (2019-20) funded Berkeley Way and 1601 Oxford and a 2019 HTF RFP of about $14,500,000. Completed projects include Jordan Court ($3,500,000), Berkeley Way (over $13,800,000) and The Grinnell ($7,300,000). In progress: BUSD workforce housing ($26,500,000, under construction since June 2025), St Paul Terrace ($12,000,000, under construction since April 2026), 1740 San Pablo ($7,500,000 Measure O). Council reserved $40,000,000 of Measure O for the BART sites: up to $20,000,000 for Ashby BART (still in planning) and $20,000,000 within a $26,500,000 City subsidy for North Berkeley BART. Supportive Housing in People's Park and Ephesian Legacy Court reservations will likely include some Measure O. Measure O cannot fund predevelopment or capitalized operating reserves, which the City covers with U1 or fee revenue.
- AMI requirement: HTF Guidelines (60% of units at or below 30% to 60% AMI) with Council-approved exceptions up to 120% AMI for BUSD educator housing; 55-year restrictions.
- Cycle: closed/inactive (next: No open Measure O round as of November 9, 2026; remaining proceeds are reserved for pipeline projects (Ashby BART up to $20,000,000, North Berkeley BART, SHiPP, Ephesian Legacy Court). On February 10, 2026 Council extended the SHiPP, Ephesian and North Berkeley BART reservations for 24 months (to about February 2028). Verify unreserved balance with HHCS or the Measure O Bond Oversight Committee.)
- Layering notes: Measure O is Berkeley's counterpart to Oakland Measure U and County Measure A1; it is permanent capital only, so projects pair it with AHMF or in-lieu funds and U1 for predevelopment and reserves, Berkeley Housing Authority PBVs for operating support, and Measure A1 or Measure W for the balance. Oversight by the Measure O committee acts in place of the HAC for bond-funded RFPs. The 2019 Council report and the November 2025 HAC packet were the documents opened; a current bond balance statement was not found on berkeleyca.gov.
- Source: https://berkeleyca.gov/sites/default/files/documents/2019-06-11%20Item%2031%20Measure%20O%20Affordable%20Housing%20Bonds.pdf
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)

**Measure U1 general fund allocation to the Housing Trust Fund (2016 rental housing business license tax increase) and CHDO operating support**
- Agency: City of Berkeley HHCS; allocation set by City Council in the biennial budget
- Type: grant
- Typical award: Measure U1 raised the business license tax on rental property owners (2016) with the stated intent of funding affordable housing and homelessness programs; Council allocates a share to the HTF each budget. Recent U1 uses: California Street Apartments $3,599,948 (BALCT, with HTF), University Homes Homekey $8,500,000, 2321-2323 10th Street $3,324,225, MLK House $2,000,988, Ephesian Legacy Court (with Measure O and AHMF), capitalized operating reserves and predevelopment loans that Measure O cannot fund, and CHDO operating grants of up to $30,000 per organization per year FY 2026 to FY 2030 (with HOME). The HAC recommendation in 2025 to add U1 to the rehab RFP was withdrawn because the FY 2026 budget projected a deficit with limited U1 available.
- AMI requirement: When loaned through the HTF, HTF Guidelines apply: at least 60% of units rent restricted, with at least 20% of all units at or below 30% AMI and the remaining restricted units (about 40%) at or below 60% AMI, rents at TCAC limits; flexible general fund otherwise.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Dependent on the FY 2027-28 biennial budget; no set-aside guaranteed. Verify with HHCS.)
- Layering notes: U1 is the only Berkeley source usable for operating reserves and predevelopment, which makes it the critical complement to Measure O and county capital for PSH deals (Berkeley Way needed up to $14,000,000 in operating reserve until BHA project-based vouchers reduced it). Competes with homelessness services for the same general fund. Documented in the 2021 HTF Guidelines, the June 2025 RFP reservations report and the November 2025 HAC packet.
- Source: https://berkeleyca.gov/sites/default/files/2021%20HTF-Approved-Guidelines%20for%20website_0.pdf
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)

**Small Sites Program (SSP) NOFA 2025, $3,800,000 (HTF subset, created 2018)**
- Agency: City of Berkeley Health, Housing and Community Services Department, Housing and Community Services Division, 2180 Milvia Street; housingdevelopment@berkeleyca.gov, (510) 981-5400
- Type: loan
- Typical award: $2,500,000 NOFA released August 18, 2025 and increased to $3,800,000; applications accepted on a rolling basis from August 25, 2025 and reviewed in order received (first three applications or twice the available funding). Three projects funded since 2018 under four NOFAs, including Bay Area Community Land Trust at 2627 California Street ($3,599,948 with U1 general funds) and Northern California Land Trust sites. No dedicated funding source; Council allocates by budget.
- AMI requirement: Acquisition and rehabilitation of rent-controlled or vacant multifamily rental buildings with 2 to 25 units under a 55-year loan and regulatory agreement; building-level average of 80% AMI (City may instead cap all incomes at 80% AMI); must accept Section 8 and Shelter Plus Care vouchers; 66% of existing households must income-certify and 75% agree to participate; requires a bank or CDFI loan; LIHTC projects not eligible; cooperatives subject to additional requirements (Exhibit H).
- Cycle: rolling (next: Rolling with no fixed deadline; still listed under Open funding opportunities on the Housing Trust Fund page as of November 8, 2026. Applications reviewed in order received until the $3,800,000 is committed; once three applications or twice the available funds are received, later applications are held, not actively reviewed.)
- Layering notes: Berkeley's analog to Oakland ACAH at much smaller scale. Pairs with the Bay Area Community Land Trust and Northern California Land Trust pipelines, county Measure A1 acquisition funds and private CDFI bridge debt. Over-the-counter approval by the City Manager, no Council action, so timing is fast relative to the HTF RFP. SSP projects follow HTF loan terms (55 years, 3% simple, residual receipts) and the City prevailing wage requirement.

### City of Burlingame

**Affordable Housing Fund NOFA (rolling, FY 2025-26 and FY 2026-27)**
- Agency: City of Burlingame Community Development Department, Economic Development and Housing
- Type: loan
- Typical award: About $12 million available (announced July 2025): $9 million for preservation of existing or naturally occurring affordable housing and $3 million for production; news reports put the fund at $14.3 million. Prior support: a $1.4 million 55-year loan considered for the 69-unit Eucalyptus Grove (1875 California Drive, CRP and Abode, 20% to 50% AMI, County AHF $5,698,107, 30 HACSM PBVs) and donated land for the 132-unit Village at Burlingame (150 Park Road, completed 2023).
- AMI requirement: Up to 80% AMI, 55-year regulatory agreement, County rent limits with utility allowances, rent increases capped at the lesser of County limits or 5%; mixed-income projects may have up to 49% restricted units.
- Cycle: rolling (next: No deadline; applications reviewed first come first served (scored against each other if several arrive within 60 days) and taken to Council. Confirm remaining balance with Joseph Sanfilippo, jsanfilippo@burlingame.org, (650) 558-7264.)
- Layering notes: County layer: every San Mateo County city project competes for the County Affordable Housing Fund NOFA (AHF 14 closed July 15, 2026, next fall 2027), HEART bridge loans and HACSM project-based vouchers; city money is usually the first commitment that unlocks those. Terms are standard county soft debt: 3% simple interest residual receipts, 55 years, DCR 1.15 (1.10 for the first two years of acquisitions), developer fee 5% to 10%, $125 per unit monitoring fee, asset management fee capped at $1,000 per unit or $25,000, 10% hard and 5% soft contingencies, City subordinates its deed of trust but not its regulatory agreement; matching funds score up to 15 points (300% match). The preservation emphasis follows the HOPE advisory committee's priorities. Source is the 2025 NOFA PDF; fund page at burlingame.org/1274.
- Source: https://burlingame.org/DocumentCenter/View/7046/City-of-Burlingame-2025-Affordable-Housing-Fund-NOFA?bidId=
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-07)

**Residential Impact Fee and Commercial Linkage Fee ordinances with on-site affordable alternative (BMC 25.44 and 25.45)**
- Agency: City of Burlingame Community Development Department, Planning Division
- Type: regulatory requirement
- Typical award: Fee-based program that replaced the former inclusionary ordinance (Ordinance 2000 of 2021; Chapter 25.45 amended by Ordinance 2046, adopted March 2, 2026; Chapter 25.44 was not amended). Residential impact fee on residential floor area with a credit for existing uses; exempt are rental projects of 10 or fewer units and for-sale projects of 6 or fewer. FY 2026-27 Master Fee Schedule rates per square foot (lower rate in parentheses where prevailing or area wage is paid): rental 11 units and above $17 ($14) up to 50 du/ac, $21 ($17) at 51 to 70 du/ac, $31 ($26) at 71 du/ac and above; for-sale 7 units and above $36 ($31). On-site alternative allowed as of right: rental projects providing 10% low income plus 5% very low income units in perpetuity, or for-sale projects providing 15% low income units for 55 years, are deemed mitigated; off-site units, preservation conversions, land dedication or other alternatives need Council approval. Commercial linkage fee (Chapter 25.44) on hotel, retail, restaurant, service and office projects adding 5,000 square feet or more: retail $7 ($5), hotel $12 ($10), office up to 50,000 square feet $18 ($15), office over 50,000 square feet $26 ($21) per square foot. Both fees feed the Affordable Housing Fund (about $12 million as of the July 2025 NOFA).
- AMI requirement: On-site alternative units: rental 10% low plus 5% very low income in perpetuity; for-sale 15% low income for 55 years; built concurrently with market units, square footage equal to or greater than market units, finishes at least 60% of market value, same amenities; regulatory agreement recorded. Density bonus projects pay the fee on all market-rate units, including bonus market-rate units, but not on affordable units, with a reduction to the extent affordable units mitigate impacts. Council may waive fees for public or nonprofit public benefit uses.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Not applicable; fees are due before the first building permit at the schedule in effect when the permit issues, and an affordable housing plan is required with the first application when the on-site or other alternative is used. No open round as of November 10, 2026.)
- Layering notes: County layer: every San Mateo County city project competes for the County Affordable Housing Fund NOFA (AHF 14 closed July 15, 2026, next fall 2027), HEART bridge loans and HACSM project-based vouchers; city money is usually the first commitment that unlocks those. Because Burlingame has no inclusionary mandate above the fee, 100% affordable projects rely on the Affordable Housing Fund NOFA (see separate record), County AHF and HACSM PBVs; the fee program is why the fund reached $12 million to $14 million by 2025. Source is the published code chapter on gocodebook.com (Burlingame's code host); residential chapter at .../chapter-25.45-residential-impact-fees. Current per-square-foot rates must be confirmed in the Master Fee Schedule with Planning at (650) 558-7250.
- Source: https://burlingameca.legistar.com/LegislationDetail.aspx?ID=11057&GUID=EE131246-D02F-4820-8342-4EBD27FD837C&Options=&Search=&FullText=1

### City of Calistoga

**Calistoga ADU Fee Assistance Program (Measure D funded connection and impact fee grants) and ADU fee waivers**
- Agency: City of Calistoga Planning and Building Department and Public Works
- Type: fee waiver
- Typical award: Adopted October 6, 2026 as Resolution No. 2026-73 (5-0): the City pays water and sewer connection and capacity charges (about $28,500 per ADU) from Measure D for the first six ADUs or JADUs with complete building permit applications each calendar year, first come first served, one per parcel, no tiered incentive; Council omitted the proposed payment of development impact fees for ADUs over 750 square feet. Funded by Measure D subject to annual appropriation. Existing policy and Gov. Code 66311.5 already exempt ADUs of 750 square feet or less from impact fees.
- AMI requirement: 15-year recorded deed restriction requiring the ADU to be rented at rents affordable to households at or below 160% AMI (per the draft resolution; the adopting motion did not change the AMI level), no rentals under 30 days; violations trigger repayment with interest at the legal judgment rate (10% simple) and a lien.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Rolling: first six complete ADU building permit applications each calendar year, first come first served; unused slots do not carry over. No fixed deadline as of November 8, 2026.)
- Layering notes: Single unit program recorded because it shows how Calistoga deploys Measure D and because the same connection fee burden (about $28,500 per unit) hits small multifamily projects, which can request similar relief as a density bonus financial concession under 17.08.030. Layers with the County Affordable ADU Forgivable Loan ($105,000 maximum, 5-year restriction) and Calistoga's PLHA share (60% ADU loans, 35% rehab through the City of Napa). Fee grants are public funds; prevailing wage exposure for a homeowner ADU is a question for counsel. Source: October 6, 2026 staff report on the City's CivicWeb host (source_url); the May 18, 2026 Housing Advisory Committee report and April 2026 ADU ordinance review were also opened.
- Source: https://calistoga.civicweb.net/document/117944/
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)

**Calistoga Affordable Housing Fund (CMC 17.08.050), capitalized by the Housing Linkage Fee (17.08.040) and inclusionary in-lieu fees**
- Agency: City of Calistoga Planning and Building Department (Senior Planner Andrew Amelung) and Administrative Services; City Council
- Type: loan
- Typical award: Special purpose fund for construction, acquisition, rehabilitation and subsidy of very low, low and moderate income housing. Balance about $2.1 million per the 2023-2031 Housing Element; the FY 2024-25 AB 1600 report shows $247,238 in the linkage fee account at June 30, 2025 to be lent to a future project once enough accumulates (the in-lieu fee account balance is shown only in an image table). Linkage fee (Resolution 2014-110, CPI adjusted): retail and restaurant $4.11, office $2.85, industrial $2.09 per square foot and $1,897.17 per guest room for tourist accommodation; inclusionary in-lieu fee $12,000 per unit (Housing Element figure). Uses to date: $650,000 for the 611 Washington site (2015), $472,000 (2017) and $500,000 (2018) for housing sites, several million dollars of in-lieu fees that funded the 30 unit Calistoga Senior Apartments (2017), and a reported $2 million impact fee loan for the 78 unit Lincoln Avenue Apartments (For the Future Housing), backfilled by future fees and Measure D.
- AMI requirement: Very low, low and moderate income households (up to 120% AMI); 55-year affordability agreements under 17.08.020. Council reviews fund programs and distribution annually.
- Cycle: rolling (next: No NOFA; City Council acts on developer requests and reviews the fund with the annual budget (FY 2026-27 budget adopted June 2026). - Layering notes: Calistoga's fund is the second largest city pool in the county after Napa's and is paired with Measure D TOT money (separate record) and County Affordable Housing Fund loans. Hotel and resort development drives linkage fee revenue, so the fund grows with the visitor economy; the per guest room linkage fee is Calistoga's hotel related housing mitigation (no separate hotel housing fee exists). Stack: CTCAC, HCD, County fund, then City fund and Measure D, HACN project based vouchers for lower income units. City loans are public funds (prevailing wage). Sources opened: FY 2024-25 AB 1600 report on the City's CivicWeb agenda host (source_url), CMC Chapter 17.08 on ecode360, the 2023-2031 Housing Element on hcd.ca.gov. calistogaca.gov pages and PDFs return 403 to scripts; CivicWeb (calistoga.civicweb.net/filepro/documents) is the working route to staff reports.

**Calistoga Affordable Housing Incentives and Density Bonus (CMC 17.08.030) with Missing Middle Housing Combining District (2026)**
- Agency: City of Calistoga Planning and Building Department; Planning Commission and City Council
- Type: density bonus
- Typical award: Entitlement incentive, not a direct subsidy. 17.08.030 implements Government Code 65915 and adds local enhancements: the City may grant an additional density bonus beyond state law, and the Council may grant financial incentives or concessions that produce identifiable cost reductions, including City subsidies for infrastructure improvements or development fees and City sponsorship of mortgage bond financing. The Planning Commission may waive lot size, setback, coverage and height standards; incentives involving City funds, public land, mixed use zoning or Public Works modifications go to the Council. Example: Calistoga Senior Apartments (30 units, 23 very low) approved in 2016 with a 58% bonus; Lincoln Avenue Apartments also used a bonus. In 2026 the Council initiated General Plan, zoning map and code amendments for a Missing Middle Housing Combining District (Opticos Design proposal received October 2026) to allow small multiplex and workforce housing near downtown.
- AMI requirement: State density bonus thresholds; inclusionary units under 17.08.020 count toward qualification; recorded agreement guaranteeing the targeted units for the period set by the Council consistent with state law.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Filed with the development application; Planning Commission hearing concurrent with entitlements, Council hearing where City funds or land are involved. Missing Middle Housing ordinance work (RFP for outreach and CEQA in mid 2026, recommended proposal October 2026) should produce code amendments in 2027; check the CivicWeb staff report folder for hearing dates.)
- Layering notes: Calistoga's code expressly authorizes fee subsidies and bond sponsorship as density bonus concessions, which is the hook for asking the Council to pay impact or connection fees from the Affordable Housing Fund or Measure D. AB 2334 unlimited density for 100% affordable projects applies in Napa County. Pair with the inclusionary record (units count toward the bonus) and the funds records. Density bonus alone does not trigger prevailing wage; City funded fee subsidies do. Code text read on ecode360 (source_url); the May 2026 Missing Middle resolution staff report and the October 2026 Opticos proposal were opened on the City's CivicWeb host (documents 114701 and 118222).
- Source: https://ecode360.com/47985322
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)

**Calistoga Inclusionary Housing Requirements (CMC 17.08.020, Ordinances 709, 733 and 780)**
- Agency: City of Calistoga Planning and Building Department
- Type: regulatory requirement
- Typical award: Requirement, not a subsidy. Applies to subdivisions of five or more parcels or condominiums and rental projects of five or more units. Ownership projects of 5 to 19 units pay the in-lieu fee ($12,000 per unit per the Housing Element, set by resolution) for every unit. Ownership projects of 20 or more units and rental projects of five or more units provide either 20% of units affordable to moderate income households (120% AMI) or 10% affordable to low income households (80% AMI), restricted 55 years; projects with 10 or more inclusionary units must make 10% of them three bedroom. Alternatives with a Commission or Council infeasibility finding: in-lieu fee, land dedication, off site units, or equivalent methods; the Council may waive or reduce the obligation for economic hardship and may assist developers with subsidies or design flexibility (17.08.020(H)).
- AMI requirement: 20% moderate or 10% low income, 55-year recorded affordable housing agreement; ADUs do not count toward the requirement; off site units do not count toward a receiving site's density bonus.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Applies at the first approval through an affordable housing plan; agreement recorded with the final map or before building permit. Ordinance 780 (adopted December 9, 2025 as the Housing Element implementation package) amended 17.08.010 to add special needs groups and set a citywide minimum density of 50% of the maximum (17.03.110).)
- Layering notes: The 20% moderate option is the loosest inclusionary standard in the county and lets market rate rental projects avoid low income units entirely; a developer wanting state density bonus concessions must instead hit the 65915 thresholds, and inclusionary units count toward the bonus. 100% affordable projects satisfy the requirement and generate no fee. In-lieu revenue flows to the Affordable Housing Fund record above. Code text read on ecode360 (source_url); the December 9, 2025 second reading staff report and ordinance were opened on the City's CivicWeb host.
- Source: https://ecode360.com/47985322
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)

**Calistoga Measure D 1% Transient Occupancy Tax for affordable and workforce housing (Resolution 2018-072, effective January 1, 2019)**
- Agency: City of Calistoga Administrative Services Department; City Council allocates
- Type: grant
- Typical award: Special tax of 1% on hotel stays (TOT 12% to 13%) held in a separate account and restricted to affordable and workforce housing programs and services, including land acquisition and donation, building acquisition, rehabilitation and demolition, housing construction, mobile home preservation, housing subsidies and preservation of expiring subsidies. Campaign estimate about $512,325 a year; an annual Government Code 50075.3 report is required. Uses: backfill of deferred fees for the Lincoln Avenue Apartments (78 units) and the proposed ADU Fee Assistance Program (annual transfer subject to appropriation). Council members questioned slow disbursement in 2024, so unspent balance is likely several million dollars; the balance was not found in a text document this pass.
- AMI requirement: Affordable and workforce housing; the City applies it to households up to 120% AMI for development and, for the ADU program, rentals at or below 160% AMI with a 10-year deed restriction.
- Cycle: rolling (next: No NOFA; allocated by City Council with the annual budget (FY 2026-27 budget adopted June 2026) and by resolution for specific projects. Confirm the fund balance with Administrative Services (707-942-2807).)
- Layering notes: Measure D is Calistoga's most flexible housing money (no nexus limits) and the natural source for moderate income units, fee backfill and land purchase (Council FY 2025-26 priorities include developing the City owned Earl and Eddy parcels). Combine with the Affordable Housing Fund for lower income units and the County fund. Parallel measures exist in Napa (F), St. Helena (E) and the County (I), each separate. Sources opened: October 6, 2026 ADU Fee Assistance staff report on CivicWeb (source_url, cites Resolution 2018-072 and the Measure D use restriction) and the Measure D City Attorney impartial analysis PDF (retrieved from calistogaca.gov via WebFetch because the site blocks scripts).

- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)

### City of Capitola

**Affordable (Inclusionary) Housing Ordinance (Municipal Code Chapter 18.02, Ordinance 1062 of 2023) and in-lieu fee**
- Agency: City of Capitola Community and Economic Development Department ((831) 475-7300), with buyer intake by the Housing Authority of the County of Santa Cruz
- Type: regulatory requirement
- Typical award: Requirement, not a subsidy. Projects creating seven or more for-sale units, residential parcels, mobile home parcels or converted condominiums must restrict 15% of units for sale to moderate, low or very low income households; rental projects are exempt from the inclusionary requirement but pay the Affordable Housing Impact Fee under Chapter 18.05 (record below). Alternatives (18.02.050): in-lieu fees at the rate in the Council fee schedule (the certified 2023-2031 Housing Element, Program 2.8, states the inclusionary in-lieu fee and the housing impact fee are both currently $25 per square foot following the 2021 feasibility study), payable at building permit with deferral to certificate of occupancy allowed if the Council finds it aids feasibility and security is provided; off-site units within one mile; land dedication yielding at least 10% more affordable units than otherwise required. In-lieu fees are deposited to the City's housing trust fund for construction of new low and very low income units. Adopted November 2004, amended 2013, 2021 and by Ordinance 1062 (introduced August 24, 2023, adopted September 14, 2023) to update definitions, mobile home sales procedures and eligibility. The City may require more than 15% only when it provides a grant, subsidy, loan, fee waiver or other fiscal benefit.
- AMI requirement: Buyers at or below 120% of Santa Cruz County AMI with assets no more than 1.5 times the income limit (excluding up to $500,000 in retirement plans); affordable price set at 35% of gross income including a 10% down payment; resale restrictions with equity sharing and release payments to the trust fund; condominium conversions of five or more units mitigate through on-site units or in-lieu fees.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Applies at entitlement; in-lieu fee per the schedule in effect at payment. Inventory to date: eight inclusionary condos at Capitola Beach Villas (2008), four other inclusionary homes, seven affordable lots at Turner Lane and 12 new units added citywide in 2025 (69 in the 6th cycle). Housing Element Program 2.8 commits the City to an economic analysis of the inclusionary ordinance during the planning period.)
- Layering notes: Lighter than the County's Measure J only in scope (same 15%, same seven-unit threshold, for-sale only) and much lighter than Watsonville. Rental developers owe the $25 per square foot Affordable Housing Impact Fee instead, so a 100% affordable rental project in Capitola should seek the impact fee exemption or deferral at entitlement. The ordinance text was read from the Council's Ordinance 1062 packet attachment on the City's public agenda host (mccmeetingspublic) because codepublishing.com returned 403 and the City's own chapter PDF link is dead; the City's Affordable Housing page and 2023-2031 Housing Element (certified August 30, 2024) were also opened.
- Source: https://mccmeetingspublic.blob.core.usgovcloudapi.net/capitolaca-meet-ccbbd673a032414cbb411229e1b0e065/ITEM-Attachment-004-f1b24ff134274c7c8e4dec361dd50b51.pdf
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)

**Capitola Affordable Housing Trust Fund (established November 2004) and Affordable Housing Impact Fee ($25 per square foot, adopted 2021)**
- Agency: City of Capitola Community and Economic Development Department ((831) 475-7300)
- Type: loan
- Typical award: Trust fund balance about $144,000 (2023-2031 Housing Element, certified August 2024); revenue to date has come only from inclusionary in-lieu fees, with donations allowed. Uses: matching funds for state and federal sources, rehabilitation loans and grants, feasibility studies, and acquisition-rehab and new construction gap assistance for households at or below 80% AMI; no loan guidelines, per-project limit or NOFA are adopted. Affordable Housing Impact Fee (adopted 2021 after a nexus study): Housing Element Programs 2.7 and 2.8 state the inclusionary in-lieu fee (ownership projects of seven or more units) and the housing impact fee (projects of fewer than seven units) are both $25 per square foot, and a separate impact fee of $6 per square foot applies to multifamily rental housing, which has no inclusionary requirement (the constraints chapter describes the impact fee generally at $25 per square foot, so confirm the rental rate on the current Council fee schedule). Exemptions or waivers for deed-restricted affordable units are not stated. PLHA: state estimate of $630,557 for Capitola over the 2020-2024 cycle. Capitola imposes no park, transportation, administration or childcare exactions; school fees ($4.08 per square foot) and Central Fire District fees ($0.53 per square foot) apply.
- AMI requirement: Trust fund monies are directed to new low and very low income units (Section 18.02.050) and to affordable units for moderate income and below; the impact fee is used exclusively to facilitate affordable housing development.
- Cycle: rolling (next: No application cycle; requests are negotiated with the Community and Economic Development Director and approved by Council. The 52-unit 100% affordable development at 1098 38th Avenue (building permit application filed, 2025 Annual Progress Report) is the first candidate for City assistance; confirm whether the impact fee is waived or deferred for that project.)
- Layering notes: Capitola's fund is too small (about $144,000) to serve as gap financing; its value is as a local match or fee offset in a TCAC or HCD application, with capital from the County's Chapter 17.10 AHIF fund being unavailable inside city limits. The $25 per square foot impact fee is a significant cost on market-rate rental projects (the County charges $2 per habitable square foot on rentals), so mixed-income sponsors should model it; the fee feasibility analysis (EPS, 2021) warned rental development was marginal even before the increase. Density increases are available under the mixed-use AHO successor provisions for 20% lower income units (record below). Sources opened: 2023-2031 Housing Element PDF (DocumentCenter 1797), 2021 fee feasibility analysis (DocumentCenter 699) and the March 23, 2026 Annual Progress Report memo. Audit reclassification: funding_type set to loan because Housing Element Program 2.7 states the City uses the Housing Trust Fund to provide loans and grants (Housing Rehabilitation Loan and Grant Program, feasibility studies, and permanent financing of acquisition-rehab and new construction affordable projects); the balance is only about $144,000. The Housing Element also states a $6 per square foot impact fee for multifamily rental housing alongside the $25 per square foot fee, so confirm the rental rate with the City.
- Source: https://www.cityofcapitola.gov/DocumentCenter/View/1797/Capitola-Housing-Element-Adopted-and-Certified-August-2024
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)

**Density Bonus Ordinance (Municipal Code Chapter 18.03, 2009, amended by the 2024-2025 Housing Element implementation ordinance) and mixed-use density increase for 20% lower income units**
- Agency: City of Capitola Community and Economic Development Department, Planning Division
- Type: density bonus
- Typical award: Chapter 18.03 (adopted 2009) was rewritten by the Council ordinance amending Title 17, Chapter 18.03 and the zoning map to implement the 2023-2031 Housing Element (certified August 30, 2024), establishing density bonus procedures consistent with current Government Code 65915 (up to 50% bonus, 80% or unlimited for 100% affordable projects, 55-year covenants, replacement units) and including specific incentives for child care facilities in affordable projects. The Housing Element also allows density increase requests on mixed-use sites in exchange for 20% of units for lower income households (or a smaller share at extremely low and very low income), with an in-lieu fee option where on-site units are infeasible. The 2025 Annual Progress Report shows zero density bonus applications and zero projects permitted with a bonus; the obsolete Affordable Housing Overlay (-AH) from the 5th cycle is being retired.

- Cycle: rolling (next: Requested with the planning application. Multifamily zoning and Capitola Mall code updates consumed 18 Council and Planning Commission meetings in 2025; the mall site is the City's largest housing opportunity. Verify the adopted date of the Chapter 18.03 amendment with Planning (the public review draft was dated August 26, 2024).)
- Layering notes: State-law mirror with no local bonus enhancement, like Watsonville and unlike the County's Chapter 17.12.065 enhanced bonus. Because rental projects are exempt from the inclusionary ordinance, a developer can combine the 20% lower income mixed-use density increase or the state bonus with the Chapter 18.02 fee structure and seek relief from the $25 per square foot impact fee as a concession. Capitola has no fee waiver program, no city NOFA and no city-controlled development funds beyond the small trust fund; Capitola projects rely on the County's state HOME tenant assistance (which covers Capitola), Housing Authority PBVs, HHAP and state capital. The amending ordinance was read from the Council agenda attachment on the City's public agenda host; codepublishing.com returned 403 and the zoneomics mirror covers only Title 17.

**Carlsbad Housing Trust Fund gap loans (Inclusionary Housing in-lieu fees, housing credit purchases and housing impact fees; CMC 21.85.110 and 21.85.120)**
- Agency: City of Carlsbad Housing and Homeless Services Department (Mandy Mills, Director); recommendations by the Housing Commission, approvals by City Council
- Type: loan
- Typical award: Residual receipts gap loans typically $500,000 to $4.25M per project. Fund sources: in-lieu fees ($4,515 per market rate unit as of 2020, fee study pending), sale of affordable housing credits, housing impact fees, loan interest and fund interest. Inclusionary rental units may not rent above 90 percent of the actual rent of a comparable market unit in the same development (CMC 21.85.090); this is not a cap at 90 percent of the lower income rent limit. **Inclusionary Housing Ordinance, Carlsbad Municipal Code Chapter 21.85 (Ordinance NS-535 as amended through CS-474, 2024), in-lieu fees and inclusionary housing credits**
- Agency: City of Carlsbad Housing and Homeless Services Department and Community Development Department (Planning)
- Type: regulatory requirement
- Typical award: Requirement, not a subsidy. Residential developments of seven or more units must build and restrict at least 15 percent of total approved units (including density bonus units) for lower income households; off-site combined projects are allowed with Council approval and the percentage is computed on total units (market units divided by 0.85). Projects of fewer than seven units pay an in-lieu fee per market rate unit equal to 15 percent of the subsidy needed to make a typical new attached unit affordable to a lower income household ($4,515 as of 2020; schedule set by Council resolution; fee study authorized). Alternatives: off-site units, land dedication, contribution to special needs housing, purchase of surplus affordable housing credits from Villa Loma and other combined projects, and inclusionary credit schedules for units serving lower tiers. Offsets (21.85.100): the City may grant density increases, standards modifications, fee waivers and subsidies at its discretion. Rental inclusionary units required since 2017 (CS-324) after the 2010 Palmer suspension. The ordinance has produced 1,708 affordable units.
- AMI requirement: Lower income households (up to 80 percent AMI); rental units restricted 55 years and no inclusionary unit may rent above 90 percent of the actual rent charged for a comparable market unit in the same development (CMC 21.85.090); inclusionary units must match the tenure of the market units; for-sale units resale restricted.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Applies at entitlement through an Affordable Housing Agreement (21.85.140) before final map or building permit; in-lieu fee per Council resolution schedule, assessed on market rate units at building permit.)
- Layering notes: Fees and credit sales fund the Housing Trust Fund (separate record). Density bonus units count in the 15 percent base, which makes Carlsbad's requirement stricter than the state density bonus tiers; the inclusionary units themselves qualify the project for state density bonus incentives (CMC 21.86, separate record). Master and specific plans must carry inclusionary provisions (21.85.035). Code read on the zoneomics mirror; Housing Element Program 2.1 on hcd.ca.gov.
- Source: https://www.zoneomics.com/code/carlsbad-CA/chapter_56
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)

Prohousing Incentive Program grant application authorized November 4, 2025 (Resolution 2025-179). Chula Vista is on HCD's Prohousing Designation list as of August 10, 2026.

- Cycle: annual NOFA (next: FY 2027-28 Annual Action Plan public review period is expected March to April 2027 (Housing and Homelessness Advisory Commission reviews in spring); PLHA and PIP uses set by Council resolution.)
- Layering notes: HOME has been the main federal layer in City NOFAs along with Low-Mod and LHTF (separate record); PLHA in Chula Vista is committed to shelter operations, not capital, so do not count on it for development. The City is a separate CDBG and HOME entitlement, outside the County Urban County and HOME Consortium (county records). Read on the City's eSCRIBE agenda portal.

**Chula Vista Housing Authority housing successor loans (Low and Moderate Income Housing Asset Fund) and Local Housing Trust Fund gap financing; 2025-2026 affordable housing NOFA**
- Agency: City of Chula Vista Housing and Homeless Services Department (Housing Manager Brian Warwick) acting for the Chula Vista Housing Authority as Housing Successor to the former Redevelopment Agency
- Type: loan
- Typical award: Residual receipts style gap loans of $3M to $4M per project. June 16, 2026: Housing Authority Resolution 2026-006 and Council Resolution 2026-130 approved up to $4,000,000 (recommended as $3,000,000 Low-Mod plus $975,000 Local Housing Trust Fund) to Wakeland Housing for the 68-unit Park Hill UMC project at 545 East Naples Street, conditioned on reducing density to 62 units; Bayview Family Apartments was the alternate. June 10, 2025: up to $4.0M Low-Mod loan to Community HousingWorks for 201 Third Avenue (HA Resolution 2025-004); March 2025: $3.0M Low-Mod for the Palomar Motel permanent supportive housing conversion with Homekey+. The 2024-2025 NOFA offered about $4,000,000 for new multifamily construction (applications due January 15, 2026). Local Housing Trust Fund seeded in 2024 with a $500,000 City match (Resolution 2024-102) and a $500,000 HCD LHTF matching grant (Resolution 2024-163, awarded January 2026). FY 2026-27 Low-Mod administration and homeless prevention appropriation $800,000.
- AMI requirement: 55 year covenants; LMIHAF rules (Health and Safety Code 34176.1: 80 percent AMI maximum, 30 percent of funds to 30 percent AMI units); LHTF units for lower income households.
- Cycle: annual NOFA (next: No open round as of November 8, 2026; no new Housing Authority or LHTF NOFA has been posted since the 2025-2026 round, and the Housing and Homelessness Advisory Commission next meets January 27, 2027. Contact the Housing and Homeless Services Department for the next round.)
- Layering notes: Chula Vista's only city gap source beyond fee waivers. Stacks with Chula Vista Housing Authority conduit bonds (separate record), County HCDS NOFA 2026-03 (Chula Vista projects are eligible for County IHTF and HOME Consortium funds because the City is in the Urban County for HOME), HACSD project-based vouchers and 4 percent LIHTC. Housing Element (2021) noted the Balanced Communities in-lieu fund held only about $1.1M in 2020 and was inadequate for gap financing; the new Housing Inclusionary Fund (CVMC 19.91.070) will add in-lieu fees. Palomar Motel used Homekey+. chulavistaca.gov blocks automated access (403); agendas, minutes and item summaries were read on the City's eSCRIBE agenda portal, but staff report PDFs (filestream.ashx) return 403, so loan terms come from the agenda item text.

**Chula Vista Housing Authority tax-exempt multifamily housing revenue bonds (conduit issuer; 2024 bond policies)**
- Agency: Chula Vista Housing Authority (City Council acting as Authority), staffed by the Housing and Homeless Services Department
- Type: bond
- Typical award: Conduit private activity bonds sized to project debt. Enclave Montecito / Sol Vista (96 units, Otay Ranch Village 2): inducement up to $25 million (HA Resolution 2025-006, August 5, 2025), TEFRA hearing and bond issuance approval April 21, 2026 with an issuance amount not to exceed $14,000,000. Resolution 2024-103 (May 21, 2024) updated the Authority's conduit bond policies so the City is the issuer in most instances rather than JPAs; Master Fee Schedule Chapter 19 sets Housing Authority application, issuance and monitoring fees. Not every Chula Vista deal uses the Authority: Otay Ranch II (270 units, Rock Mountain Road and SR 125) received a $31,220,000 bond allocation on December 10, 2025 with the California Municipal Finance Authority as issuer, and the City's May 19, 2026 TEFRA approval for that project was for the CMFA issuance.
- AMI requirement: Federal 20 percent at 50 percent AMI or 40 percent at 60 percent AMI minimum; City regulatory agreements typically mirror the inclusionary and Low-Mod covenants (55 years).
- Cycle: rolling (next: Rolling; inducement needed before CDLAC application rounds. Contact the Housing and Homeless Services Department for the bond policy and fee schedule.)
- Layering notes: The 2024 policy makes the Housing Authority the default issuer, which keeps issuer fees local, but JPA issuance (CMFA for Otay Ranch II) still occurs; when a JPA issues, the City acts only as TEFRA host. Pairs with 4 percent LIHTC, City Low-Mod and LHTF loans and parkland fee waivers (separate records). Read on the City's eSCRIBE agenda portal; bond policy PDF not downloadable (403). Otay Ranch II issuer confirmed in the CTCAC/CDLAC staff report CA-25-798.

**Inclusionary Housing Ordinance, CVMC Chapter 19.91 (Ordinance 3572, 2024; threshold amended to 20 units by Ordinance 3581, November 2024) and Housing In-Lieu Fee / Housing Inclusionary Fund**
- Agency: City of Chula Vista Housing and Homeless Services Department and Development Services Department
- Type: regulatory requirement
- Typical award: Requirement, not a subsidy. Residential and mixed-use projects of 20 or more units (applications deemed complete on or after July 1, 2024) must restrict 10 percent of units, split as evenly as possible between moderate income and low income households, for rental or for-sale product; density bonus units are excluded from the base. In-lieu fee for fractional units or in place of on-site units set by Council resolution on a square footage basis with different rates for for-sale and rental product (Master Fee Schedule Chapter 16, Resolution 2024-100, May 21, 2024, based on the RSG Inclusionary Policy and In-Lieu Fee Study); paid before the first building permit into the Housing Inclusionary Fund. Alternatives: off-site units within one mile or in TCAC high or moderate resource areas, land dedication, conversion of market rate units, preservation of at-risk units, transferable credits (10 year life), and incentive credits (for example 3.5 rental units of credit per very low income unit provided in place of a moderate unit). Replaced the 1981 Balanced Communities Policy (10 percent of 50 or more units).
- AMI requirement: 55 years rental (45 years ownership); moderate income (up to 120 percent AMI) and low income (up to 80 percent AMI) units; Chapter 19.94 marketing and lottery rules give preference to displaced Chula Vista residents and local residents and workers.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Applies at entitlement; the Council on May 21, 2024 voted 5-0 to set the threshold at 20 units (first reading) and adopted the Chapter 19.91 threshold amendment on November 12, 2024. Code is current through Ordinance 3617 (February 2026). Check the Master Fee Schedule Chapter 16 for the current per square foot in-lieu rate.)
- Layering notes: Projects of 20 to 24 units routinely pay fees, so the Housing Inclusionary Fund will grow slowly; Otay Ranch village developers (for example Village 8 East, Affordable Housing Agreement approved November 4, 2025) satisfy the requirement with dedicated affordable sites that then seek City Low-Mod loans and bonds (separate records). Inclusionary units may count toward the state density bonus (19.91.060). Ordinance text read on the zoneomics code mirror (chulavista.municipal.codes returns 403); Council actions read on the eSCRIBE agenda portal.
- Source: https://www.zoneomics.com/code/chula-vista-CA/chapter_49
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)

**Parkland Acquisition and Development fee exemption for affordable units (Ordinance 3573 amending CVMC 17.10, 2024) and project fee waivers and deferrals for affordable housing**
- Agency: City of Chula Vista Development Services Department and Housing and Homeless Services Department; waivers by City Council resolution
- Type: fee waiver
- Typical award: Ordinance 3573 (second reading May 28, 2024) exempts affordable units from Parkland Acquisition and Development (PAD) fees. Council also waives parkland dedication and in-lieu requirements case by case: Resolution 2026-087 (May 19, 2026) for the 96-unit Sol Vista (Enclave Montecito) affordable rental project in Otay Ranch Village 2 and Resolution 2024-060 (April 9, 2024) for the 100 percent affordable Chula Vista Seniors project at 178 Third Avenue. The Housing Element (Program 4.5) describes Council waivers or deferrals of development impact fees for projects with affordable units and a development fee deferral program for infill rental housing west of I-805. PAD fees in Chula Vista run tens of thousands of dollars per unit, so the exemption is a material subsidy.
- AMI requirement: Deed restricted affordable units; 100 percent affordable projects have received full parkland waivers.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Exemption applies at permit; discretionary waivers go to Council with the project's financing approvals. Confirm the current CVMC 17.10 text and whether other DIFs (transportation, public facilities) can be deferred for a specific project.)
- Layering notes: Fee relief is the second city layer after Low-Mod and LHTF loans (separate record). Waived City fees may be public funds under Labor Code 1720, so projects usually assume prevailing wage once they also take City or bond financing. County HCDS impact fee waivers (county records) do not apply inside the city. Read on the City's eSCRIBE agenda portal (May 19, 2026 and May 2024 agendas); chulavistaca.gov is blocked to scripts.

### City of Citrus Heights

**Affordable housing incentives and density bonus (Citrus Heights Zoning Code Chapter 106.32)**
- Agency: City of Citrus Heights Planning Division
- Type: density bonus
- Typical award: State density bonus law implemented in Chapter 106.32 (Ord. 2019-004, 2022-007): eligibility at 10% lower income, 5% very low income, senior housing, 10% moderate for-sale, 10% foster youth/disabled veteran/homeless, 20% low-income student housing, or land donation of at least one acre; bonus table follows Government Code 65915; minimum project size five units; bonus and incentives for projects with child care facilities; density bonus agreement recorded.

Citrus Heights is built out, so bonus use is on infill and commercial corridor sites (Sunrise Boulevard, Auburn Boulevard) and the Sunrise Tomorrow Specific Plan area at Sunrise Mall, where a 2026 public-private agreement started redevelopment; housing phases there are a future opportunity.

- Agency: City of Citrus Heights Housing and Grants Division (fund); Building Division (fee collection)
- Type: other

Per the July 9, 2026 development impact fee sheet (Resolution 2022-048): office (including medical and assisted living) $1.95, hotel $2.35, commercial and retail $1.77, industrial (flex and R&D) $1.67 per square foot on new commercial development or added commercial square footage, applying to commercial projects both under and over 5,000 square feet; residential is exempt. Rates were raised in June 2022 to the regional average after no update since 1992. Revenue goes to the City Housing Trust Fund administered by the Housing and Grants Division; fund balance and any lending terms not published.

The trust fund is small because the city is built out with little new commercial construction; the realistic city layer is the CDBG, HOME Consortium and PLHA record below plus SHRA bonds under a cooperation agreement.

**Citrus Heights CDBG entitlement, Sacramento County HOME Consortium share, and Permanent Local Housing Allocation (PLHA)**
- Agency: City of Citrus Heights Housing and Grants Division (CDBG and PLHA); SHRA administers the HOME Consortium
- Type: grant
- Typical award: CDBG: about $600,000 a year in entitlement funds plus about $50,000 program income (2024 Action Plan), used mostly for public improvements, public services (15% cap, competitive round each summer) and a housing rehabilitation revolving loan fund. HOME: the City is a member of the Sacramento County HOME Consortium with the County, City of Sacramento and Rancho Cordova; its consortium share funded $3,580,000 to the 47-unit Sunrise Pointe permanent supportive housing project (approved 2018, completed August 2023). PLHA: $1,876,554 five-year allocation from HCD, partly for the Sayonara Drive redevelopment project and a navigator program.
- AMI requirement: Per federal and PLHA rules; HOME at or below 60% AMI with 20% of HOME units at 50% AMI.
- Cycle: annual NOFA (next: No open round as of November 8, 2026. The 2027 CDBG public service application deadline was August 4, 2026 and the 2027 Annual Action Plan went to Council October 28, 2026; the next public service NOFO is expected around July 2027. Multifamily HOME requests go through SHRA's two-round schedule with a Citrus Heights consortium set-aside, confirm with SHRA (916) 440-1393.)
- Layering notes: The HOME Consortium share is the only meaningful city-level capital source: Citrus Heights directed its share to Sunrise Pointe via SHRA rather than running its own NOFA. CDBG is largely spent on infrastructure and services. Federal funds trigger Davis-Bacon (HOME at 12 or more units, CDBG at 8 or more) and NEPA. Sayonara Drive is a City-led acquisition and redevelopment site that may seek a development partner.

### City of Clovis

- Agency: City of Clovis Affordable Housing Program
- Type: fee waiver
- Typical award: Defers 40% (80% AMI units), 45% (50% AMI) or 50% (30% AMI) of City major facility sewer and water fees per restricted unit, up to 120 affordable units per fiscal year. Deferred amount becomes a 0% residual receipts loan, 17-year term for multifamily (30 years single-family) or as senior lenders require.

- Layering notes: Only sewer and water major facility fees are covered; other City impact fees remain due. The residual receipts note sits behind senior and tax credit financing. Clovis states development fees cannot be waived. Pairs with Clovis density bonus and the R-3 density increase to 20 to 30 du/ac.

**Clovis Affordable Housing Trust Fund (Martinez v. City of Clovis Judgment Action Item 2)**
- Agency: City of Clovis Affordable Housing Program (Planning and Development Services)
- Type: loan
- Typical award: Initial $1,000,000 (FY 2023-24) awarded to a senior housing project in planning; City sets aside $100,000 per year for seven years. City also holds its State PLHA formula allocation and releases it through the same webpage when available.

**Clovis Mixed Income Zoning Ordinance (MIZO, Ordinance 26-02) inclusionary requirement and in-lieu fee**
- Agency: City of Clovis Planning and Development Services, Affordable Housing Program
- Type: regulatory requirement
- Typical award: Requirement, not a subsidy. 5% of units in new residential projects of 11 or more units must be deed-restricted affordable, or pay an in-lieu fee of $2.80 per square foot of net livable area of all market-rate units; alternatives include off-site land dedication, off-site construction and acquisition-rehab.
- AMI requirement: Rental MIZO units: half at 50% AMI, half at 80% AMI, 55-year deed restriction. For-sale: 100% at 80% AMI, 45-year restriction.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Approved by City Council April 13 and 20, 2026; applies to projects not deemed complete before it took effect.)
- Layering notes: New for Clovis; required by Action Item 5 of the Martinez judgment (Keyser Marston feasibility study, October 2025). In-lieu revenue should grow the Housing Trust Fund over time, a potential future gap source. Affordable developers partnering with market-rate builders on off-site compliance may find site or fee opportunities. MIZO units cannot use the fee deferral program. The adopted ordinance PDF is a scanned image; terms were read from the City MIZO page, FAQ and December 2025 presentation.

### City of Concord

**Concord Affordable Housing Fund and Concord Housing Fund (Housing Successor Low and Moderate Income Housing Asset Fund, SB 341 report FY 2024/25)**
- Agency: City of Concord Housing and Community Services Division (Housing Successor to the former Concord Redevelopment Agency)
- Type: loan
- Typical award: Housing Successor fund at June 30, 2025: available cash $3,063,558; FY 2024/25 deposits $1,020,949 (including a $615,049 Pavilion loan repayment and $222,705 in loan payoffs); FY 2024/25 expenditures $596,214 (mostly $334,957 in first-time homebuyer loans; no multifamily loan issued); housing loans receivable $33.9 million. The 2023 Housing Element reported a combined Housing Trust Fund balance of about $6.2 million including inclusionary in-lieu fees. Track record: Spring 2018 NOFA offered $14 million of City Affordable Housing Funds and awarded $7.8 million to Resources for Community Development for the 62-unit Rick Judd Commons at 1313-1321 Galindo Street (opened 2025). The Housing Element committed to another NOFA by December 2025 for the remaining funds, including acquisition-rehab of existing affordable complexes; as of November 2026 the City's Affordable Housing Toolkit states there is currently no affordable housing development funding available and invites acquisition-rehab proposals to the Housing Manager.
- AMI requirement: Housing Successor funds must follow Health and Safety Code 34176.1: at least 30% to rental housing for households at or below 30% AMI, no more than 20% for 60% to 80% AMI, balance at or below 60% AMI; the City's five-year extremely-low-income test (July 2020 to June 2025) showed 0% spent on ELI rental housing, so the next multifamily award is likely to be steered to ELI units. City-funded projects carry long-term regulatory agreements (Rick Judd Commons is 55 years).
- Cycle: rolling (next: No NOFA open as of 2026-11-08; the Housing Element's December 2025 NOFA target was not met. Watch Council Housing and Economic Development Committee agendas (stream2.ci.concord.ca.us OnBase agenda portal) for a NOFA tied to the next TCAC rounds; contact Sophia Huckabay, Housing Manager, 925-671-3387.)
- Layering notes: Concord's own fund is modest (about $3 million liquid in the successor fund plus in-lieu balances) and is best used as the local match that unlocks County HOME, CDBG-Housing and Measure X awards (county records: Contra Costa County Affordable Housing Program, Measure X Housing Fund). Lakeside Recapitalization (RCD, Concord) received $2 million County HOME in May 2026 without City funds, showing County money can lead. The City's Resources for Housing Developers page points developers first to County Measure X and HCD. Gap order for a Concord deal: 4% credits and bonds, County HOME or Measure X, then a City successor-fund loan sized to the ELI set-aside, plus fee deferral under CDC 18.185.040(G). The OnBase agenda portal is JavaScript-only, so 2025 and 2026 council items could not be scanned for a NOFA; status taken from the Toolkit page (https://www.cityofconcord.org/1174/Affordable-Housing-Toolkit) and the SB 341 report (source_url).

**Concord Affordable Housing Incentive Program (CDC 18.185.060), Density Bonus Program (CDC 18.185.050) and Transit Station Overlay density increase**
- Agency: City of Concord Community Development Department, Planning Division (zoning@cityofconcord.org, 925-671-3152)
- Type: density bonus
- Typical award: Regulatory incentive, not a cash subsidy. Local alternative to state density bonus law for projects with at least 40% affordable units on parcels of 10,000 square feet or more in RM, RH, CO, NC, CMX, DMX and DP districts: RM density rises from 32 to about 45 units per acre (1 unit per 970 square feet, a 40% bonus), RH from 100 to about 145 units per acre (45% bonus), NC from 24 to about 33 units per acre plus FAR increases; reduced parking and other standard modifications; bonuses under 18.185.060 are not additive with 18.185.050. Separately, the Transit Station Overlay District grants a 25% density and floor area increase (Housing Element program to make it by right with objective standards). State-law density bonuses (Gov. Code 65915) are processed by the Community Development Department under 18.185.050; written findings are required to deny; an affordable housing agreement is recorded before building permit.
- AMI requirement: 18.185.060 rental eligibility: at least 20% of units at very low income plus another 20% at low or very low income (40% total); for-sale: 20% at low or very low plus 20% at up to 100% AMI. 18.185.050 follows state density bonus thresholds.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Applies at entitlement; no deadline. Concord completed its AFFH rezoning (at least 1,000 lower-income units of capacity in higher-resource areas) in March 2026 and allows multifamily by right in commercial and mixed-use districts when objective design standards are met.)
- Layering notes: The 40% affordability threshold for the local incentive program is high, so most mixed-income projects use state density bonus law instead; 100% affordable projects (which qualify for an 80% state bonus or unlimited density near transit) get the most value from the local program's FAR and parking relief in downtown districts. No City fee waiver program exists; fee deferral to first occupancy is available under 18.185.040(G) by affordable housing agreement. Pair with the County's conduit bond issuer and HACCC project-based vouchers (county records). codepublishing.com returned 403; chapter text read on the zoneomics mirror (source_url) and confirmed against the City's Affordable Housing Toolkit page.

- Agency: City of Concord Housing and Community Services Division (Sophia Huckabay, sophia.huckabay@cityofconcord.org) within the Contra Costa HOME Consortium
