**Concord Inclusionary Housing Ordinance (Concord Development Code Chapter 18.185.040, Ord. 24-1) and in-lieu fee (Fees and Charges Schedule, Res. 26-6042.1)**
- Agency: City of Concord Housing and Community Services Division (Sophia Huckabay, Housing Manager, 925-671-3387) with the Planning Division
- Type: regulatory requirement
- Typical award: Requirement, not a subsidy. Projects of 5 or more units: ownership projects 15% inclusionary (7.5% low, 7.5% moderate); rental projects 6% inclusionary (1% very low, 1% low, 4% moderate), with a fixed rotation order for each inclusionary unit. In-lieu fee effective July 1, 2026 (adjusted annually by a construction cost index): $20.13 per gross square foot of market-rate development for ownership projects and $15.10 per gross square foot for rental projects of 10 or more units; fractional-unit fee $256,497 x fractional unit (ownership) and $174,160 x fractional unit (rental). Rental projects may pay the fee for the whole obligation; ownership projects may pay only for fractional units or for 5 to 9 unit projects. In the five years before the 2023 Housing Element the City collected only about $170,000 in in-lieu fees.
- AMI requirement: Rental inclusionary units restricted 55 years and ownership units 45 years under a recorded Affordable Housing Agreement; density bonus units meeting the table income levels count toward the inclusionary requirement; projects of 1 to 4 units, replacement of units lost to natural disaster, and office-to-residential conversions of buildings commercial for at least 5 years are exempt.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Applies at entitlement; fee rate in effect at building permit. Fee schedule last adopted April 28, 2026 (Res. 26-6042.1) effective July 1, 2026; the schedule is readopted each spring. Housing Element Program 12.4 called for a fee update by July 2024, which produced the March 14, 2024 fee basis now indexed annually.)
- Layering notes: Low rental percentage (6%) and a relatively low rental in-lieu fee ($15.10 per square foot) mean most Concord apartment projects either build a handful of moderate-income units or pay the fee; this is why the City's inclusionary fund is small relative to Walnut Creek's. In-lieu revenue goes to a restricted fund alongside the Concord Housing Fund (see the Concord Affordable Housing Fund record). Chapter 18.185.040(G) also lets the City grant development incentives, including deferral of development fees until first occupancy (approved by the City Manager) and expedited processing, when an affordable housing agreement is signed. County Chapter 822-4 inclusionary ordinance does not apply inside Concord. codepublishing.com (the City's code host) returns 403 to automated access; chapter text was read on the zoneomics mirror (https://www.zoneomics.com/code/concord-CA/chapter_4) and the City's 2024 Inclusionary Housing Ordinance Summary Sheet (https://www.cityofconcord.org/DocumentCenter/View/13659). Fee amounts were read from the adopted July 1, 2026 fee schedule (source_url).
- Source: https://www.cityofconcord.org/DocumentCenter/View/15683/Fees-and-Charges-ScheduleJuly-1-2026Res-No-26-60421
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)

**Concord Naval Weapons Station Reuse Project affordable housing requirement (Concord Reuse Project Area Plan, 2012; 2026 Navy EDC Term Sheet; Brookfield master developer)**
- Agency: City of Concord Economic Development and Base Reuse Division, acting as Local Reuse Authority (1950 Parkside Drive MS/56, 925-671-3001)
- Type: regulatory requirement
- Typical award: Requirement and future land pipeline, not a current subsidy. The Area Plan and Reuse Plan call for about 12,000 housing units on roughly 2,300 to 2,400 acres, of which 25% (about 3,000 units) must be affordable to low and very low income households, including 125 supportive housing units, 195 units for people experiencing homelessness and 20 self-help units. The Council approved the Navy financial Term Sheet and revised Brookfield Term Sheet on May 26, 2026 (reported Navy price $628 million over 30 years); the Navy executed the Economic Development Conveyance Term Sheet in September 2026; SB 328 (2026) was signed; Brookfield is now preparing the Specific Plan with community engagement starting early 2027.
- AMI requirement: 25% of all units affordable to low and very low income households per the Area Plan; specific income tiers, phasing and affordable-site delivery mechanics will be set in the Specific Plan and Disposition and Development Agreement.
- Cycle: closed/inactive (next: No affordable developer solicitation yet. Brookfield-led Specific Plan work starts winter 2026-27; first phase entitlements likely 2028 or later. Monitor concordreuseproject.org news flashes and the semiannual CRP Program Report.)
- Layering notes: The largest single affordable pipeline in central Contra Costa (about 3,000 deed-restricted units over three decades), delivered through Brookfield's affordable-site dedications to nonprofit partners rather than City cash; Brookfield also has a project labor agreement with the Contra Costa Building Trades, so prevailing or union wages should be assumed on the affordable sites. Nonprofit developers should position for receiver-site selection and plan to layer County Measure X and HOME, HACCC project-based vouchers and 4% credits on each phase. The 25% figure and homeless and supportive sub-allocations were read in the City's certified Housing Element Programs Document (source_url); the term sheet milestone was read on the Concord Community Reuse Project site (http://www.concordreuseproject.org/m/newsflash/home/detail/95).

**Concord surplus and underutilized public land for affordable housing (Concord Town Center II at 1765 Galindo Street, Downtown Parcels at Laguna and Mount Diablo Streets, Housing Element surplus land program)**
- Agency: City of Concord Housing and Community Services Division and Planning Division (surplus land inventory, Housing Element sites program)
- Type: land
- Typical award: Land contribution rather than cash. City-owned surplus sites declared May 24, 2022: Concord Town Center II, 1765 Galindo Street, 3.1 vacant acres zoned DMX, Housing Element site for 309 lower-income units and an MTC Priority Site; the City issued an RFP in January 2025 and as of November 2025 is negotiating with a selected developer for sale and entitlement. Concord Downtown Parcels 1 (Mount Diablo Street, 3.2 acres, 304 lower-income units) and 2 (Oak Street, 1.1 acres, 106 lower-income units) are surplus DMX sites with an MTC technical assistance grant studying street vacations. BART's Monument Boulevard property (8.2 acres, 782 mixed-income units) is in BART's 2029-2033 solicitation window. The City committed that surplus land used for housing will provide at least 25% of units affordable to lower-income households and to notify a developer list before any disposal.
- AMI requirement: Minimum 25% lower-income units on City surplus land (Surplus Land Act and Housing Element program); the Galindo and Downtown sites are inventoried for lower-income RHNA capacity, so deeper affordability is expected in dispositions.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Town Center II negotiations under way as of November 2025; Downtown Parcels RFP timing depends on the street-vacation study. Join the City's housing interested-parties list (FormCenter link on the Housing and Community Services page) for Surplus Land Act notices.)
- Layering notes: City land write-downs are the main way Concord adds local value to a deal given its small housing fund; a land contribution plus a City successor-fund loan, County HOME or Measure X and a HACCC PBV allocation is the realistic stack. Public land dispositions trigger Surplus Land Act procedures; a below-market disposition or City financial participation is public funds under Labor Code 1720(b), subject to the 1720(c) exemptions. Inventory read from the City's publicly owned and surplus sites list (source_url), linked from the Affordable Housing Toolkit page.

### City of Corona

**Corona Affordable Housing Overlay Zone (AHO), Municipal Code Chapter 17.31**
- Agency: City of Corona Planning and Development Department
- Type: regulatory requirement
- Typical award: Requirement, not a subsidy. By-right approval for housing projects on AHO-designated parcels that reserve at least 20% of units for lower income households; mixed use allowed if at least 51% of floor area is residential; density per General Plan designation; objective design standards apply.
- AMI requirement: At least 20% of units for lower income households at affordable rent or cost, regulatory agreement for at least 30 years.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Ongoing. Adopted by Ord. 3360 (2023). The Action Plan also proposes a General Plan change to allow 100% residential in Mixed-Use designations with the AHO overlay.)
- Layering notes: By-right status removes CEQA and discretionary risk, useful for TCAC readiness. Can be combined with Chapter 17.87 density bonus. The 30-year minimum term is shorter than TCAC's 55 years, so the tax credit term governs.

**Corona CDBG, HOME and HOME-ARP (FY 2026-27 Annual Action Plan)**
- Agency: City of Corona Housing Services Division
- Type: grant
- Typical award: FY 2026-27 CDBG and HOME investment $1,844,570 (draft plan sized on 2025-26 allocations of $1,085,264 CDBG and $409,306 HOME); about $8.9M expected over the 2025-2029 Consolidated Plan. HOME is mostly programmed to tenant-based rental assistance ($656,979 TBRA, 20 households). HOME-ARP allocation $1,801,873 (as amended July 2025) with $1,531,592 for affordable rental housing; the August 6, 2024 2nd Street DDAs commit $529,875 to the Family project and $1,000,000 to the PSH project, so the HOME-ARP rental allocation is effectively fully committed.

- Cycle: annual NOFA (next: Annual Action Plan adopted each spring for a July 1 program year; FY 2027-28 cycle expected to start winter 2026-27. Little HOME is left for development after TBRA; ask Housing Services before counting on it.)
- Layering notes: Corona is its own entitlement, not part of the County Urban County. CDBG has been used for land acquisition for housing ($600K on 2nd Street). Corona does not qualify for a HOME match reduction. The Action Plan also lists SB 2 PLHA as a resource.

**Corona Housing Authority Housing Fund (Fund 291) loans and Housing Authority land (Corona 2nd Street Family Apartments DDA)**
- Agency: Corona Housing Authority (Housing Successor), Community Services Department, Housing Services
- Type: loan

Land was bought from RCTC under the SLA with $600K CDBG and $1.4M Housing Fund; repayment splits 30% to CDBG program income and 70% to the Housing Fund. Corona's Legistar (client corona) has no matters after August 2024, so newer Council items were not reachable through the API.

### City of Daly City

**Daly City Housing Development Finance Agency land offerings and housing successor fund (Carter/Martin site RFQ)**
- Agency: Daly City Housing Development Finance Agency (housing successor to the former Redevelopment Agency), Economic and Community Development
- Type: land
- Typical award: Request for Developer Qualifications issued August 14, 2026 for an approximately 12.5-acre Agency-owned site at Carter and Martin Streets in the Bayshore neighborhood next to the Cow Palace (APNs 005-050-240 and 005-380-020, zoned C-1, former RDA housing asset with Community Redevelopment Law affordability obligations), marketed under Surplus Land Act exemptions for 100 or more units with at least 25% lower income or 100% affordable mixed use. Housing Asset Fund (Fund 11) balance $4,461,128 at June 30, 2025 with net deposits of $298,048 in FY 2024-25.

**Inclusionary Housing Ordinance (DCMC Chapter 17.47, Ordinance 1423) and Affordable Housing Trust Fund**
- Agency: City of Daly City Economic and Community Development, Housing and Community Development Division
- Type: regulatory requirement
- Typical award: Requirement, not a subsidy. Residential developments of 5 or more units: for-sale projects provide 20% of units at moderate income; rental projects provide 10% at low income (rents at 30% of 70% AMI). On-site units required at 15 or more for-sale units and 20 or more rental units; smaller projects pay the Required In Lieu Fee. Rental developers may instead elect the Alternative In Lieu Fee, and rental projects over 50 units may combine on-site units (at least half the requirement or 5% of units) with Required In Lieu Fees. Fees per square foot of livable space (Resolution 18-174, November 26, 2018, as posted by the City): Required In Lieu Fee $45 ownership and $35 rental; Alternative In Lieu Fee $48 (rental only). Projects approved before July 1, 2018 pay the older Affordable Housing Impact Fee ($21 to $35 per square foot after February 1, 2020). Fees go to the Affordable Housing Trust Fund, which the City uses with state and HUD funds for 100% affordable projects (Daly City is a CDBG and HOME entitlement city).
- AMI requirement: 55-year restrictions; on-site units earn state density bonus, waivers and concessions under the Affordable Housing Plan; local preference ordinance (September 2026) gives Daly City residents and workers preference for 70% of affordable units.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Applies at entitlement; Alternative In Lieu Fees are due in full at building permit issuance. In-lieu fees are set by Council resolution (current posted schedule is Resolution 18-174). Daly City is a participant in the 2026 multi-city nexus study.)
- Layering notes: County layer: every San Mateo County city project competes for the County Affordable Housing Fund NOFA (AHF 14 closed July 15, 2026, next fall 2027), HEART bridge loans and HACSM project-based vouchers; city money is usually the first commitment that unlocks those. Daly City's rental requirement (10% low income) is the lightest among the eight cities covered, and the City's own money for 100% affordable deals comes from the Trust Fund, its HOME and CDBG entitlements and the housing successor fund rather than a NOFA; the County's $14 million Midway Village loan and City loans reported at about $7.7 million for the 72-unit 493 Eastmoor project (CMFA bonds up to $25 million authorized February 9, 2026, per news summaries not opened) show the pattern. Source is the ordinance PDF on dalycity.org; the fee amounts are unconfirmed, hence needs_confirmation. Contact hcd@dalycity.org, (650) 991-8068.

- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-07)


### City of Davis

**Affordable Housing Ordinance (Davis Municipal Code Article 18.05, Ordinance 2646) and Rental Housing Inclusionary Guidelines (Resolution 25-002, in-lieu fee)**
- Agency: City of Davis Social Services and Housing Department, Affordable Housing Manager Iris Grace and Director Dana Bailey; Community Development Department for entitlements
- Type: regulatory requirement
- Typical award: Requirement, not a subsidy. Rental projects of 20 or more units must provide 15% affordable units, half low income and half very low income (ordinance adopted July 2023). Resolution 25-002 (adopted January 7, 2025, 4 to 1) set the in-lieu fee for non-discretionary rental projects at $250,000 per required affordable unit and $125,000 for a fractional unit when the whole units are built on site. Staff had proposed $608,000 per unit (cost of the most recent all-affordable project) and the Council rejected $369,000. The fee is indexed annually by the construction cost index with a one-time payment or a multi-year option at a 10-year net present value. Ownership projects have separate land dedication and in-lieu options approved case by case.
- AMI requirement: 15% of rental units (7.5% low income at 80% AMI and 7.5% very low income at 50% AMI) with long-term covenants; alternatives (in-lieu fee, land dedication, Project Individualized Plan) must deliver equivalent affordability value and discretionary projects need Council approval of the alternative.
- Cycle: rolling (next: None (ordinance). Council on December 16, 2025 directed staff to amend the land dedication option as soon as possible; an amendment requiring land dedicators to also provide funding was introduced in March 2026 per local coverage. A broader revision of the ownership inclusionary rules is in progress. Verify current text with the Affordable Housing Manager, (530) 757-5602.)
- Layering notes: The ordinance is the engine behind Davis's two main local tools: in-lieu fees and negotiated contributions flow to the City Housing Trust Fund, and land dedication produces fully improved affordable sites (see the Housing Trust Fund and land dedication records). For a 100% affordable developer this means partnering with a market-rate applicant on a dedicated site, or seeking Housing Trust Fund gap money. Staff's October 21, 2025 informational report found production lagging RHNA and proposed a mandatory financial review when a developer claims infeasibility; Councilmembers asked staff to look at 10% extremely low income in place of part of the 15% requirement. Section 40.27.110 of the zoning code ties Article 18.05 to state density bonus law. Stack with county records: no Yolo County housing trust fund or county NOFA exists; Yolo County Housing project-based vouchers and the state CDBG and HOME competitions are the county-level layers. Access: cityofdavis.org (Akamai) returns 403 to scripts and to WebFetch; the Council minutes on documents.cityofdavis.org open and were used. The Resolution 25-002 text (showpublisheddocument/20364) and the October 21, 2025 staff report could not be opened.
- Source: https://documents.cityofdavis.org/Media/CityCouncil/Documents/PDF/CityCouncil/CouncilMeetings/Minutes/2025/Minutes-2025-01-07-City-Council-Meeting.pdf
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)

**Affordable housing land dedication sites under Article 18.05 (Village Farms 16-acre dedication, Project Individualized Plan Exhibit E)**
- Agency: City of Davis Community Development Department and Social Services and Housing Department (Council subcommittee negotiates development agreements)
- Type: land
- Typical award: Land, not cash. Village Farms Davis (Development Agreement Exhibit E, approved December 16, 2025 and revised January 13, 2026) dedicates 16 acres to the City for 280 low and very low income units on fully improved sites (no more than 4 parcels, none under 2.5 acres), to be developed with a qualified affordable housing developer selected by the City, with the City to endeavor to add 80 moderate income units. Baseline features now require construction to commence on 100 affordable units before Phase 3 and no permits beyond the first 150 until that starts; the City holds an option after 150 units. Together with the $6 million Housing Trust Fund payment the package is valued by the applicant at over $6 million plus land.
- AMI requirement: 280 low and very low income units (plus up to 80 moderate) on dedicated land; affordability covenants set in the City's developer agreement.
- Cycle: closed/inactive (next: No open round as of November 10, 2026. Village Farms dedication will not proceed after the reported Measure V defeat; watch for the Willowgrove affordable housing plan if Measure W is certified and for any other Article 18.05 dedications.)
- Layering notes: This is how 100% affordable developers get sites in Davis: the inclusionary ordinance's land dedication option plus Housing Trust Fund money, then compete for 9% credits, MHP, AHSC or HCD Super NOFA money. Vice Mayor Vaitla's December 2025 direction to amend the land dedication option (so dedicators also provide resources) led to a March 2026 ordinance introduction, so later projects should carry cash with the land. Earlier dedications (Cannery, Chiles Ranch, Bretton Woods) produced sites now built or in pipeline. Davis has no city-owned surplus land program beyond these dedications. Pair with Yolo County Housing PBVs and the CoC HHAP money for supportive units.

**CDBG and HOME entitlement allocations (2025-2029 Consolidated Plan, Resolution 25-061) and PLHA formula allocation**
- Agency: City of Davis Social Services and Housing Department, Housing and Grants Management (Director Dana Bailey)
- Type: grant
- Typical award: Davis is a CDBG entitlement city and a HOME participating jurisdiction. HUD formula allocations: FY 2025 CDBG $730,016 and HOME $323,760 (about $1.05 million combined); FY 2026 CDBG $700,471 and HOME $309,807 (about $1.01 million). Council adopted the 2025-2029 Consolidated Plan and the Program Year One (2025) Annual Action Plan on April 15, 2025 (Resolution 25-061). HOME has historically funded first-time homebuyer loans and rental project gap loans; CDBG funds public services, facilities and homelessness programs. PLHA: HCD's 2024-2028 Formula Allocation NOFA (July 16, 2026) lists Davis at $212,632 for CY 2024 and $227,760 for CY 2025, with an estimated $1,328,950 over five years; staff said in February 2025 that PLHA would go to homeownership opportunities.
- AMI requirement: CDBG at or below 80% AMI; HOME at or below 80% AMI with at least 90% of rental assistance at 60% AMI and 20% of units at 50% AMI in projects with 5 or more HOME units.
- Cycle: annual NOFA (next: No open round as of November 10, 2026. The Program Year 2027 Action Plan process is expected winter to spring 2027 with a public hearing typically in April; confirm amounts and the HOME set-aside with Grants Management, (530) 757-5602.)
- Layering notes: Federal money is the only recurring Davis source for rental projects, but the annual HOME amount is small (hundreds of thousands) and competes with homebuyer uses; combine with Housing Trust Fund gap money and state credits. Davis-Bacon applies at 12 or more HOME-assisted units or 8 or more CDBG-assisted units; state prevailing wage turns on the local or state funds in the deal and the Labor Code 1720(c) exemptions (see prevailing_wage_basis). Davis also receives HHAP through the Davis, Woodland/Yolo County CoC (see county record) for supportive housing operations. Yolo County's own CDBG and HOME (state non-entitlement) cover only unincorporated areas, so there is no overlap. Blocked: the Grants Management page and the Consolidated Plan PDF on cityofdavis.org (403); the April 15, 2025 minutes on documents.cityofdavis.org were opened and record the adoption.

**City of Davis Housing Trust Fund (in-lieu fees and negotiated developer contributions, Article 18.05)**
- Agency: City of Davis Social Services and Housing Department (Housing Trust Fund administered by the Affordable Housing Manager; Social Services Commission reviews affordable housing plans)
- Type: loan
- Typical award: Project-specific gap contributions sized by Council; no published NOFA or guidelines found. Revenue is in-lieu fees under Resolution 25-002 ($250,000 per unit) plus negotiated contributions from peripheral Measure J/R/D projects: Village Farms Exhibit E (approved December 16, 2025, revised January 13, 2026) commits $6,000,000 to the Housing Trust Fund ($2 million with dedication of the first land site, $1 million at the first building permit, $3 million before any Phase 3 building permit); Willowgrove's plan reportedly adds $1.8 million. Earlier years the fund was small (the 2023 single-family in-lieu fee was about $82,000 per unit) and the City has historically funded projects such as Paul's Place and Creekside from it. Current balance not published in any document opened this pass.
- AMI requirement: Low and very low income units with long-term covenants; Council direction prioritizes very low and extremely low income and deed-restricted ownership.
- Cycle: rolling (next: No NOFA as of November 10, 2026. Village Farms contributions will not arrive because Measure V failed in June 2026 (press reports of the certified count). Willowgrove (Measure W) is passing in Yolo County unofficial results; confirm its Housing Trust Fund contribution and timing with the Affordable Housing Manager, (530) 757-5602.)
- Layering notes: The only local soft money in Davis. Sized to projects on the dedicated land sites first (the Village Farms plan says the money should support affordable housing on the dedication sites but may be used elsewhere consistent with the plan). Local and state funds are public funds under Labor Code 1720(b), so state prevailing wage applies unless a 1720(c) exemption fits the deal, such as 1720(c)(5)(E) for below-market loans with at least 40 percent of units restricted 20 years at or below 80 percent AMI (see prevailing_wage_basis). Councilmembers raised formalizing the fund into a structured trust (April 2026). Davis has no RDA successor housing fund. Blocked: cityofdavis.org pages and the Village Farms Exhibit E staff reports (403); facts are from the December 16, 2025 and January 13, 2026 Council minutes on documents.cityofdavis.org, which did open.

**Density bonus (Davis Municipal Code Section 40.27.110, deviations under Article 18.05 and state density bonus law)**
- Agency: City of Davis Community Development Department, Planning Division
- Type: density bonus
- Typical award: Regulatory. Section 40.27.110 (Ordinance 2322, 2008) allows deviations from zoning standards in accordance with the density bonuses and incentives provided for affordable housing by Article 18.05 and state density bonus law (Government Code 65915). Davis has no local enhancement beyond the state schedule; Article 18.05 alternatives (in-lieu fee, land dedication) are the local layer.
- AMI requirement: State density bonus law thresholds (5% very low, 10% low, 100% affordable up to 80% bonus and unlimited near transit) or Article 18.05 inclusionary units.
- Cycle: rolling (next: None; applied with the entitlement application. Davis is updating its General Plan (2025 to 2027), which may fold density bonus text into a zoning rewrite.)
- Layering notes: Standard state law implementation; Davis downtown zones (Article 40.13) are form-based and the 2021-2029 Housing Element rezoned sites to meet RHNA, so the bonus matters most on R-3 and R-HD infill sites. Davis is not Prohousing designated. No fee waiver program for affordable units exists at the City level; development impact fees are set by Council annually. The code mirror (zoneomics) was used because qcode.us is blocked; confirm against the official code.

### City of East Palo Alto

**Affordable Housing Preservation Program (over-the-counter fund)**
- Agency: City of East Palo Alto Housing Division
- Type: loan
- Typical award: Council allocated just over $2 million to the program; applications accepted over the counter once the NOFA is released (anticipated March 2026 or later, launch planned for 2026). Draft guidelines (November 26, 2024) were developed with the County Equity Innovation Fund and HEART.
- AMI requirement: Conversion of market-rate housing to income-restricted housing or preservation and extension of existing restrictions; anti-displacement focus.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Over the counter after NOFA release; status of the 2026 release not confirmed. Contact housing@cityofepa.org, (650) 853-3189.)
- Layering notes: County layer: every San Mateo County city project competes for the County Affordable Housing Fund NOFA (AHF 14 closed July 15, 2026, next fall 2027), HEART bridge loans and HACSM project-based vouchers; city money is usually the first commitment that unlocks those. Small but flexible; pairs with the County's preservation financing and the Bay Area Preservation Pilot. The City's broader funding plan (Affordable Housing Strategy 2024-2028, adopted February 6, 2024) commits 50% of Measure HH office parcel tax revenue ($2.50 per square foot on office over 25,000 square feet, 2018) to creation and preservation of affordable housing, cites capacity to fund up to 122 units in 100% affordable developments, and adds Measure JJ gross receipts tax revenue (about $1.45 million to $1.7 million a year, approved November 2024); the City has not posted a new-construction NOFA, so developers should approach the Housing Division directly. Source is the preservation program page.
- Source: https://www.cityofepa.org/housing/page/affordable-housing-preservation
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-07)

**Inclusionary Housing Ordinance (Chapter 18.37) with in-lieu fees and Affordable Housing Commercial Linkage Fee**
- Agency: City of East Palo Alto Housing Division, 1960 Tate Street
- Type: regulatory requirement
- Typical award: Requirement, not a subsidy. Projects of 5 or more units: rental 20% on-site (5% at 35% AMI, 10% at 50% AMI, 5% at 60% AMI) or, with Council approval, 25% off-site or an in-lieu fee of $299,200 per required unit (FY 2025-26); for-sale 20% on-site (10% median, 10% moderate) or 25% off-site or $268,800 per unit in lieu. Projects under 5 units pay a per-unit share ($59,840 to $239,360 rental). Commercial linkage fee (Resolution 118-2020, effective October 31, 2020, ENR-indexed each April 1) applies to office, R&D and medical office; retail, restaurant, service and hotel are charged $0; the City plans to update it in 2027 after the multi-city nexus study.
- AMI requirement: Ordinance 425 (November 19, 2019) and Guidelines (Resolution 142-2020); income limits follow HCD; SB 9 lot splits exempt (September 2025); in-lieu fees reset each July (FY 2025-26 adopted July 16, 2025).
- Cycle: rolling (next: Applies at entitlement; fee schedule updated each July (comprehensive fee schedule effective July 18, 2026). East Palo Alto is a 2026 multi-city nexus study participant.)
- Layering notes: County layer: every San Mateo County city project competes for the County Affordable Housing Fund NOFA (AHF 14 closed July 15, 2026, next fall 2027), HEART bridge loans and HACSM project-based vouchers; city money is usually the first commitment that unlocks those. East Palo Alto has the deepest rental targeting in the county (a 35% AMI tier) and uses the fees plus Measure HH and Measure JJ revenue to fund 100% affordable projects such as Colibri Commons and Light Tree; 148 inclusionary units were in the pipeline in 2024. Source is the City's inclusionary housing page; fee amounts from the in-lieu fee page and the linkage fee notice (updated October 16, 2026).
- Source: https://www.cityofepa.org/housing/page/inclusionary-housing
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-07)


### City of Elk Grove

**City of Elk Grove Affordable Housing Fund and Affordable Housing Impact Fee (Municipal Code Chapters 16.88 and 16.89)**
- Agency: City of Elk Grove Housing and Public Services Division (fund and RFPs); Finance Department (fee collection)
- Type: loan
- Typical award: Fee-funded local gap loan fund. New fees adopted September 23, 2026 (Resolution 2026-202, adopting the June 30, 2026 EPS nexus study) and Ordinance 09-2026 (second reading October 14, 2026), effective January 1, 2027, replacing the 2013 per-unit fees ($6,396 per single or two-unit dwelling and $3,837 per multi-unit dwelling in 2025): residential $3.59 per square foot single-unit, $3.29 owner-occupied multi-unit and $1.46 renter-occupied multi-unit; nonresidential $2.15 shopping center, $2.29 office (was $0.00), $0.39 industrial (manufacturing and warehouse merged), $1,146.75 per hotel room, plus per-unit rates for other uses, all including the 3% administrative fee. Fees were set at roughly 7.5% of the maximum justifiable fee. The City releases an RFP when the fund balance can support a project (generally about $5 million); the City reports $84 million lent to sixteen projects since inception (developer page, not opened).
- AMI requirement: Ordinance 09-2026 expands fund uses to very low, low and moderate income households (previously very low and low) and adds EGMC 16.88.080 authorizing a local preference policy for deed-restricted rental and ownership units, consistent with fair housing law. Deed-restricted affordable housing is exempt from the residential fee.
- Cycle: rolling (next: New fee schedule effective January 1, 2027. No open RFP found as of 2026-11-10; watch elkgrove.gov/affordable-housing/developers and the City's purchasing RFP page. Contact Joshua Tovar, Management Analyst, jtovar@elkgrove.gov, or the Housing and Public Services Division, (916) 683-7111.)
- Layering notes: Elk Grove is an impact-fee jurisdiction (like the City and County of Sacramento) with no inclusionary option, so market-rate rental projects pay the fee rather than build units; the 2026 renter-occupied rate was deliberately set low ($1.46 per square foot recommended) because the nexus study found multifamily infeasible at higher fees. Elk Grove is outside the SHRA lending area (SHRA finances in other cities only under cooperation agreements), so this fund, state sources and Elk Grove's own PLHA are the local layer. Past RFPs tied fund loans to City-owned sites (Sheldon Farms North and Old Town, 2023). elkgrove.gov HTML pages and codepublishing.com return 403 to automated access, but council attachment PDFs open; facts here come from the Sept 23, 2026 staff report (item 8.2), Ordinance 09-2026 (Oct 14, 2026 item 7.5) and the Sept 23 and Oct 14 minutes. The North State BIA supported the staff recommendation at the hearing.
- Source: https://elkgrove.gov/sites/default/files/city-files/city-government/city-council/council-meetings/attachments/2026/09-23-26-8-2.pdf
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)

**Density bonus and developer incentives (Elk Grove Municipal Code Chapter 23.50) and streamlined housing approvals (Chapter 23.17)**
- Agency: City of Elk Grove Development Services, Planning Division
- Type: density bonus
- Typical award: State density bonus law implemented in Chapter 23.50 (eligibility at 10% lower income, 5% very low income, senior, 10% moderate for-sale, special needs, 100% affordable), one bonus with concessions per Government Code 65915; Section 23.50.080 (Ord. 12-2022) exempts affordable units built under the chapter from the Chapter 16.88 affordable housing fee. Chapter 23.17 provides ministerial streamlined approvals for infill affordable projects, affordable housing in commercial zones, mixed-income projects along commercial corridors, middle-class housing, adaptive reuse, faith and higher-education land, and urban subdivisions (titles confirmed; detailed standards not read this pass).
- AMI requirement: Per state law; fee exemption applies only to the deed-restricted affordable units.

The fee exemption in 23.50.080 is the useful local layer: a density bonus project avoids the per-unit affordable housing fee on its affordable units, and the 2026 fee update proposed keeping the renter multi-unit fee low. Elk Grove adopted its Chapter 23.17 streamlining menu in response to the 2021-2029 Housing Element.

- Agency: City of Elk Grove Housing and Public Services Division

### City of Escondido

**Density Bonus and Residential Incentives Ordinance (Escondido Zoning Code Article 67, Sections 33-1410 to 33-1421) and Development Fee Deferral Policy**
- Agency: City of Escondido Development Services Department, Planning Division
- Type: density bonus
- Typical award: Requirement, not a subsidy. Article 67 grants state law density bonuses (up to 50 percent; 80 percent or unlimited for 100 percent affordable projects) and incentives and concessions to projects of five or more units (three or more in some areas), including student housing and child care provisions, in-lieu incentives of equivalent land value, land donation bonuses and a sliding scale (one percent bonus per one percent increase above the 10 percent very low income minimum); amended in 2020, 2021 and 2022 for AB 2345. Agreement processing and administrative fee apply (33-1421). The 2012 Development Fee Deferral Policy lets residential projects of five or more units defer development fees to occupancy (up to one year from permit). Density transfer programs exist in the Downtown and East Valley Specific Plan areas (Resolution 2019-69; Ordinance 2023-10).
- AMI requirement: Government Code 65915 tiers; affordability tenure per 33-1418 (55 years rental).
- Cycle: rolling (next: Applies at entitlement; density bonus request form on escondido.gov. A zoning ordinance update with lot consolidation incentives was planned for 2025; confirm current Article 67 text with Planning.)
- Layering notes: State conforming with no local fee waiver: a 2024 staff report noted neither state law nor the Municipal Code requires the City to give direct financial assistance to density bonus projects. The fee deferral is the only fee relief. Escondido is not on HCD's Prohousing list (as of August 10, 2026). Pair with City HOME and recycled RDA funds (separate records) and County HCDS NOFA. Article text read on the zoneomics code mirror; Housing Element and APR read on escondido.gov.

- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)

- Agency: City of Escondido Development Services Department, Housing and Neighborhood Services Division, 201 North Broadway, Escondido 92025; Danielle Lopez, Housing and Neighborhood Services Manager, (760) 839-4841

- Agency: City of Escondido Housing and Neighborhood Services Division with the California Community Housing Agency (CalCHA)
- Type: tax abatement
- Typical award: Not a direct subsidy. As a CalCHA member, the City allows CalCHA to acquire existing market rate apartment communities with governmental purpose bonds; CalCHA's property tax exemption converts the complexes to rent restricted units for low, median and moderate income households up to 120 percent AMI with rents capped at 35 percent of the applicable AMI and annual increases capped at 4 percent; no displacement of existing tenants. Program 2.3 commits the City to identify properties for acquisition; no Escondido acquisition was confirmed this pass.

The welfare exemption for nonprofit LIHTC owners (county record) remains the tax tool for deed restricted projects. Read in the draft 2021-2029 Housing Element on escondido.gov; program status not confirmed.

### City of Fairfield

**Fairfield CDBG and HOME, multifamily rehabilitation NOFAs and PLHA formula allocation**
- Agency: City of Fairfield Housing Services Department (HUD CDBG entitlement; state HOME and CalHome grantee; HCD PLHA formula recipient)
- Type: grant
- Typical award: CDBG multifamily rehabilitation NOFAs: about $475,000 CDBG offered in 2024 (due September 24, 2024) and about $400,000 offered July 22, 2026 (due September 4, 2026, rehab complete by June 30, 2027, minimum score 75) per City news releases found in search but not opened. FY 2026-27 Annual Action Plan reportedly budgets $115,120 for multifamily rehabilitation. State HOME grant of $700,000 obtained (2024-2025) and $800,000 MORE grant applied for. PLHA formula: Fairfield CY 2024 $274,392, CY 2025 $293,914, five-year 2024-2028 estimate $1,714,950 (HCD NOFA); Housing Element dedicates 20% of PLHA to homeownership, and three PLHA down payment loans closed in FY 2025-26.

- Agency: City of Fairfield Community Development Department, Planning Division

Density bonus application fee set by Council resolution. Applications processed concurrently with the project entitlement and decided by the same review authority (Section 25.41).

**Fairfield Housing Authority Project-Based Vouchers**
- Agency: Fairfield Housing Authority (City of Fairfield Housing Services Department), 707-428-7392
- Type: rental assistance
- Typical award: HCV-only agency (about 750 vouchers to issue per the March 2026 Council Goals report; 894 vouchers administered at the start of 2024 per the 2024 Administrative Plan found in search). The FY 2026-27 PHA Annual Plan approved by Council April 7, 2026 reportedly adds 50 project-based vouchers to a program with over $10,000,000 in annual HAP. Existing PBV sites include Laurel Gardens. Council approved PBV plus housing trust fund financing for a multifamily preservation project in late 2025.

The City's Apr-Jun 2026 quarterly report says HUD determined a HAP shortfall of over $200,000 in December 2025, new voucher issuance is halted until HAP spending is resolved, and the HCV and PBV waiting lists were opened. Confirm with the Housing Authority whether any new PBV commitments are being made.)

Fairfield's PHA covers only the city; Suisun City, Vacaville, Vallejo and Solano County each have their own (separate records). As of June 2026 the Fairfield Housing Authority had spent its full HAP budget authority and halted new voucher issuance after a HUD-determined shortfall, so new PBV commitments are doubtful until funding is restored. **Fairfield Housing Trust Fund and Low/Moderate Income Housing (Housing Successor) funds, developer NOFA (August 2024 round)**
- Agency: City of Fairfield Housing Services Department (Fairfield Housing Authority as Housing Successor), 1000 Webster Street, Fairfield, 707-428-7392
- Type: loan
- Typical award: Gap loans from the City's Housing Trust Fund and former redevelopment Low/Mod funds. The August 2024 NOFA (Council goal HS 3.1, estimated $2,100,000) drew four proposals; Council approved financing for two. The March 2026 Council Goals report shows Danco approved for $1,500,000 with a Homekey+ application for a combined $23,500,000. A 2024 City press release (not opened, fairfield.ca.gov returns 403) described the round as about $1,000,000 of Local Housing Trust Fund money plus CDBG, applications due September 24, 2024. Closing of the 1600 Woolner site generated $1,121,000 in Low/Mod funds; the City also obtained a $700,000 state HOME grant and applied for an $800,000 MORE grant. Disposition of Successor Agency properties (Sem Yeto school site, Highway 12 parcel) is meant to replenish Low/Mod funds; an LOI for Sem Yeto was under review in December 2025. Council has also approved project-based voucher and housing trust fund financing for a multifamily preservation deal (Dec 2025 report).
- AMI requirement: Extremely low to moderate income households; Housing Element Action 3.1 requires long-term covenants (45 to 55 years) on City-assisted units.
- Cycle: rolling (next: No NOFA open as of November 2026. The City issues NOFAs when funds accumulate (last August 2024). Housing Element Action 3.2 commits to a NOFA a year before any tax credit compliance period ends for at-risk projects. Contact Housing Services before the next TCAC round.)
- Layering notes: Fairfield is the only Solano city with a working local trust fund plus Low/Mod successor money, so it is the first local gap source after the Solano County Housing Trust Fund (county record; the County put $4,500,000 ARPA through Fairfield for an EAH project in 2022 and proposed $400,000 for EAH's Tabor Commons in Aug 2026). Stack order for a Fairfield 9% deal: TCAC credits, City trust fund or Low/Mod loan, County SCHTF, Fairfield Housing Authority PBVs, fee deferral (separate record). Housing Element Action 1.1 says the Trust Fund is fed by a Housing Trust Fund fee and the City will study increasing it, dedicating excess property transfer tax, and a housing bond. Fairfield submitted a Prohousing Designation application in 2024 and was resubmitting for more points in 2025 (designation not confirmed), which would add scoring preference in state programs. Local and state funds are public funds under Labor Code 1720(b), so state prevailing wage applies unless a 1720(c) exemption fits the deal, such as 1720(c)(5)(E) for below-market loans with at least 40 percent of units restricted 20 years at or below 80 percent AMI (see prevailing_wage_basis). fairfield.ca.gov and its showpublisheddocument PDFs return 403 to scripts and WebFetch; the City's ClearPoint Council Goals reports on transparency.fairfield.ca.gov were the opened record.

**Fairfield affordable housing Fee Deferral Program (Municipal Code Chapter 5, Article I), Fee Credit Bank and Train Station Specific Plan fee reduction**
- Agency: City of Fairfield Community Development Department (Director approves deferrals and fee credits)
- Type: fee waiver
- Typical award: Deferral, not waiver: affordable projects defer certain building and development fees to certificate of occupancy or permanent financing. Fee Credit Bank: credits from demolished buildings (water and sewer connection fees, not school or Solano County public facilities fees) can be applied to affordable projects. Train Station Specific Plan area: 25% reduction in development fees for multifamily units above 24 units per acre. ADUs under 750 square feet exempt from park, Cordelia open space, sewer connection and County public facilities fees; all ADUs exempt from a long list of City fees. No published dollar value of deferrals.
- AMI requirement: Deferral: multifamily must be at least 50% moderate-income and 25% low-income units, 55-year rental covenant (45 years ownership). Fee credits: low- and moderate-income units with a covenant of up to 55 years.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Apply to the Community Development Department with the building permit; no cycle. The City was updating its AB 1600 traffic and Northeast (TSSP) fees in 2022-2023; confirm current fee schedule.)
- Layering notes: Deferral improves construction-period cash flow but fees are still paid, so budget them. Fee credits are a real reduction when a demolition site has banked credits; ask the Director for the current bank balance. Solano County public facilities fees cannot be deferred or credited by the City (County record: no County waiver program). A fee credit or reduction is public funds under Labor Code 1720(c) if above de minimis, hence unclear. Source is the HCD-posted October 2022 review draft of the 2023-2031 Housing Element (adopted February 7, 2023, certified April 10, 2023 per the City's housing element site, not opened); Chapter 5 of the Municipal Code itself is on a blocked code host.
- Source: https://www.hcd.ca.gov/housing-elements/docs/fairfield-6th-draft100622.pdf
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)


### City of Folsom

**Density bonus and other developer incentives (Folsom Municipal Code Chapter 17.102)**
- Agency: City of Folsom Community Development Department, Planning Services
- Type: density bonus
- Typical award: State density bonus law implemented in Chapter 17.102 (Ord. 1145, 2011) for very low, low, moderate and senior households, with additional incentives or concessions per Government Code 65915(i), an added bonus for child care facilities, and resale and occupancy restrictions on moderate income units. Multifamily objective design standards were adopted in late 2025 to enable ministerial review.
- AMI requirement: Per state law (affordable rent defined as 30% of 50% or 80% AMI).
- Cycle: rolling (next: Rolling at entitlement.)
- Layering notes: No local enhancement beyond state minimums identified; the chapter predates recent state amendments and defers to Government Code 65915 where they conflict. The 2024 General Plan and Folsom Plan Area amendments added capacity for about 6,046 units in targeted multifamily areas, which is where bonus requests will land. Inclusionary projects may also request fee waivers or deferrals under 17.104.070 and Chapter 16.60.
- Source: https://www.zoneomics.com/code/folsom-CA/chapter_53
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)

**Folsom Affordable Housing Loan (AHL) Program (Folsom Housing Fund 238 and Housing Trust Fund 221)**
- Agency: City of Folsom Community Development Department, Housing Services (loan consultant TDA, Inc.)
- Type: loan
- Typical award: Gap loans from the City's inclusionary in-lieu fee fund (Fund 238) and commercial housing trust fund (Fund 221). FY 2025-26 Mid-Year Budget (March 10, 2026): Fund 238 cash $23,960,396 at July 1, 2025, projected $23,850,147 at June 30, 2026; Fund 221 cash $951,872, projected $858,319. FY 2024-25 AB 1600 report: Fund 238 available balance $24,487,971 after $29.7M in loans receivable; Fund 221 available $978,809. Draws since mid-2025: $615,000 from Fund 238 to the General Fund for the Habitat for Humanity 300 Persifer Street sale (Res. 11467, Oct 14, 2025) and a $1.55M Fund 238 appropriation to buy two vacant Historic District housing sites on Leidesdorff Street, APNs 070-0046-026 and 070-0042-002 (Res. 11659, CEQA exemption filed June 24, 2026). Since 2019 the Council approved $13.7M in long-term loans for over 550 units in six projects; the last loan commitment was Harrington Grove, $2.7M for 52 units (2024). Guidelines adopted by Res. 11427 on August 26, 2025.
- AMI requirement: Minimum 55-year income, rent and affordability restrictions recorded senior to foreclosable liens; serves extremely low, very low and low income households; priority to sites outside concentrations of existing regulated housing and to Housing Element goals (seniors, large families, special needs). Fund 238 must spend at least 50% on construction or major rehab of multifamily rentals affordable to low and very low income households (Sacramento Housing Alliance settlement).
- Cycle: rolling (next: No open round as of November 10, 2026. No AHL NOFA or new loan award found in Council records from mid-2026 through November 2026; the 2025 guidelines allow strategic NOFAs when resources are available. Contact Housing Services via the Community Development Department, (916) 461-6000.)
- Layering notes: The largest city-controlled pool in Sacramento County outside the City of Sacramento (about $23M) with few competing applicants, because Folsom's rental projects are scarce and the Folsom Plan Area south of Highway 50 generates most in-lieu revenue. Loans are repaid from 50% of residual cash flow after allowed expenses; operating and replacement reserves required for the 55-year term; underwriting and compliance aligned to TCAC and LIHTC rules. Folsom is outside the SHRA lending area (cooperation agreement needed), so this fund plus state sources is the local layer; a Folsom Plan Area MOU committing to 890 deed-restricted affordable units (2024 General Plan amendments, not opened this pass) creates sites. Chapter 17.104.070 also allows fee waivers or deferrals and density bonuses for inclusionary units. folsom.ca.us returns 403 to automated access; the staff report and resolution were read from the City's public agenda host.
- Source: https://mccmeetingspublic.blob.core.usgovcloudapi.net/folsomca-meet-20667254009747e4aa5f68a4d63539d6/ITEM-Attachment-001-3c80e00338b5420aafa72ac45dae4a5d.pdf
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)

- Agency: City of Folsom Community Development Department (fee) and Housing Services (fund)
- Type: loan
- Typical award: Commercial linkage fee under FMC 3.90.010, indexed annually by the ENR Construction Cost Index: $2.08 per square foot through June 30, 2026 and $2.13 per square foot (office, retail, light and heavy industrial, manufacturing) from July 1, 2026 per Resolution 11601 (April 28, 2026 hearing, 2.43% adjustment). Deposited in the Housing Trust Fund (Fund 221) and used mainly to fill gaps in affordable rental projects through the AHL Program. FY 2024-25 AB 1600 report: fees collected $170,963, available fund balance $978,809 after $1.80M in loans receivable. FY 2025-26 Mid-Year Budget: cash $951,872 at July 1, 2025, projected $858,319 at June 30, 2026.
- AMI requirement: Fund supports affordable housing development; AHL Program 55-year restrictions apply to loans.
- Cycle: rolling (next: No open round as of November 10, 2026. Deployed through the AHL Program; no NOFA found. Fee paid at building permit.)
- Layering notes: Minor source compared with Fund 238. Folsom's rate ($2.13 from July 1, 2026) is below Sacramento County's $2.17 commercial and $3.26 office rates (effective March 28, 2025). Rate source is the Resolution 11601 fee schedule in the April 28, 2026 Council packet; adoption minutes were not opened. The AB 1600 report notes the fund holds fees beyond five years, reserved until enough accumulates for a project. Chapter 3.90 text itself was not opened (codepublishing.com and folsom.ca.us return 403).

- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)

**Folsom Inclusionary Housing Ordinance (Municipal Code Chapter 17.104) and in-lieu fee (Ordinance 1359, Resolution 11510)**
- Agency: City of Folsom Community Development Department, Housing Services
- Type: regulatory requirement
- Typical award: Requirement, not a subsidy. For-sale residential projects of 10 or more units (and rental projects of 10 or more units receiving City assistance) must make 10% of units affordable: 3% very low income and 7% low income; market-rate rental apartments are exempt. In-lieu fee effective February 12, 2026 (replacing 1% of the lowest sales price): $3.00 per square foot for single-family for-sale units and $2.50 per square foot for multifamily for-sale units of 1,500 square feet or less, paid at building permit into the Folsom Housing Fund (Fund 238); at least 50% of fee revenue must go to lower-income rental development. Prior-year collections exceeded $3.8M, mostly from the Folsom Plan Area. Alternatives: land dedication, off-site units, acquisition-rehab or conversion of market-rate units, inclusionary credits, combinations.
- AMI requirement: Rental inclusionary units restricted at least 30 years (or longer if state law requires); for-sale units resale-restricted; projects of nine or fewer market-rate units exempt.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Applies at entitlement; fee per unit in effect at permit issuance. Council adopted Ordinance 1359 on January 13, 2026 (first reading December 9, 2025) and set fees by Resolution 11510 the same night; next review expected with the Housing Element cycle. Developers paying fees only need a letter of intent, not a full inclusionary housing plan.)
- Layering notes: Nearly all Folsom Plan Area builders pay the fee, which is why Fund 238 holds about $22.8M and funds the AHL Program (record above). Rental multifamily was kept exempt in 2026 despite AB 1505 authority, so apartment developers owe no inclusionary units or fee. Developers who provide more than 10% can bank and sell inclusionary housing credits for five years (17.104.070). The ordinance text was read from the City Council's January 13, 2026 agenda packet on the City's public agenda host and the zoneomics code mirror.

- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)

Examples: Hazelwood Senior Apartments (49 units, 30 to 60% AMI) received pre-approval on February 24, 2025 for a height incentive (7 feet 8 inches over the 35-foot limit), reduced parking (75 stalls versus 114) and a 9% density bonus; Fort Bragg Apartments (1151 South Main, 83 units with 8 very low income) received pre-approval in November 2024.

### City of Fremont

**Development impact fee reduction and deferral for affordable housing projects, FMC Chapter 18.290**
- Agency: City of Fremont Community Development Department, Building and Housing Divisions
- Type: fee waiver
- Typical award: 50% reduction of three development impact fees (Parkland Acquisition, Park Facilities and Transportation/Traffic) for qualifying deed-restricted affordable housing units, adopted with the 2021 Comprehensive Development Impact Fee Update (Council item June 1, 2021, effective August 2, 2021 or 60 days after adoption). Capital Facilities and Fire Facilities fees are paid at the full rate. Staff estimated the reduction at about $9 million of CIP funding ($7 million parks, $2 million transportation). The FY 2024-25 Development Impact Fee Annual and Five-Year Report (December 9, 2025) fee schedule still carries the 50% rate (note 6). A separate City affordable housing fee deferral program was not confirmed in these documents; state law deferral (Government Code 66007) still applies.
- AMI requirement: Applies per deed-restricted unit (the project does not need to be 100% affordable). Deed-restricted affordable housing means units whose deed restricts occupancy by maximum income, in no case above moderate income as defined in FMC 18.155.020 (generally 120% AMI).
- Cycle: rolling (next: No deadline; reduced rates apply when impact fees are paid at building permit.)
- Layering notes: Fee relief stacks with Fund 196 loans and state fee deferral; school (FUSD), water (ACWD) and sewer (USD) fees are outside the City resolution. ### City of Fresno

**Affordable Housing Density Bonus (FMC Chapter 15, Article 22) with TOD Height and Density Bonus (Article 21) and Housing Element Program 9 by-right approval**
- Agency: City of Fresno Planning and Development Department
- Type: density bonus
- Typical award: Requirement, not a subsidy. Article 22 implements Gov. Code 65915 for projects of 5 or more units (State law governs on conflict). Article 21 adds a discretionary TOD bonus of up to 100% more density and 25% more height in MX or CMS districts within 500 feet of a BRT station or half mile of Manchester Transit Center, combinable with the affordable bonus. **Affordable Housing Development and Substantial Rehabilitation NOFA (HOME, HOME-CHDO and HOME-ARP), City of Fresno PY 2026-2027**
- Agency: City of Fresno Planning and Development Department, Housing and Community Development Division (Housing Finance)
- Type: loan
- Typical award: PY 2026-27 Annual Action Plan programs $2,804,486.73 HOME for affordable development or rehab (entitlement $2,766,057.28 plus $500,000 program income and $229,944 prior year) and a $414,909 HOME CHDO set-aside. Recent awards: $3,000,000 HOME to Sarah's Court II (120 units, 11 HOME units, January 2026). City HOME-ARP allocation was $11.9 million (HOME-ARP supportive services NOFA closed April 13, 2026). Five-year Con Plan years 3 to 5 HOME estimate $8.3 million.
- AMI requirement: HOME rents and incomes (at or below 80% AMI, with HOME rent limits on assisted units); 55-year City regulatory agreement typical for rental loans; priority for projects in areas of opportunity.
- Cycle: annual NOFA (next: No open round as of November 8, 2026. The 2026-2027 AHD NOFA (PlanetBids No. 2026/12602307) closed August 31, 2026. The separate PY 2027-28 HUD CPD NOFA (tentative release December 14, 2026, applications due January 22, 2027) follows the Consolidated NOFA model covering ESG, HOPWA, public services, infrastructure and owner-occupied repair, not HOME rental development. Expect the next AHD NOFA in mid-2027; verify with HCDD at (559) 621-8300.)
- Layering notes: City of Fresno is its own HUD entitlement (CDBG $6.9M, HOME $2.77M, ESG $624K, HOPWA $1.27M in PY 2026) and is not part of the Fresno Urban County, so City projects do not compete in the County HOME/PLHA NOFO and vice versa. The AHD NOFA is separate from the Consolidated NOFA (CDBG, ESG, HOPWA public services and infrastructure, due January 23, 2026). City HOME is usually layered with City PLHA, LHTF and Housing Successor funds and with 4% or 9% LIHTC; HOME triggers Davis-Bacon at 12 or more assisted units and federal NEPA review before choice-limiting actions. Fresno Housing (county record) PBVs and bonds stack on top. The PlanetBids NOFA document itself could not be opened by script; figures come from the City HCD page and the PY 2026-27 Annual Action Plan.
- Source: https://www.fresno.gov/planning/housing-community-development/
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)

**Affordable housing development impact fee deferral to certificate of occupancy (uncodified Ordinance 2008-51)**
- Agency: City of Fresno Planning and Development Department and Public Works Department
- Type: fee waiver
- Typical award: Defers payment of all adopted City development impact fees (street, water, sewer and others) on qualifying affordable units from building permit to certificate of occupancy. Deferral only, no reduction.
- AMI requirement: Inside the Central Area (bounded by SR 180, 99 and 41): any unit in a development with at least 15% of units restricted; outside the Central Area: restricted units only. Covenants of at least 55 years for rental and 30 years for ownership.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Ongoing; request at building permit.)
- Layering notes: Construction-period carry savings only; fees are still due before occupancy. Stacks with the Infill Incentive waiver where both apply and with density bonus concessions. Ordinance dates from 2008; confirm current implementation with Public Works since it is uncodified.
- Source: https://www.fresno.gov/wp-content/uploads/2023/04/AFFORDABLE-HOUSING-WAIVER.pdf
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)

**City of Fresno Local Housing Trust Fund (LHTF), Resolution 2021-201 and Revised Program Guidelines 02**
- Agency: City of Fresno Planning and Development Department, Housing Finance Division
- Type: loan
- Typical award: Dedicated $1,500,000 per year from the City Real Estate Transfer Tax, plus General Fund contributions, Prohousing Incentive Pilot Round 1 ($2,064,891) and State LHTF matching grants (about $8.5 million received to date, including $1,797,373 appropriated January 2026). Recent loans: $5,000,000 Cesar Chavez Apartments (54 units, 2024 commitment) and $3,727,000 The Park at South Stadium (15 LHTF units of 174, approved June 18, 2026; includes $156,800 Housing Successor funds). City applied for PIP Round 4 (up to $2,000,000) to recapitalize the fund.
- AMI requirement: Local funds (Guidelines 02) serve households at or below 80% AMI (State match dollars follow State LHTF rules, with at least 30% to extremely low income); 55-year affordability covenants on rental loans. Eviction Protection Program uses are exempt from income verification since July 1, 2025.
- Cycle: annual NOFA (next: No open round as of November 8, 2026. The LHTF Multi-Family New Construction NOFA (PlanetBids No. 12601837) released April 24, 2026 and closed May 25, 2026 with 11 applications; no new LHTF NOFA is posted on the City housing page. Next NOFA depends on the FY 2027 transfer-tax allocation and any PIP Round 4 award; verify with Housing@fresno.gov.)
- Layering notes: One of the few city-controlled flexible local sources in the Central Valley. Loans are 3% simple interest, 55-year, residual receipts, and accept third or fourth lien position behind construction/permanent debt and other public loans, so they fit as gap under 4% LIHTC and tax-exempt bonds. Guidelines 02 were rewritten in 2025 (Resolution 2025-270) and a technical amendment in April 2026 restored multifamily new construction as eligible after it was inadvertently dropped; check the current guidelines before applying. Competes for the same transfer-tax dollars as the Eviction Protection Program. County has no equivalent trust fund (see Fresno County PLHA and HOME records).
- Source: https://agendas.fresno.gov/en/legislation/id-26-146-20843
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)

**City-owned and surplus land contributions with conditional City funding commitments (Surplus Land Act RFPs, Land Bank)**
- Agency: City of Fresno Planning and Development Department
- Type: land
- Typical award: Land at nominal cost plus conditional funding. Examples: Vantage Blackstone senior modular (100 units) gets a 1.21-acre parcel on a 55-year ground lease at $1 per year plus $4,300,000 loan/grant (approved October 22, 2026); Parkview Apartments (98 units, Cesar Chavez Foundation) gets three Parkway Drive parcels plus $10,500,000 conditional commitment (December 2025); Ventura Family Apartments land contribution.
- AMI requirement: Per SLA and Gov. Code 37364 exempt-surplus terms: at least 40% of units at or below 80% AMI with half at or below 50% AMI, regulatory agreement of at least 30 years; recent deals carry 55-year covenants and 30% to 80% AMI targeting.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Site by site; Vantage Blackstone commitment expires September 30, 2027 if financing is not secured. Watch City SLA notices and RFPs on PlanetBids.)
- Layering notes: City land plus a conditional funding resolution is the standard Fresno package for TCAC 4% and HCD MFSN applications (commitments are reissued each round, as with Parkview since 2024). Funding sources behind the commitments vary (CDBG-acquired land on Blackstone carries CDBG national objective requirements). Below-market ground leases count as public subsidy for prevailing wage. The City also adopted a Land Bank program to acquire sites for future reuse.
- Source: https://agendas.fresno.gov/en/legislation/id-26-1294-21998
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)

**Downtown and Chinatown Housing Development NOFA, City Revolving Loan Fund (RLF) construction loans**
- Agency: City of Fresno Planning and Development Department
- Type: loan
- Typical award: Construction gap loans of up to $8,000,000 per project from the City Revolving Loan Fund (Round 2 awards: Helm Lofts $8M, Uptown Apartments $8M, The Park at South Stadium $8M). 60-month term, variable rate estimated at 4.81%, secured by deed of trust.
- AMI requirement: None required for RLF dollars; market-rate projects are eligible (Uptown is 48 market-rate units). Affordability comes from layered sources or Surplus Land Act terms (South Stadium 70 of 174 units restricted to very low and low income for 55 years).
- Cycle: rolling (next: Round 2 NOFA (PlanetBids No. 12601560) opened February 13, 2026 and closed April 14, 2026; conditional commitments expire December 31, 2026 unless financing closes. No Round 3 announced as of 2026-11-08.)
- Layering notes: Short-term construction money, not permanent soft debt: it must be taken out at conversion, so it suits 4% LIHTC or mixed-income deals with a permanent loan sized to repay. Pairs with City PLHA, LHTF and FHS land in the Downtown/Chinatown area, and with the TOD height and density bonus. RLF capital is State money: $20 million of the State's $250 million Downtown Fresno appropriation (FY 2025-26 installment, Resolution 2025-256) plus a further $5 million appropriated in 2026 for a $25 million fund (Council item 25-1713). The executed RLF Agreement form (item 26-440) nonetheless contains boilerplate federal compliance language; confirm with the City whether any federal cross-cutters attach.
- Source: https://agendas.fresno.gov/en/legislation/id-26-145-20842
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)

**HUD Section 108 Affordable Housing Development Loan Pool (Substantial Amendment 2025-02)**
- Agency: City of Fresno Planning and Development Department, Community Development Division
- Type: loan
- Typical award: $15,000,000 pool (City borrowing capacity $15,494,680) for land acquisition and acquisition of manufactured housing units; no minimum or maximum loan; loans generally forgivable at end of affordability term. City repays HUD over 20 years from future CDBG (estimated 3.94% rate).
- AMI requirement: Nonprofit developers only. At least 51% of units on land acquired with the pool for low and moderate income households (80% AMI), or at least 20% for non-elderly multifamily rental where CDBG share is proportional; 100% LMI for manufactured units; up to 55-year covenants. Borrower must secure outside senior financing and commit up to 10% equity.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Council hearing to adopt Substantial Amendment 2025-02 and authorize the HUD application scheduled November 12, 2026 (ID 26-1506). If approved, a NOFA will be posted on PlanetBids; timing unknown, verify with the Community Development Division.)
- Layering notes: Land acquisition gap, so it fits early in the stack ahead of LIHTC applications, and can help secure site control for TCAC/CDLAC rounds. CDBG/Section 108 rules apply (Davis-Bacon at 8 or more units for assisted construction, NEPA, URA relocation). Competes with future City CDBG public infrastructure spending because CDBG is pledged for repayment. Separate from the City's earlier $20M Section 108 loan for the Senior Activity Center.
- Source: https://www.fresno.gov/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Section-108-Loan-Guarantee-Application-Affordable-Housing-Development-Loan-Pool-10w1789.pdf
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)

**Housing Successor to the Redevelopment Agency of the City of Fresno, Low and Moderate Income Housing Asset Fund (LMIHAF) program income and FHS-owned sites**
- Agency: City of Fresno in its capacity as Housing Successor (FHS) and Fresno Revitalization Corporation
- Type: loan
- Typical award: FY 2026-27 budget $4,188,073 (carryover $4,138,073 plus about $50,000 program income); unencumbered and available for development $2,523,599, all restricted to units at or below 30% AMI because FHS exceeded the 20% cap for 60-80% AMI. LMIHAF assets under management $28.9 million; FY 2024-25 ending balance $6,856,360. Historic per-unit contributions range from about $25,000 to $331,000; recent uses include Heritage Estates ($1.2M), B Street ($836,200 encumbered) and 33 E Atchison ($275,000).
- AMI requirement: HSC 34176.1: at least 30% of funds for extremely low income (30% AMI) rentals, no more than 20% for 60-80% AMI, remainder at or below 60% AMI; 55-year covenants for rentals.
- Cycle: rolling (next: No standalone NOFA as of November 8, 2026. Funds and FHS-owned parcels are committed through City NOFAs, RFPs and disposition agreements (FY 2026-27 program income budget approved June 11, 2026; $2,523,599 unencumbered, restricted to 30% AMI rentals). Contact the Housing Successor.)
- Layering notes: Small cash pool but useful for deep (30% AMI) targeting and as a match: PLHA allows LMIHAF dollars to be matched into a housing trust account. FHS land is being paired with LHTF, RLF and PRO Housing applications in Downtown and Chinatown (South Stadium used $156,800 FHS plus FHS parcels at 829 and 835 Fulton). Excess surplus test is met (unencumbered $4.08M versus $6.24M threshold at FY 2024-25), so there is no pressure to transfer funds to HCD.
- Source: https://agendas.fresno.gov/en/legislation/id-26-752-21456

**Infill Incentive Program development impact fee waiver (FMC Article 12-4.16, Ordinance 2021-029) and Residential BUILD Act waivers**
- Agency: City of Fresno Public Works Department (Traffic and Land Planning), with City Manager approval
- Type: fee waiver
- Typical award: Waives City park, police, fire and street facilities impact fees and reimburses up to 50% of curb, gutter and sidewalk costs. Backfilled from the City budget, first come first served. Cumulative waivers since 2014: $10.19 million across programs ($3.62M Infill Incentive, $659K Residential BUILD). FY 2025 waivers totaled only $45,825 (five single-family homes).
- AMI requirement: None; the waiver is location-based (Infill Opportunity Zone, outside the South Industrial Priority Area, sites up to 6.5 net acres or commercial-to-residential conversions of any size).
- Cycle: rolling (next: Likely expired: the City application form (July 2025 update) states the waiver is not valid on building permits issued after June 30, 2026 and only when backfill funds exist. No extension was found as of November 8, 2026; the December 18, 2025 fee waiver report shows $0 Infill waivers in FY 2025. Confirm with Public Works before underwriting.)
- Layering notes: Market-rate and affordable infill both qualify, so it is not affordable-specific, but it lowers impact fees for downtown and BRT corridor projects that also use the TOD bonus. Applied at certificate of occupancy, not at permit, so the full fee must be carried in the construction budget. Use near zero in FY 2025 suggests limited backfill funding. Fee waivers backfilled with City funds may be public subsidy under Labor Code 1720.
- Source: https://agendas.fresno.gov/en/legislation/id-25-1584-20563
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)

**Permanent Local Housing Allocation (PLHA), City of Fresno 2024-2028 Five-Year Plan and PLHA development loans**
- Agency: City of Fresno Planning and Development Department, Housing Finance Division
- Type: loan
- Typical award: Estimated $14,949,413 over 2024-2028 (first allocation $2,391,906, second $2,562,083). 45% of each year to multifamily rental development, 50% to owner-occupied rehab and down payment assistance, 5% admin. Recent award: $1,600,000 PLHA to Helm Lofts (9 restricted units of 98, conditional award February 9, 2026).
- AMI requirement: Rental activity up to 120% AMI under State rules, with a portion of units reserved at or below 60% AMI; 55-year regulatory agreement; loans are low-interest deferred (Helm Lofts: 3% simple, 55-year term).
- Cycle: annual NOFA (next: No open round as of November 8, 2026. Last standalone PLHA NOFA ran August 1 to August 29, 2025. The draft 2024-2028 PLHA plan (public comment September 21 to October 10, 2026; hearing November 5, 2026; Council adoption pending) states PLHA rental funds are offered through the City's Affordable Housing Development and Substantial Rehabilitation NOFAs, the latest of which closed August 31, 2026. Expect the next round with the mid-2027 AHD NOFA; verify with Housing@fresno.gov.)
- Layering notes: Separate from the Fresno County PLHA (county record covers the unincorporated area and participating cities, not the City of Fresno). The City plan devotes only 45% to rentals, so expect roughly $1.1M per year available for multifamily. PLHA is used as soft gap alongside City HOME and LHTF and with LIHTC; it was also paired with the market-rate-oriented Revolving Loan Fund on Helm Lofts. State PLHA funds count as public funds for prevailing wage purposes.

### City of Garden Grove

**Affordable Housing and Permanent Supportive Housing Development RFP and Housing Element Program 4 (Affordable Housing Construction assistance)**

- Type: loan

Housing Element Program 4 commits the City to technical and financial assistance for about 10 affordable units a year (80 units over the cycle) through land cost write-downs and construction assistance from General Fund, HOME, LMIHAF and PLHA, plus expedited processing. The FY 2025-30 Consolidated Plan earmarks part of about $2,900,000 of HOME-ARP for one PSH development, and the Housing Successor is buying the Civic Center Parcel for housing.

The Affordable Housing and Permanent Supportive Housing Development RFP page (ggcity.org/news/afford-rfp) still returns 403; search results date the City announcement to January 2024, so it is likely closed. Contact Neighborhood Improvement (714-741-5144).)

Local and state funds are public funds under Labor Code 1720(b), so state prevailing wage applies unless a 1720(c) exemption fits the deal, such as 1720(c)(5)(E) for below-market loans with at least 40 percent of units restricted 20 years at or below 80 percent AMI (see prevailing_wage_basis). **Residential Density Bonus and Affordable Housing Regulatory Agreements (Garden Grove Municipal Code Chapter 9.60, Secs. 9.60.040 and 9.60.050; Housing Element Program 10)**
- Agency: City of Garden Grove Community and Economic Development Department, Planning Services Division
- Type: density bonus
- Typical award: Requirement and entitlement, not a subsidy. Chapter 9.60 implements the State Density Bonus Law, Housing Accountability Act, Housing Crisis Act and No Net Loss law: density bonus, incentives, concessions, waivers and parking ratios per Government Code 65915 and 65915.5 as amended, processed concurrently with the land use application; ministerial review for qualifying housing development projects; replacement of protected units; regulatory agreement required for every affordable unit (Sec. 9.60.050) including a rule that voucher holders pay the affordable rent, not FMR. The 2021-2029 Housing Element reports surveyed projects averaging 183% of base density through bonuses and commits the City to the updated ordinance by 2025 (Program 10) and to study an inclusionary ordinance (Program 11).
- AMI requirement: State thresholds (5% very low, 10% low, 10% moderate for-sale, 100% affordable) with 55-year rental covenants in the City regulatory agreement.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Applies at project application. Program 11 inclusionary study was due within the Housing Element cycle; no inclusionary ordinance or in-lieu fee exists as of this pass.)
- Layering notes: Garden Grove has no inclusionary ordinance, in-lieu fee, local housing trust fund or affordable housing fee waiver; density bonus plus Housing Element Program 4 (technical and financial assistance for 10 affordable units a year, expedited processing, land write-downs from General Fund, HOME, LMIHAF and PLHA) is the full local toolkit beyond the Housing Successor land and GGHA vouchers. Garden Grove is not a Prohousing designated city. Density bonus does not trigger prevailing wage. Chapter 9.60 read on the zoneomics mirror; 2021-2029 Housing Element PDF opened on ggcity.org.

- Agency: City of Grass Valley Community Development Department
- Type: fee waiver
- Typical award: Fee deferral for affordable housing is available on request, but the City reports it has received no requests. Program 13 commits the City to apply for grants and support developers seeking funding (objective 25 very low and 40 to 60 low income new units in 2019-2027); Program 14 supports tax-exempt bonds and mortgage credit certificates. The City won a $2 million DTSC Equitable Community Revitalization Grant in 2024 to clean up a brownfield site of interest to affordable developers, and expedited a Habitat for Humanity SB 9 lot split for three deed-restricted homes.
- AMI requirement: Lower income units per the funding source; Program 28 targets units at or below 30% AMI with Nevada County and the Regional Housing Authority.
- Cycle: rolling (next: unknown, verify with agency. The 7th cycle Housing Element is due in 2027.)
- Layering notes: Deferral terms are not codified in a published resolution; negotiate case by case. City sites have historically attracted County-sponsored supportive housing (Brunswick Commons, 41 units) and RHA projects. The City joined the October 30, 2025 regional housing workshop with the County, Nevada City, Truckee and HCD. Source is the 2024 General Plan Annual Progress Report (March 2025) on the City's meeting host; a 2025 APR was not located this pass.

### City of Hayward

**HOME Investment Partnerships funds through the Alameda County HOME Consortium and CDBG entitlement (Cooperation Agreement FY 2027-2029)**
- Agency: City of Hayward Development Services Department, Housing Division; Alameda County HCD as Consortium lead

The County proposes to centralize HOME administration, compliance and allocation during the FY 2027-2029 term, with Consortium members reviewing future allocations.

Pairs with the County HOME Consortium RFP, Measure A1 and HACA PBVs. **Hayward Affordable Housing NOFA (local housing funds with Alameda County Measure A1 base allocation; last round 2018)**
- Agency: City of Hayward Development Services Department, Housing Division, 777 B Street, Hayward; housing@hayward-ca.gov, (510) 583-4454
- Type: loan
- Typical award: 2018 NOFA: about $7,000,000 in local housing funds plus recommendations for Hayward's Measure A1 base allocation ($18,200,000 available at the time) and local match to position projects for the A1 regional pool. Maximum City loan 10% of total residential development cost of the affordable units; HOME per-unit limits for HOME-assisted units ($144,050 studio to $285,149 four bedroom in 2018); 24-month commitment with one-year extension. CDBG available for predevelopment or acquisition by request. No NOFA has been issued since; the City reports only one City-supported project remaining in the pipeline and limited general fund for housing.

The December 2024 Housing Policy and Resource Committee report floated an annual general fund allocation for a regular NOFA but no funding was identified. Watch the Doing Business with Hayward page and the Housing Division mailing list.)
- Layering notes: Hayward's role is mainly as pass-through for its Measure A1 base allocation (county record) and HOME Consortium share; local dollars are limited to the Affordable Housing Trust Fund balance and CDBG. Developers should expect to rely on Measure A1, Measure W, HACA project-based vouchers and state sources with the City providing land (surplus sites), entitlements under the Streamlined Affordable Housing Overlay, and its Prohousing designation points.
