**Hayward Affordable Housing Ordinance (HMC Chapter 10, Article 17; Ordinance 17-20, amended April 11, 2023), in-lieu fees (Resolution 17-167 as amended 2023) and Affordable Housing Trust Fund**
- Agency: City of Hayward Development Services Department, Housing Division, 777 B Street, Hayward; housing@hayward-ca.gov, (510) 583-4454
- Type: regulatory requirement
- Typical award: Requirement, not a subsidy. Applies to all projects of two or more net new units: on-site units, in-lieu fee, off-site units or alternatives. In-lieu fees (10 or more units, per sq ft of habitable space, 2023 schedule): high-density condominiums 35 units per acre or more $19.35; lower-density ownership under 35 units per acre $26.00; all other dwelling types including rental $23.46; plus 10% if paid at occupancy; projects of 2 to 9 units pay 50% to 89% of the calculated fee. Fees fund the Affordable Housing Trust Fund, used solely to increase and preserve housing for extremely low to moderate income households (land acquisition and development subsidies). Collections 2020 to mid-2026 total $8,926,851: $3,599,171 (2020), $2,193,532 (2021), $2,013,770 (2022), $199,507 (2023), $489,948 (2024), $378,237 (2025), $52,687 (2026 YTD).

Compare Fremont ($44 per sq ft for-sale) and Berkeley ($62.83).

- Agency: City of Hayward Development Services Department, Planning Division
- Type: density bonus
- Typical award: Entitlement streamlining, not a subsidy. ### City of Hollister

**Density Bonus Ordinance (Municipal Code Chapter 17.34, Ordinance 1230 of 2023 as amended by Ordinance 1267 of 2025)**
- Agency: City of Hollister Community Development Department, Planning Division
- Type: density bonus
- Typical award: Implements Government Code 65915 to 65918 for housing developments of five or more units: bonuses from 20% (5% very low or 10% lower income) up to 50%, 80% for 100% affordable projects (up to 20% moderate), no density maximum for 100% affordable projects within one-half mile of a major transit stop with a height waiver of up to three stories or 33 feet, 15% base bonus plus increments for land donation (Table 17.34-4), 20% senior bonus, 35% student housing bonus, child care facility bonus (17.34.080), one to four incentives or concessions (17.34.060), reduced parking, density bonus housing agreement and deed restrictions (17.34.120 to 17.34.150). Section 17.34 B allows the City to grant a greater bonus than state law requires but no local enhancement schedule is codified.
- AMI requirement: State density bonus law thresholds: very low (50% AMI), lower (80% AMI) and moderate income for-sale units (120% AMI); rental affordability covenants of 55 years; equity sharing on for-sale units.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Submitted with the planning entitlement (17.34.100). Housing Element Policy Action H3.6 states the ordinance update was adopted October 2025 (Ordinance 1267, Zoning Ordinance Overhaul Phase 2) with annual review; goal of two density bonus projects per year. The 2025 Annual Progress Report shows 2 applications requesting a bonus (23 units) and 0 projects permitted with a bonus.)
- Layering notes: Mirrors state law with no extra local bonus, so it is comparable to the San Benito County Chapter 21.03 Section 13 density bonus. Inclusionary units required under Chapter 17.36 count toward the bonus thresholds (17.36.050 C), and bonus units are excluded from the inclusionary base, so a 15% inclusionary project of 10 or more units in Hollister can claim at least a 20% to 27.5% bonus plus concessions at no extra affordability cost. Housing Element Policy Action H3.3 commits to continuing lower sewer, water connection and traffic impact fees for multifamily and to adopting a permit fee reduction or waiver program for affordable and special needs housing by August 2026 (2025 APR status: not yet started); Phase 3 zoning procedure amendments and Housing Element implementation rezonings (ZOA 2026-1) were heard April 20, 2026. Code text read on the zoneomics mirror; municode blocks automated access.

**Hollister Housing Trust Fund ($300,000 initial deposit, Housing Element Policy Action H5.12 and 2026 stipulated judgment with HCD and the Attorney General)**
- Agency: City of Hollister Planning and Housing Divisions (program procedures subject to HCD approval)
- Type: other
- Typical award: Initial capitalization of $300,000 from the City general fund, required by the March 26, 2026 stipulated judgment (People of the State of California and HCD v. City of Hollister) and carried into the adopted 2023-2031 Housing Element as Policy Action H5.12. The fund must support housing for extremely low, very low and low income households, including migrant housing, emergency shelters, supportive housing, single-room occupancy and transitional housing. Award form (grant or loan), per-project limits and the application procedure are to be set in a program document approved by HCD. Any money remaining five years after deposit transfers to the State Building Homes and Jobs Trust Fund unless HCD agrees otherwise. On June 22, 2026 the City Council adopted a resolution approving the Housing Trust Guidelines and a FY 2026-27 budget adjustment moving $300,000 from General Fund 101 to the HOME Program Revolving Loan Fund 809 (5-0 roll call), and directed staff to submit the guidelines to HCD for review. The guideline text is attached to the agenda item but could not be opened (eScribe attachments behind a bot check), so award form and limits remain unconfirmed.
- AMI requirement: Extremely low, very low and low income households (at or below 80% AMI); affordability terms to be set in the HCD-approved procedures.
- Cycle: rolling (next: No open round as of November 10, 2026. Guidelines and the $300,000 deposit were approved June 22, 2026 and sent to HCD for review; no HCD approval or funding round has been posted. Contact housing@hollister.ca.gov for status.)
- Layering notes: This will be the only city-controlled capital source for affordable development in Hollister; there is no inclusionary in-lieu fund (Chapter 17.36 requires on-site units) and the former redevelopment agency's housing assets are limited to a Housing Division loan and resale monitoring portfolio (Successor Agency page opened). At $300,000 it is predevelopment-scale money; realistic use is a predevelopment loan or local match that strengthens a TCAC, HCD or AHSC application, layered under county sources (San Benito County PLHA, HHAP, CMFA conduit bonds) and Housing Authority of the County of Santa Cruz PBVs. The five-year sunset creates pressure to commit funds quickly, which favors shovel-ready sponsors. H5.12 also commits the City to annual developer meetings, one-on-one technical assistance and support letters. The $300,000 sits in the HOME Program Revolving Loan Fund 809 alongside HOME program income, so trust awards may carry HOME-style terms; confirm once HCD approves the guidelines. Sources opened: judgment text (oag.ca.gov Exhibit B), adopted Housing Element PDF, and the June 22, 2026 City Council minutes on eScribe.

- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)

**Inclusionary Housing Program (Municipal Code Chapter 17.36, Ordinance 1252)**
- Agency: City of Hollister Community Development Department, Planning Division and Housing Division (housing@hollister.ca.gov, (831) 636-4360 x1254)
- Type: regulatory requirement
- Typical award: Requirement, not a subsidy. All for-sale and rental residential projects of 10 or more units must provide 15% of base units (before any density bonus) as on-site inclusionary units: at least 6% very low income, at least 5% very low or low income, and at least 4% very low, low or moderate income (Section 17.36.050). Fractions of 0.25 or more round up. No in-lieu fee option exists; the only alternatives (Section 17.36.060) are affordable rental units inside a for-sale project or acquisition and rehabilitation of existing market-rate units (rehab value at least 25% of pre-rehab value including land, City-approved physical needs assessment, residentially zoned site, applicant-funded relocation). Ordinance 1252 (ZOA 2023-4) adopted August 6, 2024; Housing Element goal of 150 inclusionary units during 2023-2031.
- AMI requirement: Inclusionary units sold or rented only to very low, low or moderate income households (up to 120% AMI, San Benito County HCD limits) or to the City or its designee; units must average at least 85% of the square footage of market units with the same bedroom count, match unit type proportions, bedroom ratio, finishes and exterior design, and be dispersed on site with equal access to common areas; buyers and renters screened by the Administrator through an open public process (no private selection). For-sale units: affordable price restricted 30 years under a recorded agreement, resetting on resale, owner occupancy within 60 days and at least 10 months a year, no rental. Rental units: affordable for 55 years under a recorded affordable housing agreement.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Applies at entitlement; an affordable housing agreement is required and inclusionary units must be permitted and occupied in proportion to market-rate units in each phase (Section 17.36.050 F). Exempt: ADUs, projects under 10 units, vesting tentative maps and development agreements in effect at the effective date, complete applications with fees paid before that date, and projects exempted by Gov. Code 66474.2, 66498.1 or other state law. Council may adopt guidelines and administration and monitoring fees by resolution (Section 17.36.080).)
- Layering notes: Hollister's program is stricter than the San Benito County Chapter 21.03 ordinance (15% on site or 20% off site, with a $30 per square foot in-lieu fee) because it allows no fee payment and requires on-site units for both rental and for-sale projects; as a result the City has no inclusionary in-lieu fund to redeploy as gap financing. Inclusionary units may be used to qualify for a density bonus under Chapter 17.34 (Section 17.36.050 C), so a 15% inclusionary project can stack the state bonus and concessions. The City's Below Market Rate Housing Program (affordable_housing.php) administers waitlists for inclusionary units; all waitlists were closed as of this pass. Hollister's prior Housing Developer Resources page (opened) states the City previously had no inclusionary ordinance; the code text was read on the zoneomics mirror because library.municode.com blocks automated access. Pairs with the Housing Authority of the County of Santa Cruz PBVs and the CMFA conduit bonds recorded at the county level (Baler Place, 340 Bridgevale Road, is a Hollister project).
- Source: https://files.hollister.ca.gov/Community%20Development%20Department/Planning/Zoning%20Ordinance%20Update/ZOA%20_Adopted%20Ordinances/2024-08-06%20ORD%201252.pdf
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)

**Permit fee waiver program for affordable and special needs housing and reduced multifamily impact fees (Housing Element Policy Action H3.3)**
- Agency: City of Hollister Planning, Building and Finance Divisions and Engineering Department
- Type: fee waiver
- Typical award: Existing: lower sewer and water connection fees and traffic impact fees for multifamily development (per-unit basis; the City is considering a square-foot basis). Committed: a reduction or waiver of permit processing fees for affordable and other special needs housing projects, to be established by August 2026 following the user fee study now underway; the Housing Element also calls for waiving permit fees for ADUs under certain sizes or deed restricted as affordable to lower income households, and the sites strategy table contemplates reducing development fees for key sites. Amounts not yet set.

Density bonus concessions under Chapter 17.34 remain the only guaranteed path to fee or standard relief until the program is adopted. Recorded as negative information per schema rule 4 and so the August 2026 commitment can be tracked.

### City of Huntington Beach

**Affordable Housing (Inclusionary Housing) Ordinance, Huntington Beach Zoning and Subdivision Ordinance Sec. 230.26, and in-lieu fee**
- Agency: City of Huntington Beach Community Development Department, Housing Division (Charles Kovac, Housing Manager, charles.kovac@surfcity-hb.org; Gregory Hoang, Senior Housing Analyst, 714-536-5473)
- Type: regulatory requirement
- Typical award: Requirement, not a subsidy. New residential projects of three or more units (including conversions) must restrict at least 10% of units: rental units at the lower income level (or very low or extremely low at the developer's choice), ownership units at moderate income, with fractional units rounded up or paid as fee. In-lieu fees may be paid by ownership projects of any size and rental projects of 100 units or fewer, per a fee schedule set by Council resolution and indexed annually to Orange County new home prices; fees are paid before building permit (pro rata for phased projects) and deposited in the Affordable Housing Trust Fund. Land dedication is allowed at Council discretion. Projects that exceed the requirement on-site are eligible for reduced City fees (the 2025 Annual Progress Report cites over $1,000,000 of development impact fee exemptions for a 78-unit project with 8 ELI, 32 VL and 37 low units). A 6-1 Council vote amended the ordinance and the fee formula to make payment more flexible (date not confirmed).
- AMI requirement: Affordability term at least 55 years for rental and 45 years for ownership; affordable rental units built by a separate affordable developer on a parcel within an ownership project may not request City financial assistance; at least 40% of such units must have two or more bedrooms; interior standards equal to LIHTC minimums.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Applies at entitlement; fee per the current Council resolution at building permit. Council must review the Trust Fund and fee within 180 days after each fiscal year end (by late December).)
- Layering notes: A low 3-unit threshold but a fee-out for all ownership and all rental projects up to 100 units, so in practice most Huntington Beach projects pay the fee; the Trust Fund (next record) is the resulting local source. The ordinance's fee-reduction incentive is the only affordable housing fee relief found among the five cities. Housing Element status matters here: HCD's March 6, 2026 letter found the 2021-2029 element cannot be certified until the Program 2A and 2B rezonings (Affordable Housing Overlay) are complete, and the state litigation over the element continues, which exposes projects to builder's remedy and limits state funding points. Code read on the zoneomics mirror; Legistar attachments (HCD letter, 2025 APR) opened via the Legistar web API.
- Source: https://www.zoneomics.com/code/huntington-beach-CA/chapter_4
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)

**Affordable Housing Density Bonus (Zoning and Subdivision Ordinance Sec. 230.14) and Affordable Housing Overlay (Beach and Edinger Corridors Specific Plan)**
- Agency: City of Huntington Beach Community Development Department, Planning Division
- Type: density bonus
- Typical award: Requirement and entitlement, not a subsidy. Sec. 230.14 implements Government Code 65915: 20% base bonus for 10% lower income units rising 1.5% per additional 1% to 35%, 5% base bonus for 10% moderate income for-sale units rising 1% per 1% to 35%, one to three incentives or concessions by affordability tier, land donation option under 65915(h). The Beach and Edinger Corridors Specific Plan Affordable Housing Overlay provides non-discretionary review for qualifying affordable projects, and the HBHA Pathways RFQ sought 100% affordable supportive housing at 60% AMI or less with by-right processing for projects with at least 20% affordable units.
- AMI requirement: State thresholds; 55-year rental covenants; in-lieu fees under Sec. 230.26 are calculated on units before the density bonus.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Applies at project application. Housing Element Program 2B (expand the Affordable Housing Overlay) is the rezoning HCD requires before certification; Resolution 2026-25 to adopt the element was heard June 2 and June 8, 2026.)
- Layering notes: Huntington Beach's local code mirrors the pre-2020 state schedule (35% cap), but state law controls and allows larger bonuses; the practical constraint is political and legal (Measure U voter control, State v. City of Huntington Beach over the Housing Element). Until the element is certified, projects may use builder's remedy and the City cannot earn Prohousing points. No local fee waiver ordinance beyond the Sec. 230.26 fee-reduction incentive. Density bonus does not trigger prevailing wage. Code read on zoneomics; HCD March 6, 2026 letter and Legistar matter list opened.

**Affordable Housing Trust Fund (Sec. 230.26.E and F) and City inclusionary loans**
- Agency: City of Huntington Beach Community Development Department, Housing Division; Huntington Beach Housing Authority
- Type: loan
- Typical award: In-lieu fees collected under Sec. 230.26 are placed in the Affordable Housing Trust Fund and may be used for predevelopment, land or air rights acquisition, rehabilitation, land write-downs, administration, gap financing or interest rate buy-downs on construction or permanent loans. Current balance and annual receipts were not published in an opened document. Example of use: the City holds an Inclusionary Housing promissory note on Pelican Harbor Apartments that was amended (First Amendment to City Inclusionary Housing Promissory Note) with a HOME note amendment and CMFA bond TEFRA approval on October 21, 2025 (Resolution 2025-65) to allow the project's refinancing; Five Points Senior Villas covenants were extended by amendment in August 2025.

Combine with the City's CDBG and HOME, County 2026 Supportive Housing NOFA loans ($95,000 to $105,000 per unit inside Huntington Beach), OCHA PBVs (Oasis Huntington Beach took 62) and OCHFT. The Huntington Beach Housing Authority is also the housing successor; its LMIHAF balance was not opened this pass. Local and state funds are public funds under Labor Code 1720(b), so state prevailing wage applies unless a 1720(c) exemption fits the deal, such as 1720(c)(5)(E) for below-market loans with at least 40 percent of units restricted 20 years at or below 80 percent AMI (see prevailing_wage_basis). Code text on zoneomics; Legistar matter 25-856 attachments list opened (the inclusionary note PDF itself is an image scan with no text).

**CDBG and HOME entitlement (FY 2025-2029 Consolidated Plan, Resolution 2025-32; annual CDBG Notice of Funding Availability)**
- Agency: City of Huntington Beach Community Development Department, Housing Division (Charles Kovac, Housing Manager; Gregory Hoang, Senior Housing Analyst, gregory.hoang@surfcity-hb.org, 714-536-5473)
- Type: grant
- Typical award: FY 2025-26: CDBG grant $1,121,195 plus $258,868 carryover ($1,380,063 total); HOME grant $538,328 plus $306,100 program income ($844,428 total). HOME uses FY 2025-26: Families Forward TBRA $200,000, Mercy House TBRA $200,000, Mobile Home TBRA $128,841, CHDO Reserve/Affordable Housing $261,754, administration $53,833. CDBG capital: code enforcement $246,506, housing rehabilitation $381,139, TBRA administration $235,000, ADA improvements $125,000; public services $168,179 across six agencies. The 2026-27 CDBG NOFA opened October 2, 2025 with applications due December 11, 2025.
- AMI requirement: HOME rents and 80% AMI limits; the City states its HOME CHDO acquisition-rehab rental properties are restricted to households at or below 60% of Orange County AMI for a minimum of 15 years under each CHDO agreement; CHDO reserve for nonprofit-owned or developed affordable housing; CDBG national objectives with at least 70% of funds benefiting households at or below 80% AMI.
- Cycle: annual NOFA (next: FY 2027-28 CDBG NOFA open: application packets available October 8, 2026; completed applications due by 5:00 p.m. December 10, 2026 (original signed applications only, postmarks not accepted).)
- Layering notes: Huntington Beach's HOME is small ($538,328) and goes almost entirely to TBRA; only the CHDO reserve (about $260,000 a year) is available for development, so City HOME is a token layer next to County and OCHFT money. Davis-Bacon applies at 12 or more HOME-assisted units. The City's Pathways Project (Jamboree Housing ENA extended 18 months in May 2024 for a permanent shelter and supportive housing at the Navigation Center site, Beach and Edinger Corridors Affordable Housing Overlay) was budgeted from IIG, AHSC, TCAC, BHCIP, Community Care Expansion, OCHFT ($2,500,000), OCHA PBVs ($3,720,000) and Behavioral Health Services funds ($5,000,000), illustrating the stack the City expects. Legistar attachments (FY 2025-26 funding tables, 2026-27 NOFA notice, Pathways funding matrix, ENA extension) opened via the Legistar web API; The City CDBG and HOME program page (huntingtonbeachca.gov, opened 2026-11-08) posts the FY 2027-28 NOFA, handbook and application.

- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)

**Pathways Project supportive housing and shelter site (Huntington Beach Housing Authority Exclusive Negotiations Agreement with Jamboree Housing; Navigation Center site, Beach and Edinger Corridors Affordable Housing Overlay)**
- Agency: Huntington Beach Housing Authority and Community Development Department; Jason Austin, Deputy Director of Homeless and Behavioral Health
- Type: zoning incentive
- Typical award: City-controlled site (current Navigation Center, about 3,000 deed-restricted affordable units in the City's overall portfolio per the RFQ) offered to Jamboree Housing under a 2022 Exclusive Negotiations Agreement extended 18 months on May 14, 2024 to plan and secure funding for a permanent homeless shelter, sobering center, services and low income supportive housing. June 2024 funding matrix prepared by the City: IIG $3,900,000, BHCIP $60,000,000, TCAC/CDLAC equity $23,000,000, Community Care Expansion $3,800,000, AHSC $17,000,000, OCHFT $2,500,000, OCHA PBVs $3,720,000, Behavioral Health Services (Prop 1) $5,000,000. No City cash commitment is listed.
- AMI requirement: Housing Authority goal of 100% affordable units at 60% AMI or below qualifying as supportive housing under Government Code 65650; at least 20% affordable for by-right processing in the overlay.
- Cycle: closed/inactive (next: ENA extension ran 18 months from May 2024 (to about November 2025); status of a further extension or disposition agreement not confirmed. Check Housing Authority agendas.)

Any developer other than Jamboree would need the ENA to lapse. Public land conveyed below fair market value and local loans are public funds under Labor Code 1720(b)(1) and (b)(3), so state prevailing wage applies unless a 1720(c) exemption fits the deal (see prevailing_wage_basis). ENA extension and funding matrix PDFs opened via Legistar web API (matter 24-397).

### City of Irvine

**Affordable Housing Credits Program (Irvine Zoning Ordinance Sec. 2-3-6)**
- Agency: City of Irvine Community Development Department (credits database and three-party credits agreements)
- Type: regulatory requirement
- Typical award: Market mechanism, not a subsidy. Projects that build more affordable units than the 15% requirement earn transferable credits in three income categories (extremely low or very low, low, moderate) that they may sell to market-rate projects or mixed projects with a shortfall; credits become available after building permits are issued for the excess units and a completion bond or certificate of occupancy is in place. A three-party credits agreement (buyer, seller, City) must be executed before the buyer's building permits; sale prices are not disclosed to the City.
- AMI requirement: Credits track the income level of the excess units; the receiving project satisfies its required affordable component at that level.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Agreement before building permit; City maintains the credits database on request.)
- Layering notes: Reclassified from other to regulatory requirement: the credits program is part of the Chapter 2-3 inclusionary procedure (15% requirement, 5% each extremely low or very low, low and moderate) and is a compliance-trading mechanism, not a public subsidy. For a 100% affordable developer it can still be a revenue source: excess units earn credits (for example 2.0 credits per ownership unit sold to lower income buyers, 1.6 extremely low or very low credits per qualifying rental unit, one credit releasing 19 market-rate units) that can be sold to market-rate builders. Confirm with the City how many credits are outstanding and the recent trading range. Read on the zoneomics mirror because the City-linked Municode page is Cloudflare-blocked; the City in-lieu fee page (cityofirvine.gov/node/94569) confirms the 15% requirement and menu options.
- Source: https://www.zoneomics.com/code/irvine-CA/chapter_2
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)

**Affordable Housing In-Lieu Fee Fund (Irvine Zoning Ordinance Sec. 2-3-5.B.3.c; fee set by City Council resolution)**
- Agency: City of Irvine Community Development Department
- Type: loan
- Typical award: In-lieu fees are deposited in the City's affordable housing fund and used for projects implementing the Housing Element needs assessment or serving low, very low and extremely low income households; the fee is charged per market-rate unit under a Council-approved formula, determined at building permit, and has not been updated since 2011 (a legacy $17,000 per unit rate applied only to pre-2007 Irvine Business Complex filings). A May 2026 Draft Affordable Housing and In-Lieu Fee Analysis was released August 10, 2026; staff recommends keeping the existing formula with updated inputs. Finance Commission reviewed it October 19, 2026; Planning Commission and Council hearings are not yet scheduled. Fund balance and any developer allocation process are not published.
- AMI requirement: Fund uses limited to low, very low and extremely low income households and Housing Element implementation; recipients record 55-year covenants under Chapter 2-3.
- Cycle: rolling (next: No NOFA located as of November 8, 2026. In-lieu fee update pending Planning Commission and City Council hearings (dates TBD). Ask Community Development (cd@cityofirvine.org) for the fund balance and whether a developer round is planned.)
- Layering notes: Because most Irvine builders provide units on-site or through credits, the in-lieu fund is smaller than Santa Ana's; its visible use is land and loans to Irvine Community Land Trust projects (Salerno, Parc Derian, Doria, Alegre, Sage Park) which then take LIHTC, HOME, OCHFT and County MHSA money. Local and state funds are public funds under Labor Code 1720(b), so state prevailing wage applies unless a 1720(c) exemption fits the deal, such as 1720(c)(5)(E) for below-market loans with at least 40 percent of units restricted 20 years at or below 80 percent AMI (see prevailing_wage_basis). Code text read on zoneomics because the City-linked Municode page is Cloudflare-blocked; the City In-Lieu Fee Formula Update page (cityofirvine.gov/node/94569) and its September 8, 2026 FAQ were opened and confirm the 15% requirement, the formula-based fee and the update schedule.
- Source: https://www.zoneomics.com/code/irvine-CA/chapter_2
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)

**Inclusionary Housing Ordinance, Affordable Housing Implementation Procedure (Irvine Zoning Ordinance Chapter 2-3, Secs. 2-3-1 to 2-3-11; Ord. 04-15, 24-13, 25-16)**
- Agency: City of Irvine Community Development Department, Planning Services and Housing staff
- Type: regulatory requirement
- Typical award: Requirement, not a subsidy. Residential projects must provide 15% of units as affordable: 5% extremely low or very low income, 5% low income, 5% moderate income (ownership units for very low or low earn 2:1 credit; extremely low units 1.6:1; three- and four-bedroom units 1.4:1 and 1.6:1). Projects with at least 10% very low or extremely low units satisfy the combined 10% lower income requirement. Alternatives (menu option) are allowed only when on-site units are infeasible or in the City's interest: converting market units for 55 years, extending expiring covenants 55 years, in-lieu fees set by Council resolution, transferring units to a nonprofit, buying affordable housing credits (Sec. 2-3-6), alternative housing (SROs, special needs, shelters at 1:1), or dedicating land or resources of at least equal value. Projects up to 100% affordable may be approved in any planning area and can only be denied under Government Code 65589.5(d). Community preference policy in Sec. 2-3-11.
- AMI requirement: Covenants of at least 55 years at the income level provided; bedroom mix must match the market units and affordable units must be dispersed; affordable housing plans and annual compliance reports required; revocation of entitlements for noncompliance.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Applies at entitlement; in-lieu fee amount determined at building permit under the current Council resolution (fee study drafted August 3, 2023; current schedule not confirmed). Chapter last amended June 24, 2025 (Ord. 25-16).)
- Layering notes: Irvine's 15% requirement is the highest of the five Orange County priority cities and is the engine behind the Irvine Company planning area affordable sites that nonprofits (Jamboree, C&C, Related, ICLT) build with 4% and 9% credits; a nonprofit taking an inclusionary site typically gets the land at low cost plus City or Irvine Community Land Trust support, then layers County MHSA/BHSA, OCHFT and OCHA PBVs. Sec. 2-3-7 states the City has no obligation to provide financial incentives, so there is no guaranteed city subsidy. cityofirvine.gov returned 403 to all fetch methods this pass; the ordinance was read on the zoneomics mirror.
- Source: https://www.zoneomics.com/code/irvine-CA/chapter_2
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)

**Irvine Community Land Trust (ICLT) land and development partnerships**
- Agency: Irvine Community Land Trust, 501(c)(3) created by the City of Irvine in 2006, 503 Nightmist, Irvine 92618; Board chaired by Ryan Aeh (2026)
- Type: land
- Typical award: ICLT acquires or receives land (including City conveyances such as the four-acre site reported in the City's FY 2023-25 budget) and ground leases it to development partners so that units stay affordable permanently. Portfolio: Alegre Apartments, Doria Apartments, Parc Derian Apartments, Salerno Apartments (501 Nightmist) and Sage Park (affordable ownership); it reports hundreds of affordable units in Irvine and, since its 2017 mission expansion, elsewhere in Orange County. ICLT finances projects with LIHTC, HOME, Orange County Housing Finance Trust loans, FHLB AHP and HUD programs; dollar values of land contributions are not published.
- AMI requirement: Permanent affordability through recorded ground lease covenants; rental projects have served extremely low to low income households and Sage Park serves moderate income buyers.
- Cycle: rolling (next: No solicitation open as of November 8, 2026; contact ICLT through its partnerships page.)
- Layering notes: ICLT is how Irvine converts inclusionary land dedications and City-owned parcels into 100% affordable projects without a city loan program; a developer partnering with ICLT gets site control at nominal ground rent and then stacks 4% or 9% credits, County MHSA/BHSA capital, OCHFT (Cypress Village Irvine took $3,500,000 in the 2024 OCHFT round) and OCHA PBVs. ICLT is a nonprofit, not a public agency, so its land alone does not trigger prevailing wage, but City land conveyed through it may. ICLT home, about, history, process, partnerships and properties pages and the September 23, 2026 letter opened on irvineclt.org.
- Source: https://irvineclt.org/our-process/
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)

**Residential Density Bonus Standards (Irvine Zoning Ordinance Sec. 2-3-10)**
- Agency: City of Irvine Community Development Department, Planning Services
- Type: density bonus
- Typical award: Requirement and entitlement, not a subsidy. Implements Government Code 65915 to 65918 by reference: density bonuses, incentives and concessions, waivers and parking ratios per state law, documented in a density bonus housing agreement recorded as a condition of the discretionary approval; development standards may be modified under Sec. 2-3-10.C for projects providing the Chapter 2-3 affordable units.
- AMI requirement: State thresholds (5% very low, 10% low, 10% moderate for-sale, 100% affordable); 55-year rental covenants.

Irvine receives its own CDBG, HOME, PLHA and HHAP allocations (HHAP Round 6 $5,947,855 per the County record) but those pages could not be opened this pass. Irvine is not a Prohousing designated city per the HCD list opened 2026-11-08.

### City of Lincoln

**Lincoln 2021-2029 Housing Element Actions 2.6 and 2.7: project-by-project incentives (deferred development fees, reduced parking, expedited review) for affordable housing in Villages 1, 5 and 7**
- Agency: City of Lincoln Community Development Department, Planning Division (916-434-3370; 600 6th Street)
- Type: fee waiver

The Housing Element (adopted January 2023 per the City's 2025 Annual Progress Report, 2021 to 2029 cycle, RHNA 5,120 units) commits the City to offer incentives on a project-by-project basis for lower-income housing in Village 1, Village 5 and Village 7, including deferred development fees, reduced parking requirements, expedited application review and technical assistance (Action 2.7), and to provide financial or in-kind assistance and incentives beyond the density bonus for extremely low income housing (Action 2.6). Action 2.9 commits only to explore a local inclusionary program; none has been adopted. No dollar amounts, fee schedules or fund are attached.

- Layering notes: Lincoln's village specific plans (Lincoln Crossing, Village 7 and others) carry no fixed inclusionary percentage, unlike Roseville's 10% goal, so affordability in Lincoln depends on developer-by-developer agreements plus County and state money. The Consolidated Plan notes two-story height limits and two spaces per unit parking standards as constraints the City may relax for affordable projects. The Housing Element PDF itself could not be located on the redesigned lincolnca.gov site (housing element and general plan URLs returned 404); the actions were read from the City's 2026-30 Consolidated Plan, hence needs_confirmation.

- Agency: City of Lincoln City Manager's Office (Nita Wracker; publiccomments@lincolnca.gov, 916-434-2427; 600 Sixth Street)
- Type: grant

**Lincoln density bonus (state Government Code 65915 applied directly; Housing Element Action 2.3 reported implemented, no stand-alone zoning chapter located)**
- Agency: City of Lincoln Community Development Department, Planning Division
- Type: density bonus
- Typical award: Regulatory incentive, not a subsidy. Lincoln does have a local density bonus chapter: Municipal Code Chapter 18.59, Density Increase and Incentive Program (Ord. 881B, April 23, 2013, replacing a 1995 chapter). It applies in all zones allowing residential use and grants qualifying projects and land transfers a density bonus, incentives and concessions in the amounts specified in Government Code 65915 et seq., as amended, so current state tiers apply (20% to 50% bonuses, 80% for 100% affordable projects, up to four concessions, parking caps). The Housing Element (Action 2.3) identifies Section 18.59 as the City's density bonus provision; Action 2.5 also lists a 35% bonus for market-rate rental projects with 20% low or 10% very low income units, a figure superseded by state law.
- AMI requirement: State thresholds (5% very low, 10% lower, 10% moderate for-sale, senior housing, 100% affordable); the City and applicant agree on a method to ensure continued availability of the bonus units before approval (18.59.060), with 55-year rental covenants under state law.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Processed with entitlements; application filed in writing with the Planning Division concurrently with other entitlements (18.59.050). No deadline.)
- Layering notes: No local enhancements beyond state law, and no local trust fund, fee waiver ordinance, inclusionary fund or city NOFA in Lincoln beyond the negotiated Housing Element incentives (record above) and CDBG. Chapter 18.59 incorporates Government Code 65915 by reference, so it tracks state amendments automatically. Chapter text was read on the zoneomics mirror (the official host, municode, returns 403); the City's Housing Element confirms that Section 18.59 is the density bonus provision.

- Agency: City of Lodi Community Development Department
- Type: fee waiver
- Typical award: Not yet adopted as a standing program. Program 1.6 commits the City to adopt by 2025 one or more incentives for infill housing at 20 or more units per acre: parking credits, fee waivers, reductions or deferrals when financially feasible, priority processing. Program 1.12 commits to incentives (reduced standards, fee waivers or financial assistance) for housing for persons with disabilities by 2026. - AMI requirement: State density bonus thresholds; affordability covenants per Government Code 65915 (55 years rental).

Housing Element Program 1.1 commits the City to update 17.36.050 to the current state tier framework; the 2025 Housing Element Annual Progress Report lists the Development Code amendments as in progress, and the 2025 code amendments (Ordinances 2030 and 2034) did not address the density bonus. No density bonus applications were filed in 2025.)
- Layering notes: Lodi has no inclusionary ordinance (Housing Element confirms) and no local in-lieu fee, so the density bonus is the only land-use subsidy. Because the code defers to state law, developers can claim the full state bonus despite the outdated 35% text. Pair with County HOME, SJRHF, HACSJ PBVs and the City surplus land program (next record). Read from the zoneomics mirror of Title 17 Article 3 because municode blocks scripts.
- Source: https://www.lodi.gov/DocumentCenter/View/8317/2023-2031-Certified-Housing-Element

### City of Madera

**Affordable Housing Density Bonus (Madera Municipal Code Chapter 10-3-5.1) with Housing Element incentives: fee reductions (Program B-7), impact fee waivers (MMC 10-8.17) and fee waivers or deferrals (Program A-4)**
- Agency: City of Madera Community Development Department, Planning (Planning Manager David Brletic, (559) 661-5433)
- Type: density bonus
- Typical award: Requirement, not a subsidy. The density bonus follows state law; the chapter was amended in February 2025 to track recent state changes, including parking for 100% affordable projects near transit. Program B-7 fee reductions: downtown projects and vacant or aging buildings get up to 100% off Engineering fees and 75% off Planning and Building fees. Non-profit buildings get up to 50%, with building fee reductions capped at $4,000. MMC 10-8.17 lets the Community Development Director approve impact fee adjustments, waivers or exemptions. Program A-4 offers fee waivers and deferrals for affordable projects as technical assistance.
- AMI requirement: State density bonus thresholds (for example 10% lower income or 5% very low income units); 55-year affordability for bonus units.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Available at entitlement, no deadline. The Housing Element commits to local density bonus standards beyond state law by Q1 2028 and to fee reductions for at least 20 qualifying projects by Q3 2026.)
- Layering notes: Madera has no inclusionary ordinance or in-lieu fund. These fee tools are the only local cost reductions beyond HOME and PLHA. Program B-7 targets downtown revitalization, so it fits best for an affordable rental project downtown. Elsewhere, use the Director's waiver authority in MMC 10-8.17 and ask for a deferral under A-4. A fee waiver is a public subsidy and, depending on its size, can trigger state prevailing wage. The 6th Cycle Housing Element was adopted February 4, 2026. Madera County's density bonus (county record, Chapter 18.114) applies only in unincorporated areas.
- Source: https://media-001-us.cdn.govstack.com/madera-003-us/media/fqwd5cjj/clean-madera-6th-cycle-housing-element-2-4-2026.pdf
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)

**City of Madera HOME Investment Partnerships (new participating jurisdiction) and CDBG entitlement, 2025-2029 Consolidated Plan**
- Agency: City of Madera Grants Division (Finance), Grants Administrator Marcela Zuniga, (559) 661-3692
- Type: loan
- Typical award: HOME: about $353,555 per year (5-year estimate $1,767,777). The first allocation, in 2024, was $372,065, plus a one-time City match of $127,935, for $500,000. Over 2025-2029 the ConPlan housing goal budgets HOME $1,590,999.90, CDBG $322,982 and PLHA $1,361,913. CDBG: about $989,791 per year. The PY 2027/28 tentative allocation is about $990,000 (up to 20% admin, up to 15% public services, about $643,500 capital).
- AMI requirement: HOME rental rules (24 CFR 92.252): HOME rents for households at or below 60% AMI, with 20% of HOME units at 50% AMI in projects with 5 or more units. CDBG must benefit households at or below 80% AMI.
- Cycle: annual NOFA (next: CDBG PY 2027/28 applications opened November 2, 2026 and are due January 29, 2027 by 5:00 p.m. via grantsinfo@madera.gov. No HOME rental NOFA found; request HOME gap funding directly from the Grants Division ahead of tax credit rounds.)
- Layering notes: Madera became a HOME participating jurisdiction in June 2024, so HOME is now the City's only recurring federal source that can fund new rental construction. The ConPlan lists owner rehab or new affordable housing as HOME uses. The amounts are small (about $354K per year), so the City would likely save several years of HOME for one gap loan, as the City of Merced does. Stack with PLHA (separate record), Housing Authority of the City of Madera project-based vouchers (county record) and 4% or 9% credits. Federal Davis-Bacon wages apply at 12 or more HOME-assisted units. HOME also requires NEPA review, and grants from 2024 on carry Build America Buy America requirements. The CDBG NOFA mostly funds public services and public improvements, but CDBG can pay for acquisition and site work for new housing. Sources read: 2025-2029 Consolidated Plan, PY 2027/28 CDBG Notice of Funding (media-001-us.cdn.govstack.com/madera-003-us/media/guann5xv/notice-of-funding-final.pdf) and the 6th Cycle Housing Element.

- Agency: City of Madera Grants Division (Finance)
- Type: loan
- Typical award: 2022 PLHA award of $1,801,097 (FY 2019, 2020 and 2021 allocations), notified February 15, 2023. The ConPlan lists $1,361,913 remaining for housing. The 2026 Housing Element estimates $1,455,181 available from award years 2021-2023, earmarked for housing construction and rehabilitation.

**Successor Housing Agency to the former Madera Redevelopment Agency (Low and Moderate Income Housing Asset Fund)**
- Agency: City of Madera as Successor Housing Agency (Resolutions MRA-1498 and CC 12-09)
- Type: loan
- Typical award: No published lending program. The City's FY 2024-25 ACFR shows the Low and Moderate Income Housing special revenue fund (former RDA housing funds) with a fund balance of $3,458,285 at June 30, 2025, up from $2,486,663, after FY 2024-25 revenue of $1,179,511 in property taxes and $117,379 in investment income, $8,828 of expenditures and a $316,440 transfer out; about $1.4 million budgeted for low and moderate income housing went unspent. Remaining RDA-era developer notes receivable total $7,000. The latest SB 341 reports posted are FY 2014-15 and FY 2015-16.

Up to $500,000 a year may go to homeless prevention and rapid rehousing. An unencumbered balance above the greater of $1,000,000 or the prior four years of deposits is excess surplus that must be committed within three years or sent to HCD.
- Cycle: rolling (next: unknown, verify with agency. Ask the City for the latest SB 341 report or the Housing Successor section of the Annual Progress Report.)
- Layering notes: Recorded so the asset fund is not overlooked. The FY 2024-25 ACFR shows about $3.5 million in the fund and roughly $1.2 million a year of incoming property tax revenue, but the City has no NOFA or lending guidelines for it; ask the City how it plans to deploy the balance and whether successor-owned parcels remain. Any award would layer with City HOME and PLHA, and the 30% extremely low income targeting rule favors deeply affordable rental projects.

### City of Marina

**Affordable Housing Overlay fee waivers and deferrals (Municipal Code Section 17.48.130, Ordinances 2023-01 and 2023-12) and state density bonus adopted by reference (Section 17.48.040, Ordinance 2023-07)**
- Agency: City of Marina Community Development Department, Planning Services Division
- Type: fee waiver
- Typical award: Projects on Affordable Housing Overlay (AHO) sites mapped for Housing Element opportunity sites receive ministerial administrative approval by the Community Development Director (no hearing), AHO development standards instead of the base zone (42-foot height, 48 feet on Reservation Road and Del Monte Boulevard), and one of three incentives: waived, reduced or deferred planning, plan check or construction permit fees; deferral of City construction and impact fees to completion or occupancy; or payment of construction and impact fees over twelve months or longer after completion. Section 17.48.040 adopts Government Code 65915 to 65918 by reference and caps bonuses, concessions, waivers and parking at the state maximums unless a development agreement provides more. Approvals lapse after two years with a one-year extension.
- AMI requirement: To use the AHO a project must restrict at least 12% of units to very low income or 15% to low income households (Section 17.48.130(F)(1)(b)) under an agreement of at least 55 years executed before building permit; minimum density 30 units per acre. Inclusionary ratios in Table 17.48.030-1 still apply. Density bonus target units above the inclusionary requirement are restricted 30 years.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Not applicable; ministerial on AHO-mapped sites. Housing Element Program 2.3 committed the City to evaluate its incentives by end of 2024 and strengthen them by end of 2026 if 200 lower income units are not on track.)
- Layering notes: The AHO is the only fee relief program found among Monterey County priority cities and was cited in Marina's August 2025 Prohousing Designation application (Enhancement Category 3). Fee deferral to occupancy helps construction-period cash flow on tax credit deals such as Lightfighter Village (EAH and Veterans Transition Center, 71 units) and future Dunes and Downtown Marina AHO sites. It does not waive school, water (Marina Coast Water District) or Fort Ord Reuse Authority successor fees. Code read on the zoneomics mirror (Title 17, Chapter 17.48) because marina.municipal.codes returns 403.
- Source: https://www.zoneomics.com/code/marina-CA/chapter_5
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)

**Below Market Rate housing program and project affordable housing agreements (Lightfighter Village, The Dunes BMR, Sea Haven BMR; BMR Administrative Policies adopted March 1, 2021)**
- Agency: City of Marina City Manager's Office, Housing Program Division
- Type: regulatory requirement
- Typical award: Program, not a cash subsidy. The City records affordable housing agreements under Section 17.48.080 for each project: Lightfighter Village (Veterans Transition Center and EAH Housing, 229-239 Hayes Circle, 71 permanent supportive units, Resolution 2023-34 of April 4, 2023) must keep 40% of units affordable with at least 15% very low income; the agreement restricts 11 units to 30% AMI and 18 units to 50% AMI at TCAC rents for 55 years and the project is securing 17 project-based vouchers. The Dunes BMR site 1 delivered 93 affordable units (occupancy May 1, 2024) and Sea Haven BMR for-sale homes were sold through a 2023 lottery. Housing Element Program 2.5 reserves 30% of BMR units for Marina workers and residents under the BMR Administrative Policies and Procedures (2021).
- AMI requirement: Project-specific: Lightfighter 30% and 50% AMI for 55 years; BMR ownership units resale-restricted 45 years; rental inclusionary units 55 years or perpetual.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Agreements are approved by Council before building permit on each project. Housing Element objective: assist 60 lower income Marina households through the BMR program and facilitate 200 affordable units by 2031.)
- Layering notes: Marina's role is regulatory and site-based; the money for Lightfighter Village came from County Housing Trust Fund ($500,115), HHAP, state and tax credit sources (county records), and the City contributed entitlements, the AHO process and the 40% affordability agreement. Marina also submitted a draft Prohousing Designation application in August 2025 (draft read on cityofmarina.org) which, if approved, adds state scoring points for Marina sites; designation status not confirmed. The Housing Element APR for 2024 is posted only as a SharePoint link that could not be opened. Documents read: Resolution 2023-34 with the Lightfighter agreement (Archive ADID 13198), Resolution 2025-18 (ADID 14723), the certified Sixth Cycle Housing Element (DocumentCenter View 13793) and the Housing page (cityofmarina.org/190/Housing).
- Source: https://cityofmarina.org/Archive.aspx?ADID=13198
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)

**Inclusionary Housing (Municipal Code Section 17.48.030 as amended by Ordinance 2025-07) and Affordable Housing Trust Fund (Section 17.48.090)**
- Agency: City of Marina Community Development Department, Planning Services Division; City Manager's Office, Housing
- Type: regulatory requirement
- Typical award: Requirement, not a subsidy. Ordinance 2025-07 (introduced May 20, 2025, adopted June 3, 2025, effective 30 days later, implementing Housing Element Program 2.4 with General Plan Amendment Resolution 2025-48) lowered the threshold from 20 to 5 or more units and set a citywide 20% requirement for new or substantially rehabilitated for-sale or rental housing: 6% very low, 7% low, 7% moderate, plus a voluntary incentive-based 10% middle income (up to 135% AMI for-sale) tier; existing occupied housing on the former Fort Ord also 20% (6/7/7), down from 40% (15/15/10). Market-rate density bonus units are exempt. Alternatives approved by Council (17.48.030(D)): land dedication, acquisition and rehabilitation, preservation of at-risk units, conversion of market-rate units, special needs housing, or a tailored program for 500-unit specific plan projects. No in-lieu fee is codified; the Affordable Housing Trust Fund (17.48.090) receives only enforcement recoveries. Rental units restricted 55 years (in perpetuity if allowed), for-sale resale restrictions 45 years, rents capped at 90% of comparable market rent.
- AMI requirement: 20% of units: 6% very low (rent at 30% of 50% AMI), 7% low (30% of 60% AMI rental), 7% moderate (30% of 110% AMI rental); middle income tier voluntary.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Applies with the first discretionary application (affordable housing plan required). Housing Element objective: 200 lower income units through inclusionary and density bonus by 2031.)
- Layering notes: Marina has no in-lieu fee revenue and therefore no local gap fund; its contribution to affordable deals is land and entitlement through specific plans (The Dunes, Sea Haven, Marina Heights, Cypress Knolls each at 20%) and the Affordable Housing Overlay (record below). Marina is in the Monterey Urban County for CDBG and does not receive PLHA directly (county records). Lightfighter Village received a County Housing Trust Fund loan of $500,115 (county record). Ordinance 2025-07 and Resolution 2025-48 were read as PDFs from cityofmarina.org Archive.aspx; the current code text was read on the zoneomics mirror because marina.municipal.codes returns 403.
- Source: https://www.cityofmarina.org/ArchiveCenter/ViewFile/Item/14532
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)


### City of Menlo Park

**Below Market Rate (BMR) Housing Fund NOFA 2026/27**
- Agency: City of Menlo Park Community Development Department, Housing Division
- Type: loan
- Typical award: Approximately $4 million available for the production and preservation of permanent affordable housing, awarded competitively by the City Council; PlanetBids listing cites award sizes of about $300,000 to $800,000. Additional consideration for extremely low income units, special populations and preservation or rehabilitation of multifamily housing. Emergency shelters and transitional housing are not eligible. The prior round (January 2023) offered $1.5 million to $2 million; the City also contributed $1 million to a teacher housing project in November 2024.
- AMI requirement: Permanent affordability consistent with the BMR Housing Program Guidelines (October 21, 2025) and the Housing Element; priority to extremely low income and special needs units.
- Cycle: annual NOFA (next: Applications due 5:00 pm Friday, November 20, 2026 on PlanetBids (invitation 2026-100926-101526; questions closed November 6, 2026); Housing Commission review winter 2027, Council award spring 2027. Housing Element Program H1.I requires a NOFA at least every two years.)
- Layering notes: County layer: every San Mateo County city project competes for the County Affordable Housing Fund NOFA (AHF 14 closed July 15, 2026, next fall 2027), HEART bridge loans and HACSM project-based vouchers; city money is usually the first commitment that unlocks those. The BMR fund is capitalized by commercial in-lieu fees (office and R&D $23.26 per square foot in FY 2026-27) and residential in-lieu payments, so its size tracks Meta and life science approvals; $4 million is enough for one gap loan or a preservation deal and is typically paired with County AHF and HACSM PBVs. Source is the City's 2026 NOFA page; contact Arianna Milton, ANMilton@menlopark.gov, (650) 330-6705.
- Source: https://www.menlopark.gov/Government/Departments/Community-Development/Housing/NOFA
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-07)

**Below Market Rate (BMR) Housing Program: residential inclusionary and commercial in-lieu fees (MPMC 16.96)**
- Agency: City of Menlo Park Community Development Department, Housing Division
- Type: regulatory requirement
- Typical award: Requirement, not a subsidy. Residential: 10 to 19 units at least 10% BMR, 20 or more units at least 15% BMR (very low, low and moderate income); 5 to 9 units provide a unit if feasible or pay a graduated in-lieu fee of 1% to 3% of sales price; for-sale projects of 10 or more may pay 3% of the sales price per market-rate unit in lieu; rental in-lieu fee set by Council resolution based on the cost of a one-bedroom unit. Each on-site BMR unit earns one additional market-rate unit up to 15% above zoned density. Commercial: buildings of 10,000 square feet or more provide BMR units or pay in-lieu fees of $23.26 per square foot (office and R&D, Group A) or $12.62 (other commercial and industrial, Group B) for July 1, 2026 to June 30, 2027, adjusted each July 1 by a five-year CPI shelter average.
- AMI requirement: BMR rents at or below 30% of the income category limit and no more than 75% of market rents; income categories from 30% to 120% AMI; one-year live or work preference; BMR housing agreement recorded before permits.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Applies at application; Menlo Park leads the 2026 San Mateo County multi-city nexus study (Strategic Economics) that may raise inclusionary percentages and add a residential impact fee later in 2026 or 2027.)
- Layering notes: County layer: every San Mateo County city project competes for the County Affordable Housing Fund NOFA (AHF 14 closed July 15, 2026, next fall 2027), HEART bridge loans and HACSM project-based vouchers; city money is usually the first commitment that unlocks those. The commercial in-lieu fee is the engine of the BMR fund (see NOFA record); office projects in the Bayfront and downtown specific plan areas often negotiate on-site or off-site BMR units instead. Source is the City's residential BMR requirements page; commercial rates from the companion commercial page and the October 21, 2025 Guidelines (Resolution 7003).
- Source: https://www.menlopark.gov/Government/Departments/Community-Development/Housing/Developers/Residential-development-BMR-requirements
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-07)

**Mill Valley Affordable Housing Requirements: inclusionary units and affordable housing impact fee, MVMC Chapter 20.80 (Ordinance 1295 of 2017, inclusionary update adopted 2026 under Housing Element Programs 7 and 11)**
- Agency: City of Mill Valley Planning and Building Department
- Type: regulatory requirement
- Typical award: Requirement, not a subsidy. Impact fee: 1% of construction valuation on single-family and small multifamily residential work at or above the valuation threshold ($100,000 in 2018, $105,000 in 2020, $130,000 in 2023, $142,000 from May 1, 2024, indexed to the California Construction Cost Index), paid at building permit into the Affordable Housing Trust Fund; collection was extended five years by Council resolution on March 20, 2023. The 2026 update lowered the inclusionary requirement from 25% to 15%, exempted 2 to 6 unit projects from building affordable units and waived their impact fee when units stay under 850 square feet (one bedroom), 1,000 (two bedrooms) or 1,200 (three bedrooms), and eliminated micro-unit caps. Fractional units of 0.50 or more may be met by an in-lieu payment calculated by applying the fraction to the impact fee formula.
- AMI requirement: Projects of 7 to 9 units: 15% affordable with at least one unit for moderate income households. Projects of 10 or more units: 15% affordable, at least half of the affordable units for low income households and the rest moderate income. Rental affordable units restricted in perpetuity or the maximum term allowed by law (20.80.060). Exempt: ADUs, micro units, projects below the valuation threshold, projects vested before November 1, 2018. Off-site units, land dedication or acquisition-rehabilitation alternatives at the City's sole discretion; Chapter 20.80.080 allows reducing moderate income unit counts when units are instead restricted to very low or low income.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Threshold adjusts each calendar year. Housing Element Program 11 requires a further look at inclusionary ratios at the 2028 RHNA mid-point; Program 12 calls for considering a commercial linkage fee and single-family impact fee changes with other Marin jurisdictions.)
- Layering notes: The 2026 drop from 25% to 15% (half low, half moderate) brings Mill Valley below Novato (20%) and the County (20%) and closer to San Rafael's 5% to 10%; combined with the Housing Overlay Districts (17 to 40 units per acre) it is meant to make 7-plus unit infill feasible on commercial corridors. The impact fee is the engine of the Trust Fund record above; no commercial linkage fee exists yet. The 2026 ordinance PDF (Attachment 1, as adopted per the City zoning updates page), the Zoneomics mirror of Chapter 20.80, the 2024 APR and the Housing Element were opened; the City's eCode360 host was not needed.
- Source: https://www.cityofmillvalley.gov/DocumentCenter/View/12336
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)

**Mill Valley Affordable Housing Trust Fund (MVMC 20.80.070, Ordinance 1295, Resolution 20-26 Administrative Guidelines, Resolution 24-60 Local Housing Trust Fund match)**
- Agency: City of Mill Valley Planning and Building Department (Danielle Staude, dstaude@cityofmillvalley.org), with Housing Advisory Committee priorities and City Council approval of every award
- Type: loan
- Typical award: Funded by the 1% affordable housing impact fee on residential permits at or above the construction valuation threshold ($142,000 since May 1, 2024) plus inclusionary in-lieu payments and donations; collections were $345,000 by Feb 2020, roughly $300,000 a year per the Housing Element and about $600,000 a year per the 2024 Annual Progress Report, with about $1,000,000 unencumbered in 2024. Resolution 24-60 (Sept 5, 2024) committed $1,000,000 of Trust Fund match for an HCD Local Housing Trust Fund application ($1,200,000 requested; HCD's Round 5 applicant list shows the City with a self-score of 60) so that $2,400,000 total would be available: $1,000,000 ($500,000 grant plus $500,000 match) for Bayfront Terrace at 1 Hamilton Drive and $1,400,000 for other projects to be solicited. Loans at simple interest of no more than 3% as construction or deferred-payment permanent financing; up to 5% administration. Ongoing uses: Marin Housing Authority BMR administration, Home Match contract (up to $30,000 a year), Bayfront Terrace predevelopment, and the Lease to Locals pilot ($3,500 to $14,000 per converted rental, running through 2027).
- AMI requirement: Low income households per Chapter 20.80 covenants; LHTF-matched awards target 60% AMI and below with a 30% extremely low income set-aside. Projects must be inside Mill Valley, scored on feasibility, funding needed, unit count and location outside the very high fire severity zone. Council approves each award at a public hearing. The City adopted HCD's Uniform Multifamily Regulations for underwriting.
- Cycle: rolling (next: unknown, verify with agency. The City said it would announce a solicitation in early 2025 contingent on the HCD LHTF award; no award or solicitation was found on the City site as of November 2026, and the 2028 Mitigation Fee Act five-year review and impact fee extension decision are the next fixed milestones.)
- Layering notes: Mill Valley's fund is unusually well capitalized for a 14,000-person city because the 1% fee hits every large remodel; it is the only Marin priority city with a committed state LHTF match strategy. Money has gone almost entirely to the City's own site (Bayfront Terrace, EAH Housing, 45 units) and to tenure programs, so a third-party developer should expect the $1,400,000 remainder and future fee receipts (about $600,000 a year) as the ceiling. Layer under the Marin County Affordable Housing Fund (the County awarded 1 Hamilton $500,000 in 2022 and $1,000,000 total by 2024 per County documents cited in search results, not opened), County HOME ($360,000 to the Eden Housing Mill Valley rental project in FY 2026-27, see County record) and PLHA; CDBG and HOME flow through the Marin Urban County. City loans are public funds for prevailing wage. - Agency: City of Mill Valley Planning and Building Department
- Type: density bonus
- Typical award: Requirement framework, not a cash subsidy. The 2024 Housing Overlay Districts, applied on top of base zoning to Housing Element sites, allow 17 to 40 units per acre (20 to 40 in the Opportunity Site overlay), 40-foot height, one parking space for units of 1,000 square feet or less, waived lot merger fees, and let projects also use State Density Bonus to modify standards; projects reserving 20% of units for lower income households get streamlined review. - Type: density bonus
- Typical award: Incentive, not a subsidy. Section 38-112.5 adopts State Density Bonus Law and adds local bonuses in subsection (J) that are independent of and additional to the state bonus: 10% for consolidating two or more parcels into a lot of at least 0.50 acre; 10% for projects with 70% two- and three-bedroom units (plus one extra story in the Alvarado District and the Pacific, Munras and Cass MF2 overlay); 10% for projects with 40% moderate income units; and 50% for 100% affordable projects under Government Code 65915(b)(1)(G). Rental affordability agreements run 55 years. The RHNA Overlay District (Sections 38-99.9 and 38-99.10) allows multifamily on nonvacant commercial sites carried over from the fourth and fifth cycle inventories, and the Multifamily Residential Overlay sets 60 units per acre.
- AMI requirement: State density bonus thresholds; local bonuses require 40% moderate income or 100% affordable (80% AMI and below with up to 20% moderate) as applicable; 55-year covenants for rental units.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Not applicable; requested with the first planning application on the City form. Coastal zone projects must also meet the Local Coastal Program except for density.)
- Layering notes: The stackable local bonuses (up to 50% extra for 100% affordable) are the strongest zoning incentive among Monterey County cities and can be combined with the state bonus, inclusionary unit credit and the RHNA overlay sites. No local fee waiver program was found; the City's main constraint is water allocation (Housing Element Program 2-J). Code text read on the zoneomics mirror (Chapter 38, Articles 16E and 17) because the City's municode host blocks scripts.
- Source: https://www.zoneomics.com/code/monterey-CA/chapter_4

- Type: grant

FY 2026-27 uses: Affordable Housing Opportunities $940,000 (inclusionary unit acquisition, rehabilitation and resale, minor and major homeowner rehabilitation loans), public services $207,400 (eleven nonprofits including shelters at about $20,000 each), administration $118,000; backup projects include a MidPen project ($1,500,000). - Agency: City of Monterey Community Development Department, Housing Programs

- Typical award: Requirement, not a subsidy. The City Code (Section 8-1.00 et seq., Ordinance 3346 C.S. of 2004 requiring permanent affordability) requires a minimum of 20% permanently affordable low and moderate income units in projects of six or more new housing units and in condominium conversions (2015-2023 Housing Element Program i.2.1), with payment of in-lieu fees allowed; the 2015-2023 Housing Element reported that court rulings had limited the ordinance to ownership projects and that it did not apply to apartment projects; the 2023-2031 Housing Element Program 2-I directs the City to codify the requirement in the Zoning Code. **Affordable housing over-the-counter Notice of Funding Availability (Housing Impact Fund, BMR In-Lieu Fees Fund, Local Housing Trust Fund grant)**
- Agency: City of Mountain View Housing Department and Council NOFA Review Committee

- Agency: City of Mountain View Housing Department
- Type: regulatory requirement
- Typical award: Requirement, not a subsidy. Projects of 7 or more units: 15 percent BMR for rental and non-townhome ownership, 25 percent for rowhouse and townhouse projects; projects under 7 units pay fractional in-lieu fees with a new graduated reduction for 1 to 6 units. Rental BMR units at over 50 to 80 percent AMI with a 65 percent AMI weighted average; ownership at over 80 to 120 percent AMI (100 percent weighted average) plus a further 10 percent of townhome units at 120 to 150 percent AMI. Affordable in perpetuity; rents may rise at most 3 percent a year. In-lieu fees (now only a valuation yardstick for alternative compliance, since Council removed fee payment as a compliance option): rental $118 per net new habitable square foot in 2025 falling to $98 in FY 2026-27; townhome $153 to $118; other ownership $67 to $91; escalated by the California Construction Cost Index. Alternative compliance (land dedication, off-site units, or acquisition and preservation of existing housing) requires Council approval and a $32,000 cost-recovery fee.
- AMI requirement: Rental 65 percent AMI weighted average (range over 50 to 80 percent AMI); ownership 100 percent AMI weighted average; perpetual affordability; 15 percent of BMR units (or one unit) to be accessible under the 2026 amendments.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Not applicable; requirement applies at entitlement. No application round as of November 9, 2026.)
- Layering notes: BMR in-lieu fees historically funded the City's NOFA (for example $10 million to 1012 Linda Vista in 2023 and $6.3 million to Lot 12), so removing fee compliance will shrink the BMR Housing Fund over time; the City seeded the Affordable Housing Initiative Fund with $1 million from this fund in January 2026. The new acquisition and preservation compliance path lets a market-rate developer buy and deed-restrict existing units, a potential partnership for nonprofit preservation buyers.
