### City of Napa

**Napa 1% Transient Occupancy Tax for Affordable and Workforce Housing Fund (Measure F, November 2018)**
- Agency: City of Napa Housing Division
- Type: loan
- Typical award: Special tax of 1% on hotel and short term rental stays (TOT raised from 12% to 13%), effective January 1, 2019, dedicated solely to affordable and workforce housing projects, programs and services in the City of Napa. FY 2025-26 revenue about $2.5 million; fund balance at June 30, 2026 about $8.9 million unaudited, of which only about $264,000 was formally reserved for a specific project (FY 2025-26 draft CAPER), so most of the balance is uncommitted. The $3.7 million committed in 2021 and 2022 to the Crescent ownership project (15 moderate and 25 low income units, construction started summer 2026) was expended in Program Year 2025. Prior year: $10.2 million balance with $4 million reserved and $2.8 million revenue (FY 2024-25 CAPER). Measure F campaign estimate was $2.1 million a year. Awards are low or no interest deferred loans under the same rolling NOFA as the impact fee fund.
- AMI requirement: Households at or below 120% AMI. Under the NOFA the TOT fund is targeted primarily to the missing middle (81% to 120% AMI, rents at 30% of 110% AMI) and applications serving that band receive automatic full leverage points. 55-year rental and 45-year ownership regulatory agreements.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Rolling through the Neighborly portal under the combined Affordable Housing and TOT NOFA; City commits to a NOFA at least every two years. No 2025 or 2026 NOFA document found online as of 2026-11-08; confirm availability with the Housing Division (707-257-9628).)
- Layering notes: The only sizable local source in Napa County for moderate income and workforce rental or ownership units, which state programs rarely fund. Pairs with the impact fee loan (80% AMI units) in a mixed income project: impact fee dollars on the low income units, TOT dollars on the 81% to 120% AMI units. The County (Measure I) and the other four cities adopted parallel 1% TOT measures in 2018; each is a separate fund with its own geography, so a Napa city project cannot draw on the County or St. Helena funds. Sources opened: FY 2024-25 CAPER (source_url, fund balance and revenue), 2023 NOFA, Measure F argument in favor, HCD Prohousing designation release (Napa designated 2024) and Prohousing matrix.
- Source: https://www.cityofnapa.org/DocumentCenter/View/15932/2025---2026-DRAFT-CAPER
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)

**Napa Affordable Housing Impact Fee (NMC Chapter 15.94, Ordinance O2018-011) and alternative equivalent proposals**
- Agency: City of Napa Community Development Department (Chief Building Official) and Housing Division
- Type: regulatory requirement
- Typical award: Requirement, not a subsidy. Fee per gross square foot set by implementing resolution; schedule effective January 1, 2017 (phased in from May 2016): multifamily $4.05, single family and condominium $4.75, office and retail $3.55, hotel $6.00, industrial $3.50 per square foot. Collections ran $0.4 million to $3.6 million a year in FY 2014-15 through FY 2018-19 and about $1.7 million in FY 2024-25. An impact fee nexus study was underway in 2023 (Housing Element Program H2-2.7, fee schedule update due by 2028), so expect a higher schedule.
- AMI requirement: Exemption requires rents at 30% of 60% AMI (low), 30% of 50% AMI (very low) or 30% of 30% AMI (extremely low) with a 55-year rental or 45-year ownership affordable housing agreement under 15.94.080. Market rate units, including units for median and moderate income households, pay the fee.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Fee due before building permit issuance, or deferred under a recorded secured building agreement (Government Code 66007) to final inspection or certificate of occupancy, whichever occurs first; the City routinely defers fees for affordable projects to occupancy. Developers may propose an alternative equivalent proposal (on or off site affordable units, land dedication, conversion of market rate units, preservation) with City Council approval under 15.94.070. A petition for reduction, adjustment or waiver under 15.94.100 must be filed with the City Clerk at least 10 days before the first public hearing on the discretionary approval, or within 10 days after paying the fees under protest if no discretionary approval is required. A developer contesting the Director's fee determination for an unlisted nonresidential use has 30 days under 15.94.040(E).)
- Layering notes: Napa replaced its 1999 inclusionary ordinance with this fee in 2012, so market rate apartments owe no on site affordable units and 100% affordable projects (15% or more affordable) pay nothing. The fee stream capitalizes the Affordable Housing Impact Fee Fund record above. Compare the County fee under County Code 18.107 (Pass 2 record), which was overhauled on October 21, 2025 and phases in from January 16, 2026; the City schedule still dates from 2017 until the nexus study update is adopted. A fee exemption is not a City expenditure, but the City's loans are, so prevailing wage turns on the loan not the exemption. Code text read on the ecode360 mirror (source_url) and the 2018 ordinance PDF; the 2017 rate sheet is at cityofnapa.org/DocumentCenter/View/102.
- Source: https://ecode360.com/43395059
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)

**Napa Affordable Housing Impact Fee Fund (Affordable Housing Trust Fund) development loans, rolling NOFA**
- Agency: City of Napa Housing Division (Housing Manager Stephanie Gaul, 707-257-9628)
- Type: loan
- Typical award: Gap loans sized by the joint City and County Multi Family Transaction Underwriting Guidelines (Jan 21, 2020). Minimum award $100,000, no set maximum. Fund balance at June 30, 2026 was $6.3 million unaudited, of which $2.4 million was formally reserved for specific projects; FY 2025-26 fee collections were about $1.2 million, and $3.1 million of impact fees plus Homekey+ funds acquired the 24 unit 4th and Division Apartments that year (FY 2025-26 draft CAPER). Prior year: $8.7 million balance with $5 million reserved at June 30, 2025. Track record: $2.2 million general fund plus trust fund money each to Heritage House (90 units, 40 PSH) and Valley Lodge (54 units PSH) in 2022; four projects held reservations from the impact fee and TOT funds at the time of the 2023 Prohousing application. Application fee 1% of the loan request, minimum $10,000 ($5,000 cashier's check at pre-application, $5,000 at award).
- AMI requirement: Units must serve households at or below 80% AMI (rents at 30% of 30%, 50% or 60% AMI by tier). 55-year regulatory agreement for rental, 45 years for ownership, recorded under NMC Chapter 15.94. Mixed income projects are funded only for the proportional share of affordable units. Units must count toward the City RHNA (new construction, adaptive reuse, or qualifying rehab); transitional housing and shelters not eligible. Scoring gives 15 points for at least 20% PSH units and 10 points for 100% affordable.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Rolling, first come first served through the Neighborly portal (portal.neighborlysoftware.com/NAPACA/Participant). The 2023 NOFA accepted applications until June 30, 2024 or until funds were allocated; the City states funds are released at least once every two years by NOFA. No 2025 or 2026 NOFA document was found on cityofnapa.org as of 2026-11-08; contact the Housing Division before preparing an application.)
- Layering notes: The largest city controlled pool in Napa County and the normal local gap layer for 4% and 9% deals inside Napa city limits (Heritage House, Valley Lodge, Jamboree Silverado Trail PSH). Terms mirror the Napa County Affordable Housing Fund record: 3.0% simple interest, 55-year term, 50/50 residual receipts split, subordinate to senior debt, 90% maximum senior LTV, $100 per unit monitoring fee. Stack order: CTCAC credits and CMFA or CalHFA conduit bonds first, then HCD programs (MHP, AHSC, NPLH, Homekey), then City impact fee loan, then City 1% TOT loan for moderate income or missing middle units, with HACN project based vouchers for PSH units. County Affordable Housing Fund money is usually not available for sites inside the city (County preference for unincorporated projects) but the two agencies share underwriting guidelines and have co-funded projects. Local and state funds are public funds under Labor Code 1720(b), so state prevailing wage applies unless a 1720(c) exemption fits the deal, such as 1720(c)(5)(E) for below-market loans with at least 40 percent of units restricted 20 years at or below 80 percent AMI (see prevailing_wage_basis). Sources opened: 2023 NOFA (source_url), FY 2024-25 CAPER for fund balances, Prohousing Designation matrix, 2023 Housing Element APR.
- Source: https://www.cityofnapa.org/DocumentCenter/View/9332/Notice-of-Funding-Availability-2023-PDF
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)

**Napa CDBG entitlement program (Community Development Improvements category) and state HOME and CalHome program income**
- Agency: City of Napa Housing Division (CDBG Advisory Committee recommends, City Council approves)
- Type: grant
- Typical award: About $600,000 of CDBG a year (FY 2026-27 estimate about $600,000, HUD amount pending). After the 15% public service cap and 20% administration cap, the remainder (roughly $390,000) funds physical improvements, housing rehabilitation, property acquisition and nonprofit capital improvements with no category cap. Requests typically total twice the money available. FY 2024-25 rehab loans and grants totaled $135,650 for 10 households. The City is not a HOME participating jurisdiction; it recycles program income from past state HOME and CalHome grants into deferred homebuyer loans.
- AMI requirement: Must meet a CDBG national objective (principally low and moderate income benefit, 80% AMI or below) and a Consolidated Plan 2025-2030 priority: housing rehabilitation, emergency shelter services, nonprofit capital improvements, fair housing, outreach for Latino residents, services for youth aging out of foster care, infill sidewalks in low income block groups.
- Cycle: annual NOFA (next: Annual application cycle each winter for the Annual Action Plan adopted in spring (the 2026-2027 draft Annual Action Plan is posted); next cycle for FY 2027-28 applications expected about January 2027. Contact the Housing Division at 707-257-9543.)
- Layering notes: Napa is the only CDBG entitlement jurisdiction in Napa County (the County and other cities are state non-entitlement, see Pass 2 HOME and CDBG record), but the dollars are small and mostly committed to rehab and services, so CDBG is a predevelopment or site improvement layer rather than a construction gap source. Davis-Bacon applies at 12 or more HOME-assisted units or 8 or more CDBG-assisted units; state prevailing wage turns on the local or state funds in the deal and the Labor Code 1720(c) exemptions (see prevailing_wage_basis). CDBG-DR and CDBG-MIT contract reporting also runs through this office. Source page and the FY 2024-25 CAPER and 2025-2030 Consolidated Plan were opened.
- Source: https://www.cityofnapa.org/181/Community-Development-Block-Grant
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)

**Napa Density Bonus (NMC 17.52.130) with Supplemental Density Bonus up to 100%, and :AH Affordable Housing Overlay District incentives (NMC Chapter 17.36)**
- Agency: City of Napa Community Development Department, Planning Division
- Type: density bonus
- Typical award: Requirement and entitlement incentive, not a direct subsidy. State density bonus law implemented through 17.52.130 (O2010-3, O2011-2). Local enhancement: a Supplemental Density Bonus allows the decision making body to grant bonuses, incentives or concessions above the state maximum up to a total of 100% for projects that exceed the state affordability tables or provide amenities and public benefits (underground parking, superior design, common space). Small project bonus lets duplexes and triplexes exceed pod density if the extra units are very low or lower income (30-year restriction). :AH overlay sites (over 2.5 acres, under 10% slope, within one half mile of transit or services) must deliver 10% very low plus 10% low income units in RM, MU or MP districts and receive priority processing, fee deferral to occupancy for all affordable units, access to local affordable housing funds, Housing Authority marketing and density flexibility under 17.52.140.
- AMI requirement: State density bonus thresholds (5% very low, 10% lower income, 10% moderate for sale, senior, etc.) with 55-year restrictions; supplemental bonus requires affordability above the state tables or public benefits. :AH overlay requires 20% affordable (10% very low and 10% low) or an approved alternative equivalent proposal.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Applies at entitlement; large project density bonus decisions are made by the City Council. The 2023-2031 Housing Element (adopted October 17, 2023, certified December 5, 2023) found 17.52.130 out of date with AB 682, AB 1551, AB 2334, AB 571 and SB 290 and committed to update it (Program H2-2.1) in the comprehensive zoning ordinance update that was underway in 2024-2025; check the current code before relying on local terms.)
- Layering notes: Napa is one of the few California cities with a codified local bonus above the state maximum (to 100% total), which matters for small infill sites downtown and along the four General Plan corridor focus areas. AB 2334 (unlimited density and three extra stories for 100% affordable projects in Napa County, a very low vehicle travel area) applies by state law even before the local text is updated. :AH overlay sites in the Housing Element site inventory (including City owned sites under Program H2.F) carry the fee deferral and local fund incentives, which pair with the impact fee and TOT loans above. Density bonus alone does not trigger prevailing wage; City funds do. Code text read on the official ecode360 code (17.52.130 at ecode360.com/43397951; 17.36 at ecode360.com/43397139); the Housing Element PDF and 2023 APR were opened on cityofnapa.org.
- Source: https://ecode360.com/43397951
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)

**Napa Land Banking Program and City sponsored affordable housing sites (Jefferson/Trower, The Crescent at Old Sonoma Road, Harvest Middle School Program H2-3.3)**
- Agency: City of Napa Housing Division and Housing Authority of the City of Napa
- Type: land
- Typical award: City acquires or controls land for affordable development and selects developers by RFP. Current pipeline: the 2.75-acre Jefferson/Trower site at 3875 Jefferson Street (bought 2023; 19 affordable ownership units on a housing land trust model for low and moderate income buyers; developer selected, development phase expected to begin early 2026); The Crescent, 77 deed restricted units on the former County HHSA campus on Old Sonoma Road (first 40 units for low and moderate income households, financing expected to close January 2026 with construction in 2026; AHSC application was not funded). Housing Element Program H2-3.3 had targeted at least 53 low income units on the former Harvest Middle School site (2447 Old Sonoma Road), but the City bought the 26.6-acre site from Napa Valley Unified for $25 million and now lists it as a Future Public Recreation Complex (interim operations since December 13, 2025, long-term vision still to be set), so housing on that site is unconfirmed.
- AMI requirement: Deed restrictions of 55 years (rental) or 45 years (ownership) for City assisted units; Crescent first phase targets low and moderate income; Jefferson/Trower targets low and moderate income first time buyers.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Developer RFPs issued as sites become available (Jefferson site RFP released 2024). Watch items: Crescent financing close and 2026 construction start, later Crescent phases seeking state grants, and the City's long-term plan for the City-owned former Harvest Middle School site. Monitor City Council agendas (Legistar client napacity) for RFP notices.)
- Layering notes: City land plus impact fee and TOT loans is the model Napa uses to make 100% affordable projects pencil; the Crescent is a joint City and County effort on a County campus, so both the County Affordable Housing Fund and City funds are in the stack. Public land conveyed below fair market value and local loans are public funds under Labor Code 1720(b)(1) and (b)(3), so state prevailing wage applies unless a 1720(c) exemption fits the deal (see prevailing_wage_basis). Source: Council Focus Areas FY 2025-2027 page (opened); the 2023 Housing Element APR and Housing Element Program H2-2.6 were also opened.
- Source: https://www.cityofnapa.org/1358/Council-Focus-Areas-for-FY-2025-2027

**Napa Permanent Local Housing Allocation (PLHA) formula share and Junior Unit Initiative Program (ADU and JADU forgivable loans)**
- Agency: City of Napa Housing Division (also delegated administrator of PLHA for American Canyon, Calistoga, St. Helena and Yountville)
- Type: loan
- Typical award: Napa's PLHA formula allocation is programmed 80% to Junior and Accessory Dwelling Unit creation, 15% to homeless services and 5% to administration. The Junior Unit Initiative provides a 0% forgivable loan of up to $75,000 to create a JADU or converted ADU (forgiven 5% per year over 20 years), an additional interest free deferred loan of up to $25,000 for converted ADUs, grants up to $5,000 for ADA improvements, design and engineering grants, and free construction management (2026 flyer). Owner must occupy one unit and rent the other to a low income tenant under a recorded regulatory agreement.
- AMI requirement: Rental unit affordable to a household at or below 80% AMI at the City's posted affordable rents for 20 years under a recorded regulatory agreement; owner occupies the other unit. (The delegated city PLHA plans use a 10 year term.)
- Cycle: rolling (next: Rolling while PLHA and program funds last; 2026 program flyer posted. Not a multifamily source.)
- Layering notes: Recorded because PLHA is the only state formula money the City controls directly and because the City runs the same ADU program for the other four Napa jurisdictions under delegation agreements (November 15, 2022 Council action), which is why no city in the county has a PLHA multifamily set aside. For multifamily deals this is a negative finding: PLHA in Napa County goes to ADUs and rehab, not construction gaps. See the Pass 2 County PLHA record and the County Affordable ADU Forgivable Loan record for the parallel county program. Sources opened: PLHA page (source_url) and the Junior Unit Initiative page.
- Source: https://www.cityofnapa.org/1197/Permanent-Local-Housing-Allocation
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)

**Napa Successor Agency housing funds: 20% Low and Moderate Income Housing Fund (Fund 229) and Local Housing Fund (Fund 230)**
- Agency: Housing Authority of the City of Napa as housing successor to the Napa Community Redevelopment Agency; City Housing Division staff
- Type: loan
- Typical award: Small and declining. Housing Authority FY 2026-27 mid-cycle budget: 20% Low/Mod fund beginning balance $1,458,803 (July 1, 2025), projected $1,173,898 at June 30, 2026 and $812,439 at June 30, 2027 after a $221,984 increase for the Continuity rental assistance program; revenue is limited to loan repayments and interest (about $175,500 to $205,611 a year). Local Housing Fund beginning balance $941,673, projected $906,414 at June 30, 2026 and $825,959 at June 30, 2027; it pays Housing Authority administration and services to the smaller cities. The FY 2025-27 budget notes the Successor Agency Low-Mod fund that formerly supplemented the Local Housing Fund has closed. Current uses are loan monitoring, home sharing, landlord mitigation and rental assistance rather than new development loans.
- AMI requirement: Health and Safety Code 34176.1 rules for housing successors: funds for households at or below 80% AMI with at least 30% of expenditures for 30% AMI households over each five year period, 55-year rental covenants.
- Cycle: rolling (next: No separate NOFA. Any development use would go to the Housing Authority Board (City Council plus two resident commissioners), usually alongside the rolling impact fee and TOT NOFA; confirm with the Housing Division (707-257-9543).)
- Layering notes: Unlikely to fund new construction at current balances and uses; treat as a possible small gap or predevelopment add-on next to the impact fee and TOT funds. Balances from the Housing Authority FY 2026-27 mid-cycle budget (source_url, Legistar 239-2026) and the FY 2025-26 and 2026-27 adopted budget (Legistar 184-2025); the FY 2017-19 City budget describes the original Fund 229 and 230 structure. Housing successor funds are public funds under Labor Code 1720(b), but 1720(c)(4) excludes affordable units paid for solely from Low and Moderate Income Housing Fund money; other funds in the deal decide coverage (see prevailing_wage_basis).

**Napa fee deferral and reduced building permit fees for affordable and workforce housing (Housing Element Programs H2-2.8 and H2-1.1)**
- Agency: City of Napa Community Development Department (Building Division) and Housing Division
- Type: fee waiver
- Typical award: Affordable Housing Fee Reduction Pilot Program, adopted by City Council Sept 15, 2026 (Legistar matter 352-2026; Resolutions R2026-111 and R2026-112). Building permit fees (fee numbers 2.1.6-2.1.10 multifamily, 2.1.26-2.1.30 single family, 2.1.36 ADU) are reduced 100 percent for very low and extremely low income units, 75 percent for low income units, and 50 percent for moderate income units (120% AMI) and ADUs or JADUs of 749 sq ft or less; this replaces Resolution R2021-119 (flat 50 percent). Development impact fees (Fire and Paramedic, Street Improvement, Park Development, Park Land Dedication, Orchard Avenue, North Jefferson, High-Priority Improvement Payback, Big Ranch Road, Lone Oak Drainage) are reduced 100 percent for very low and extremely low income units and 75 percent for low income units, capped at 250 very low and 250 low income units, first come first served. Staff estimated about $8,622 per very low income unit and $6,275 per low income unit in impact fee savings. Separately, NMC 15.94.040 lets affordable housing impact fees be deferred to final inspection or certificate of occupancy under a recorded secured building agreement.
- AMI requirement: Units must be deed restricted at least 55 years (rental) or 45 years (for-sale) under an NMC 15.94.080 affordable housing agreement, use HCD income limits unless a funding source requires otherwise, and be reportable on the City's RHNA annual report; units in an approved alternative equivalent to paying affordable housing impact fees do not qualify. Building permit reductions reach moderate income (120% AMI); impact fee reductions apply only to low, very low and extremely low income units.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Building permits must be applied for or issued by December 31, 2028, or until the unit caps are reached.)
- Layering notes: Fee relief now covers most City impact fees for lower-income units and is routinely combined with affordable housing impact fee and TOT loans. The Director may limit reductions to projects where they move the project to construction and no other funding gap exists. Napa Valley Unified School District and Napa Sanitation District fees are outside the City's control. Waived or reduced fees can count as public funds under Labor Code 1720(b)(4), so confirm with counsel. Resolution text read from the staff-attached drafts (R2026-XX) on Legistar; the matter history records adoption on Sept 15, 2026 with enactment numbers R2026-111 and R2026-112.

### City of Novato

**Novato Affordable Housing Fund (inclusionary in-lieu fee fund) gap financing and development fee waivers for affordable projects**
- Agency: City of Novato Community Development Department, 922 Machin Avenue, Novato, (415) 899-8989
- Type: loan
- Typical award: No published guidelines or NOFA. The Affordable Housing Programs Fund (Fund 210) receives in-lieu fees, BMR resale and monitoring fees and interest, and mainly pays for BMR program administration, with occasional project support: past loans to Eden Housing ($1,500,000), Homeward Bound Oma Village ($600,000) and Habitat northwest quad ($427,438). For Habitat for Humanity's 80-unit Redwood Boulevard ownership project the Council granted $350,000 for development impact fees plus waivers of several City fees (March 14, 2023) and a further grant of up to $1,000,000 ($800,000 from Fund 210 plus $200,000 transferred from the General Fund) for processing fees (March 11, 2025). Staff projected a Fund 210 balance of $1,132,422 at June 30, 2025, leaving about $332,422 for other projects after reserving $650,000 for BMR buybacks, and said the fund no longer has large balances because developers build inclusionary units on site.

Inclusionary requirement 10% for 7 to 10 units rising to 20% at 20 or more units (19.24.030).

**Novato Affordable Housing Requirements (inclusionary), Novato Municipal Code Division 19.24 (Ordinances 1576, 1676 and 1718), with in-lieu fees to the City housing fund**
- Agency: City of Novato Community Development Department, 922 Machin Avenue, Novato, (415) 899-8989
- Type: regulatory requirement
- Typical award: Requirement, not a subsidy. In-lieu fee amounts are set by Council resolution (not published on the code mirror); fees are paid before building permit issuance into a separate City fund earmarked for very low, low and moderate income housing (19.24.040). Council approval of an in-lieu payment is discretionary for projects of 7 or more units and by right for 3 to 6 unit projects and for fractions below 0.70.
- AMI requirement: Sliding scale by project size: 3 to 10 units 10%, then one percentage point per unit from 11 units (11%) to 20 or more units (20%). Rental projects: half of the required units at 50% AMI rents and half at 60% AMI rents (very low and low income). Ownership: half low income (65% AMI pricing) and half moderate income (90% AMI pricing). Fractions of 0.70 or more round up. Affordable units restricted for a minimum of 99 years from first occupancy (rental) or first sale (ownership) unless state law requires a shorter term (19.24.070E), through a recorded Inclusionary Housing Agreement; one-for-one replacement of demolished deed-restricted units. Exempt: ADUs and JADUs, residential care facilities for the elderly, single or two-unit projects with homes of 3,000 square feet or less, and AHO overlay projects that meet the overlay's 20% requirement.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Ordinance 1718 (Sept 10, 2024) was the latest amendment read. Confirm the current in-lieu fee resolution and any Housing Element Program 3.F (Evaluate and Adjust Impact Fees) follow-up with the Planning Division.)
- Layering notes: Novato's 20% at 20-plus units with a 50/50 very low and low split is the strictest rental inclusionary standard among the three Marin priority cities and matches the County's 20% in unincorporated Marin; State Density Bonus units are excluded from the base count. Because in-lieu payment needs Council approval above six units, fund revenue is small and lumpy; a 2019 Planning Commission record cited a housing fund balance of about $1,200,000 (search snippet, not opened). Habitat for Humanity's 80-unit Redwood Boulevard project shows how the City layers: about $1,000,000 in City fee reductions and waivers approved March 2025 on top of $1,000,000 allocated in 2023 from the City's Affordable Housing Fund, with a $5,239,098 Marin County Housing Trust Fund loan (April 15, 2025, see County record). novato.gov and novato.org returned 403 to every request this pass (HTML pages, showpublisheddocument PDFs and the news module); Novato has no Legistar API client and no Granicus or IQM2 host was found, so City pages, the 2023-2031 Housing Element, the 2025 Annual Progress Report and Council staff reports could not be opened. The Zoning Ordinance was read on the Zoneomics mirror and HCD's April 12, 2023 review letter was opened on hcd.ca.gov. marincounty.gov remained Cloudflare-blocked this pass; County programs are referenced from the Marin County records in this database.
- Source: https://www.zoneomics.com/code/novato-CA/chapter_3
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)

### City of Oakland

- Agency: City of Oakland HCD, Housing Preservation Services, with the San Francisco Housing Accelerator Fund (HAF) as program administrator; applications go to HAF

- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)

**Affordable Housing Impact Fee, OMC Chapter 15.72 (2025 amendments, Ordinance 13853 C.M.S.), with exemption for affordable housing projects and Fund 1872**
- Agency: City of Oakland Planning and Building Department (collection, impactfees@oaklandca.gov) and HCD (expenditure through NOFAs)
- Type: fee waiver
- Typical award: Requirement on market-rate housing and a funding source for affordable housing. July 15, 2025 amendments converted the fee from per unit to per square foot (AB 602): multifamily Zone 1 $36.17 per sq ft (was $29,658 per unit), Zone 2 $29.18 (was $23,929), Zone 3 $19.73 but set at 0% through FY 2027-28; townhome $14.98 / $10.97 / $5.99 (Zone 3 at 0%); single family $12.66 / $9.08 / $4.40 (Zone 3 at 0%). Annual Marshall and Swift inflation adjustment each July 1. Exempt: 100% affordable projects, projects providing the on-site or off-site affordable units specified in 15.72.100-110, ADUs, 2 to 4 unit projects, single-family homes under 1,750 sq ft, SB 684 projects, and the first four smallest units in larger projects. All impact fee payments deferred to certificate of occupancy for 100% affordable and density bonus projects (SB 937 alignment). FY 2024-25 AHIF fund: start $18,162,106, end $10,737,051, $6,577,455 spent, $5,893,752 committed, $4,843,299 being committed to NOFA pipeline projects.
- AMI requirement: Exemption requires 100% affordable (manager units excepted) or the on-site mix in 15.72.100 (chosen to align with state density bonus thresholds); fee revenue funds 100% affordable developments for extremely low to moderate income households through the NC NOFA.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Fee due at building permit (installments) or deferred to certificate of occupancy for affordable and density bonus projects; rates adjust each July 1. Zone 3 zero rate expires June 30, 2028 unless extended.)
- Layering notes: Oakland has no general permit or impact fee waiver program; the AHIF exemption plus SB 937 deferral of transportation and capital improvement fees is the relevant relief. Affordable projects still pay the Transportation Impact Fee (Ch. 15.74) but are exempt from the Capital Improvements Impact Fee. AHIF revenue (Fund 1872) is one of the non-bond sources commingled with Measure U in the NC NOFA, so this record both reduces developer cost and feeds the Oakland NOFA record. No county impact fee exists for comparison. Fee rate schedule read in the July 2025 Master Fee Schedule exhibit on Legistar; the annual report FY 2024-25 (November 2025) supplied balances.
- Source: https://oakland.legistar1.com/oakland/attachments/b2194064-f7d7-4deb-b57e-d33d286c32be.pdf
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)

**Density Bonus and Incentive Procedure, Oakland Planning Code Chapter 17.107 (Ordinance 13684 C.M.S., 2022), and S-13 Affordable Housing Combining Zone**
- Agency: City of Oakland Planning and Building Department, Bureau of Planning
- Type: density bonus
- Typical award: Requirement and entitlement, not a subsidy. Implements Government Code 65915 with the state tables (20% to 50% bonus for 10% to 24% low income; 20% to 50% for 5% to 15% very low; 80% bonus for 100% affordable projects). Local additions: 100% affordable projects within one-half mile of a major transit stop may waive all density maximums and receive up to three additional stories or 33 feet; condominium conversions with 33% moderate or 15% lower income units get a 25% unit bonus or equivalent incentive; incentive counts of one, two, three or four follow state tiers; parking ratio reductions per 65915(p) and no parking required for qualifying transit-adjacent 100% affordable projects; incentives expressly exclude fee waivers and City land.
- AMI requirement: State thresholds (10% low, 5% very low, 10% moderate for sale, 100% affordable with up to 20% moderate); 55-year restriction for rental.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Submitted concurrently with the planning application; no deadline.)
- Layering notes: Oakland does not offer a local bonus above state law except the transit-adjacent height add for 100% affordable projects. Fee relief comes separately through the AHIF on-site exemption (Ch. 15.72), which was deliberately keyed to density bonus thresholds so a mixed-income project can satisfy both with one affordability mix. Code read on the zoneomics mirror because the City's codepublishing site blocks scripts.
- Source: https://www.zoneomics.com/code/oakland-CA/chapter_84
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)

**Jobs/Housing Impact Fee (commercial linkage fee), OMC Chapter 15.68, Fund 1871**
- Agency: City of Oakland Planning and Building Department (collection) and HCD (expenditure)
- Type: loan
- Typical award: Linkage fee on office and warehouse projects over 25,000 sq ft: $7.87 per sq ft for permits applied July 1, 2024 to June 30, 2025 per Table 4 ($8.05 for July 1, 2023 to June 30, 2024), inflation adjusted; paid 25% at permit, 50% at certificate of occupancy, 25% eighteen months later. The 2025 amendments extended the fee to additional nonresidential categories. FY 2024-25 JHIF fund (Fund 1871): start $13,964,433, end $12,546,460, fee revenue $0 in FY 2024-25, $12,060,074 committed to affordable developments, $486,386 being committed to pipeline projects. Past JHIF awards include $2,500,000 (2700 International, 75 units) and $3,472,130 (34th and San Pablo, 60 units).
- AMI requirement: Revenue restricted to acquisition, new construction, substantial rehabilitation and preservation of affordable housing, awarded through HCD NOFAs.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Fee collected continuously; funds flow to the NC NOFA pipeline (next round late 2026 or early 2027).)
- Layering notes: Oakland is one of only two priority cities in the county with a commercial linkage fee (Fremont also has one). Classified as loan because the fund balance is deployed as City development loans through HCD NOFAs (New Construction and ACAH); the fee itself is a cost to commercial developers, not to affordable housing sponsors. Revenue is modest relative to Measure U (FY 2024-25 JHIF fee revenue was $0) but is flexible local money with no bond restrictions, which HCD uses for early predevelopment commitments. Developers do not apply to this fund directly; it is part of the NOFA sources table.

**Low and Moderate Income Housing Asset Fund (LMIHAF, Fund 2830), boomerang Affordable Housing Trust Fund (Fund 1870) and HOME program income authorizations (Resolution 90894 C.M.S., 2025)**
- Agency: City of Oakland HCD (housing successor to the Oakland Redevelopment Agency) and Community Development Division (HOME entitlement)
- Type: loan
- Typical award: Program income from residual receipts and payoffs: LMIHAF collected $5,634,227 (FY 2021-22), $5,820,444 (FY 2022-23), $2,132,775 (FY 2023-24) and $2,309,139 (FY 2024-25); HOME program income reallocated through the budget. October 2025 resolution authorized HCD to commit accumulated and future LMIHAF and HOME program income to NOFA pipeline projects without returning to Council, alongside an additional $40,000,000 of Measure U Tranche 2 and just under $30,000,000 from other sources. Boomerang Fund 1870 (former RDA residual property tax) seeded the R2H2 program and remains an eligible NOFA source for predevelopment, acquisition, new construction, operating subsidies and homeless prevention.
- AMI requirement: LMIHAF (Fund 2830): up to 80% AMI, at least 30% of units at or below 30% AMI and no more than 20% at 60% to 80% AMI (Health and Safety Code 34176.1); HOME: up to 80% AMI with at least 90% of rental units at or below 60% AMI and at least 20% at or below 50% AMI in rental projects of 5 or more units, HOME rents; boomerang AHTF funds: rental up to low income with priority for very low income, ownership assistance up to 120% AMI.
- Cycle: rolling (next: No separate application; funds are awarded within the NC NOFA, R2H2 RFP, ACAH and Rehab NOFA processes.)
- Layering notes: Oakland is a HOME participating jurisdiction and CDBG entitlement city in its own right (not in the Alameda County HOME Consortium), so its HOME dollars are separate from the County's consortium RFP recorded at county level. County boomerang funds (county record) and City boomerang Fund 1870 are distinct pots from the same RDA dissolution. These sources are the most flexible local money for predevelopment and operating subsidy where Measure U bond proceeds cannot be used.
- Source: https://oakland.legistar1.com/oakland/attachments/ccf0850a-3465-4736-aeec-d4a8b6c1734c.pdf
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)

**Measure U Affordable Housing Bond: New Construction Notice of Funding Availability (NC NOFA), Resolutions 90419, 90552, 90894 and 91377 C.M.S.**
- Agency: City of Oakland Housing and Community Development Department (HCD), Housing Development Division, 250 Frank H. Ogawa Plaza, Suite 5313; Fay Darmawi, Deputy Director, fdarmawi@oaklandca.gov, (510) 238-3714
- Type: loan
- Typical award: Measure U (Nov 2022, $850,000,000 bond, $350,000,000 for affordable housing in three tranches). Tranches 1 and 2 committed $248,000,000 to 32 projects (New Construction 15 projects, 1,172 units, $167,035,412; R2H2/Homekey 6 projects, $31,564,588; ACAH 11 projects, $37,000,000; 5% admin $12,400,000), leveraging about $5 outside per $1 City. 2024 NC NOFA: 24 applications requesting $424,000,000; January 2025 awards $80,500,000 to 5 projects (583 units); November 2025 pipeline awards $63,500,000; 13 unfunded pipeline applications (919 units, $246,000,000 requested) remain. Tranche 3: $50,000,000 appropriated in the FY 2026-27 midcycle budget and authorized by Resolution 91377 C.M.S. (October 2026), about $35,000,000 of it for the NC NOFA. Typical City loans run roughly $8,000,000 to $20,000,000 per project, 55-year residual receipts.
- AMI requirement: 2024 NC NOFA: 100% of City-assisted units restricted to low income households at or below 60% AMI with rents no more than 30% of 60% AMI (and at least 10% below market rents within one mile); threshold of at least 20% of affordable units at rents no more than 30% of 30% AMI reserved for extremely low income households, with points for deeper ELI and homeless or special needs targeting; no more than 15% of unassisted affordable units may be moderate income; 55-year regulatory agreement; loans typically 3% simple interest, 55-year term, repaid from residual receipts. Scoring favors public land, ministerial approvals, readiness for tax credits, emerging developer joint ventures, displacement-risk neighborhoods.
- Cycle: biennial (next: Next NC NOFA planned for late 2026 or early 2027 after state HDFC rules settle; awards timed to the spring 2027 tax credit round. Existing pipeline applicants may be advanced ahead of a full round. Confirm release date with HCD (NOFA mailing list).)
- Layering notes: Oakland is the largest city funder in the county (42% of Alameda County affordable permits 2024-25). Stacks with Alameda County Measure A1 Oakland base allocation and Measure W Home Together New Construction RFP (five Oakland projects won Measure W in March 2026: Liberation Park, 500 Lake Park, 3135 San Pablo, East 12th Circle, Brighter Bancroft), county PBVs via OHA, and state HDFC/TCAC. City commitment is intended as the first local layer so projects can show match for county and state rounds. Measure U loans carry Oakland local hire, First Source and prevailing wage requirements; a Project Labor Agreement debate for Measure U projects occurred in 2024. Measure KK (2016, $100,000,000 housing) is fully committed and reported with Measure U. Non-bond sources commingled in the same NOFA: Affordable Housing Impact Fee Fund 1872, Jobs/Housing Impact Fee Fund 1871, boomerang Fund 1870, LMIHAF 2830, HOME 2109, PLHA 2145, excess redevelopment bond funds. oaklandca.gov returns 403 to scripts; all material read from Oakland Legistar attachments and the City's OpenCities prelive host.
- Source: https://oakland.legistar1.com/oakland/attachments/6fffddd8-44d0-4cb6-9f7a-bd7e5972ecb2.pdf
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)

**Prohousing Designation (renewed 2025, Resolution 90836 C.M.S.) and Prohousing Incentive Pilot Program grants**
- Agency: City of Oakland HCD, Housing Policy Unit
- Type: grant
- Typical award: Oakland was the first Bay Area jurisdiction designated Prohousing (December 2022); renewal for a 3-year term authorized September 16, 2025. Prohousing Incentive Program awards: $2,390,000 (Round 1, 2023) dedicated to capitalized service reserves for deeply affordable housing; Rounds 2 and 3 unsuccessful ($1,390,000 requests); Round 4 application for up to $1,600,000 authorized March 2026 for capitalized service reserves for PSH units in R2H2 or NC NOFA projects.
- AMI requirement: Capitalized service reserves for permanent supportive housing and deeply affordable units identified through City NOFAs.
- Cycle: annual NOFA (next: HCD PIP Round 5 NOFA released October 13, 2026 (about $8 million statewide); applications due March 31, 2027, Prohousing Designation required by March 31, 2027, awards expected June 2027. Oakland Round 4 result not confirmed.)
- Layering notes: Developers benefit indirectly: Oakland projects receive Prohousing scoring points in AHSC, IIG, TCC and other state programs, and PIP dollars are routed to service reserves that make PSH projects feasible. Hayward and San Leandro also hold or expect Prohousing status. No county equivalent.

**Rapid Response Homeless Housing (R2H2) and local Homekey program (Resolutions 89977 and 90419 C.M.S.)**
- Agency: City of Oakland HCD, Homeless Housing Development unit
- Type: grant
- Typical award: Program capitalized in 2023 with boomerang Fund 1870 and LMIHAF: $10,400,000 capital plus $19,600,000 operating subsidy; $21,000,000 Measure U Tranche 2 capital added September 2024 for $31,400,000 total capital. Four awards to date (Mandela House, Friendly Manor, Covenant House, the Holland), leveraging over $87,000,000 outside funds (about $4 to $1). About $7,000,000 of Measure U Tranche 2 remained available for new applications as of September 2026; Tranche 3 may add more. City also co-applies for state Homekey+: 2025 awards $7,100,000 The Maya (23 units), $33,000,000 Mark Twain Homes (109 units), $6,500,000 34th and San Pablo (15 PSH units).
- AMI requirement: Permanent supportive housing or permanent transitional housing for people experiencing homelessness; quick-build, ready to house residents within 12 months of award and fully operational within 15 months; Housing First.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Rolling RFP since November 2023; apply any time while capital remains. Confirm remaining balance with HCD.)
- Layering notes: Oakland analog to state Homekey; projects typically combine R2H2 capital with Homekey+, county Measure W Housing dollars, HHAP and county BHSA. Operating subsidy is the binding constraint; the Prohousing Incentive Program award ($2,390,000 in 2023, up to $1,600,000 requested in Round 4, 2026) is dedicated to capitalized service reserves for R2H2 and NC NOFA PSH units. OHA may add project-based vouchers or operating subsidy.

- Agency: City of Oakland HCD, Asset Management Services unit
- Type: loan
- Typical award: Rehab NOFA: last issued FY 2019-20; $7,000,000 of Measure U Tranche 2 earmarked in 2024 and a competitive round planned for 2027 using already authorized Tranche 2 funds plus Tranche 3. Health and Safety Loan Program: over-the-counter emergency loans to owners of City-subsidized multifamily housing, generally up to $250,000 per project, 0% interest, 55-year term; balance fully committed ($250,000 Christian Church Homes, $100,000 Coliseum Connections) and a $2,000,000 recapitalization was recommended in October 2026.

### City of Oceanside

**Inclusionary Housing Ordinance, Oceanside City Code Chapter 14C (Ordinance 24-OR0004-1, 2024) and Inclusionary Housing In-Lieu Fee**
- Agency: City of Oceanside Housing and Neighborhood Services Department (Housing Division) and Development Services Department (Planning)
- Type: regulatory requirement
- Typical award: Requirement, not a subsidy. Ordinance 24-OR0004-1 (introduced January 24, 2024, adopted February 14, 2024, effective outside the Coastal Zone) raised the set-aside from 10 to 15 percent, added unit mix, dispersal and equal amenity rules for reserved units, and clarified ADU use. The Coastal Commission approved the amendment on February 5, 2026 (LCP-6-OCN-25-0030-2) with seven suggested modifications. The City Council introduced an ordinance adopting the modifications on June 3, 2026 (5-0) and adopted it June 17, 2026; it applies citywide. Current rules: applies to residential projects of 7 or more units (including mixed-use, condo conversions and time extensions); at least 15 percent of units reserved (for-sale units for lower and moderate income, rental units for lower income); acutely low income category added; affordability for at least 55 years for rental and for-sale; ADUs may satisfy the requirement in any residential project; affordable housing agreement recorded before building permit, final map or Coastal Development Permit. In-lieu fee per reserved unit is set by Council resolution, deferrable on impact fee terms, and deposited in the affordable housing trust account. Rental projects have been covered since the September 9, 2020 Phase 1 amendment.
- AMI requirement: 15 percent of base units (density bonus units excluded): for-sale units for lower and moderate income households, rental units for lower income households; minimum 55 year restrictions for rental and for-sale units.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Applies at entitlement. Confirm the current in-lieu fee rate with the Housing Division.)
- Layering notes: In-lieu fee revenue is Oceanside's only recurring local housing fund; the Housing Element lists inclusionary fees with HOME, Housing Asset Funds, project-based vouchers and PLHA as sources for the Affordable Housing Strategy (separate record). Compare Carlsbad (15 percent at 7 or more units) and the unincorporated County ordinance (county record). ci.oceanside.ca.us returns 403, but oceanside.legistar.com serves agendas, staff reports and attachments (calendar year selection by form postback).
- Source: https://oceanside.legistar.com/LegislationDetail.aspx?ID=8043739&GUID=7C8992C1-38FE-4F71-BDD0-7FC43EF4E401&Options=&Search=&FullText=1
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)

**Oceanside Affordable Housing Strategy RFP/NOFA (Housing Element Program 4): HOME, Housing Successor Agency asset funds, inclusionary in-lieu fees, PLHA and project-based vouchers**
- Agency: City of Oceanside Housing and Neighborhood Services Department, Housing Division, and the Housing Successor Agency to the Oceanside Community Development Commission; recommendations through the Housing Commission
- Type: loan
- Typical award: Amounts vary; no standing developer NOFA. The Council on September 9, 2020 directed an RFP/NOFA implementing the Affordable Housing Strategy with priority to homelessness and extremely low income housing (temporary shelters, bridge housing, vouchers, permanent supportive housing). Funding sources named: HOME entitlement, remaining Housing Asset Funds (former redevelopment), inclusionary in-lieu fees, project-based vouchers and PLHA (PLHA earmarked for emergency shelter operations). The FY 2026-27 Annual Action Plan (approved May 6, 2026) budgets $1,484,745 of HOME (entitlement $467,836, program income $106,909 and $1,037,649 unallocated prior funds) for tenant-based rental assistance, affordable housing development and homeownership gap assistance, with stated targets of 30 TBRA households and 10 to 15 homebuyers rather than a named development project; CDBG entitlement is $1,123,152, mostly rehab, services and Section 108 repayment. The Housing Element set objectives of 634 extremely low income and 1,268 lower income units for 2021-2029.
- AMI requirement: Lower income and extremely low income households, with priority to people experiencing homelessness and ELI households; affordability term set per agreement (HOME term rules apply to HOME units; the Housing Element does not state a City term).
- Cycle: rolling (next: No open round as of November 10, 2026. HOME development funds are allocated through the Housing Commission as projects arise; contact the Housing Division.)
- Layering notes: Oceanside projects also compete in the County HCDS NOFA 2026-03 only for IHTF (the City is its own HOME participating jurisdiction and CDBG entitlement, outside the County consortium), and can use HACSD or Oceanside Housing Authority project-based vouchers. The City last issued its own multifamily revenue bonds in 2016 (Villa Storia, 38 units; Program 1) and otherwise relies on CMFA or CSCDA. Fee deferrals for affordable units are offered on the same terms as impact fee deferrals. Program text read in the 2021-2029 Housing Element (October 2022 revision, HCD-hosted); the certified September 2023 re-adoption and current Annual Action Plan could not be opened because City document hosts block or time out.

**Oceanside Density Bonus Ordinance (Zoning Ordinance, Housing Element Program 2) and development impact fee deferral for affordable units**
- Agency: City of Oceanside Development Services Department, Planning Division
- Type: density bonus
- Typical award: Requirement, not a subsidy. Housing Element Program 2 commits the City to amend its density bonus ordinance (Zoning Ordinance Article 30) to conform to AB 1763, SB 1227 and AB 2345. State law allows up to a 100 percent bonus for projects reserving at least 15 percent of base units for very low income, 24 percent for lower income or 44 percent for moderate income households. Coastal zone: the certified Article 30 density bonus provisions do not apply to the Downtown District. The Coastal Commission approved the Downtown density amendment (LCP-6-OCN-25-0029-2, 86 units per acre base density, 5,500 unit figure treated as a target) with modifications on February 5, 2026, including a requirement that the City submit updated density bonus regulations covering the Downtown District by January 1, 2029; the Council adopted the modifications (introduced June 3, 2026, ordinance adopted June 17, 2026). Inclusionary in-lieu fee deferral on the same terms as impact fee deferral is available.
- AMI requirement: Government Code 65915 tiers; 55 year rental affordability.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Applies at entitlement. Confirm the current Zoning Ordinance Article 30 text with Planning; updated density bonus regulations for the Downtown District are due to the Coastal Commission by January 1, 2029.)
- Layering notes: No local enhancements beyond state law were found; the practical local tools are the inclusionary in-lieu fund and the Affordable Housing Strategy NOFA (separate records). Smart and Sustainable Corridors Plan (Program 9) adds capacity along transit corridors. Read in the 2021-2029 Housing Element (HCD-hosted) and the Coastal Commission February 2026 staff report.

### City of Oxnard

**Oxnard Affordable Housing Additive Zones, -AHP (by-right) and -AHD (discretionary) (City Code Chapter 16, Division 7C, Ordinance No. 2999)**
- Agency: City of Oxnard Community Development Department, Planning Division
- Type: zoning incentive
- Typical award: Zoning entitlement, not a subsidy: adds the right to build multifamily or mixed use at up to 30 units per acre on Housing Element sites; ministerial site plan review in -AHP; lot merger fees waived when merging parcels under 0.5 acre. The FY 2026-27 Action Plan cites an inventory of 2,466 potential units in these zones.

Impact fees still apply (Sec. 16-420D(D)), so fee relief must come from Policy H-4.2 waivers negotiated separately. State density bonus (Division 7A) can be layered for more density. Useful for 100% affordable tax credit projects seeking ministerial certainty on smaller sites.

**Oxnard Density Bonus and Related Incentives and Concessions Program (City Code Chapter 16, Division 7A, Sec. 16-410 et seq.)**
- Agency: City of Oxnard Community Development Department, Planning Division
- Type: density bonus
- Typical award: Density bonus, incentives, waivers and parking modifications per Gov. Code 65915; no direct funding.
- AMI requirement: Per state density bonus law; rental affordability at least 55 years; affordable housing agreement and equity sharing agreement for for-sale units (Sec. 16-410.19). Units dispersed, phased proportionally and architecturally consistent (Sec. 16-410.17).

**Oxnard Inclusionary Housing Program and Affordable Housing In-Lieu Payments (Uncodified Ordinance No. 2980, as amended by Ordinance No. 2999)**
- Agency: City of Oxnard Housing Department (Housing Director) and Community Development Department
- Type: regulatory requirement
- Typical award: Requirement, not a subsidy. In-lieu payments are allowed only if City Council grants the request at pre-application. The April 8, 2020 Harris and Associates nexus study proposed per-unit fees of $36,000 (single-family for-sale), $35,000 (multifamily for-sale) and $28,000 (multifamily rental), replacing 2006 fees of $7,000, $5,500 and $7,735; fees are indexed every July 1 since 2021 to the ENR Building Cost Index (Los Angeles). Current indexed schedule not opened.
- AMI requirement: Projects of 10 or more units. For-sale: at least 10% of units sold to lower income (80% AMI) households, affordable units at least 3 bedrooms. Rental: at least 5% very low income (50% AMI) plus 5% lower income (80% AMI), proportional by bedroom size. Covenants of at least 20 years; Oxnard-resident preference list required. Inclusionary units are figured on the pre-bonus unit count and do not count toward density bonus.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Ordinance applies at entitlement; in-lieu fee due per unit at building permit. An update of the Inclusionary Housing Ordinance is underway (discussed at the April 20, 2026 Housing Element and Prohousing workshop, including possible location-based percentages); no adoption date set as of 2026-11-08.)
- Layering notes: Ordinance 2980 (adopted June 2, 2020) replaced Ordinance 2721; specific plan areas with equal or higher requirements are exempt. Off-site units or land dedication (MAI appraisal) can substitute for the payment with Council approval. Payments go to the City's Affordable Housing Trust Fund (see separate loan record). Projects in the -AHP/-AHD additive zones must provide units and cannot pay in lieu. The 20-year covenant is far shorter than TCAC's 55-year term, so a tax credit deal on the same site carries the longer restriction. Ventura County has no adopted inclusionary ordinance (postponed June 2026), so Oxnard's requirement is local only. Oxnard's Prohousing application was pending as of April 2026. oxnard.gov HTML pages return 403 (Cloudflare) to scripts, but wp-content PDFs open directly.

### City of Paso Robles

**Affordable housing fee deferral loans (deferral of development impact, water and sewer connection and building permit fees; Housing Element Program 7)**
- Agency: City of El Paso de Robles Community Development Department and City Council (case-by-case resolution)
- Type: fee waiver
- Typical award: Case-by-case Council approval of long-term deferral of City water connection, sewer connection, development impact and building permit fees, structured as General Fund loans repaid several years beyond occupancy. Oak Park Public Housing (Paso Robles Housing Authority) phases one through four received fee deferral loans of $1.018 million (Resolution 12-031), $889,000 (14-019), $999,423 (17-019) and $1,438,160.71 (Resolution 18-020, 2018). Resolution 18-020 terms: promissory note repaid over up to 30 years from building permit at 3.75% simple interest from residual receipts, secured by a deed of trust. News reports (not agency sources) describe a March 2026 Council resolution deferring water, sewer, development impact and building permit fees for affordable housing, a 30-year deferral of about $1.2 million for Highland's Senior Affordable Apartments (298 Niblick Road), a 30-year deferral of about $1.8 million for Sunrise Villas Apartments, a roughly 50% impact fee waiver for a nine-unit Habitat for Humanity project on Vine Street, and February 2021 deferrals for a 79-unit senior project at Woodland Plaza II.
- AMI requirement: Units affordable to lower-income households (Health and Safety Code 50079.5), including extremely low income; City practice requires a recorded affordability covenant for the longest feasible time and not less than 30 years (Resolution 18-020).
- Cycle: rolling (next: Rolling; no open round or deadline as of November 8, 2026. Requests go to Council with the entitlement or before building permit; contact Community Development at (805) 237-3970 or planning@prcity.com.)
- Layering notes: This is the only City-controlled financial tool in Paso Robles; it substitutes for a housing trust fund. City fee deferrals have been the local match for Paso Robles Housing Authority tax credit deals (Oak Park) and are expected to pair with County Title 29 or Regional Housing Fund awards, HASLO or Paso Robles Housing Authority vouchers, SLO County Housing Trust Fund loans and the Urban County HOME NOFA (county record). The City receives about $165,000 per year of CDBG through the Urban County, which cannot fund new construction or impact fees. The 2026 resolution and project-specific deferrals were found only in local news; the City's eScribe agenda host (pub-pasorobles.escribemeetings.com) renders listings in JavaScript and returns 403 on document downloads, so the HCD-hosted 2020-2028 Housing Element is the agency source. Paso Robles is now preparing its 7th cycle Housing Element (consultant RFP due September 8, 2026).

**Community Development Block Grant (CDBG) city allocation through the San Luis Obispo Urban County**
- Agency: City of El Paso de Robles Community Development Department, Housing Programs Division (County of San Luis Obispo is lead agency)
- Type: grant
- Typical award: City page states about $165,000 per year, but the County's 2027 Action Plan NOFA estimates Paso Robles' 2027 CDBG share at $295,492 ($192,070 available for project applications after admin and the 15% public services cap). At least 70% must benefit low income persons (80% AMI or below), no more than 15% for public services, up to 30% for blight elimination; projects must complete within about 1.5 years. CDBG cannot pay new housing construction costs or development impact fees; eligible uses include land acquisition for low income housing, street improvements serving low income housing, rehabilitation and public facilities.

- Cycle: annual NOFA (next: No open round as of November 8, 2026. The County runs one combined Action Plan NOFA each fall; the next round (2028 Action Plan) is expected to open in late September 2027.)
- Layering notes: The City recommends use of its own CDBG share but the County Board adopts the Action Plan (county record: Urban County Action Plan NOFA). HOME and ESG are not allocated to the City; the City may apply to the County for HOME annually, and County HOME has funded Peoples' Self-Help Housing projects in Paso Robles (Canyon Creek, Creekside Gardens). Useful only for acquisition, site work or rehab components and must be paired with other local or state sources for construction. Davis-Bacon applies.

Chapter 21.65 implements SB 9 urban dwelling units for individual owners. Both were part of the 2024 comprehensive Zoning Code Update.

Recent projects: a 79-unit senior low-income development approved February 16, 2021 with fee deferrals, and Highland's Senior Affordable Apartments (30 units, 298 Niblick Road, CEQA notice January 2026) using a density bonus. ### City of Petaluma

**Petaluma Commercial Development Housing Linkage Fee (Ordinance 2171 N.C.S. of 2004, as amended 2011)**
- Agency: City of Petaluma Community Development Department, Housing Division; collected by Building at permit
- Type: regulatory requirement
- Typical award: Requirement, not a subsidy. Fee on new or expanded nonresidential square footage, effective July 1, 2024: commercial $3.47, retail $6.00 and industrial $3.57 per square foot of building space (July 2022 rates were $3.36, $5.81 and $3.46), due before building permit issuance, escalated annually by the ENR Construction Cost Index 20-city average. Exempt: public facilities, public and private schools, churches. Fund balance $2,158,717 as of July 1, 2022 (Housing Element).

- Layering notes: The linkage fund is one of three revenue sources for Petaluma's Local Housing Trust Fund (see Housing Fund record) and is the only local source aimed at 80-100% AMI workforce units, which makes it a possible match for moderate-income or mixed-income deals that cannot use LIHTC. Petaluma's rates are far higher than Rohnert Park's 2008 linkage fee ($0.69 to $1.19 per square foot) and the County's Workforce Housing fee applies only in unincorporated areas. - Agency: City of Petaluma Community Development Department, Housing Division

**Petaluma Inclusionary Housing Program (Implementing Zoning Ordinance Section 3.040, Ordinance 2663 N.C.S.) and Housing In-Lieu Fee (Resolution 2018-142 N.C.S.)**
- Agency: City of Petaluma Community Development Department, Housing Division
- Type: regulatory requirement
- Typical award: Requirement, not a subsidy. Residential projects of five or more units, including residential components of mixed-use projects, must provide 15% of units on site as affordable (rental and ownership alike). Alternatives require City Council approval as alternative compliance: land donation, an in-lieu payment to the City Housing Fund equal to a 20% inclusionary requirement, or other methods. In-lieu fee for fractional units under 0.5 or approved alternative compliance: $10.12 per square foot (2024 Development Impact and Capacity Fees booklet, effective July 1, 2024), collected at close of escrow for for-sale homes and at final inspection or certificate of occupancy for multifamily. Projects deemed complete before January 1, 2019 use the prior rules.
- AMI requirement: Rental projects: 15% of units on site, half (7.5% of total units) affordable to very low income and half (7.5%) to low income households, restricted at least 55 years. Ownership projects: 15% on site, half (7.5%) low income and half (7.5%) moderate income, restricted at least 45 years. The 2023-2031 Housing Element targets 1,000 inclusionary units (400 very low, 400 low, 200 moderate) over eight years.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Applies at entitlement. Housing Element Program 11 called for a 2024 review of thresholds, in-lieu options and fee structure and a fee recalculation at least every four years; no 2025 or 2026 ordinance or resolution amending the program was found (cityofpetaluma.org blocks scripts, so recent council actions could not be checked). Fee schedule for FY 2025-26 and FY 2026-27 could not be opened.)

Petaluma's 15% rental requirement is higher than Santa Rosa's 8% low income rule and lower than the City of Sonoma's 25%. The County's Affordable Housing Program fee (county record) applies only in unincorporated areas. ### City of Placerville

**Affordable Housing Density Bonus, Placerville City Code Title 10 Chapter 12 (Sections 10-12-1 to 10-12-13; 2015 text, state-law update ZC 24-05 pending under ROI 2024-01)**
- Agency: City of Placerville Development Services Department, Planning Division, 3101 Center Street, (530) 642-5252, pv.planning@gmail.com
- Type: density bonus
- Typical award: Requirement, not a subsidy. The local chapter still reflects the 2015 version of Government Code 65915: bonus up to 35% for 5% very low, 10% lower or 10% moderate (for-sale) units, 20% for senior housing, land donation bonus up to 35% combined; one to three incentives (reduced lot size, setbacks, lot coverage, height, parking, mixed-use zoning, other cost-reducing regulatory relief) and by-right parking ratios of 1 space (0 to 1 bedroom), 2 (2 to 3 bedrooms) and 2.5 (4 or more). Where the chapter conflicts with state law, state law controls (10-12-1), so the current 80% bonus for 100% affordable projects, unlimited bonus near major transit and up to five concessions apply by operation of state law. The 2025 Annual Progress Report (March 2026) reports the full density bonus ordinance update was deferred to 2026 because of evolving state law.
- AMI requirement: Per state law: income-restricted units for very low (50% AMI), lower (80% AMI) or moderate (120% AMI, for-sale) households with a recorded density bonus housing agreement (10-12-12); rental affordability term per Government Code 65915 (55 years).
- Cycle: rolling (next: Request with the entitlement application (optional pre-application conference). Watch for the Planning Commission and City Council hearings on text amendment ZC 24-05 (density bonus update), dates still TBD on the City's project list; adoption targeted in 2026.)
- Layering notes: No local enhancement beyond state law. Placerville has no local housing trust fund, no inclusionary ordinance or in-lieu fee, no commercial linkage fee, no city NOFA and no redevelopment successor housing funds; the City's affordable housing tools are this chapter, the Housing Opportunity Overlay by-right sites, fee deferral under SB 937, SCIP impact fee financing and sponsorship of state CDBG, HOME and PLHA applications (separate records). Stack with the El Dorado County density bonus and the County PLHA, Trust Fund, HOME/CDBG, PBV and welfare exemption records; the County Traffic Impact Fee offset (Policy B-14) does not apply inside the city, which levies its own traffic impact mitigation fee. Chapter text read from the City's own zoning ordinance PDF; the City page links the amlegal code library, which was not opened.

- Agency: City of Placerville Development Services Department (applicant and lender of record for state CDBG and PLHA competitive funds) with El Dorado County Housing Authority (HHSA) and Housing El Dorado
- Type: loan
- Typical award: Pass-through loans sized to each state award, no local cash. Mallard Apartments (Mallard Lane and MacIntosh, 72 units): City CDBG loan $756,000 for acquisition, Competitive PLHA (CPLHA) loan $756,000 for architecture and engineering, IIG $1,105,000 for frontage and offsite work, MHP $11,000,000. Middletown Apartments (Cold Springs Road and Middletown Road, 82 units): CDBG loan $861,000 for acquisition, CPLHA loan $861,000, IIG $2,158,000, MHP $13,000,000. Program C-4 commits the City to meet annually with nonprofit developers, apply or co-apply for state and federal funds (CDBG, HOME, PLHA, Section 202 and 811, CalHome), and to establish priority processing and fee deferrals for extremely low income projects.

Gap order used on the two Placerville projects: 4% LIHTC and bonds (CMFA TEFRA via the County), MHP, IIG, City CDBG and CPLHA loans. The City has no local trust fund, inclusionary fee, linkage fee or RDA successor housing funds; a first-time homebuyer program and workforce housing study (Program C-8, CDBG planning grant by spring 2025) were not advanced as of the 2025 progress report. Source is the City's 2023 Housing Element Annual Progress Report tables (October 8, 2024 Council packet); the 2025 APR staff report of March 24, 2026 was also read.

- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)

**Development impact fee deferral for affordable projects (SB 937 implementation, Housing Element Program C-5), ADU impact fee reductions, and Statewide Community Infrastructure Program (SCIP) impact fee financing (Program C-7)**
- Agency: City of Placerville Development Services Department (Planning and Building Divisions) and Finance; SCIP bonds issued by California Statewide Communities Development Authority (CSCDA)
- Type: fee waiver
- Typical award: Timing relief, not a reduction, for multifamily: the City reports it implemented fee deferrals under SB 937 in 2025 so impact fees on qualifying affordable projects are collected at certificate of occupancy rather than permit issuance. Housing Element Program C-5 also offers deferment to completion or occupancy, payment over 12 months or longer after completion, or fee reductions where the applicant documents lower facility demand. Impact fee reductions (water, sewer, traffic impact mitigation, park fees) have been implemented only for ADUs and JADUs consistent with state law. SCIP lets a developer finance City impact fees and public improvements through tax-exempt CSCDA bonds repaid by a special assessment on the parcel; the City intends to offer it for all projects, especially housing, but no development had used SCIP as of the 2023 and 2025 progress reports. No general fee waiver for affordable housing exists.
- AMI requirement: SB 937 deferral applies to projects meeting the statute's affordability definitions (generally 100% affordable or qualifying mixed-income projects); Program C-5 options are for affordable housing providers. SCIP has no affordability requirement.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Request deferral at building permit; SCIP participation requires a City resolution and CSCDA application ahead of permit issuance. Confirm the current fee schedule and deferral form with the Building Division.)
- Layering notes: Placerville levies its own traffic impact mitigation, park and utility fees, so the El Dorado County Traffic Impact Fee offset (Board Policy B-14) does not apply to city projects; deferral is the only local fee tool. SCIP assessment financing of impact fees is senior to other liens and must be cleared with TCAC and permanent lenders. Pair with the HO overlay by-right sites and City-sponsored CDBG, PLHA and HOME loans (separate records). Sources read: the March 24, 2026 City Council staff report accepting the 2025 Housing Element Annual Progress Report (SB 937 deferral statement), the City's Housing Resources page describing SCIP (updated March 4, 2025) and Programs C-5 and C-7 of the 2021-2029 Housing Element.
- Source: https://www.cityofplacerville.org/media/City%20Council%20Staff%20Reports/2026/03%2024%202026/12.3_SR%202025%20Housing%20Element%20APR%20(CK,DW-Fully%20Executed).pdf
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)

**Housing Opportunity Overlay Zone (HO, Title 10 Chapter 5 Section 24, Zone Change 2016-01) by-right affordable sites and Housing Element Programs A-3 and A-5**
- Agency: City of Placerville Development Services Department, Planning Division
- Type: zoning incentive
- Typical award: Regulatory. Sites in the HO overlay (and the R-5 Very High Density Multi-Family zone) allow owner-occupied or multifamily housing by right at a minimum 20 and maximum 24 units per acre with compliance with local design standards and no discretionary action (Government Code 65583.2 sites). The overlay covers about 17 acres with three additional sites proposed for 2026. Two of the four original HO parcels produced Mallard Apartments (72 units, 30% to 60% AMI, 55 years) and Middletown Apartments (82 units, 30% to 60% AMI, 55 years), both by Pacific Southwest Community Development Corporation and under construction in 2025 (82 Middletown permits issued in 2025). Objective design standards (LEAP $65,000 and SB 2 $160,000 funded) were still being completed as of March 2025.
- AMI requirement: By-right status is tied to lower income housing need under state law; projects on HO sites have been 100% affordable at 30% to 60% AMI with 55-year covenants. No local inclusionary percentage.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Ministerial site plan review on HO or R-5 sites at any time. Three additional HO sites were proposed for 2026 rezoning; confirm status and the objective design standards with Planning.)
- Layering notes: The HO overlay is where Placerville's deal flow has actually occurred; both recent projects paired by-right siting with City-sponsored CDBG and CPLHA loans, IIG and MHP (see the City state-funding record). The 2025 APR reports 244 lower income units of site capacity against a 90-unit lower income RHNA, so no-net-loss is not a constraint. Combine with the state density bonus (Chapter 12) and SB 35 or AB 2011 streamlining. Source is the City's 2021-2029 Housing Element policy document (Programs A-3 and A-5); the 2016 draft HO ordinance was also read on the City's EvoGov agenda host. No local trust fund or NOFA exists in Placerville.
- Source: https://www.cityofplacerville.org/media/Planning%20Division/Housing%20Element/2021-2029%20Housing%20Element%20-%20Amended/PolicyDocSect%20II%20-%202021%20HE%20(12-16-22,%20lmh).pdf

### City of Rancho Cordova

**Affordable Housing Plan requirement for new growth areas (Housing Element policy, south of Highway 50)**
- Agency: City of Rancho Cordova Planning Department and Housing Division
- Type: regulatory requirement
- Typical award: Requirement, not a subsidy. Per the May 6, 2026 Keyser Marston survey prepared for Sacramento County, Rancho Cordova has no formal inclusionary ordinance but its Housing Element requires new residential projects in newly developing areas (generally south of Highway 50, mostly high-resource areas) to include an Affordable Housing Plan showing how the project contributes to affordable housing production; compliance options are on-site units, land dedication, rehabilitation of existing affordable units, or in-lieu fees negotiated through development agreements for master plans and specific plans.
- AMI requirement: No fixed percentage. Housing Element Policy H.1.5 and Action H.1.5.1 require an Affordable Housing Plan approved at the earliest entitlement (Specific Plan, Development Agreement or other primary entitlement) projecting units by extremely low, very low, low and moderate income and the ownership and rental split, set case by case by City Council.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Applies at specific plan or development agreement approval.)
- Layering notes: For affordable developers the practical effect is land: master plan developers (Rio del Oro, Suncreek, Arboretum, Westborough, etc.) often satisfy the plan by dedicating sites or paying per-door in-lieu fees, which creates site opportunities and sometimes developer contributions for 9% and 4% deals. Per Action H.1.5.1, contributed land may be used by the City and its nonprofit partners, and the City will pursue supplemental funding to reach below 50% AMI. Sources: May 6, 2026 Keyser Marston memo for Sacramento County, and the HCD-hosted 2021-2029 Housing Element draft (March 24, 2021); the City site itself blocks automated access.

- Type: density bonus

- Agency: City of Rancho Cordova Housing Division (Community Development)
- Type: loan
- Typical award: Rancho Cordova Local Housing Trust Fund (LHTF), carried over from Sacramento County at incorporation and funded by the Housing Development Impact Fee on nonresidential development, paid per square foot at building permit. The Housing Element names the LHTF as a local source for new construction support, preservation of at-risk units and acquisition-rehabilitation by nonprofits. ### City of Redwood City

**Affordable Housing NOFA and Preservation Program (impact fee fund loans)**
- Agency: City of Redwood City, Housing Services
- Type: loan
- Typical award: NOFA issued October 23, 2025 for $7,960,000 ($4,650,000 former RDA LMIHF plus $3,310,000 Affordable Housing Impact Fees), with about $5.8 million in expected Elco Yards (1601 El Camino Real) housing impact fees added. Two applications. May 11, 2026 staff recommendation: Rise City Apartments (1304 Middlefield Road, Sand Hill Property Company, 94 units, 20% to 70% AMI, 24 PSH units) $7,960,000 in new permanent loans, for a total City commitment of $12,326,460 including $4,366,460 (HOME and housing funds) awarded February 2024; 1580 Maple Street (MidPen Housing, 79 units, 20% to 40% AMI, City-owned land appraised at $5,140,000 contributed by ground lease) $5,000,000 ($500,000 predevelopment loan plus $4,500,000 permanent loan conditional on receipt of the Elco Yards fees). Total City funding allocated $17,326,460. Permanent loan terms: residual receipts, 3% simple interest, 57-year term, 55-year regulatory term. Redwood City Pulse reported Council approval on May 11, 2026. Separate Affordable Housing Preservation Program: over-the-counter gap loans to convert market-rate units to deed-restricted units or preserve expiring restrictions; first project 417 Stambaugh Street (8 units, about $1.2 million loan, June 2025); about $5.8 million remained in HPP funds; guideline amendments were on the May 11, 2026 agenda.
- AMI requirement: New construction multifamily rental of 5 or more units; all City-funded units at or below 80% AMI and at least 15% of units at or below 30% AMI (extra points for more extremely low income units); 55-year City regulatory agreement (HOME units also carry the 20-year HOME term).
- Cycle: annual NOFA (next: No open round as of November 8, 2026. The last NOFA was issued October 23, 2025 and awarded May 11, 2026; no new NOFA appears on City Council agendas through November 9, 2026. Preservation Program is over the counter.)
- Layering notes: County layer: every San Mateo County city project competes for the County Affordable Housing Fund NOFA (AHF 14 closed July 15, 2026, next fall 2027), HEART bridge loans and HACSM project-based vouchers; city money is usually the first commitment that unlocks those. City loans are residual receipts loans repaid from cash flow after operating expenses, hard debt and reserves, and are sized to leverage County AHF, HACSM PBVs and 4% or 9% credits; 1580 Maple shows the City-County land plus City fee money pattern. Marked needs_confirmation because redwoodcity.org (NOFA page, Preservation Program guidelines, fee schedule) returned 403 to automated access and figures come from the May 12, 2026 Redwood City Pulse report (source) and the City's meetings portal; confirm award terms with Housing Services.
