### City of San Ramon

**San Ramon Affordable Housing Commercial Linkage Fee (Inclusionary Housing and Commercial Linkage Ordinance, April 2019) and Affordable Housing Fund**
- Agency: City of San Ramon Community Development Department, Planning Services Division
- Type: regulatory requirement
- Typical award: Requirement, not a subsidy. A per square foot fee on net new gross floor area of all new commercial construction, including the commercial portion of mixed-use projects, regardless of zoning; exempt: projects adding 5,000 square feet or less, schools and places of public assembly, public facilities, and like-for-like replacement of buildings destroyed by calamity. Developers may instead build affordable units on an appropriate site, dedicate land or provide other housing resources. Mixed-use developments that meet the inclusionary policy are exempt from in-lieu fees. Fees are deposited into the City's Affordable Housing Fund ($4.28 million as of March 3, 2022, before Canopy and other recent payments). The per square foot rate is set in the Master Fee Schedule and was not found on an opened page.
- AMI requirement: Not applicable to the payer; the fund supports very low (including extremely low), low and moderate income rental and ownership housing in San Ramon.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Applies at building permit. Housing Element Program 8 called for a 2024 review of the linkage fee structure to reflect affordable construction costs; the Council considered updated nexus fee studies with the FY 2026-27 Master Fee Schedule in March 2026 (confirm adopted rate).)
- Layering notes: Bishop Ranch and the City Center office base make this the City's steady fund source; the Affordable Housing Fund has no published NOFA and is deployed by Council through development agreements and project-specific commitments (the City adopted Priority Access System guidelines for City-funded projects), so developers should request Affordable Housing Fund support directly in entitlement negotiations. Stack with County HOME and Measure X (San Ramon is in the Urban County for HOME and CDBG, county records), HACCC project-based vouchers and the City's fee waiver policy (separate record). Read from the HCD-hosted 2023-2031 Housing Element draft (source_url, Sections 11.3.1.4, 11.4.7.1 and Program 8); the adopted element (Resolution 2023-017) is linked from https://www.sanramon.ca.gov/news/what_s_new/adopted_2023_2031_housing_element.
- Source: https://www.hcd.ca.gov/housing-elements/docs/san-ramon-6th-draft122922.pdf
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)

**San Ramon Affordable Rental Housing Fee Waiver Policy (adopted October 11, 2022) for 100% affordable rental projects**
- Agency: City of San Ramon Community Development Department, Planning and Building Divisions
- Type: fee waiver
- Typical award: Waiver of development impact fees and a capped waiver of City service fees for rental projects in which all units are affordable to households at or below 80% AMI. Impact fee waiver options: City Traffic Impact Fee, School Age Child Care Fee, Park and Recreation Facility Impact Fee, Private Sector Art and Beautification Fee, Open Space Development Impact Fee, Specific Plan Recovery Fees, General Plan Recovery Fee, Zoning Ordinance Recovery Fee and the Tri-Valley Transportation Development Fee (already waived for affordable units). City service fee waivers (building plan check and inspection, planning plan check, engineering plan check and inspection) capped at 25%. City example: a typical 100-unit affordable project receives about $24,000 per unit in impact fee waivers and $5,865 per unit in service fee waivers, over $2.5 million total. The City counts waived fees as local match for State funding applications; value calculated at building permit.
- AMI requirement: 100% of units (except managers' units) affordable to households at or below 80% AMI under a recorded affordable housing or density bonus agreement; San Ramon's 2026 rent table caps 80% AMI rents at $2,376 (1 person) to $3,938 (6 persons).
- Cycle: rolling (next: Applies at building permit issuance; no application deadline. The Canopy (BR 8) Eden Housing project (161 units, 2026 entitlements) and Eden's 2453 Camino Ramon project are the first users; confirm the policy remains in the FY 2026-27 Master Fee Schedule.)
- Layering notes: The only formal fee waiver program among the five priority cities and worth roughly $3 million on a 100-unit deal; combined with Bishop Ranch land dedications it makes San Ramon unusually feasible for 100% affordable 4% credit deals despite high land costs. Waivers are public funds for Labor Code 1720 purposes (prevailing wage) and are reported as local match to TCAC and HCD. Layer with County HOME and Measure X, HACCC PBVs and County conduit bonds (county records); the County has no comparable fee waiver program (county record: development fee waiver for affordable housing, discretionary only). Policy terms read from the HCD-hosted Housing Element (source_url) and confirmed in the January 13, 2026 Canopy staff report on the City's IQM2 host.
- Source: https://www.hcd.ca.gov/housing-elements/docs/san-ramon-6th-draft122922.pdf
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)

**San Ramon Density Bonus Ordinance (Zoning Ordinance Division D4, Chapter VIII, Sections D4-76 to D4-80) and Priority Access System for City-funded housing**
- Agency: City of San Ramon Community Development Department, Planning Services Division
- Type: density bonus
- Typical award: Regulatory incentive, not a cash subsidy. Chapter VIII implements Government Code 65915 by reference: any changes to state density bonus law supersede local text; waivers of development standards are granted unless specified findings are made; parking may be modified or covered-parking requirements waived for affordable units; a density bonus housing agreement is recorded before final map or building permit; a processing fee set by resolution applies. No local bonus beyond state law. Separately, the City's Priority Access Guidelines give San Ramon residents and workers priority in City-funded affordable projects, and the Housing Element targets 200 very low or extremely low, 200 low and 400 moderate income inclusionary units over 2023-2031 against a RHNA of 5,111 units.
- AMI requirement: State density bonus law thresholds (Gov. Code 65915); density bonus units are excluded from the inclusionary unit count under C4-177, so they stack on top of the 15% inclusionary requirement.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Applies at entitlement; no deadline.)
- Layering notes: San Ramon has no city-run NOFA, no RDA successor housing fund (the City never had a redevelopment agency) and its Affordable Housing Fund is deployed by Council through development agreements rather than competitive rounds; local tools are the inclusionary receiver-site model, the fee waiver policy and state density bonus. Most existing affordable stock in Dougherty Valley sits under Contra Costa County affordability agreements (county records: Inclusionary Housing Ordinance Ch. 822-4 and Residential Density Bonus Ch. 822-2) rather than City agreements. Zoning text read on the zoneomics mirror (source_url); the City's code host (qcode) is blocked.
- Source: https://www.zoneomics.com/code/san-ramon-CA/chapter_4
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)

**San Ramon Inclusionary Housing Ordinance (Ordinance 520, adopted October 24, 2023; San Ramon Municipal Code Sections C4-175 to C4-183) and Affordable Housing Fund (C4-180)**
- Agency: City of San Ramon Community Development Department, Planning Services Division (Lauren Barr, Director; Planning@sanramon.ca.gov, 925-973-2560)
- Type: regulatory requirement
- Typical award: Requirement, not a subsidy. Applies to all residential projects of 2 or more units (ADUs excluded). Projects of 2 to 9 units (for-sale or rental) may pay an affordable housing fee equal to 25% of total new livable square footage times the per square foot rate in the City Fee Resolution (about $15.16 per square foot per the City of Antioch's January 2026 countywide comparison). For-sale projects of 10 or more units (single-family and multifamily) must build 15% affordable units allocated 20% very low, 30% low and 50% moderate income (must-build added in 2023). Rental projects of 10 or more units must provide 15% affordable units, half very low and half low income. Alternatives (C4-179): voluntary rental units in a for-sale project, off-site construction within San Ramon, preservation of at-risk units with 55-year extensions, land dedication (fully improved with impact fees paid) or combinations. Fees go to the Affordable Housing Fund with an annual report to Council on balance and commitments; the balance was $4.28 million as of March 3, 2022.
- AMI requirement: 55-year affordability (raised from 30 years in 2023) for rental and for-sale units, renewed for 55 years on each resale; resale price capped at purchase price grown by AMI; City first right of refusal on affordable ownership units.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Applies at first approval with an Affordable Housing Plan; Affordable Housing Agreement before final map or building permit. Housing Element Program 8 scheduled a 2024 review of the inclusionary and commercial linkage fee structure; the Council heard a FY 2026-27 Master Fee Schedule and nexus study update in March 2026, so confirm the current per square foot rate with Planning Services.)
- Layering notes: San Ramon's 15% rental requirement with half the units at very low income is the deepest in the county among the priority cities and, combined with Bishop Ranch's build-out, produces receiver-site deals: the Canopy (BR 8) Affordable Site Development Agreement introduced January 13, 2026 (Ordinance 536, adopted January 27, 2026) has Sunset Development dedicating a rough-graded site with impact fees paid to Eden Housing for 161 affordable units that absorb the inclusionary obligations of 255 Canopy single-family homes (raised from 15% to 22.5%) and the CityWalk apartments, plus $3,000 per market-rate unit (about $765,000) paid into the Affordable Housing Fund. Dougherty Valley affordable units (Highlands Point, Muirlands, Seville, Valencia, Cornerstone at Gale Ranch and others, about 1,886 affordable units citywide) are governed by Contra Costa County affordability agreements under the Dougherty Valley Settlement Agreement and the County's Chapter 822-4, not this ordinance, and several 20-year moderate-income agreements expire in 2026. Ordinance text read at source_url; the Canopy staff report was read on the City's IQM2 agenda host (https://sanramonca.iqm2.com/Citizens/Detail_LegiFile.aspx?ID=4882).
- Source: https://www.sanramon.ca.gov/UserFiles/Servers/Server_10826046/File/Our%20City/Departments/Community%20Development/Planning/ORD%20520%20Amended%20Inclusionary%20Housing%20Ordinance%202023.pdf

Reviewed concurrently with other entitlements; approved if State law is met.

No fee deferral policy page, current impact fee schedule or council resolution implementing Programs 15 or 19 was found on ci.sanger.ca.us (the only fee document is a scanned 2008 file); confirm terms with the Community Development Department. ### City of Santa Ana

**Affordable Housing Development RFP No. 26-004A (Inclusionary Housing Fund, HOME, HOME-ARP and Housing Successor Agency loans)**
- Agency: City of Santa Ana Community Development Agency, Housing Division, 20 Civic Center Plaza M-26, (714) 667-2250; bid contact Jacques Lam, JLam@santa-ana.org; solicitation on PlanetBids portal 20137
- Type: loan
- Typical award: Open RFP issued May 1, 2026 with $17,507,926 available: Inclusionary Housing Funds $2,628,194, HOME $11,533,196, HOME-ARP $715,622 (permanent supportive housing only), Housing Successor Agency Funds $2,630,914, plus Housing Authority project-based vouchers and Housing Successor land. Available funds are republished each quarter in the Housing Division Quarterly Report and added to the RFP by addendum. Recent City awards: Crossroads at Washington $4,600,000 plus 15 PBVs (86 units), WISEPlace $5,200,000 plus 25 PBVs (48 units), Estrella Springs $1,600,000 plus 89 PBVs (89 units), Wellington $920,000 (9 ownership units, approved July 1, 2025), Richard Lehn Intergenerational Housing $2,021,319 HHAP plus 8 PBVs (11 units).
- AMI requirement: At least 55-year covenants; Inclusionary and Housing Successor funds serve moderate (120% AMI), low, very low and extremely low income households and may fund mixed-income and mixed-use projects; HOME units at High and Low HOME rents with 20% of HOME-assisted units at 50% AMI in projects of five or more HOME units; HOME-ARP units are permanent supportive housing only. Priority points for substantial rehabilitation and adaptive reuse (motel and office conversions), homeownership, and by-right or shovel-ready projects.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Quarterly proposal deadlines: January 11, 2027 and May 3, 2027 at 4:00 p.m. (July 1 and October 1, 2026 rounds have passed); question deadlines November 30, 2026 and April 5, 2027. The City's stated objective is to issue one affordable housing RFP per year and finance at least one multifamily project per year.)
- Layering notes: Santa Ana is the deepest city pool in Orange County: about $17,500,000 in one RFP, mostly HOME, with loans at 3% simple interest, 55-year term, repaid from 50% of residual receipts, TCAC developer fee limits and a Review Panel scoring process under the 2020 Affordable Housing Funds Policies and Procedures (opened). Any City-funded affordable housing project is covered by the June 6, 2023 Community Workforce Agreement (Section 2.2.4, no dollar threshold): contractors sign a Letter of Assent, hire through union hiring halls and pay prevailing wage rates, and the project must reach 30% of craft hours from Santa Ana and Orange County ZIP codes, veterans or MC3 graduates; budget a labor premium even for small or ownership projects that might otherwise be exempt under Labor Code 1720(c). Davis-Bacon applies to HOME projects of 12 or more assisted units. Stack with County 2026 Supportive Housing NOFA loans and OCHA or SAHA PBVs, OCHFT gap loans (WISEPlace took $2,500,000 OCHFT MHSA plus $1,500,000 County ARPA) and 4% or 9% credits. The County NOFA pays $95,000 to $105,000 per unit inside Santa Ana, so the City loan is normally the larger local layer. RFP PDF, RFP page, policies PDF and FY 2025-26 Q4 quarterly report opened on santa-ana.gov and its Google Cloud document store.
- Source: https://storage.googleapis.com/proudcity/santaanaca/2026/05/8841f39e-rfp-26-004a-affordable-housing-development_final.pdf
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)

**Affordable Housing Opportunity and Creation Ordinance (Municipal Code Chapter 41, Article XVIII.I, Secs. 41-1900 to 41-1909; Ordinance NS-3019) and in-lieu fee to the Inclusionary Housing Fund**
- Agency: City of Santa Ana Planning and Building Agency (inclusionary housing plans) and Community Development Agency Housing Division (Inclusionary Housing Fund)
- Type: regulatory requirement
- Typical award: Requirement, not a subsidy. Applies to projects of five or more units (lowered from 20 by NS-3019, adopted April 19, 2022) that receive a discretionary density or land use increase. Rental projects: 15% low income, or 10% very low, or 5% extremely low, or a 10% mix (5% low, 3% very low, 2% extremely low). For-sale projects: 5% moderate income. In-lieu fee per habitable square foot of the entire project, tiered by size: $6.00 (5 to 9 units), $9.00 (10 to 14), $12.00 (15 to 19) and $15.00 (20 or more) (Sec. 41-1904(c)(1)). Effective January 1, 2026, a project of 20 or more units that elects the $15.00 fee must also sign an enforceable commitment that 30% of the construction workforce is a skilled and trained workforce (Public Contract Code 2601), with at least 35% of those work-hours under City local hire policies; the fee drops to $10.00 at 60% and $5.00 at 90% skilled and trained workforce. From November 16, 2021 through December 31, 2025 the workforce commitment was optional ($10.00 at 30% and $5.00 at 60%, with 20% local hire). The earlier NS-2994 amendment had cut the fee from $15 to $5 per square foot before the 2022 rewrite. Inclusionary Housing Fund receipts since inception: $31,147,483 (FY 2009-2020 $10,800,251; FY 20/21 $3,709,875; FY 21/22 $6,933,320; FY 22/23 $0; FY 23/24 $834,000; FY 24/25 $0; FY 25/26 $1,685,995 from the 408-unit Lowe Enterprises project at 2828 N. Main St.). Fund expenditures to date $20,558,250 for 224 units plus The Link interim shelter ($7,893,866); commitments $1,357,021. Only 35 on-site inclusionary units (25 ownership, 10 rental) have been built since 2011, so the ordinance functions mainly as a fee.
- AMI requirement: On-site units restricted 55 years; fund may be spent on moderate, low, very low and extremely low income rental and ownership housing, shelter and down payment assistance. Sec. 41-1904.1 incentives for on-site production: up to 25% setback reduction, up to 20 feet of added height, and a local density bonus of 1.5% for each 1% of for-sale units above 5% moderate income, up to 35%.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Applies at entitlement. The in-lieu fee amount is set at issuance of the first building permit and must be paid no later than the first occupancy approval for construction that adds net residential units (Sec. 41-1904(c)(2)). Fee schedule may be changed only by a five-vote Council supermajority. The Housing Element programs commit the City to periodic review of the threshold and fee.)
- Layering notes: This fee stream feeds the Inclusionary Housing Fund that is offered through the City's annual Affordable Housing Development RFP (record above), which is the only Orange County city in-lieu fund with a regular competitive outlet. Orange County has no county inclusionary ordinance, so this is a city-only requirement. Market-rate developers often use the ordinance's local density bonus with the state bonus; the Housing Element notes the 2022 rewrite was meant to recover fee revenue lost after NS-2994 cut the rate to $5. Ordinance page, NS-3019 PDF and the zoneomics code mirror for Article XVIII.I opened; fund figures from the FY 2025-26 Q4 Housing Division Quarterly Report (opened).
- Source: https://santa-ana.gov/2021-affordable-housing-opportunity-and-creation-ordinance/
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)

**Density Bonus for Affordable Housing (Municipal Code Chapter 41, Article XVI.I, Secs. 41-1600 to 41-1607) and Density Bonus Agreements**
- Agency: City of Santa Ana Planning and Building Agency, Planning Division, (714) 667-2700
- Type: density bonus
- Typical award: Requirement and entitlement, not a subsidy. The local article grants a 25% density bonus plus one additional development incentive under a recorded Density Bonus Agreement, with waivers or modifications of development standards decided under Sec. 41-1607; state law (Government Code 65915) now governs bonus amounts up to 50% or more, up to five incentives or concessions and unlimited waivers, and the City applies the state schedule. The FY 2025-26 Q4 Housing Division report lists the Density Bonus Agreements executed to date, including 415 and 547 rental units restricted under two agreements and smaller sets of 92, 19, 11 and 2 very low income units.
- AMI requirement: State law thresholds: 5% very low, 10% low, 10% moderate for-sale, or 100% affordable; local code covenants of 30 years when an additional incentive is granted (state law requires 55 years for rental); a monitoring fee set by resolution applies.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Applies at project application; agreements recorded before building permit.)
- Layering notes: Santa Ana projects routinely combine the state density bonus with the AHOCO local bonus and the Transit Zoning Code (SD-84) and Metro East overlays; the Housing Element credits the City with 5,130 permits from 2021 to 2024, 152% of its very low, low and moderate RHNA progress through 2025. No fee waiver or impact fee deferral ordinance for affordable housing was found; the County NOFA treats city fee waivers as match but Santa Ana offers none. Density bonus alone does not trigger prevailing wage. Code text read on the zoneomics mirror; the Q4 quarterly report lists agreements.

**HOME Investment Partnerships, CDBG and ESG entitlement (FY 2025-2029 Consolidated Plan)**
- Agency: City of Santa Ana Community Development Agency, Housing Division (HOME Participating Jurisdiction since 1994)
- Type: grant
- Typical award: Five-year Consolidated Plan FY 2025-2029 anticipates $41,700,000: CDBG $30,123,118, HOME $9,093,495, ESG $2,504,870. HOME development funds are deployed as loans through the Affordable Housing Development RFP ($11,533,196 of HOME and $715,622 of HOME-ARP available in RFP 26-004A), with 15% of each annual HOME allocation reserved for certified CHDOs. CDBG funds public services, infrastructure, the Residential Rehabilitation Program (grants up to $25,000, closed in Q4 FY 2025-26 when funds ran out) and shelter; HOME also funds the My First Home mortgage assistance program.
- AMI requirement: HOME rental units at or below 80% AMI at High and Low HOME rents, 20% of HOME-assisted units at 50% AMI in projects of five or more HOME units; CDBG national objective benefit to low and moderate income persons.
- Cycle: annual NOFA (next: Annual Action Plan adopted each spring for the July 1 program year; developer requests go through the Affordable Housing Development RFP quarterly deadlines (next January 11, 2027). Public service and CDBG applications are solicited in the winter before the Action Plan.)
- Layering notes: Santa Ana's HOME grant (about $1,800,000 a year) is larger than the County Urban County HOME grant ($1,244,583) and the City lends most of it to multifamily deals rather than TBRA, which is why HOME is the largest line in the RFP. Davis-Bacon applies at 12 or more HOME-assisted units; HOME brings NEPA, Section 3 and a HUD subsidy layering review. HOME-ARP is limited to permanent supportive housing. Santa Ana is outside the County Urban County program, so County HOME is not available inside the city. Consolidated Plan page, CDBG page, HOME page and Grants page opened on santa-ana.gov; RFP PDF supplies the HOME terms.

### City of Santa Clara

**Affordable Housing Fee (Ordinance 1974, December 5, 2017) and City Affordable Housing Fund gap loans**
- Agency: City of Santa Clara Community Development Department, Housing and Community Services Division
- Type: loan
- Typical award: Fee on new market-rate for-sale and rental housing and on non-residential development, indexed annually to the ENR San Francisco Building Cost Index; rates were set well below the nexus maximum to encourage rental and smaller units (current per square foot rates are in the City fee schedule, not opened this pass). Fund 565 balance June 30, 2025: $10,408,762 (FY 2024-25 receipts $3,479,128 fees and $394,430 interest; no expenditures to date). Committed use: $4,944,484 loan (RTC 23-952, November 14, 2023) to Charities Housing for 106 affordable units at 1601 Civic Center Drive (30 to 50 percent AMI), alongside a County loan of up to $12.1 million and $1.6 million of housing impact fees moved into the City Affordable Housing Capital Fund. The City Affordable Housing Fund also carries about $223,677 a year of ongoing appropriations for services in the Annual Action Plan.
- AMI requirement: City Affordable Housing Agreement and Regulatory Agreement; 1601 Civic Center restricted to 30 to 50 percent AMI households.
- Cycle: rolling (next: No NOFA and no open round as of November 9, 2026. Fund 565 held $10,408,762 at June 30, 2025, but that balance still includes the $4,944,484 Charities Housing loan for 1601 Civic Center Drive (the transfer to Fund 165 was restated to zero because the project had not commenced), so roughly $5.5 million is uncommitted. Approach the Housing and Community Services Division directly. Watch the Related Santa Clara project (5155 Stars and Stripes Drive), whose affordable housing obligations and 2026 litigation could change fee or unit delivery.)
- Layering notes: Santa Clara has not run a competitive round; awards have been negotiated per project (Charities Housing 2023, Klamath and Bracher loan extensions 2024). Stack with County Measure A or SHDF (1601 Civic Center has a $12.1 million County commitment), SCCHA PBVs and CMFA bonds. The City's housing successor fund (see separate record) is a second small source. santaclaraca.gov returns 403 to automated access; the AB 1600 report and resolutions were read from the Legistar attachment host.

### City of Santa Cruz

**CDBG and HOME entitlement grants (HUD Consolidated Plan 2025-2030, Annual Action Plan PY 2026-2027)**
- Agency: City of Santa Cruz Community Development Department, Housing and Community Development Division (housing@santacruzca.gov)
- Type: grant
- Typical award: PY 2026 (July 2026 to June 2027): $497,393 CDBG and $237,080.42 HOME from HUD, both lower than PY 2025; CDBG total available $512,553 with about $15,000 program income; HOME total available $793,841 including about $100,000 program income and $456,761 of prior-year funds for reprogramming. The City describes typical levels as about $600,000 CDBG and about $400,000 HOME per year. CDBG funds community programs (public services capped at 15%), infrastructure and facility improvements and delivery costs for two housing programs; HOME funds acquisition, homebuyer assistance, homeowner rehabilitation and rental development, with repaid rehabilitation and homebuyer loans automatically reprogrammed to affordable housing. Santa Cruz receives no ESG.
- AMI requirement: CDBG benefits households at or below 80% AMI; HOME rental units at or below 60% AMI (High HOME rents) with HUD affordability periods of 5 to 20 years depending on subsidy; Section 3 applies to construction and rehabilitation.
- Cycle: annual NOFA (next: PY 2027-2028 application period open as of this pass; the cycle normally opens in October with applications due mid-December, proposals advertised in November, public review and Council approval February through May, and the Action Plan submitted to HUD by May 15. Applications: online CDBG form, HOME application (DOCX) and CDBG supplemental budget; CBDO certification available. Email housing@santacruzca.gov to join the HUD notification list.)
- Layering notes: Small but predictable; HOME is the realistic development piece (under $800,000 available in PY 2026) and is typically paired with an AHTF loan and PBVs from the Housing Authority of the County of Santa Cruz. Federal Davis-Bacon applies to HOME projects of 12 or more assisted units and CDBG projects of 8 or more units. The County administers state HOME and CDBG for the unincorporated area, Watsonville (CDBG entitlement separately), Capitola and Scotts Valley, so Santa Cruz is the only Santa Cruz County city with its own HOME entitlement. Documents opened via WebFetch: HUD Consolidated Plan Documents page and the PY 2026-2027 Annual Action Plan PDF.
- Source: https://www.santacruzca.gov/Government/City-Departments/Community-Development/Housing-Assistance-Information-and-Resources/HUD-Consolidated-Plan-Documents
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)

**Density bonus (Municipal Code Chapter 24.16 Part 3) and fee deferrals for 100% affordable developments (Part 4, Resolution NS-30,634)**
- Agency: City of Santa Cruz Community Development Department, Planning Division and Housing Division
- Type: fee waiver
- Typical award: Chapter 24.16 Part 4 is now Fee Deferrals for Affordable Units (Sections 24.16.300 Units Eligible for Fee Deferrals and 24.16.310 Procedure for Deferral of Fees). Resolution NS-30,634 (adopted March 10, 2026) lets staff defer development review fees for 100 percent affordable housing projects: Building, Fire, Community Development, Parks, Police, Public Works, Water and similar fees may be deferred up to five years, or until certificate of occupancy if a substantially complete building permit application is filed, then up to about five more years on a payment plan with interest set annually by the Finance Director. Third-party review cost fees are collected in full; impact fees (Gov. Code 66007, SB 937), the Parks and Recreation Facilities Tax and the Quimby Fee cannot be deferred past certificate of occupancy; the Traffic Impact Fee is deferred under separate procedures. Fee waivers are not granted by staff and must still be requested from City Council; Resolution NS-30,635 waivers apply only to projects on City-owned land or buildings. Part 3 density bonus text and the childcare impact fee reduction for 100% affordable projects were not read (codepublishing.com 403).
- AMI requirement: 100 percent affordable housing developments for the staff deferral policy; a 2019 City form indicated only very low and low income units were eligible for Part 4 fee relief (not re-confirmed).
- Cycle: rolling (next: Rolling. Submit the supplemental fee deferral application with the 100 percent affordable planning application (or with building plan check if no planning fees apply), then sign a fee deferral agreement and payment plan.)
- Layering notes: Treat as a cost reduction layered on top of the AHTF loan and Measure O compliance; the County's enhanced density bonus (Chapter 17.12.065, up to 50% for 21% or more low income units) and County AHIF exemption apply only in the unincorporated area. Santa Cruz also created Flexible Density Units in four commercial zones (auxiliary units allowed up to the full floor area ratio regardless of density) and the My House My Home senior ADU program, both cited in the 2023 Prohousing application. Marked needs_confirmation because the code text was not opened; the zoneomics chapter index listing Parts 3 and 4 and the City Prohousing page were. Childcare impact fee: the City Childcare Impact Fee page lists rates with no affordable housing provision; search results suggest Chapter 18.48 exempts 100 percent affordable projects. Confirm before counting it.

**Measure O Inclusionary Housing Program (Municipal Code Chapter 24.16 Part 1, Ordinance 2021-04) and inclusionary in-lieu fee**
- Agency: City of Santa Cruz Housing and Community Development Division, with tenant and buyer eligibility intake by the Housing Authority of the County of Santa Cruz (2160 41st Avenue, Capitola)
- Type: regulatory requirement
- Typical award: Requirement, not a subsidy. Voter-approved Measure O requires residential projects to provide a share of units affordable to very low, low or moderate income households under Chapter 24.16 Part 1 as revised by Ordinance 2021-04 (effective April 13, 2021); units may be built as rental or for-sale and carry long-term or permanent deed restrictions. Before the 2021 revision the ordinance required 15% of new rental units at or below 80% AMI; the City's June 2018 Keyser Marston feasibility analysis tested 15%, 25% and 35% alternatives and Downtown versus non-Downtown subareas under AB 1505, and the revised percentage (reported as 20%) was not confirmed from code text this pass. In-lieu fees under Section 24.16.030(6) are calculated project by project on the affordability gap between market and inclusionary rents (2018 sample: $168,478 gap per unit, $25,271 per market-rate unit or $34.86 per square foot at 15%), are usually paid before building permit issuance and are deposited to the Affordable Housing Trust Fund for new low income units with long-term restrictions or preservation. No refunds or interfund transfers occurred 2021-2025 (2026 AB 2663 report). Measure O rents and incomes are set annually by resolution (2025 schedule effective July 1, 2025, Resolution NS-16,452 series; eight implementing resolutions listed through NS-29,463).
- AMI requirement: Very low, low and moderate income households per the City resolution governing each unit; Measure O rentals restricted to very low and low income tenants or Housing Choice Voucher holders with annual income recertification; eligibility letters issued by the Housing Authority expire after three months; $250 processing fee paid by the seller or landlord.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Applies at entitlement; in-lieu fee due at building permit. Annual rent and income schedules take effect July 1. Confirm the current inclusionary percentage and any Downtown subarea rate with the Housing Division (affordablehousing@santacruzca.gov) because the code publisher (codepublishing.com) and the Measure O resolution PDFs (scanned images) could not be read this pass.)
- Layering notes: Primary feeder of the AHTF (record above). Compared with the County's Measure J (15% of for-sale projects of seven or more units, rental projects pay the Affordable Housing Impact Fee), the City program applies to rental projects, so market-rate apartment developers downtown face either on-site units or a gap-based fee; recent mixed-income downtown projects show the pattern (175 condos with 20 affordable at Front Street Riverfront, 276 market-rate with 37 affordable at 530 Front Street, 233 market-rate with 35 affordable at 130 Center Street). Inclusionary units can qualify for the state density bonus under Chapter 24.16 Part 3. The 2022 ballot Measure O (library and housing site) outcome was not addressed on any City page opened; the Downtown Library and Affordable Housing Project on City Lot 4 is under construction with 124 units (all but one manager unit affordable), so the project proceeded. Sources opened: Measure O program page, Resolutions and Ordinances page, FAQ page, For Rent Units page, KMA 2018 analysis PDF and the 2026 in-lieu fee report PDF, all via WebFetch because santacruzca.gov blocks scripted fetches.
- Source: https://www.santacruzca.gov/Government/City-Departments/Community-Development/Housing-Assistance-Information-and-Resources/Measure-O-Inclusionary-Housing
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)

**Prohousing Designation (awarded August 4, 2023; renewal application 2026, Resolution NS-30,681) and Downtown Library and Affordable Housing Project on City Lot 4**
- Agency: City of Santa Cruz Economic Development and Housing (Housing Division) with the Planning Division
- Type: policy/designation
- Typical award: Not a direct subsidy. The designation (57 points, 7th highest of 47 jurisdictions as of April 2024) gives City projects scoring preference or priority processing in AHSC, Infill Infrastructure Grant, Transformative Climate Communities and other state programs and made the City eligible for Prohousing Incentive Program Round 2 ($9.5 million statewide pool). Example: the Downtown Library and Affordable Housing Project on City-owned Lot 4 (Cathcart, Cedar and Lincoln Streets) received a $33.5M AHSC award, a $55.1M TCAC tax credit award and $55.6M of CDLAC bond authority for 124 units (all affordable except one manager unit) above a new library funded by Measure S, with child care, 240 parking spaces and a $250,000 Economic Development Trust Fund contribution for the farmers market. The 2023 designation expires January 1, 2027; the City applied for renewal in 2026.
- AMI requirement: Not applicable to the designation; the Lot 4 housing is 100% affordable (income levels not stated on the project page; Eden Housing manages the interest list for studio to three-bedroom units).
- Cycle: rolling (next: Renewal decision by HCD pending; current designation valid through January 1, 2027. Lot 4 housing framing was underway on levels 4 through 8 as of the latest project update, with completion dates not stated.)
- Layering notes: Prohousing points are additive to the AHTF and HOME layers and have been decisive for Santa Cruz downtown projects competing in AHSC. The City disposes of its own land for 100% affordable projects (Lot 4, Pacific Station North 125 units and Pacific Station South 70 units with Santa Cruz Community Health and Dientes, 119 Lincoln Street ground lease) and accepts land dedications from market-rate developers under Measure O (Anton Pacific). Santa Cruz County does not hold a Prohousing designation in the records compiled; Watsonville, Capitola and Scotts Valley pages opened this pass do not mention one. The Prohousing page, the May 2024 Economic Development journal article and the Downtown Library project page were opened; the 2026 resolution PDF returned 403 to scripted access.
- Source: https://www.santacruzca.gov/Government/City-Departments/Community-Development/Housing-Assistance-Information-and-Resources/Prohousing-Designation-Program
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)

**Santa Cruz Affordable Housing Trust Fund (AHTF), Resolution NS-26,410, guidelines revised September 10, 2024**
- Agency: City of Santa Cruz Community Development Department, Housing and Community Development Division (affordablehousing@santacruzca.gov, (831) 420-5150)
- Type: loan
- Typical award: Construction and deferred-payment permanent loans at simple interest of no more than 3% per year, plus gifts, grants, loan guarantees and credit enhancement. Revenue: Chapter 24.16.030 inclusionary in-lieu fees, the City's PLHA formula allocation (HCD estimate about $1.5 million over five years, deposited directly to the AHTF) and donations. Pipeline list dated September 2024 of 100% affordable rental projects eligible after the first-phase funding review: 136 River Street (For the Future Housing) $1,800,000 loan commitment, predevelopment; 119 Lincoln Street (Eden Housing with For the Future Housing) ground lease plus $5,555,000 loan commitment, predevelopment. Income targets: 30% of funds for extremely low income, up to 70% for lower income, maximum 20% for moderate income, 15% contingency; administrative costs capped at 5%. Fund balance is not published; the 2026 AB 2663 in-lieu fee report (opened) lists fee descriptions but no balance.
- AMI requirement: Rental housing for low (80% AMI) and very low (50% AMI) income households; for-sale housing for moderate, low and very low income; priority first to projects guaranteeing perpetual affordability and second to at least 55 years with recapture; extra points for lowest rents, highest share of affordable units, committed other sources, leverage of tax credits and state and federal programs, and sponsor track record.
- Cycle: rolling (next: No NOFA; requests are reviewed on a rolling basis through a first-phase funding review that places eligible 100% affordable rental projects on the AHTF pipeline list, followed by Council approval of loan commitments. Contact the Housing Division before submitting; the pipeline list was last updated September 2024.)
- Layering notes: The City's primary local gap source and the usual local match for TCAC, HCD and AHSC applications (the Downtown Library and Affordable Housing Project secured $33.5M AHSC, $55.1M of tax credits and $55.6M of CDLAC bond authority). Separate from the County of Santa Cruz Housing Funds NOFA (LMIHAF, County PLHA and County AHIF), which covers unincorporated projects only, and from the County's Chapter 17.10 Measure J program; city projects stack AHTF with Housing Authority of the County of Santa Cruz PBVs, City HOME and CDBG (record below) and Prohousing scoring bonuses. In-lieu fee revenue depends on how many Measure O projects pay fees rather than build units, so balances fluctuate; the City also takes land dedications (Anton Pacific dedicated land for the Pacific Station expansion). cityofsantacruz.com now redirects to santacruzca.gov, which returns 403 to scripted fetches; the AHTF page, guidelines PDF, pipeline list and in-lieu report were opened through the WebFetch tool.
- Source: https://www.santacruzca.gov/Government/City-Departments/Community-Development/Housing-Assistance-Information-and-Resources/Affordable-Housing-Trust-Fund
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)


### City of Santa Rosa

**Permanent Local Housing Allocation (PLHA), City of Santa Rosa formula allocation and 2024-2028 PLHA Plan**
- Agency: City of Santa Rosa Housing and Community Services Department; loans awarded by the Housing Authority through its NOFA
- Type: loan
- Typical award: Five-year 2024-2028 formula allocation of up to $3,046,056 ($487,369 for 2024 and $522,044 for 2025 applied for after an October 13, 2026 public hearing); up to 5% ($152,303) for administration. The prior 2019-2023 allocation of $4,012,612 was committed to four projects totaling 196 units. Funds are loaned at 3% simple interest, deferred, repaid from surplus cash, secured by deed of trust and regulatory agreement.
- AMI requirement: Priority for multifamily rental housing affordable to households at or below 60% AMI (predevelopment, development, acquisition, rehabilitation and preservation); PLHA statute allows up to 120% AMI for some activities. Preference for the most units at the deepest affordability.
- Cycle: annual NOFA (next: No open round as of November 8, 2026. PLHA funds are loaned through the Santa Rosa Housing Trust annual NOFA, next expected about May 2027 based on prior cycles. HCD award for the 2024 and 2025 allocations pending after the Council hearing.)
- Layering notes: Santa Rosa is a direct PLHA entitlement recipient, so its allocation is separate from the County PLHA record (which covers the unincorporated area and non-entitlement cities such as Sonoma and Rohnert Park). Petaluma also receives its own PLHA (see Petaluma record). Because PLHA, CDBG, PIP, HOME and local Housing Trust money all flow through the same NOFA, one application reaches all City sources. Read from the Council staff report and Exhibit A PLHA Plan on the City's Legistar agenda host (matter 26-0770).

**Santa Rosa Affordable Housing Capital Facilities Fee Pilot Program (Resolution RES-2024-175)**
- Agency: City of Santa Rosa Planning and Economic Development Department with Housing and Community Services (deed restrictions through the Housing Authority)
- Type: fee waiver
- Typical award: Capital Facilities Fee (Chapter 21-04) set at $0 for new units deed-restricted through the City's Housing Authority at very low (0-50% AMI, including acutely and extremely low), low (50-80% AMI) and moderate (80-120% AMI) income levels, for building permits for vertical construction issued during the pilot. RES-2024-175 was adopted November 12, 2024 and took effect 60 days later (about January 11, 2025); the pilot ends three years after the effective date (about January 2028) or on adoption of a new CFF nexus study, whichever is first. The zero fee for the Low Income category stops once the City reaches its RHNA Low Income unit total. The 2026 Prohousing renewal application (source) describes the CFF pilot and streamlined design review for 100% affordable projects but does not state a 50 percent permit fee reduction, so that claim is unconfirmed. The CFF for a multifamily unit is several thousand dollars, so the waiver is worth roughly $100,000 to $500,000 on a typical project (confirm with the current fee schedule).
- AMI requirement: Units must be deed-restricted through the Housing Authority at the AMI categories above. Units receiving locally sourced financial assistance from the City or Housing Authority loan programs are NOT eligible for the CFF waiver. Low Income units lose eligibility once the City meets its RHNA Low Income unit total for the current cycle.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Applies to building permits for vertical construction issued before the pilot ends, about January 11, 2028 (three years after the RES-2024-175 effective date), unless a new CFF nexus study ends it sooner.)
- Layering notes: Key conflict: a project cannot take both the CFF waiver and a Santa Rosa Housing Trust NOFA loan, so model both paths; for a 100% affordable LIHTC deal the NOFA loan is usually larger than the CFF waiver, but the waiver has no competition and no application cycle. The waiver stacks with the Chapter 21-01 deferral of other impact fees, state density bonus and the County welfare exemption (county record). The County's 2025-2026 traffic and parks fee waiver (county record) applies only in unincorporated Sonoma County. Read from the resolution text included in the City's draft 2026 Prohousing Designation renewal application (Legistar matter 26-0547, Council hearing August 4, 2026); the City's designation expires January 1, 2027 and renewal is pending with HCD.
- Source: https://legistar.granicus.com/santarosa/attachments/21130e8e-5174-46fe-8b07-7f926d718e3d.pdf
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)

**Santa Rosa Density Bonus and Other Developer Incentives, Zoning Code Chapter 20-31 (state density bonus plus local Supplemental Density Bonus up to 100%)**
- Agency: City of Santa Rosa Planning and Economic Development Department; Density Bonus Housing Agreements through the Housing Authority
- Type: density bonus
- Typical award: Regulatory, not cash. State density bonus up to 50% with incentives and concessions; 100% affordable rental projects (very low and low income, up to 20% moderate) get a 100% density bonus. Local enhancements: (1) an Additional Density Bonus of up to 100% above maximum density for projects that reach the 50% base bonus and add very low income units (5% additional VLI units earns 20%, up to 10% VLI earns 38.75%) or moderate income units; (2) a Supplemental Density Bonus through a Minor Conditional Use Permit using Eligibility Points, at least 60% earned by on-site affordable units and up to 40% by community benefits (public open space, park or capital facilities fee contributions, landmark rehabilitation, family-sized affordable units), with three total incentives or concessions; (3) incentives for specialized housing (10% of units for special needs at very low income rents, 55 years) and child care facilities.
- AMI requirement: Affordable units restricted 55 years under a recorded Density Bonus Housing Agreement; inclusionary units may count toward both Chapter 21-02 and the density bonus.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Density bonus application filed with the first entitlement application and processed concurrently; Supplemental Density Bonus requires a Minor CUP. Chapter last amended by Ordinance 2023-006 (June 6, 2023); further Title 20 amendments to implement the 2023-2031 Housing Element were introduced December 2025 (PLN25-0397).)
- Layering notes: Santa Rosa's supplemental bonus goes beyond state law and beyond the County's Chapter 26 density bonus program (county record), which is useful on infill sites near the two SMART stations and Downtown where the Downtown Station Area Specific Plan already allows high densities. A single affordability agreement can cover inclusionary and density bonus units. Pairing a 100% density bonus with the CFF pilot waiver and the Housing Trust NOFA is the standard local stack. Read from the ecode360 mirror of the Santa Rosa City Code.
- Source: https://ecode360.com/42981356
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)

**Santa Rosa Housing Trust annual Notice of Funding Availability (Housing Authority affordable housing loans: local Housing Trust, CDBG, PLHA and Prohousing Incentive Program funds)**
- Agency: Housing Authority of the City of Santa Rosa, Housing and Community Services Department (Santa Rosa Housing Trust)
- Type: loan
- Typical award: FY 2026-27 NOFA (issued May 1, 2026, due June 5, 2026): about $3.6 million, made up of about $1,399,000 local Housing Trust funds, $1,056,071 CDBG and $1,187,500 state Prohousing Incentive Program (PIP) funds; two applications received for $4 million and 93 units; August 24, 2026 awards: $2,000,000 to Ponderosa Village Phase II (CRDC and Danco, 30 units, 250 Roseland Ave) and $1,642,571 to Caritas Homes Phase II (360 Seventh St). FY 2025-26 NOFA: about $3.5 million (about $2,210,500 local, $1,082,310 CDBG); awards Sept 2025: $489,228 Zane-Wolff Veterans Village rehab, $1,238,310 Apple Valley Scattered Sites rehab, $2,000,000 Ridley Family Apartments (50 units). FY 2024-25: about $3.1 million for 170 units. Local Housing Trust revenue is one half of the City's real property transfer tax allocation ($2.275 million total in FY 2026-27, split equally with Homeless Services) plus housing impact fees and commercial linkage fees (about $1.44 million collected in 2025). Application fee $2,203.
- AMI requirement: Units restricted to extremely low, very low and low income households up to 60% AMI (unless another source restricts further) for 55 years from initial occupancy under a recorded Regulatory Agreement. Standard loan: 3% simple interest, principal and interest deferred 55 years, residual receipts split 75% to the Authority and 25% to the developer.
- Cycle: annual NOFA (next: No open round as of November 8, 2026. No FY 2027-28 Housing Trust NOFA has been issued; based on prior cycles expect a May 2027 release with an early June 2027 deadline. Contact housingtrust@srcity.org, (707) 543-3300.)
- Layering notes: This is the primary local gap source inside Santa Rosa city limits and is separate from the County CFH, County HOME/CDBG (Santa Rosa is its own CDBG entitlement and is not in the Urban County) and County PLHA records. Santa Rosa is also a HOME participating jurisdiction and has run a continuous HOME NOFA in the past (2020); HOME TBRA guidelines were revised September 2026. The City's own PLHA 2024-2028 allocation (separate record) and the $1.25 million PIP grant (accepted April 7, 2026, must be spent by June 30, 2028) are folded into this NOFA, so a single application reaches all City sources; applicants cannot pick the source. Typical stack: City NOFA loan plus RED Housing Fund (county record) plus County CFH or PBVs, then 4% or 9% LIHTC. The FY 2026-27 round had a five-point preference for rehabilitation and a five-point deduction for applicants that previously declined or failed to close an award. Prevailing wage: the NOFA requires compliance with California prevailing wage and, for federal funds, Davis-Bacon. Note the City's Capital Facilities Fee pilot waiver (separate record) is not available to units receiving City or Housing Authority loan funds, so developers must choose between the fee waiver and NOFA funds. Access notes: srcity.org returns 403 to scripts; records were read from the Legistar web API (client santa-rosa) and legistar.granicus.com attachments, and the ca-santarosa.civicplus.com mirror for some pages.
- Source: https://legistar.granicus.com/santarosa/attachments/b3d1890e-abad-405d-b6fe-7256e122c83c.pdf
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)

**Santa Rosa Inclusionary Housing Ordinance, City Code Chapter 21-02 (Housing Allocation Plan): on-site allocated units, housing impact fee and commercial linkage fee**
- Agency: City of Santa Rosa Planning and Economic Development Department (compliance) and Housing Authority (affordability agreements and fee proceeds)
- Type: regulatory requirement
- Typical award: Requirement, not a subsidy. For-rent projects: 8% of units for low income or 5% for very low income households; for-sale: 10% moderate income; Downtown multifamily: 4% low or 3% very low (rental) and 5% moderate (for-sale). Projects of six or fewer units pay the housing impact fee. Any project may instead pay the housing impact fee set by Council resolution, indexed to CPI each July (rate not opened this pass; the fee is paid before final inspection for rentals). Commercial linkage fee applies to new commercial development, due at building permit. Collections in 2025: $1,436,870 ($1,257,641 housing impact fees and $179,229 commercial linkage fees), down from $1.52 million in 2024. In 2025, permits were issued for 23 on-site allocated units (20 very low, 2 low, 1 moderate) out of 661 qualifying units.
- AMI requirement: Allocated units restricted 55 years by recorded affordability agreement with the Housing Authority; deed-restricted affordable projects (units restricted 55 years under agreement with the City), homeless shelters, SROs and ADUs are exempt. Fee revenue must fund housing within City limits for lower and moderate income households with 55-year agreements; Downtown fees are reserved two years for Downtown projects.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Not applicable; applies at entitlement and the fee rate in effect at payment is charged. Next Inclusionary Housing annual review expected in March 2027.)
- Layering notes: Fee proceeds feed the Santa Rosa Housing Trust NOFA (record above), so market-rate pipeline volume drives local loan capacity. Developers providing on-site units get one incentive or concession under Chapter 20-31 and may count the same units toward a state density bonus (bonus units are excluded from the base when computing the inclusionary share). Alternatives (off-site units in the same quadrant, land dedication, conversion of market-rate units, preservation of at-risk units, inclusionary credits usable for 10 years) require Director approval; off-site units cannot receive City or Housing Authority subsidy. The County's separate Affordable Housing Program fee applies only in unincorporated areas. Read on the ecode360 mirror of the Santa Rosa City Code because qcode.us and srcity.org block scripts; collection data from the 2025 Annual Review (Legistar matter 26-0150).
- Source: https://ecode360.com/42997624
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)

**Santa Rosa development fee deferral for affordable housing units, City Code Chapter 21-01 (Section 21-01.020)**
- Agency: City of Santa Rosa Planning and Economic Development Department; agreements approved by City Council
- Type: fee waiver
- Typical award: Deferral, not a waiver: Government Code 66000(b) development impact fees on affordable units under contract with the City may be deferred up to two years from the date otherwise due, secured by a deed of trust, with the balance (at the rate in effect when originally due) payable on sale, transfer or placement of permanent financing. Separately, all City development impact fees are due at final inspection rather than permit issuance (Section 21-01.030), which is itself a cash-flow benefit, and water and sewer demand fees may use a Board of Public Utilities payment plan.
- AMI requirement: Only units under an affordability contract with the City or Housing Authority qualify.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Application must be filed with Planning and Economic Development at least 120 days before fees are due; each deferral agreement needs Council approval. No standing deadline.)
- Layering notes: Stacks with the Capital Facilities Fee pilot waiver (separate record) for remaining fees such as park and utility fees, and with the Housing Trust NOFA. The County's Multi-Family Development Fee Deferral Program (county record) applies only to unincorporated projects. Deferral agreements are not assignable without City Attorney consent, which matters when a LIHTC partnership takes title after entitlement. Read from the ecode360 mirror; the Housing Element implementation ordinance introduced December 2025 (PLN25-0397) amended Titles 20 and 21 but the redline was not reviewed for changes to this chapter.
- Source: https://ecode360.com/42997580
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)

**Santa Rosa tax-exempt multifamily housing revenue bonds (City Council conduit issuance under the City Bond Policy and Term Sheet)**
- Agency: City of Santa Rosa Housing and Community Services Department (Housing Authority) and City Council as issuer
- Type: bond
- Typical award: Conduit tax-exempt and taxable multifamily housing revenue bonds issued by the City Council on request under Council Policy 000-15 (RES-2018-071) and City Code Chapter 4-52; amounts set per project within CDLAC allocation (non-profit borrowers may not need an allocation). Bonds are non-recourse to the City and Housing Authority. Issuer fees per the Bond Policy Term Sheet: $5,000 non-refundable application fee (covers initial review and TEFRA hearing, credited at closing), issuance fee of 25 basis points of principal with a $20,000 minimum at closing, and annual compliance monitoring fee of 12.5 basis points of original principal paid semi-annually. Borrower pays all City, bond counsel, financial advisor, CDLAC, trustee and other costs. Rated issues need AA or better unless privately placed under Exhibit A.
- AMI requirement: Must satisfy CDLAC regulations and Section 142(d) (20% at 50% AMI or 40% at 60% AMI minimum); Council may impose more restrictive terms per issue. Qualified Project Period set in each Regulatory Agreement (typically 15 years after 50% occupancy, or longer if bonds remain outstanding or CDLAC requires). Project must show positive cash flow after year one or cover any operating deficit for five years.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Request to Council timed to CDLAC application rounds; confirm issuer fee schedule and TEFRA hearing lead time with Housing and Community Services, (707) 543-3300.)
- Layering notes: Alternative to CSCDA, CMFA or CalHFA conduit issuance for 4% LIHTC deals in Santa Rosa; using the City as issuer can simplify coordination with Housing Authority loans and regulatory agreements. The Developer Information page confirms the program and lists local funds (real property transfer tax and housing impact fees), CDBG, HOME and HCD funds used by the Housing Authority. The Bond Policy and Term Sheet were opened this pass (srcity.org DocumentCenter 21065 and 21066); contact is the Housing Trust Division, HousingTrust@srcity.org, (707) 543-3300. Whether the City is actively issuing versus deferring to JPAs was not confirmed.
- Source: https://ca-santarosa.civicplus.com/678/Developer-Information

### City of Scotts Valley

**Density Bonus Ordinance (Municipal Code Chapter 17.62, Ordinance 16.142 adopted December 4, 2024)**
- Agency: City of Scotts Valley Planning Department
- Type: density bonus
- Typical award: Chapter 17.62 was replaced in its entirety on December 4, 2024 to implement State Density Bonus Law (Government Code 65915 to 65918) and the 2023-2031 Housing Element: concurrent request with the first permit application, summary density table, eligibility under 65915(b)(1) and additional bonuses under 65915(v)(1), incentives and concessions (65915(k)), waivers (65915(e)), reduced parking (65915(p)), land donation bonuses, replacement housing documentation, regulatory agreements (17.62.060) and affordable unit design standards (17.62.050). No local bonus beyond state law is codified; the chapter states that state law definitions and limits control.
- AMI requirement: State density bonus law thresholds with 55-year rental covenants recorded in a regulatory agreement; affordable units comparable in design and construction to market units.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Submitted with the first permit application; the Maximum Allowable Density Worksheet is available from the Community Development Department for sites without a units-per-acre standard. The City is filing a 2026 technical update to the Housing Element sites inventory (projects at 4444 Scotts Valley Drive, 75 Mount Hermon Road and 4575 Scotts Valley Drive).)
- Layering notes: Mirrors state law, like Watsonville and Capitola; the County's enhanced bonus does not apply inside Scotts Valley. Pairs with the inclusionary exemption for subsidized projects and the Chapter 17.41 ministerial path for 20% or 100% affordable projects (record below); the City Housing page also lists SB 35 procedures and an AB 1332 pre-approved ADU program. Scotts Valley offers no fee waiver program; the Housing Element lists permitting fee waivers only as a possible case-by-case action for special needs housing. Code text read on the zoneomics mirror.
- Source: https://www.zoneomics.com/code/scotts-valley-CA/chapter_39
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)

**Housing Element Opportunity Site Combining District (Municipal Code Chapter 17.41, Ordinance 16.142.1 adopted June 18, 2025): ministerial approval and standards relief for affordable projects**
- Agency: City of Scotts Valley Planning Department
- Type: zoning incentive
- Typical award: Not a subsidy. On Housing Element opportunity sites (Table F-10 sites outside the Town Center Specific Plan), multifamily projects with 20% or more of units affordable to lower income households get by-right approval (objective standards only) with ministerial design review under 17.50.045; other projects follow normal zoning review. Rezone sites carry a 20 du/ac minimum and 40 du/ac maximum, 60% coverage, three stories and a 35-foot top plate (40 feet for vertical mixed use), and at least 16 units are allowed on every site. Any project may request a deviation from a standard that physically precludes its proposed density, limited to the minimum needed. Lot consolidation incentives (deviations from development and subdivision standards) are available only to projects that merge a parcel under one-half acre with an adjacent parcel and are 100% deed restricted for 55 years (rentals at or below 80% AMI, ownership at or below 120% AMI, residential at least 85% of mixed-use floor area). On Mixed-Use Rezone sites residential uses must occupy less than 70% of gross floor area; no affordable exception is stated. Chapter adopted December 4, 2024 (Ordinance 16.142) and rewritten June 18, 2025 (Ordinance 16.142.1) to carry out Housing Element Programs H-1.1 and H-1.2.
- AMI requirement: At least 20% lower income units for by-right approval; lot consolidation incentives require 100% affordable units for 55 years (rental 80% AMI, ownership 120% AMI) on merged parcels that include one under one-half acre.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Available now for sites mapped in the combining district; Program H-1.1 required the rezonings within the Housing Element timeline and Program H-1.2 maintains by-right approval for lower income sites. Confirm site eligibility with the Planning Department.)
- Layering notes: Scotts Valley's main local incentive for tax credit projects, substituting for the absence of a trust fund or fee waiver; it stacks with the Chapter 17.62 state density bonus and the inclusionary exemption for subsidized projects, and with Housing Authority PBVs and state capital. The 4444 Scotts Valley Drive 100% affordable project (first under the 6th cycle element, using state density bonus and SB 35) is the template. Code text read on the zoneomics mirror; the HCD certification letter (April 2, 2024) and the City Housing Element page were also opened.
- Source: https://www.zoneomics.com/code/scotts-valley-CA/chapter_22
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)

**Inclusionary Housing (Below Market Rate) Ordinance (Municipal Code Section 14.01.030, Affordable Housing Committee) and affordable housing in-lieu fee fund**
- Agency: City of Scotts Valley Planning Department (planningdepartment@scottsvalley.gov, 1 Civic Center Drive) with the Council's Affordable Housing Committee setting project terms
- Type: regulatory requirement
- Typical award: Requirement, not a subsidy. Within the former redevelopment project area boundary (unchanged since 1990), residential developments of seven or more units (for sale or rental) must set aside 15% of units for very low, low and moderate income households on site, or off site in limited cases; developments of six or fewer units pay an in-lieu fee; projects of seven or more units with average lot sizes over one acre may pay the fee with Council approval. The in-lieu fee equals the median sales price of a home in the project minus the City-determined affordable price. The two-member Affordable Housing Committee recommends unit counts, sizes and affordability levels for each project, subject to Council confirmation. The ordinance has produced 84 affordable rental and 50 affordable ownership units; in-lieu fees from small projects have subsidized smaller rental projects (the City loaned funds to Emerald Hill Apartments, 46 units with MidPen Housing, including impact fee offsets). Exempt: subsidized projects deed restricted through state or federal programs, single homes on existing lots, additions, ADUs and hardship cases. Housing Element Program H-1.8: comprehensive study by July 2026 and a citywide amendment with income-tier standards by January 2027.
- AMI requirement: Very low, low and moderate income households as set per project by the Affordable Housing Committee; inclusionary units carry restricted equity accrual, resale price and rental price limits; subsidized affordable projects meeting the standard are exempt.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Applies at entitlement; the Affordable Housing Committee meets as special meetings noticed 24 hours ahead. Watch for the July 2026 inclusionary study and the January 2027 citywide ordinance amendment (Program H-1.8), which may change the boundary, percentage and in-lieu formula.)
- Layering notes: The in-lieu fee fund is the City's only local housing money; no balance, guidelines or NOFA are published, so treat it as a small negotiated gap or fee-offset source, as with Emerald Hill. The 15% standard matches Capitola and the County's Measure J but applies to rentals as well; it is lighter than Watsonville's 20%. 100% affordable projects are exempt and instead use Chapter 17.41 ministerial approval and the Chapter 17.62 state density bonus (records below); the 4444 Scotts Valley Drive project is the first 100% affordable project under the 6th cycle element. Regional sources: County state HOME tenant assistance (covers Scotts Valley), Housing Authority PBVs, Housing Trust Silicon Valley loans (Beverly Gardens, 25 units, $3,277,500 acquisition loan), HHAP. The 2023-2031 Housing Element PDF (certified April 2, 2024), the City Housing page (scottsvalley.gov/220) and the Affordable Housing Committee page were opened; the municode text of Section 14.01.030 was not (blocked host).
- Source: https://www.scottsvalley.gov/DocumentCenter/View/4812/2023-2031-Housing-Element---Adopted-and-Certified
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)


### City of Seaside

**Affordable Housing Incentives (Zoning Code Chapter 17.33, density bonus)**
- Agency: City of Seaside Community Development Department, Planning Division
- Type: density bonus
- Typical award: Incentive, not a subsidy. Chapter 17.33 grants density bonuses by Council determination on the state sliding scale (10% lower income units earn 20%, rising to 35% at 20%; 5% very low income units earn a 20% bonus on a parallel scale), with incentives and concessions, reduced parking (17.33.050), child care bonuses (17.33.060), processing rules and a recorded density bonus agreement (17.33.100). Bonus units do not count toward the 20% inclusionary requirement. The fifth cycle Housing Element (Program 13) acknowledged the chapter had not been updated to current state law and committed to do so in the comprehensive zoning update.
- AMI requirement: State density bonus thresholds; affordability terms per Government Code 65915 (55 years rental).
- Cycle: rolling (next: Not applicable; state law controls where the local chapter is less generous. Check for the Seaside 2040 zoning update adoption before relying on local tables.)
- Layering notes: No local fee waiver, trust fund NOFA or city NOFA was found for Seaside beyond the inclusionary in-lieu fund and CDBG (records above and below). Seaside is a CDBG entitlement city (about $365,000 a year per the fifth cycle Housing Element; FY 2026-27 funding plan adopted March 2026 with about $581,000 including carryover, unverified) and is not in the Urban County. Water connection moratorium relief (Council July 2026) matters more than zoning for multifamily feasibility. Code read on the zoneomics mirror because the City site is JavaScript-only for agendas.

**Affordable Housing Requirements (Zoning Code Chapter 17.32, 20% inclusionary), in-lieu fund and Campus Town Affordable Housing Agreement**
- Agency: City of Seaside Community Development Department, Planning Division
- Type: regulatory requirement
- Typical award: Requirement, not a subsidy. Every residential development and condominium conversion must provide at least 20% of units as inclusionary units for moderate, low and very low income households (first third low, second third very low), calculated before any density bonus; equivalents allow one very low unit to count as two moderate units and one low unit as 1.5. Affordability 40 years for rental and for each sale of ownership units. Alternatives (17.32.060): off-site units, land dedication, or any combination of on-site, off-site, in-lieu fees and land dedication equal to the on-site cost. Exemptions: government-built housing, second units, replacement after disaster. The fifth cycle Housing Element reported about $2.6 million in the inclusionary in-lieu fund as of 2017, used for grants to nonprofits. Campus Town (KB Bakewell, Fort Ord, 1,485 units) carries an Affordable Housing Agreement for 225 affordable units (74 very low, 78 low, 73 moderate), equivalent to 350 units, with 161 affordable units in Phase 1 including off-site very low and low income units and land dedicated for a nonprofit rental project.
- AMI requirement: Very low (50% AMI), low (80%) and moderate (120%) households; 40-year covenants; tenants may be drawn from the HACM Section 8 waiting list.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Applies at tentative map, use permit or building permit. Campus Town Phase 1 final map approved and ground broken in 2025; the City bought a 1.62-acre MST parcel in Campus Town in December 2025 and streamlined Campus Town review in February 2026. The 2023-2031 Housing Element (draft May 2023) and Seaside 2040 General Plan were still being finalized in the documents opened.)
- Layering notes: Seaside's 20% requirement with no ten-unit threshold is the broadest in the county, but the code sets no fee schedule; in-lieu payments are negotiated case by case. The in-lieu fund (about $2.6 million in 2017, about $9 million across two restricted housing funds in 2018 per candidate statements, unverified) plus former RDA successor agency land in the Long Range Property Management Plan are the City's local layers for a nonprofit partner on the Campus Town dedication site or Seaside East. Blocked: ci.seaside.ca.us AgendaCenter is JavaScript-only and the CivicClerk portal only lists meetings from October 2026; code text read on the zoneomics mirror, program history from the fifth cycle Housing Element PDF on hcd.ca.gov. Confirm the current fund balance and any 2024-2026 fee resolution with Planning.
- Source: https://www.zoneomics.com/code/seaside-CA/chapter_3
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)

**CDBG entitlement, Inclusionary Housing In-Lieu Fund and Successor Agency properties (Housing Element funding resources)**
- Agency: City of Seaside Community Development Department (Housing and CDBG administration); Successor Agency to the Seaside Redevelopment Agency
- Type: grant
- Typical award: FY 2026-27 Annual Action Plan (draft, City CDBG page): about $275,000 CDBG entitlement plus $256,750 program income and $49,250 prior year funds, $581,000 total, allocated by Council on March 19, 2026. The FY 2026-28 NOFA anticipated $525,000 (FY 2026-27) and $500,000 (FY 2027-28) and caps planning and administration at 20% and public services at 15%, with the remaining 65% for public facilities and infrastructure; public service grants are guided to $5,000 to $12,000. New housing construction is ineligible except by Community Based Development Organizations, and FY 2026-27 awards went to public services and facility projects (including the Elm House transitional housing roof). The fifth cycle Housing Element (HCD review draft, March 2020) reported an Inclusionary Housing In-Lieu Fund of about $2.6 million as of 2017, historically granted to nonprofit developers to buy existing housing or build new affordable units; no current balance was found. Successor Agency Long Range Property Management Plan sites were identified for residential and mixed use sale.
- AMI requirement: CDBG 80% AMI benefit; in-lieu fund projects serve very low, low and moderate income households under Chapter 17.32 covenants.
- Cycle: biennial (next: No open round as of November 8, 2026. The next two-year CDBG NOFA (FY 2028-30) is expected in late 2027 if the City repeats the prior cycle timing; in-lieu fund awards are ad hoc.)
- Layering notes: Seaside controls three small local layers (CDBG entitlement, in-lieu fund, successor agency land) but CDBG is used for public services and public facilities, not new housing construction, so it is not a gap source for multifamily development. A developer should approach Community Development about the in-lieu fund or sites such as Campus Town (about 297 planned affordable units), the North 40, Parker Flats and 1620 Broadway; the Action Plan also cites the Seaside Housing Collaborative for acquisition and rehabilitation. County HHAP, County Housing Trust Fund and HACM project-based vouchers (county records) are the larger sources. CDBG figures come from the City's CDBG page, the draft FY 2026-27 Annual Action Plan and the FY 2026-28 NOFA; the in-lieu fund figure is from the 2020 Housing Element draft hosted by HCD.

**Inclusionary Housing (Municipal Code Chapter 17.41, Ordinance 620 of 2005 as amended by Ordinance 757 of 2023), in-lieu housing fee and Affordable Housing Fund (Section 17.41.080)**
- Agency: City of Soledad Community and Economic Development Department; Finance Director administers the Affordable Housing Fund
- Type: regulatory requirement
- Typical award: Requirement, not a subsidy. Applies to residential projects of five or more lots or units and commercial projects of 2,500 square feet or more; the percentage of affordable units is set by the Housing Element (20% is the figure applied to the Miramonte Specific Plan). Compliance by on-site units, land dedication, in-lieu fees or a combination approved by Council; affordable units built concurrently with market-rate units unless an affordable housing developer takes them under an affordable housing agreement (2023 amendment). The in-lieu fee amount and payment method are set by Council case by case (17.41.070) and deposited in the Affordable Housing Fund (17.41.080), which Council may spend only on affordable housing. Exempt: 100% affordable projects, projects of four or fewer units, public and nonprofit service projects. In June 2025 Council voted 3-2 to revise the 132-unit Miravale agreement to replace moderate income units with in-lieu payments and a parcel contribution (press report, about $25,000 a unit proposed), and a Miramonte Affordable Housing Advisory Subcommittee reviewed the ten-phase Miramonte Affordable Housing Plan on May 20, 2026.
- AMI requirement: Per Housing Element affordability policies; incentives in 17.41.100 and real property dedication in 17.41.090; eligibility screening and anti-overconcentration rules in 17.41.140 and 17.41.150.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Applies at tentative map or permit; obligations due before first certificate of occupancy or final map. Miramonte Affordable Housing Plan expected back to Council in 2026-27; confirm the Miravale in-lieu fee resolution.)
- Layering notes: Soledad's Affordable Housing Fund will be capitalized by Miravale and Miramonte in-lieu payments and could pair with the County PLHA workforce housing set-aside the City requested (record below) for a moderate income for-sale project. Soledad delegated its PLHA to the County in 2024 and is in the state CDBG non-entitlement program, not the Urban County (county records). Blocked: cityofsoledad.gov timed out or refused every connection and cityofsoledad.com fails TLS; the code was read on the zoneomics mirror and the Miravale and Miramonte actions are known only from press and a meeting-aggregator listing, so confirm with the City Clerk.
- Source: https://www.zoneomics.com/code/soledad-CA/chapter_22
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)

The City receives RHNA credit for the units.
