### City of Sonoma

**City of Sonoma Affordable Housing Fees for Nonresidential Development (Resolution 12-2020) and planned residential affordable housing impact fee (Housing Element 2023-2031 Program 8)**
- Agency: City of Sonoma Planning Department
- Type: regulatory requirement
- Typical award: Requirement, not a subsidy. Resolution 12-2020 established Affordable Housing Fees for Nonresidential Development, charged per gross square foot by nonresidential use type including additions; the rate schedule itself was not opened. The City's FY 2023-24 AB 1600 fee report shows the Affordable Housing Impact Fee account (732-00000-000-30120) collected $7,452.98 in FY 2023-24 with an ending balance of about $104,000 to $137,000 at June 30, 2024 (the report's summary and detail pages differ), no projects yet identified, and a plan to earmark funds in the FY 2025-26 budget. Housing Element Program 8 directs the City to adopt by December 2023 a per-square-foot impact fee on single-family homes and 2 to 4 unit projects and by December 2025 to expand the nonresidential fee after nexus studies. The FY 2023-24 report lists no residential affordable housing fee, so the residential fee had not been adopted as of June 30, 2024.
- AMI requirement: Fee proceeds go to the Affordable Housing Trust Fund (Resolution 18-2019) for low and moderate income housing development, preservation, and loan and grant programs.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Unknown, verify with agency. Confirm whether the residential impact fee (due December 2023) and the expanded nonresidential fee (due December 2025) were adopted and at what rates; the City's 2026 Fee Study and Master Fee Schedule Update is underway and may carry them.)
- Layering notes: Any new fee revenue would flow to the Affordable Housing Trust Fund (separate record) and expand the City's gap capacity, which is now mostly TOT-based. The County's Affordable Housing Program fees (county record) do not apply inside the city. Source is the adopted Housing Element on the City's ProudCity storage; Resolution 12-2020 and council fee resolutions could not be opened on the civicweb portal.
- Source: https://storage.googleapis.com/proudcity/sonomaca/2024/10/Housing-Element-2023-2031-FINAL.pdf
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)

**City of Sonoma Affordable Housing Trust Fund (established May 2019, funded by 1% of Transient Occupancy Tax and inclusionary in-lieu fees)**
- Agency: City of Sonoma City Manager's office and Planning Department; grants approved by City Council
- Type: grant
- Typical award: Small, case-by-case grants and loans approved by Council. Most recent award: $250,000 grant approved June 18, 2025 (agreement authorized July 16, 2025) to Burbank Housing toward acquisition and 55-year preservation of 18 units at Setzer Senior Apartments (8 units, 673 First St West) and Maysonnave Apartments (10 units, 270 First St East), leveraged with a $4.5 million BAHFA Housing Preservation Loan Pilot loan and San Francisco Housing Accelerator Fund financing; closed fall 2025. Revenue: Council approved on June 10, 2019 the final 1% of the Measure S TOT increase (TOT now 13%) effective September 1, 2019 to address affordable housing, estimated at the time at about $350,000 to $400,000 per year, plus in-lieu fees under Section 19.44.030. Press accounts put the balance at roughly $1.4 million to $1.9 million in 2025-2026; no City balance figure was opened.
- AMI requirement: Grant terms set per project; the 2025 preservation deal requires affordability for at least 55 years with rents averaging 30% of 80% AMI and tenants protected on modest income increases. The fund is earmarked for very low, low and moderate income housing (Section 19.44.030).
- Cycle: rolling (next: No NOFA. Requests go to City Council; the Council's 2026 priorities include creating a funding plan and policy for use of the Housing Trust Fund, so an allocation policy may be adopted in 2026-2027 (verify with the City Manager's office, (707) 938-3681).)
- Layering notes: Sonoma is a non-entitlement city inside the County's Urban County and County PLHA area, so projects in the city should combine this fund with County CFH, County HOME and CDBG, County PLHA, RED Housing Fund and County PBVs (county records); the 2025 Burbank deal shows the pattern with BAHFA regional preservation money. Housing Element Program 7 commits the City to pursue a Prohousing Designation and to request RED JPA membership in 2024 (status not confirmed). The City also runs an ADU fee waiver program (housing strategies page) and lists Policy H-4.6 fee waivers for affordable housing, but no multifamily fee waiver ordinance was found. Council staff reports on the civicweb portal could not be reached by meeting date; the City's press release and TOT page were used as sources.
- Source: https://www.sonomacity.org/city-of-sonoma-preserves-18-affordable-homes-through-landmark-partnership
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)

**City of Sonoma Density Bonus and incentives, Development Code Sections 19.44.040 through 19.44.080 (Housing Element Program 19)**
- Agency: City of Sonoma Planning Department and Planning Commission (reductions in standards); City Council for other incentives
- Type: density bonus
- Typical award: Regulatory. Adopts state density bonus law (Government Code 65915 through 65918) by reference; bonus percentage calculated under 65915(f), inclusionary units count toward the bonus, one bonus per project, Planning Commission may waive or modify standards to fit bonus units, incentives include reduced standards, mixed-use zoning, other cost-reducing incentives and state parking ratios. No local bonus beyond state law, though Housing Element Program 19 contemplates streamlined processing and a density bonus or incentives for projects not otherwise eligible under state law, and reduced parking for affordable and special needs housing (Program 18). Density bonus and inclusionary units are exempt from the Chapter 19.94 growth management allocation.
- AMI requirement: State thresholds; affordable units restricted in perpetuity under Section 19.44.060 (2016 amendments raised the term from 30 to 55 years and 2021-2023 amendments made it perpetual).
- Cycle: rolling (next: Density bonus request filed with the first entitlement application; Housing Element Program 19 schedules an update of Chapter 19.44 to current state law (Program 15 code amendments noticed January 2026).)
- Layering notes: Past projects using the bonus include Firehouse Village and Maysonnave Apartments. In a city with low base densities and an urban growth boundary, the state bonus plus the 25% inclusionary rule is the main production tool; pair with the Affordable Housing Trust Fund and County sources. Read from the zoneomics mirror of the Sonoma Development Code (codepublishing.com and sonoma.municipal.codes return 403).
- Source: https://www.zoneomics.com/code/sonoma-CA/chapter_4
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)

**City of Sonoma Inclusionary Housing requirement and in-lieu fee, Development Code Chapter 19.44 (Sections 19.44.020 and 19.44.030, Ordinance 06-2021)**
- Agency: City of Sonoma Planning Department
- Type: regulatory requirement
- Typical award: Requirement, not a subsidy. Projects of five or more parcels or units must make at least 25% of units affordable: rental projects 5% extremely low, 10% very low and 10% low income (sequenced ELI, VLI, LI, then middle income); ownership projects 5% low, 10% moderate and 10% middle income. Projects of four or fewer units pay an in-lieu fee per Section 19.44.030; fractions below 0.5 may be paid as a fee. In-lieu fees are paid before building permit into the City's housing trust fund. Fee amount is set by Council resolution (amount not opened); Housing Element Program 1 called for a nexus-supported in-lieu fee by December 2023 and a July 2024 amendment requiring perpetual affordability. Units of 850 square feet or less, ADUs and additions under 850 square feet are exempt. Affordability is in perpetuity under Section 19.44.060.
- AMI requirement: Rental: 25% of units split 5% ELI, 10% VLI, 10% LI; ownership: 25% split 5% LI, 10% moderate, 10% middle income; restricted in perpetuity by recorded affordability agreement; affordable units must average at least 75% of market-rate unit floor area with the same bedroom count.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Applies at entitlement. Housing Element Program 1 schedules a review of the inclusionary provisions and Development Code amendments by 2026; Program 15 Development Code amendments were noticed under CEQA in January 2026. Check with Planning (707) 938-3681 for the current in-lieu fee resolution.)
- Layering notes: At 25% with deep targeting, this is the strictest inclusionary rule among the Sonoma County priority cities, and the City says it has produced about 293 inclusionary and density bonus rental units inside 40 market-rate projects (about six units a year). Because the required ELI and VLI units can also qualify a project for a state density bonus (Chapter 19.44 counts inclusionary units when calculating the bonus), most market-rate rental projects in Sonoma pair the two. In-lieu revenue feeds the Affordable Housing Trust Fund (separate record). Growth management (Chapter 19.94 Housing Allocation Process) exempts affordable and density bonus units from the annual allocation. Code read from the zoneomics mirror (codepublishing.com returns 403); the City's Housing Policies page confirms the 25% rule.
- Source: https://www.zoneomics.com/code/sonoma-CA/chapter_4
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)


### City of South Lake Tahoe

**City direct gap and predevelopment financing for affordable housing (HOME program income, Housing Successor and Redevelopment Agency program income, PLHA formula funds, Prohousing Incentive Program funds, general fund, residential units of use) and state application sponsorship**
- Agency: City of South Lake Tahoe Development Services Department, Housing Division (Housing Manager, mmanuel@cityofslt.gov, 530-542-7417); City Council approves each commitment
- Type: loan
- Typical award: Deal-by-deal Council commitments, no NOFA or written guidelines. Track record: over $2.5 million of HOME program income, Redevelopment Agency program income and general fund to Sugar Pine Village (248 units, Related California and Saint Joseph Community Land Trust on state surplus land; Phase 1A 68 units opened fall 2024, Phase 2A 60 units fall 2025, Phase 1B 60 units summer 2026, Phase 2B seeking financing), plus City-sponsored AHSC ($17,359,470), MHP ($19.6 million), IIG, LGMG, HOME and PLHA awards; a $564,073 predevelopment loan plus $500,000 of Prohousing Incentive Program funds to Novin Development for the 75-unit 3900 and 3908 Lake Tahoe Boulevard project (SB 35 approval 2025, AHSC pending); about $1,791,669 CDBG-CV and $120,000 PIP for rehabilitation of three Homekey properties (72 supportive units) with Tahoe Coalition for the Homeless; 21 multifamily residential units of use donated to Lake Tahoe Community College's 100-bed dorm (about $315,000 market value); three Al Tahoe lots donated to Saint Joseph Community Land Trust. City awards 2020 to 2025 included PLHA formula about $880,000 total, PLHA competitive $15 million over three awards, HOME $6,538,240 and PIP Round 2 $620,000. Legacy RDA Low and Moderate Income Housing Fund loans (AB 987 database) total $16.46 million HOME, $2.15 million RDA and $1.18 million CDBG across 296 units in eight projects.
- AMI requirement: Follows the state source layered in: Sugar Pine Village and 3900 Lake Tahoe Boulevard are 55-year deed restrictions at 30% to 80% AMI; TRPA deed restriction also required when bonus units are used. HOME program income follows HOME rules.
- Cycle: rolling (next: No NOFA; no open round as of November 8, 2026. Approach the Housing Division (housing@cityofslt.us) ahead of the AHSC, MHP and PLHA competitive rounds; the draft Housing Element commits the City to apply for at least one grant per year. The draft 2027-2035 Housing Element was open for public comment through September 12, 2026 and no adopted version was posted on the City Housing Element page as of November 8, 2026; Phase 2B of Sugar Pine Village is still pursuing financing.)
- Layering notes: South Lake Tahoe is a non-entitlement city that has out-raised most small cities by sponsoring state applications (PLHA competitive, AHSC, HOME, IIG, LGMG) for a nonprofit or private developer, so the City's own cash is small but its sponsorship is the key to the state layer. Gap order used on Sugar Pine Village: LIHTC and bonds, AHSC and MHP, IIG and LGMG, HOME and PLHA, City program income last. County layers available in the Tahoe Basin: El Dorado County PLHA formula and County HOME/CDBG participation requests, County Affordable Housing Trust Fund (no development NOFA), County PHA project-based vouchers, CMFA TEFRA approvals, welfare exemption, BHSA housing funds; the County Traffic Impact Fee offset (Policy B-14) does not apply inside the city because the City levies its own fees. TRPA layer: bonus units and the allocation exemption are required for any deed-restricted project (see the TRPA record), and TRPA application fees are waived for affordable projects. Residential allocations are scarce (33 market-rate per year citywide, one third reserved for multifamily), which is why deed-restricted projects using bonus units are the only route to scale. Workforce Housing Fund in-lieu fees (inclusionary record) are a separate, newer pool. No local housing trust fund, no city NOFA, no local tax-exempt issuer. Source is the City's August 2026 public review draft 2027-2035 Housing Element on the City DocumentCenter; the City's CivicPlus pages opened directly but council packets were not reachable (Granicus and Legistar hosts not found).
- Source: https://www.cityofslt.gov/DocumentCenter/View/24379/SLT_Housing-Element_Public-Review-Draft_August-2026
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)

**City permit fee waiver for nonprofit and public agency affordable housing (City Code Section 6.55.090), lot consolidation fee waiver for deed-restricted units (Housing Element Program 1-7) and Sugar Pine Village inspection fee reduction**
- Agency: City of South Lake Tahoe Development Services Department (Planning and Building Divisions); waivers approved by the City Council at a public hearing
- Type: fee waiver
- Typical award: Case by case. Nonprofits and public agencies developing affordable housing may request waiver of City permit fees, granted by Council resolution (about 45 days from request to approval, run concurrently with permit review). The City also reduced building inspection fees for Sugar Pine Village because HCD inspects the modular units. Program 1-7 commits the City to waive the lot line adjustment fee when the resulting project includes deed-restricted affordable units. City planning fees are modest relative to TRPA fees; City multifamily impact charges are mainly utility connection fees set by South Tahoe Public Utility District (not waived; $7,500 deposit and 10% of capacity fees at plan review). No waiver of TRPA water quality ($1.86 per sq ft) or excess coverage mitigation fees ($8.50 per sq ft), though TRPA application fees are waived for affordable, moderate and achievable bonus-unit projects and the mobility mitigation fee may be waived.
- AMI requirement: Affordable housing project sponsored by a nonprofit or public agency; deed restriction consistent with TRPA affordable, moderate or achievable definitions when bonus units are used. No specific AMI threshold published for the City waiver.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Request with the entitlement or building permit application; Council hearing required. Verify current practice with the Housing Division (530-542-7417) because the code text could not be opened.)
- Layering notes: Fee relief is small in dollar terms; the real cost drivers in the Basin are TRPA mitigation fees, land coverage purchases and development rights, which the TRPA bonus unit program (separate record) addresses. Combine with the TRPA application fee exemption and with the Phase 2 Housing Amendments height, coverage and density relief. Private for-profit developers are not eligible for the 6.55.090 waiver unless partnered with a nonprofit or public agency. The County Traffic Impact Fee offset (Board Policy B-14) is not available inside the city. The City's code host (codepublishing.com) returned 403 and the gocodebook mirror had no Chapter 6.55 page, so Section 6.55.090 was not read directly; the description is taken from the fees and exactions analysis in the City's August 2026 public review draft 2027-2035 Housing Element (pages 4-203 to 4-206) and from Program 1-7 of the adopted 2022-2027 Housing Element.
- Source: https://www.cityofslt.gov/DocumentCenter/View/24379/SLT_Housing-Element_Public-Review-Draft_August-2026
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)

**Inclusionary Housing Ordinance (City Code Chapter 6.27, Ordinance 1180) and Workforce Housing Fund in-lieu fees**
- Agency: City of South Lake Tahoe Development Services Department, Planning Division and Housing Division (fund held by the Finance Director); 1052 Tata Lane, 530-542-7417
- Type: regulatory requirement
- Typical award: Requirement, not a subsidy. New residential construction, redevelopment of 50% or more of a building with dwellings, or condo conversion must provide inclusionary units or pay an in-lieu fee scaled to unit size (habitable square feet): 2,000 sq ft or less exempt; 2,001 to 2,500 sq ft 5% of units or $5.29 per sq ft; 2,501 to 3,000 sq ft 6% or $5.84 per sq ft; 3,001 to 5,000 sq ft 9% or $16.77 per sq ft; over 5,000 sq ft 17% or $17.65 per sq ft. Fees are paid before building permit issuance (by phase for phased projects) into the Workforce Housing Fund for housing affordable to low and moderate income households. Fund balance and collections to date are not published; the 2027-2035 draft Housing Element commits the City to post requirements, fee amounts and annual collections by mid-2027 and to publish a five-year in-lieu fee report under AB 2663.
- AMI requirement: Inclusionary units deed restricted for rent or sale to lower income households (80% AMI or below, El Dorado County), priced at no more than 30% of gross income including utilities, dispersed on site, comparable in exterior quality and bedroom mix, built concurrently with market-rate units. No affordability term is stated in the chapter text that was read.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Applies at building permit. The Master Fee Schedule adopted May 5, 2026 keeps the in-lieu rates unchanged from the March 26, 2024 schedule ($5.29, $5.84, $16.77 and $17.65 per square foot by size tier) plus a $157 inclusionary housing plan check fee. Draft Housing Element Program 2-10 commits to posting requirements and fee amounts by mid-2027 and annual monitoring; first AB 2663 fee report due in 2027.)
- Layering notes: This is the only locally generated housing fund in South Lake Tahoe. Multifamily rental projects are exempt from both the unit requirement and the fee (chapter text on the gocodebook mirror), so apartment developers owe nothing; the fund is fed by large single-family and condo construction, which is the dominant product in the Basin. Spending the Workforce Housing Fund is at Council discretion with no NOFA or guidelines published; pair requests with the City's HOME program income, PLHA formula and Prohousing Incentive Program dollars (see the City direct financing record) and with the County Affordable Housing Trust Fund, County PLHA and County HOME/CDBG records, which also have no standing NOFA. The ordinance grew out of Housing Element Program 2-11 (2022 to 2027 cycle) and the January 2023 Analysis of Local Funding Sources. Adoption date conflict: the August 2026 draft Housing Element says Council adopted the ordinance in December 2024, but the March 26, 2024 Master Fee Schedule already lists the inclusionary fee tiers, so the fee was in place by early 2024. Fee amounts are confirmed on the official Master Fee Schedule; unit percentages and exemptions were read on the gocodebook mirror because codepublishing.com returns 403.
- Source: https://www.cityofslt.gov/DocumentCenter/View/24191
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)

**TRPA Residential Bonus Unit Program (TRPA Code Chapter 52), allocation exemption (Chapter 50.5.1) and Phase 2 Housing Amendments as applied in South Lake Tahoe Town Centers (Tourist Core, Tahoe Valley and Midtown Area Plans)**
- Agency: Tahoe Regional Planning Agency (TRPA), with City of South Lake Tahoe Planning Division as lead reviewer inside Area Plan boundaries; City holds a voting seat on the TRPA Governing Board
- Type: density bonus
- Typical award: Regulatory, not cash, but it substitutes for development rights that otherwise must be bought. Deed-restricted affordable (80% AMI), moderate (120% AMI) or achievable (TRPA-set percentage tied to median home price) units receive residential bonus units at no cost in place of a residential unit of use (potential unit plus allocation), are exempt from the City's annual allocation (33 market-rate allocations per year citywide, one third reserved for multifamily), and are exempt from TRPA application fees. About 946 of the 1,124 bonus units set aside in 2018 remained as of the 2026 draft Housing Element, all reserved for deed-restricted housing and prioritized for Centers and multifamily zones. Phase 2 Housing Amendments (TRPA Governing Board, December 2023; MAP settlement July 2024) remove the maximum density cap for 100% deed-restricted projects in Town Centers, allow heights up to 65 feet in Centers (step-back, shade and scenic findings above 56 feet), allow 100% deed-restricted projects outside Centers to transfer in coverage up to 70% of high-capability land if runoff is treated by a public stormwater system, and allow use of the TRPA basin-wide parking study to reduce parking. Affordable projects using these tools have reached 61 to 67 units per acre in the city (Sugar Pine Village, 3900 Lake Tahoe Boulevard).
- AMI requirement: Permanent TRPA deed restriction recorded as a permit condition: occupancy limited to affordable, moderate or achievable households (or local employees for achievable units), no second-home or vacation rental use, annual compliance report to TRPA (penalties up to $5,000 per day), real estate disclosure on transfer; project within one half mile of transit. Height, coverage and density incentives under Phase 2 require 100% deed-restricted units plus stormwater and transportation contributions.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Bonus units assigned at TRPA permit (about 120 days of TRPA review, or City-only review for qualifying projects inside the TCAP and TVAP). Watch: TRPA Phase 3 (Cultivating Community, Conserving the Basin) EIS scoping closed March 16, 2026 with further code changes pending; City Midtown Area Plan (MTAP) adoption was pending a September 2026 hearing; TRPA 2025-2026 income limits and achievable percentages are updated each July.)
- Layering notes: Flag for every South Lake Tahoe deal: the Tahoe Basin is dual-jurisdiction. The City cannot grant a state density bonus law bonus or concessions that exceed TRPA standards; TRPA gives full density relief only to 100% deed-restricted projects and gives no comparable benefit or mandatory concessions to mixed-income projects that set aside a share of units, which the draft 2027-2035 Housing Element names as a continuing constraint (Program 2-8 asks TRPA to allow state density bonus compliance). Land coverage (Bailey system, 30% base outside Area Plans, 70% inside TCAP and TVAP), scenic and height limits and the allocation system govern feasibility more than zoning. Projects using bonus units must carry a TRPA deed restriction in addition to TCAC, HCD or City covenants; coordinate the three so income limits (TRPA uses county AMI for a family of three) and terms do not conflict. The TRPA application fee waiver stacks with the City Section 6.55.090 waiver (separate record). County layers (PLHA, Trust Fund, PBVs, welfare exemption) apply as in the rest of El Dorado County. Source pages at trpa.gov opened directly; City-specific figures (946 bonus units remaining, 61 to 67 du per acre, 65-foot height, MTAP status) come from the City's August 2026 draft Housing Element on the City DocumentCenter.
- Source: https://www.trpa.gov/housing/
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)


### City of South San Francisco

**Commercial Linkage Fee fund (Fund 823) and Affordable Housing Trust Fund loans**
- Agency: City of South San Francisco Economic and Community Development Department, Housing Division
- Type: loan
- Typical award: Commercial Linkage Fee (SSFMC 8.69, adopted 2018): office and R&D $17.38 per square foot, hotel $5.80, retail, restaurant and services $2.90 (January 2025 handout). Fund 823 revenue swung from $7.5 million (FY 2022-23) to a projected $1.5 million in FY 2025-26, $19.3 million in FY 2026-27 and $8.5 million in FY 2027-28 (Genentech, Trammell Crow and Healthpeak payments); projected year-end FY 2024-25 balances were $14 million in Fund 823, $200,000 in the Affordable Housing Trust Fund (Fund 205) and $1 million in the housing successor fund (Fund 241). City loans: Rotary Gardens Phase 1, 500 Linden Avenue, up to $7,867,409 (August 11, 2026); Synergy Community Development acquisition of the Metropolitan Hotel, 220 Linden, up to $3,115,000 from Fund 823 (February 24, 2026); 1051 Mission Road (BRIDGE, 158 units, PUC site) $2,000,000 raised to $2,362,000 as the LHTF match plus up to $14.6 million committed April 22, 2026 from the first market-rate phase for Measure K and tax credit applications; 428-432 Baden (For the Future Housing, 36 units) $4,050,000; 201-219 Grand and 418 Linden (ROEM, 84 units) $3,500,000; 201 Baden (Eden, 82 units) $2,362,500 LHTF. City also holds a $28,817,500 IIG grant for 1051 Mission and $890,000 PIP.
- AMI requirement: Trust Fund serves low and moderate income households; LHTF-matched loans require extremely low and very low income units; 55-year City regulatory agreements.
- Cycle: rolling (next: No standing NOFA; the Affordable Housing Financing Plan (May 2025, FY 2025-27) says the City will time NOFAs, acquisitions and rehabilitation around linkage fee payouts, with 66% of projected revenue arriving in FY 2026-27. Requests go to Council through the Housing Division (housing@ssfca.gov, (650) 829-6620).)
- Layering notes: County layer: every San Mateo County city project competes for the County Affordable Housing Fund NOFA (AHF 14 closed July 15, 2026, next fall 2027), HEART bridge loans and HACSM project-based vouchers; city money is usually the first commitment that unlocks those. South San Francisco has the largest city housing fund in the county after the linkage fee rebound and uses it as the first-in local loan (residual receipts) ahead of County AHF, state IIG and LHTF money; the City also waives or pays permit fees from Fund 823 for public housing work (C Street electrification, August 2026) and holds TEFRA hearings for CMFA bonds (Rotary Gardens, August 2026). City-owned sites: 1051 Mission Road (PUC site, Development Agreement amended April 24, 2026), 220 Linden and 905 Linden under negotiation in 2026. Source is the Housing Division funding page; figures from the Affordable Housing Financing Plan PDF and Council files on ci-ssf-ca.legistar.com (Legistar API client ci-ssf-ca).
- Source: https://www.ssfca.gov/Departments/Economic-and-Community-Development/Divisions/Housing-Division/Funding-Sources-for-Affordable-Housing
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-07)

**Inclusionary Housing Ordinance (SSFMC Chapter 20.380) and replacement housing rules**
- Agency: City of South San Francisco Economic and Community Development Department, Housing Division
- Type: regulatory requirement
- Typical award: Requirement, not a subsidy. Market-rate projects of 5 or more units: rental 15% (10% lower income, 5% very low income); homebuyer 15% (7.5% moderate, 7.5% lower income); extended to rental housing in 2018. In-lieu fee amounts are not posted on the developer page. Demolition requires one-for-one replacement, relocation assistance and right of first refusal.
- AMI requirement: County income and rent limits (2026-27 schedule posted), utility allowances deducted, regulatory agreements control; Procedures and Guidelines for Inclusionary Units updated September 2024.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Applies at entitlement; the City is not listed among the 2026 multi-city nexus study participants, so no change is pending.)
- Layering notes: County layer: every San Mateo County city project competes for the County Affordable Housing Fund NOFA (AHF 14 closed July 15, 2026, next fall 2027), HEART bridge loans and HACSM project-based vouchers; city money is usually the first commitment that unlocks those. The 15% rental requirement with a very low income tier plus the linkage fee is why South San Francisco's biotech corridor funds housing elsewhere in the city; 100% affordable projects are exempt and instead draw on Fund 823 loans (see separate record). Source is the Housing Requirements for Developers page.
- Source: https://www.ssfca.gov/Departments/Economic-and-Community-Development/Divisions/Housing-Division/Housing-Requirements-for-Developers
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-07)


### City of St. Helena

**St. Helena Affordable Housing Program: 20% inclusionary requirement, housing in-lieu fee and nonresidential Housing Impact Fee (SHMC Chapter 17.30, Ordinance 23-4)**
- Agency: City of St. Helena Community Development Department
- Type: regulatory requirement
- Typical award: Requirement, not a subsidy. Inclusionary: at least 20% of all new dwelling units in any residential project (no project size threshold; new units under 850 square feet and ADUs are excluded) must be affordable units of the same tenure, built concurrently. Rental projects with four or more affordable units split them by RHNA need (as of March 2022: 55% very low, 31% low, 14% moderate); three or fewer units are assigned one each to very low, low then moderate. Ownership projects: half the affordable units at or below 100% AMI (or 80% AMI, which earns an extra 5% density bonus beyond state law) and half at moderate income, 45-year resale restrictions renewed at each resale. In-lieu fee (per square foot of net new floor area, set by Council resolution) is available by right only to projects of four or fewer units; larger projects need a Council infeasibility finding that density bonus concessions cannot cure. Housing impact fee on nonresidential development and conversions per the master fee schedule (wineries, nonprofits, schools, public uses and small day care exempt); the Council considered a 2024 proposal to raise the hotel fee to about $41,797 per room and commercial to $14 per square foot (press report, adoption not confirmed).
- AMI requirement: Rental affordable units restricted by recorded agreement (very low, low and moderate by RHNA ratio); ownership units 45 years. The Council may forgive part of a rental project's obligation for undue hardship where the project contributes significantly to affordable housing.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Applies at the first discretionary or ministerial approval through an inclusionary housing plan and recorded affordable housing agreement before building permit. Code is current through Ordinance 26-4 (May 12, 2026). Biennial review of fees and requirements due 2026. Current master fee schedule amounts were not located online; confirm with Community Development (707-968-2740).)
- Layering notes: The strictest inclusionary rule in Napa County (20% with no threshold) means almost every market rate project in St. Helena produces deed restricted units or fee revenue for the trust fund record above. 100% affordable projects satisfy the requirement by definition and pay no in-lieu fee; nonresidential impact fees and in-lieu fees capitalize Fund 751. Chapter 17.29 (Density Bonus) implements state law and is cross referenced for concessions. Code text read on the Zoneomics mirror of the City zoning code (source_url); cityofsthelena.gov pages opened but the agenda search returned nothing to scripts, and codepublishing and gocodebook mirrors return 403.
- Source: https://www.zoneomics.com/code/saint-helena-CA/chapter_4
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)

**St. Helena Affordable Housing Trust Fund (Fund 751, SHMC 17.30.050) development loans and project commitments**
- Agency: City of St. Helena Community Development Department and Administrative Services Director (fund administrator); City Council approves commitments
- Type: loan
- Typical award: Fund 751 beginning balance July 1, 2025 of $2,404,218, projected $2,448,125 at June 30, 2026 and $2,492,032 at June 30, 2027 before new commitments, but the budget states the fund balance includes unavailable long-term receivables of $1,249,684 in loans and interest, so cash available is roughly $1.2 million before the Fountain Street pledge. Recurring revenue is small (about $62,400 a year of housing fees plus about $7,200 interest; $583,991 of fees in FY 2023-24). Track record: about $2,450,000 committed to Turley Flats (8 units, $700,000 incl. deferred fees), Brenkle Court (8 units) and 963 Pope Street (5 units) through 2021, and the Housing Element states the City has funded every developer request since 2015. Press reports (not confirmed on the City site) describe a $1.4 million loan to Our Town St. Helena for the Christine Apartments and a March 2026 commitment of $2.2 million ($1.5 million early, $700,000 later) to the 40 unit Fountain Street project by Our Town St. Helena and Burbank Housing (about $27 million total cost, land donated).
- AMI requirement: Fund must be used solely to increase and improve housing affordable to moderate, low and very low income households, with priority for extremely low income households and the western part of the city (Programs H-DD and H-MM). Rental affordability agreements recorded; the City targets 55-year terms on assisted rental projects.
- Cycle: rolling (next: No NOFA; developers request funds directly and the City Council acts by resolution (typically one to two actions a year). Remaining uncommitted balance after the Fountain Street pledge should be confirmed with Community Development (707-968-2740, Director Leza Mikhail). The biennial review of fees and inclusionary requirements under 17.30.050(B) is due in 2026.)
- Layering notes: Small but reliable: St. Helena has funded every request since 2015 and pairs trust fund loans with reduced or deferred City fees (Program H-CC) and Measure E money (separate record). Stack order for a St. Helena deal: CTCAC credits, HCD programs, County Affordable Housing Fund (the County funded Turley Flats $798,000 and 963 Pope $200,000, see Pass 2 record), then City trust fund and Measure E, with HACN project based vouchers. Local and state funds are public funds under Labor Code 1720(b), so state prevailing wage applies unless a 1720(c) exemption fits the deal, such as 1720(c)(5)(E) for below-market loans with at least 40 percent of units restricted 20 years at or below 80 percent AMI (see prevailing_wage_basis). Figures from the adopted FY 2025-26 and 2026-27 budget (source_url, Fund 751 worksheet); the 2023-2031 Housing Element draft on hcd.ca.gov and the code mirror were also opened. The City AgendaCenter search returned no results to scripts, so 2026 council actions rest on press coverage and are marked as such.
- Source: https://www.cityofsthelena.gov/ArchiveCenter/ViewFile/Item/625
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)

**St. Helena Measure E 1% Transient Occupancy Tax for affordable and workforce housing (Fund 752)**
- Agency: City of St. Helena Administrative Services and Community Development Departments; City Council
- Type: grant
- Typical award: Special tax of 1% on hotel stays (TOT 12% to 13%) effective January 1, 2019, restricted to programs and services for affordable and workforce housing. Revenue about $300,000 to $315,000 a year (FY 2024-25 estimate $287,718 including interest; FY 2025-26 budget $322,504; FY 2026-27 $328,684). Fund balance $636,312 at July 1, 2025, projected $858,816 at June 30, 2026 and $1,187,500 at June 30, 2027 (includes a $160,000 long term receivable for an affordable housing loan). Only $100,000 of Planning and Building services is budgeted against it, in FY 2025-26, and nothing in FY 2026-27, so most of the balance is available for projects.
- AMI requirement: Households earning up to 120% AMI (rental and for sale), per the fund description; the City prioritizes extremely low and very low income units in its Housing Element programs.
- Cycle: rolling (next: No NOFA; City Council allocates by resolution. Press coverage indicates Measure E money is part of the two fund total (about $1.5 million) the Council pledged to Fountain Street in March 2026; confirm the uncommitted balance with the City.)
- Layering notes: Measure E is the City's only source for moderate income (81% to 120% AMI) units, which neither the trust fund's nexus based dollars nor state programs cover well; use it on workforce units in a mixed income project while the trust fund covers lower income units. Parallel to Napa's Measure F, Calistoga's Measure D and the County's Measure I, each a separate fund with its own geography. Figures from the adopted FY 2025-26 and 2026-27 budget (source_url, Fund 752 worksheet); the Housing Element estimate of $280,000 a year was also read.
- Source: https://www.cityofsthelena.gov/ArchiveCenter/ViewFile/Item/625
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)

**St. Helena reduced, deferred or waived fees for affordable housing (Housing Element Program H-CC) and Density Bonus Chapter 17.29**
- Agency: City of St. Helena Community Development Department; City Council
- Type: fee waiver
- Typical award: The City reduces, defers or waives application and impact fees for affordable developments case by case; through January 1, 2022 it had reduced, deferred or waived fees for 21 affordable units (Turley Flats, Brenkle Court, 963 Pope Street), in part by lending trust fund money to cover deferred fees. The 2023-2031 Housing Element sets a goal of fee relief for 30 extremely low or very low income units and commits to adopt eligibility criteria and higher incentives for extremely low and very low income units. Chapter 17.29 implements the state density bonus (one to three concessions at 10%, 17% and 24% lower income, etc.) with the 5% local bonus add on for ownership projects under 17.30.030(G).
- AMI requirement: Affordable housing developments, with priority for extremely low and very low income units; deed restrictions required under the City affordable housing agreement.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Request with the entitlement application; Council approves fee relief with the funding commitment. Housing Element program timelines run through 2031.)
- Layering notes: Fee relief is routinely bundled with trust fund and Measure E commitments, so a St. Helena request should ask for all three at once. St. Helena's PLHA share (95% rehab loans up to $60,000 through the City of Napa) and its Housing Services Agreement with HACN (Section 8, regulatory monitoring, loan servicing) round out the local layer; there is no HOME or CDBG entitlement. Waived or reduced fees can count as public funds under Labor Code 1720(b)(4). Source: 2023-2031 Housing Element HCD review draft on hcd.ca.gov (source_url; the City adopted the element in 2023 and the final version was not located on the City site); the City budget and code mirror were also opened.

### City of Stockton

**Affordable Housing Incentives and Density Bonus Provisions, Stockton Municipal Code Chapter 16.40 (State bonus to 50%, Tier-1 to 75%, Tier-2 to 100%; Ord. 2020-12-01-1502, 2022-07-12-1601-02, 2025-06-03-1601)**
- Agency: City of Stockton Community Development Department, Planning Division
- Type: density bonus
- Typical award: Requirement and entitlement incentive, not a subsidy. State Density Bonus up to 50%; Tier-1 supplemental bonus 50% to 75% with 30 eligibility points; Tier-2 76% to 100% with 50 points. Points: one per additional percent of very low or low income units, LEED 15 to 30, CALGreen Tier I up to 20, 10% on-site renewable 15, adaptive reuse of historic buildings 20, plus other community benefits. Projects not qualifying for state concessions get three local concessions: setback reduction up to 25%, parking reductions of 25% to 100% scaled to the share of lower income units, lot coverage or FAR increases of 5% to 20%, lot coverage up to 25%, height plus 12 feet or 10%.
- AMI requirement: State law thresholds (5% very low, 10% low, 100% affordable, senior, moderate for-sale) for the base bonus; supplemental tiers require additional affordable units or community benefits scored under 16.40.050; density bonus housing agreement recorded per 16.40.070.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Applies at entitlement. Title 16 was amended June 3, 2025 and again in 2025-2026 (Chapter 16.20, 16.80.310, 16.244.010) to implement the 2023-2031 Housing Element; check the current code before design.)
- Layering notes: Stockton's 100% bonus exceeds state law and was one of HCD's stated reasons for the Prohousing Designation. Pair with the PFF exemption and the Housing NOFA; the Housing Element also allows duplexes by right in single-family zones. Parking can go to zero for projects with 75% or more lower income units, which matters for downtown and transit sites. Read from the zoneomics code mirror of Title 16 Division 3 because the City's code publisher blocks scripts.
- Source: https://www.zoneomics.com/code/stockton-CA/chapter_3
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)

- Agency: City of Stockton Housing, Homelessness, Events and Parking Department (formerly Economic Development Department Housing Division)
- Type: grant
- Typical award: 2026-27 allocations: CDBG $3,229,216 plus about $350,000 program income, HOME $1,382,561, ESG $284,821. HOME budget: $1,324,906 HOME Housing Loans for multifamily rehab or new construction, $207,384 CHDO set-aside, $150,000 program delivery, $138,256 admin. CDBG largely to public infrastructure ($4,914,998 with carryover) and public services; 2026-27 CDBG/ESG public service NOFA awarded $498,509 CDBG and $262,528 ESG to nonprofits. 2024 Real Property Acquisition NOFA offered about $4,551,524 of CDBG and PIP for nonprofit site acquisition (5 applications, $10.0 million requested; awards included $1,500,000 to Parents by Choice for transitional youth housing at 523 E. Main and up to $800,000 CDBG to STAND for scattered-site acquisition).
- AMI requirement: HOME rents and incomes (at or below 60% AMI for rental, 15% CHDO set-aside), CDBG national objective, ESG homeless eligibility. HOME preference policy (2024, in 2025-2029 Consolidated Plan) favors projects serving targeted populations named in the Consolidated Plan.

HOME match is currently 100% waived by HUD. HOME money is the backbone of the City Housing NOFA and has been combined with PLHA, LMIHF, HHAP and PIP in every recent award. CDBG has been used for land acquisition NOFAs for nonprofits, which is unusual in the region. HACSJ has secured City NOFA funds for its DCDC projects (Danny Drive, Sierra Vista). Draft 2026-27 AAP read from the Stockton Legistar attachment; the City housing page lists the same plans.

**City-Wide Affordable Housing Development Public Facilities Fee (PFF) Exemption Program (with Greater Downtown Residential PFF Exemption; Resolutions 2015-11-17-1602, 2018-02-06-0504, 2018-11-06-1402, 2020-12-15-1105)**
- Agency: City of Stockton Economic Development Department (fee programs) with Community Development Department Permit Center
- Type: fee waiver
- Typical award: Full exemption from seven Public Facilities Fee categories (city office space, libraries, fire stations, parkland, community recreation centers, police stations, street improvements) for qualifying new affordable housing anywhere in city limits; the same categories are exempt for all new residential development in the Greater Downtown area. Dollar value depends on the current PFF schedule (not published on the program page); the program was cited by HCD as a basis for Stockton's 2023 Prohousing Designation. Other PFFs (water, wastewater, air quality, habitat, school fees) and the SJMSCP habitat fee still apply.
- AMI requirement: Qualifying affordable housing development as defined in the authorizing resolutions (deed-restricted units); confirm the affordability threshold and covenant term with the Economic Development Department before relying on it.
- Cycle: rolling (next: No application deadline; rolling. Apply before building permit issuance through the Economic Development Department. The exemption sunsets when the City completes its Master Infrastructure Plans and PFF Nexus Study and adopts new fees; as of November 8, 2026 the nexus study is still in progress (Parks Master Plan approved, draft Transportation Master Plan out for comment in 2026), so the exemption remains listed as active.)
- Layering notes: Most valuable local incentive in Stockton after the NOFA; the exemption reduces per-unit soft costs by the PFF categories listed and the downtown exemption applies to market-rate units too, which helps mixed-income deals. A non-residential short-term PFF deferral program (through December 31, 2027) and the non-residential 5 or 10 year deferral do not apply to housing. Stacks with the Chapter 16.40 density bonus and the Housing NOFA; fee exemptions count as public assistance for Labor Code 1720 analysis, so confirm prevailing wage exposure with counsel. Read from the City Business Assistance page (financial_assistance.php); authorizing resolutions are linked there.

**Low and Moderate Income Housing Fund (LMIHF), Successor Agency to the Stockton Redevelopment Agency (housing successor)**
- Agency: City of Stockton as Housing Successor; administered by the Housing Division through the Housing NOFA
- Type: loan
- Typical award: Fund balance not published in the 2026 NOFA documents; the Housing Source Funds Description lists LMIHF as a NOFA source for acquisition, new construction and conversion or rehabilitation for households up to 120% AMI. Recent uses: part of $1,614,000 HOME and LMIHF allocated to Sierra Vista III in 2019 and 2020 (de-obligated March 2026 and returned to the NOFA pool); part of $1,126,893 PLHA and LMIHF to Kentfield Apartments rehab (2024).
- AMI requirement: Housing successor rules (Health and Safety Code 34176.1): 55-year rental covenants, income targeting by statute with at least 30% of expenditures for extremely low income households over each five-year period; City NOFA applies a 55-year regulatory agreement.
- Cycle: annual NOFA (next: Deployed only through the City Housing NOFA; no standalone LMIHF application. No open round as of November 9, 2026: no 2026 Housing NOFA is posted on the City Housing page. Check the annual housing successor report filed with the City's HCD Annual Progress Report for the current balance.)
- Layering notes: Stockton is one of the few San Joaquin County cities with legacy redevelopment housing money; Tracy, Manteca and Lodi records show none in active use. LMIHF is the most flexible source in the Stockton pool (local money, up to 120% AMI, no federal cross-cutting rules) and is usually paired with HOME to cover costs HOME cannot. Treat as a small, lumpy source: the only recent LMIHF commitments were under $1.7 million each. Combine with HACSJ PBVs and SJRHF gap loans (county records). Fund description opened from the Stockton Legistar attachment for the April 2026 award item; the Successor Agency meets concurrently with Council.

**Prohousing Designation and Prohousing Incentive Pilot (PIP) funds, City of Stockton (2023 designation, 2026 renewal application, PIP Rounds 1 to 4)**
- Agency: City of Stockton Housing, Homelessness, Events and Parking Department with HCD
- Type: grant
- Typical award: Stockton received $2,370,000 in PIP funds from the first PIP round (NOFA December 15, 2022) after its 2023 designation (one of 22 jurisdictions then designated). Stockton applied for PIP Round 4 (NOFA September 30, 2025; $1,000,000 base plus up to $500,000 bonus) but HCD's Round 4 awardee list shows it unfunded (Prohousing score 38, deprioritized under Guidelines Section 401(D) for receiving a prior award). PIP funds are placed in the Housing NOFA for predevelopment, construction, acquisition, rehabilitation or capitalized operating subsidies for households up to 120% AMI, and PIP was part of the $4.55 million 2024 property acquisition NOFA. The 2026 renewal application is out for public comment November 2 to December 8, 2026 (Council hearing December 8, 2026, 1:00 PM) and would keep the City eligible for PIP and HHAP through 2029.
- AMI requirement: PIP: affordable to extremely low through moderate income households, or workforce housing up to 120% AMI (150% in high-cost areas); City NOFA covenants apply.
- Cycle: annual NOFA (next: No open City round as of November 9, 2026: PIP money reaches developers only through the City Housing NOFA, and no 2026 Housing NOFA is posted. Prohousing renewal public hearing December 8, 2026. HCD PIP Round 5 is open to designated jurisdictions October 13, 2026 through March 31, 2027, with awards estimated June 2027.)
- Layering notes: Designation also gives Stockton projects scoring preference in state competitive programs (AHSC, IIG, MHP, HHAP), which helps the local stack indirectly. Stockton Measure M (Strong Communities sales tax) funds libraries and recreation, not housing, and Measure W funds public safety; neither is a housing source despite appearing in the brief. Read from the City housing page, which also lists the 2025-2029 Consolidated Plan and 2026-27 AAP documents.

**Stockton Affordable Housing NOFA (annual Housing NOFA; HOME, HOME-ARP, PLHA, LMIHF, NSP, CDBG, HHAP and PIP loan pool)**
- Agency: City of Stockton Economic Development Department, Housing Division (underwriting consultant TDA Consulting Inc.)
- Type: loan
- Typical award: 2025 Housing NOFA released October 30, 2025, closed December 18, 2025: 8 proposals requesting $28.2 million for 522 units; $11,979,838 available after de-obligating $1,614,000 of HOME and LMIHF from Sierra Vista III. Awards: Fairview Terrace (Mutual Housing California, 76 senior units) $2,800,000 gap loan approved March 31, 2026 (Resolution 2026-03-31-1601) on top of $7,037,865 HOME awarded November 19, 2024; Don Shalvey Apartments (Visionary Home Builders, 108 family units, TDC $84.0 million) $5,000,000 and Danny Drive (DCDC, 66 senior units, TDC $39.7 million) $4,179,838 recommended April 2026 after Council deferred them on March 31. 2024 NOFA (January 29, 2024) offered about $16.1 million and funded Fairview Terrace $7,037,865 HOME, Kentfield Apartments rehab $1,126,893 PLHA and LMIHF, Casa de Mariposa $747,055, plus two HHAP projects. Typical award $0.7 million to $7 million per project.
- AMI requirement: 55-year regulatory agreement and loan term at 3% simple interest, repaid from residual receipts proportionate to the City share of permanent financing; projects served 30% to 80% AMI (families) and 30% to 60% AMI (seniors). HOME-funded units carry the HOME affordability period inside the 55-year term. Article XXXIV authority: voters allow Council to approve up to 500 assisted units per year.
- Cycle: annual NOFA (next: No open round as of November 9, 2026. The City Housing page posts no 2026 Housing NOFA (it currently lists the Prohousing renewal comment period and the 2025-2029 Consolidated Plan and 2026-27 Action Plan substantial amendments, hearing November 10, 2026). The prior round was released in late October 2025 and closed in mid December 2025; under the Council-approved process (Motion 2025-11-04-1601) the due date is at least 45 days after release, so a release now would close no earlier than early 2027. Confirm timing with hhep@stocktonca.gov, (209) 937-8538.)
- Layering notes: Stockton is the only city in San Joaquin County running a competitive gap-loan NOFA, and it is the main local soft source after the SJCOG San Joaquin Regional Housing Fund (county record). Pool is HUD and state pass-through plus housing successor LMIHF, so awards must fit each source's rules and deadlines; the City requires the full stack to be committed before executing loan documents and de-obligates allocations older than three years that cannot start within three years (Sierra Vista III lost $1.6 million in 2026). Scoring: developer capacity 30, proforma 30, populations served 15, design 15, leverage 10; an AI score was averaged with three human raters in 2025. Stacks with HACSJ project-based vouchers, County HOME (Urban County does not cover Stockton), BHSA and managed care plan grants (county records), the City PFF exemption and the 100% density bonus (records below). 2026 awards included HOME-ARP and PIP as eligible sources. Source documents read through the Stockton Legistar API and Granicus attachments; stocktonca.gov Economic Development pages have moved to /business/economic_development/housing_index.php.

### City of Suisun City

**Suisun City Housing Authority Project-Based Vouchers (2023 RFP, up to 96 PBVs) and Almond Gardens Apartments**
- Agency: Suisun City Housing Authority (City Council plus two tenant commissioners), 701 Civic Center Boulevard; Jason Goltiao, Housing Program Manager, 707-421-7332, jgoltiao@suisun.com

**Suisun City land contribution and impact fee waiver for affordable housing (Almond Gardens; Successor Agency and Housing Authority property)**
- Agency: City of Suisun City, Suisun City Housing Authority and Successor Agency to the Redevelopment Agency (Bret Prebula, City Manager and Executive Director, 707-421-7300)
- Type: fee waiver
- Typical award: Case by case, no ordinance. The CTCAC staff report for Almond Gardens (CA-24-602, December 11, 2024; 97 units, 96 restricted) lists Suisun City land at $850,000 and an impact fee waiver of $1,535,881 in both construction and permanent sources, alongside Citibank bonds, deferred developer fee and tax credit equity. The Housing Authority owned 707 Main Street and the Successor Agency 701, 711, 713 and 717 Main Street; the City announced on September 1, 2026 that 707 Main Street and two downtown parking lots transferred to California Forever in the first phase of a downtown sale agreed in June 2026.
- AMI requirement: Negotiated; Almond Gardens is 100% affordable (48 units at 30% AMI, 48 at 50% AMI) with a 55-year CTCAC term and Section 8 PBVs on all 96 restricted units.
- Cycle: rolling (next: No program or deadline. Any waiver or land write-down requires Council or Housing Authority action; Housing Element Program 1.B promises impact fee deferrals and density bonuses for mixed-use and residential projects in the Downtown Waterfront Specific Plan area.)
- Layering notes: Suisun City has no trust fund, inclusionary fee or LMIHAF report found online, so land and fee concessions are its only local contribution. The Main Street sales to California Forever entities (CF Suisun LLCs) may generate Successor Agency or Housing Authority proceeds; ask the City whether housing asset proceeds will be re-deployed. A fee waiver on a 97-unit project is public funds under Labor Code 1720(c), hence prevailing wage true (the project is also bond and credit financed). Source is the CTCAC report; the Housing Authority DDA and the May 26, 2026 staff reports were not opened (suisun.com 403; Granicus agenda PDF opened but attachments not).
- Source: https://www.treasurer.ca.gov/sites/default/files/ctcac/CA-24-602.pdf
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)

**Suisun City local housing fund, inclusionary ordinance and PLHA (no trust fund or inclusionary; Housing Element Programs 1.B, 1.C, 1.E; PLHA formula share)**
- Agency: City of Suisun City Development Services Department and Suisun City Housing Authority
- Type: grant
- Typical award: Negative finding for local funds. The adopted 2023-2031 Housing Element (adopted March 21, 2023, modified May 16, 2023) has no trust fund, in-lieu fee or fee waiver program. Program 1.E: research an inclusionary ordinance, seek developer input, determine appropriateness within two years after adoption (by spring 2025) and adopt within one year of that determination if appropriate. Program 1.C: the City applies for state and federal subsidies (HOME, CDBG, MHP, CalHFA) to assist nonprofit and for-profit developers. Program 1.B: priority processing, fee deferral where possible, flexible standards and density bonuses for mixed-use and residential projects in commercial zones, focused on the Downtown Waterfront. Program 1.F: meet annually with the County and other Solano cities on mortgage revenue bonds or mortgage credit certificates, first allocation application in 2025 if feasible. Suisun City is not a CDBG or HOME entitlement (state programs). PLHA formula (HCD 2024-2028 NOFA): CY 2024 $80,369, CY 2025 $86,957, five-year estimate $502,306.
- AMI requirement: PLHA: at or below 60% AMI unless the plan targets higher; state HOME and CDBG rules when the City applies as grantee.
- Cycle: annual NOFA (next: PLHA allocations arrive annually from HCD. No inclusionary ordinance or local fund found as of November 10, 2026; ask Development Services whether Council acted on Program 1.E and how PLHA is programmed.)
- Layering notes: A Suisun City project must bring its own subsidy: state HOME or CDBG with the City as applicant, CMFA bonds and TCAC (Almond Gardens model), County SCHTF (county record), and the City's land or fee concessions (separate record). About $85,000 a year of PLHA is too small for gap loans unless pooled. Source is the adopted element PDF on suisun.com (read via WebFetch; curl returns 403).

**Housing Mitigation Fund and BMR In-Lieu Fund biennial Notice of Funding Availability**
- Agency: City of Sunnyvale Community Development Department, Housing Division (Housing and Human Services Commission advisory)
- Type: loan
- Typical award: Biennial NOFA. 2022: $16 million to four developments. 2024 (issued May 2, 2024, due June 6, 2024): $29,533,000 awarded August 13, 2024, including $14.03 million to MidPen's 1171 Sonora Court (172 units; $12.5 million City acquisition of the site plus $1.53 million predevelopment, about $84,500 per unit with earlier PLHA), $1.5 million predevelopment to MidPen's 295 South Mathilda (126 units, City-owned site bought for $7.3 million in 2023), and $14 million to Pacific Companies and Miramar's 352 East Java Drive (308 units, about $45,000 per unit). 2026 NOFA released January 2026 for $18 million with awards announced spring 2026; priorities include senior and age-friendly projects and units for people experiencing homelessness. Minimum award $500,000; FY 2024-25 budget appropriated $32.5 million.
- AMI requirement: Deed restricted to lower income households for a minimum of 55 years; scoring favors deep affordability, homeless-serving units (at least 20 to 25 percent in recent awards), high resource locations, readiness and leverage. Funding agreement must be executed within two years of award.
- Cycle: biennial (next: 2026 round awards were expected spring 2026; next NOFA expected in FY 2027-28 (about early 2028), when 295 South Mathilda is expected to seek about $7.5 million in construction funds and 1171 Sonora about $12 million. Confirm award results and the next release with the Housing Division (NOFA documents are posted on the City housing page, which is blocked to scripts).)
- Layering notes: The best-funded city NOFA in the county after San Jose. Awards are structured as predevelopment, acquisition (with the City taking title and ground leasing, which locked in TCAC High Resource status for 1171 Sonora) and construction loans, and are meant to leverage County Measure A or SHDF, AHSC, IIG, BAHFA and 4 percent credits. Sunnyvale's HHSC scoring sheet is public. Also uses PLHA for predevelopment ($500,000 to 1171 Sonora in 2022). sunnyvale.ca.gov blocked; APR and award reports read from Legistar.
- Source: https://legistar.granicus.com/Sunnyvale/attachments/d5ab8b14-34d8-439e-99c0-2db362a22f77.pdf

**Inclusionary Below Market Rate Housing Program, Municipal Code Chapters 19.67 (ownership) and 19.77 (rental), BMR in-lieu fees (Council Priority Project HO-9)**
- Agency: City of Sunnyvale Community Development Department, Housing Division
- Type: regulatory requirement
- Typical award: Requirement, not a subsidy. 15 percent of units must be deed-restricted BMR units distributed through the project: rental projects of 3 or more units (5 percent very low income and 10 percent low income) and ownership projects of 7 or more units (all 15 percent moderate income); 100 percent affordable projects are exempt. The 2026 Strategic Economics feasibility study found 20 percent is not supportable, so staff recommend keeping 15 percent and converting fees: ownership in-lieu fee from 7 percent of sales price (about $70 per square foot) to $93 per square foot for 7 or more units; rental in-lieu fee from $33 to $93 per square foot for 7 or more units and from $16.50 to $46.50 per square foot for 3 to 6 units; four-year review cycle added to Council Policy 2.3.3. Fees deposit to the Housing Mitigation Fund. Alternative compliance plans require Council approval (2025 examples: 777 Sunnyvale-Saratoga Road, 1124 West El Camino Real). Ordinance 3239-25 (March 2025) allows reduced requirements for qualifying retail preservation projects in low and moderate resource areas. Inventory: 366 BMR rental, 516 BMR ownership and 1,768 units in 100 percent affordable developments.
- AMI requirement: Rental BMR units: 15 percent of units, split 5 percent very low income and 10 percent low income, for projects of 3 or more rental units. Ownership BMR units: 15 percent of units at moderate income for projects of 7 or more ownership units. MTC TOC policy minimums (15 percent, rental average 80 percent AMI or less, ownership average 120 percent AMI or less) are met.
- Cycle: rolling (next: City Council hearing on the in-lieu fee conversion and Policy 2.3.3 amendment scheduled November 10, 2026 (Planning Commission October 12, HHSC October 28, 2026); fees take effect 60 days after adoption. Next full review in four years.)
- Layering notes: The in-lieu fee increase (nearly triple for rental) will push more market-rate projects to build units on site and will enlarge the Housing Mitigation Fund NOFA pool in the meantime. Affordable developers benefit indirectly through the NOFA and through BMR alternative compliance partnerships (off-site units). State density bonus applies on top of the 15 percent. Sunnyvale also reduced park dedication in-lieu fees for affordable and DUO projects in 2024. sunnyvale.ca.gov returns 403 to automated access; the report was read from the Legistar attachment host.

- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)

**Non-Residential Housing Mitigation Fee (Housing Impact Fee), Municipal Code Chapter 19.75**
- Agency: City of Sunnyvale Community Development Department, Housing Division
- Type: regulatory requirement
- Typical award: Requirement, not a subsidy. Fee on new office, R&D, industrial, retail and lodging square footage in any zone since 2015; over $47 million collected 2015 to 2022. January 24, 2023 action (BAE nexus study) raised office and R&D to $11 per square foot for the first 25,000 square feet and $22 per square foot above that, left retail, lodging and industrial unchanged, and kept CPI indexing; one legacy project pays $13 per square foot versus the prior $19.50 standard rate. Revenue funds the Housing Mitigation Fund, which supplies the biennial NOFA ($16 million in 2022, $29.5 million awarded in 2024, $18 million offered in 2026).
- AMI requirement: Projects funded from the Housing Mitigation Fund are restricted to lower income households for at least 55 years.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Current FY 2026-27 rates are in the City's Master Fee Schedule (not opened this pass); confirm with the Housing Division. No fee update is pending beyond annual indexing.)
- Layering notes: Sunnyvale's linkage fee, driven by Moffett Park and Peery Park office growth, is the engine behind one of the county's largest city housing funds. Fee revenue will slow with the office downturn, so the 2026 NOFA ($18 million) is smaller than 2024. Compare with San Jose's CLF ($6.1 million cumulative) and Mountain View's Housing Impact Fee. sunnyvale.ca.gov blocked; staff report read from Legistar.

**Prohousing Designation, Prohousing Incentive Program applications and City-owned sites for affordable housing (295 South Mathilda Avenue)**

City-owned site: 295 South Mathilda Avenue purchased September 2023 for $7,325,000 and held under an Exclusive Negotiating Agreement (August 30, 2023) and short-term ground lease with MidPen Housing for a 126-unit project with at least 25 percent of units for families experiencing homelessness; the 2024 NOFA awarded $1.5 million for predevelopment; cumulative City support including land about $13.3 million ($105,000 per unit) before construction funds. - Agency: City of Thousand Oaks Community Development Department, Planning Division
- Type: density bonus
- Typical award: State density bonus with local add-ons. Small and underutilized parcel incentives (Art. 7, Ord. 1568-NS): 100% affordable projects (all units except a manager unit for extremely low, very low or low income households, under recorded agreement) at a minimum 20 units per net acre on an existing parcel under 1/2 acre (alone or combined with contiguous parcels) or a Housing Element underutilized site may request any two extra incentives beyond density bonus incentives. - Typical award: Requirement, not a subsidy. Staff-recommended in-lieu fees (September 11, 2023 Planning Commission report): $25.70 per leasable sq ft for apartments, $14.60 per saleable sq ft for townhomes, $16.80 per saleable sq ft for detached homes, indexed annually; adopted by Resolution 2023-056 (resolution text not opened).
- AMI requirement: Projects of 10+ units. Apartments: 10% at low income, covenant 55 years or as long as residential use; no off-site production for apartments. Townhome/condo: 10% moderate; detached: 5% moderate, 45-year cumulative resale covenant. Ownership projects only, with Council approval: off-site or separate on-site rental parcel at 15% of total units at low income (very low at developer option) within 1 mile, at most 15% studios and at least 40% two-bedroom or larger. Land dedication at Council discretion: 15% of units at very low income, within 1 mile or in a TCAC moderate or higher resource area, with overconcentration limits.
- Cycle: rolling (next: In-lieu fee due before first building permit. In-lieu allowed for fractional units, for-sale projects, and rentals of 20 or fewer units; rentals over 20 units only on an extreme hardship finding.)
- Layering notes: Off-site rental and land dedication options let a market-rate developer partner with a tax credit developer, creating a site or capital source for a 9% or 4% deal. Projects that build inclusionary units on site may request one Gov. Code 65915(d)(2) incentive even without a density bonus (9-10.307). Density bonus units are excluded from the inclusionary count. toaks.gov opens; agenda documents were read from the PrimeGov host (toaks.primegov.com).
- Source: https://toaks.primegov.com/api/compilemeetingattachmenthistory/historyattachment/?historyId=9ab9904d-ef6e-40e3-bc8f-c8e68e9f4266
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)


### City of Tracy

- Agency: City of Tracy Economic Development (CDBG/HOME) and Homeless Services Division; funds pass through San Joaquin County Neighborhood Preservation Division
- Type: grant

Tracy's own FY 2026-27 CDBG and HOME share and the City NOFA could not be confirmed (City notice returns 404). City uses of flexible funds have gone to the Temporary Emergency Housing Facility shelter: $331,794 CDBG recommended for shelter operations (January 30, 2026), $18,650 County CDBG for furnishings (March 3, 2026), a $786,574 PLHA application for shelter operations (February 20, 2026), HHAP Round 3 $251,795 and Round 4 $436,246 and a Round 5 application (December 19, 2025), plus $7.17 million County ARPA and a $3 million HUD EDI grant for shelter site work.
- AMI requirement: HUD CDBG national objective and HOME rent and income limits; County Urban County rules apply.
- Cycle: annual NOFA (next: No open round as of November 10, 2026. The County FY 2026-27 CDBG, HOME and ESG NOFA ran December 8, 2025 to January 23, 2026; the FY 2027-28 round has not been posted and, based on the prior cycle, would open about December 2026. Confirm Tracy's own cycle with cdbg.home@cityoftracy.org.)

PLHA and HHAP have been used for shelter operations rather than capital. Layer County HOME, SJRHF, HACSJ PBVs and BHSA (county records) with the Tracy density bonus. The City news article announcing the CDBG/HOME application returned 404 and the govaccess PDF host refused connections; facts above were read from the City's homelessness actions page (opened) and the county record.

**Density Bonus, Tracy Municipal Code Title 10 Chapter 10.08 Article 36.5 (Sections 10.08.4650 to 10.08.4686; Ordinance 1378 adopted January 20, 2026)**
- Agency: City of Tracy Community and Economic Development Department, Planning Division
- Type: density bonus
- Typical award: Requirement and entitlement incentive, not a subsidy. Ordinance 1378 (adopted January 20, 2026) repealed the 2008 article (Ord. 1113) and re-enacted Article 36.5 (Sections 10.08.4650 to 10.08.4686). Density bonus tables in 10.08.4659 run from 20% (10% low income or 5% very low income) up to 50% (24% low or 15% very low); lower income student housing 35% to 50%; moderate income for-sale common interest developments 5% to 50%; senior housing or mobile home park a flat 20%. The 10.08.4653 definition still says no more than 35%, but the tables control. One to five concessions or incentives (10.08.4677), five for 100% lower income projects plus up to three stories or 33 feet near major transit; parking caps, land donation (15% base) and child care bonuses; recorded density bonus housing agreement (10.08.4686).
- AMI requirement: Bonus under 10.08.4659 for any one of: 10% low income, 5% very low income, a senior housing development or mobile home park, 20% lower income students in student housing, or 10% moderate income units in a for-sale common interest development. Section 10.08.4656 still lists older thresholds (10% very low, 20% low, 50% senior, 20% moderate condominium). Code defines low income eligibility at 70% AMI and very low at 50% AMI, with affordable rent set at 60% and 50% AMI; 100% lower income projects may include up to 20% moderate income units.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Applies at entitlement; no application deadline. Ordinance 1378 is in effect and no further hearing is scheduled.)
- Layering notes: Tracy's bonus is the state minimum with no local enhancement, unlike Stockton's 100% tier. The 2023-2031 Housing Element (adopted July 1, 2025, HCD compliance letter August 11, 2025, RHNA 8,830) relies on rezoning rather than local subsidy. Tracy's Residential Growth Management Ordinance governs allotments for market-rate units; confirm whether affordable projects are exempt. Read from the zoneomics mirror of Title 10 because cityoftracy.org returns 403 to scripts and its Municipal Code host blocks automated access.

### City of Ukiah

**City of Ukiah state HOME and CDBG awards (City as State Recipient), including the Summercreek Village HOME application**
- Agency: City of Ukiah Community Development Department, Housing Services Division
- Type: grant
- Typical award: City applies to HCD as a non-entitlement State Recipient and relends to projects. Track record: $5 million State HOME grant (2018) for Ukiah Senior Apartments; a $5 million HOME application for a 32-unit project (FY 2019-20 budget narrative). HOME 2025 Projects NOFA: the City applied as State Recipient for $2,300,000 for the rehabilitation of DANCO's 64-unit Summercreek Village Apartments (listed by HCD as Acorn Valley Phase II, 8 HOME units, 9% tax credits); the City newsletter had described up to $5 million. 2025 State CDBG application approved by Council February 2, 2026: up to $2.1 million for the Orchard Manor Apartments multi-unit residential rehabilitation (Rural Communities Housing Development Corporation) plus up to $1.5 million for business assistance. CDBG also funded a Housing Conditions Survey (3,000-plus units). The owner-occupied Housing Rehabilitation Program has no funding for 2026.
- AMI requirement: HOME rental units at or below 60% and 80% AMI with 55-year state affordability (20-year federal minimum); CDBG benefits households at or below 80% AMI.
- Cycle: annual NOFA (next: No open round as of November 9, 2026. HCD HOME 2025 Projects NOFA applications closed March 30, 2026 with awards anticipated July 2026, but no 2025 award list is posted yet; the 2025 CDBG application outcome is also pending. Developers must ask the City to sponsor before the next HCD HOME or CDBG deadline.)
- Layering notes: Davis-Bacon applies at 12 or more HOME-assisted units or 8 or more CDBG-assisted units; state prevailing wage turns on the local or state funds in the deal and the Labor Code 1720(c) exemptions (see prevailing_wage_basis). City-sponsored HOME is distinct from Mendocino County's HOME program income pool, and both can sit in one project. HOME repayments recycle into City program income. City CDBG is not currently used for multifamily construction.

**Ukiah Housing Successor Low and Moderate Income Housing Asset Fund (LMIHAF)**
- Agency: City of Ukiah as Housing Successor to the former Ukiah Redevelopment Agency (Housing Services Division)
- Type: loan
- Typical award: Former RDA housing bond proceeds deposited in the LMIHAF and used to seed the Ukiah Housing Trust Fund in 2017. The City Council authorized $500,000 for affordable housing activities in FY 2019-20 (2019 Housing Element). Current balance not published on the City site; check the annual Housing Successor report (Health and Safety Code 34176.1).
- AMI requirement: Health and Safety Code 34176.1(a)(3)(A): after allowed administration and homeless prevention spending, remaining LMIHAF funds must be spent developing housing for households at or below 80% AMI, with at least 30% for rental housing at or below 30% AMI (extremely low income) and no more than 20% for households between 60% and 80% AMI, tested in five-year compliance reports. The 2019 Housing Element describes an older two-thirds at or below 60% AMI standard. Eligible uses include rental rehab, acquisition-rehab and new construction.
- Cycle: rolling (next: unknown, verify with agency; funds are offered through Ukiah Housing Trust Fund rounds rather than a separate application.)
- Layering notes: Treat as part of the UHTF capital stack, not a separate window. Housing successor income targeting (two-thirds at 60% AMI or below) is stricter than the UHTF NOFA's 120% AMI ceiling, so the City will steer LMIHAF dollars to lower-income units. Balance and five-year expenditure deadlines should be confirmed from the City's latest Housing Successor annual report, which was not located on the City site this pass. Source is the adopted 2019-2027 Housing Element hosted by HCD.
- Source: https://www.hcd.ca.gov/housing-elements/docs/ukiah-6th-adopted102819.pdf
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)

**Ukiah Housing Trust Fund (UHTF) NOFA, funded with PLHA, Prohousing Incentive Pilot (PIP) and housing successor funds**
- Agency: City of Ukiah Community Development Department, Housing Services Division (Housing and Grants Manager, housing@cityofukiah.com, 707-463-6708)
- Type: loan
- Typical award: Most recent round: June 10, 2024 NOFA for about $1,000,000 to acquire infill parcels for affordable housing, combining a $455,000 Prohousing Incentive Pilot award (October 2023) with up to $617,000 of the City's 2019-2022 PLHA allocation. Loans at 0 to 3% simple interest, 55-year term, repaid from residual cash flow after operating costs, senior debt, reserves and deferred developer fee; due on sale or refinance. Commitments last 24 months from Council approval (one-year extension possible). Earlier UHTF capital came from former RDA housing bond proceeds; the 2019 Housing Element notes a $500,000 NOFA in 2018. Acorn Valley Plaza (DANCO, 74 units, opened March 2025) was built with UHTF funds.
- AMI requirement: Units affordable at or below 60%, 80% or 120% AMI with a recorded 55-year rent or resale covenant; bonus points for units at 0 to 30% AMI. Funding-source rules (PLHA, PIP) add restrictions.
- Cycle: annual NOFA (next: unknown, verify with agency. The 2024 round closed July 8, 2024 and no newer NOFA is posted on the Housing Services page as of 2026-11-08. Projects must deploy UHTF funds and start construction within two years of award.)
- Layering notes: Ukiah is the only priority city in Mendocino County with a standing local trust fund and was the first rural Northern California city with a Prohousing Designation (April 2023), which earns state Prohousing points on AHSC, IIG and similar applications. The 2024 round targeted parcels in TCAC High and Highest Resource areas and favored scattered-site or non-traditional infill. The Housing Element says the fund exists partly to supply local match points for tax credit applications. Stacks with County HOME program income (about $351,767, for example the Marigold Villas request in Ukiah) and the City's own state HOME awards; County PLHA is a separate formula pool. Local and state funds are public funds under Labor Code 1720(b), so state prevailing wage applies unless a 1720(c) exemption fits the deal, such as 1720(c)(5)(E) for below-market loans with at least 40 percent of units restricted 20 years at or below 80 percent AMI (see prevailing_wage_basis).
- Source: https://cityofukiah.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/06/2024-HTF-NOFA.pdf
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)

Section 9253 (Ord. 945, 1993) grants at least the bonus and incentives in Government Code 65915 and lets the City deliver them through Planned Development zoning regardless of parcel size or a Council variance waiving development standards. The 2019 Housing Element reports a fee deferral program for housing developers (water and sewer hookups are the largest fees; typical multifamily fees about $12,500 per unit, 9.5% of development cost) and that affordable developers may receive funding and fee deferrals for infrastructure.

Fee deferral terms were not found in a current resolution, so confirm amounts and timing with Planning (707-463-6268). A deferral of City fees is likely a public subsidy under Labor Code 1720(b)(4) unless repaid at market terms. The County density bonus ordinance (Chapter 20.234) does not apply inside city limits.
