- AMI requirement: Households at or below 50% AMI at admission (75% at 30% AMI); PBV units capped at 25% of a building unless serving elderly, disabled or supportive-services households; project preferences for homeless referrals.
- Cycle: rolling (next: No RFP open as of November 2026; the Authority has run rounds roughly annually (2019, mid 2024, December 2024). Watch the HACV news page and PlanetBids portal 42510 for the next PBV RFP; HUD's 2026 guidance to pause new PBV commitments may delay it.)
- Layering notes: The 2024 round offered up to 200 PBVs, the largest project-basing opportunity in the county and the key operating subsidy for the Step Up Housing and Sacramento Street Apartments conversions financed with CMFA bonds (county record). The Authority was understaffed in 2024-2025, so allow time for HAP contract execution. PBVs alone do not trigger state prevailing wage; Davis-Bacon applies to PBV new construction or rehab of 9+ contract units. Opened the HACV Recent News page, which carries the RFP notices and PBV site list.

**Vallejo Housing Successor Low and Moderate Income Housing Asset Fund (LMIHAF), Housing Authority of the City of Vallejo**
- Agency: Housing Authority of the City of Vallejo acting as Housing Successor; City of Vallejo Housing and Community Development Department, 200 Georgia Street, 707-648-4507 (Alicia Jones, Housing Director)
- Type: loan
- Typical award: FY 2023-24 report (dated December 5, 2024): deposits $376,807, expenditures $2,404,145 (of which $2,403,420 for extremely low-income housing development), ending balance $605,550, LMIHAF loans and grants receivable $15,773,272, no real property held. FY 2022-23: deposits $1,747,828, no expenditures, ending balance $3,534,099, receivables $13,199,965. $182,210 of a 2015-16 $500,000 excess surplus transfer to HOME match remains encumbered. Four properties in the Long-Range Property Management Plan are used for affordable housing. FY 2024-25 report (due December 2025) not located.

- Cycle: rolling (next: No NOFA; the Housing Authority board (City Council) commits funds project by project and reviews the annual report each December. Ask the HCD Department what the $2,400,000 FY 2023-24 commitment funded and what remains after the FY 2024-25 report.)

Housing successor funds are public funds under Labor Code 1720(b), but 1720(c)(4) excludes affordable units paid for solely from Low and Moderate Income Housing Fund money; other funds in the deal decide coverage (see prevailing_wage_basis). **Vallejo Inclusionary Housing Ordinance (Municipal Code Chapter 16.216, Affordable Housing Requirements; Housing Element Program B 2.1.1)**
- Agency: City of Vallejo Planning and Development Services Department, Long Range Planning (Hector Rojas, 707-553-7283)
- Type: regulatory requirement
- Typical award: Requirement, not a subsidy. Introduced October 27, 2026; Council directed the Planning Commission version: applies to residential projects of 10 or more units; rental projects provide 4% affordable (2% very low, 2% low); ownership projects of 10 to 100 units 7% (4% low, 3% moderate), over 100 units 10% (6% low, 4% moderate). Staff had proposed a 20-unit threshold with 5% rental (1% VLI, 4% LI). In-lieu fee may be paid for some or all units, set by a later Council resolution and deposited in a separate City affordable housing fund; fractional units under 0.50 may be paid as fee. Alternatives: off-site units in the same census tract, rental units in ownership projects. EPS feasibility (March 13, 2026) found a subsidy gap of about $369,000 per very low-income apartment and $471,614 per low-income single-family unit, which are the equivalent in-lieu fee ceilings. Effective 90 days after final passage. Exemptions: disaster rebuilds, ADUs, residential care facilities, applications complete before the effective date.
- AMI requirement: Rental units at 30% of HCD income limits less utilities (2026 Solano three-person limits: VLI $61,850, LI $98,950, MOD $134,550); 55-year minimum covenants for rental and ownership units; Affordable Housing Plan and recorded Affordable Housing Agreement required; one-for-one replacement of demolished deed-restricted units.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Second reading and adoption scheduled November 10, 2026; in-lieu fee resolution to follow before the effective date (about February 2027). Planning Commission asked for annual reports and a new feasibility study about two years after enactment. A Commercial Linkage Fee ordinance is to be drafted after adoption.)
- Layering notes: Vallejo's RHNA is 2,900 units with 1,446 lower and moderate units still unmet after 2025. This is the first inclusionary ordinance in Solano County; its in-lieu fund will be a new, small local gap source alongside the Housing Successor LMIHAF (separate record). Developers of 10+ unit rentals should model 4% affordable units or the fee once set. Underwriting in Vallejo is weak (EPS found rental yields of 4.7% to 5.0% against a 5.5% threshold), so the fee is expected to be modest. Staff report and draft ordinance opened on the City's inclusionary project page.

**Walnut Creek Inclusionary Housing Ordinance (Zoning Code Article 9, Sections 10-2.3.903 et seq., amended November 2017) and housing in-lieu fee**
- Agency: City of Walnut Creek Housing Division (Housing Programs), Community and Economic Development Department
- Type: regulatory requirement
- Typical award: Requirement, not a subsidy. Applies to all residential development of one or more units except ADUs and disaster replacement units. New ownership projects: 10% moderate, or 7% low, or 6% very low income units, or pay the in-lieu fee (ownership projects of any size may pay the fee). New rental projects: 10% low or 6% very low income units, or pay the fee (rental units restored after AB 1505). Condominium conversions: 15% low or 11% very low. Fractions of 0.7 or more round up; partial fee payment allowed pro rata; blended income levels allowed. In-lieu fee reset to $18.00 per square foot effective January 1, 2018 with annual construction-price-index adjustments ($19.27 in 2021; about $26.04 per square foot in 2026 per the City of Antioch's January 2026 countywide comparison). Walnut Creek Transit Village alone paid over $4 million in in-lieu fees and is expected to generate $6 to 7 million for the City's Housing Trust Fund.
- AMI requirement: Rental inclusionary units affordable 55 years and ownership units 45 years; units dispersed on site with the same bedroom mix and comparable quality; one-for-one replacement of demolished low-income units built within 30 years.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Applies at entitlement; fee indexed each January. Housing Element Program H-2.D (6th cycle) continues the ordinance and contemplates an updated nexus study; confirm the current per square foot fee with the Housing Division (brynen@walnutcreekca.gov).)
- Layering notes: Walnut Creek's fee-first ordinance is the engine of its Local Housing Trust Fund (separate record): most downtown and BART-area apartment projects pay the per square foot fee rather than build 6% very low income units, which is why the City can fund 42 to 97 unit affordable projects itself. The County's Chapter 822-4 ordinance does not apply inside the city. walnutcreekca.gov (including showpublisheddocument PDFs) returns 403 to automated access; ordinance terms were read from the City's 2023-2031 Housing Element hosted by HCD (source_url, Chapter 3 Section 3.3.7 and Chapter 6) and the 2026 fee level from the Antioch comparison table.

### City of Watsonville

**Affordable Housing Ordinance (Municipal Code Chapter 14-46, Ordinance 1480-25 effective October 9, 2025) with in-lieu and commercial fees**
- Agency: City of Watsonville Community Development Department, Housing Division (275 Main Street, Suite 400, (831) 768-3080)
- Type: regulatory requirement
- Typical award: Requirement, not a subsidy. Projects of 7 to 50 units: for-sale 15% (5% above moderate, 5% median, 5% moderate), rental 20% (5% low, 5% median, 10% very low or Housing Choice Voucher and other subsidy recipients). Projects over 50 units: 20% for both tenures (for-sale 10% above moderate, 5% moderate, 5% median). In-lieu fees are required from projects of six or fewer units or lots, from new commercial and industrial development over 1,000 square feet (a commercial linkage fee) and from condominium conversions; fees are set by Council resolution and indexed annually at 50% of the Santa Cruz-Watsonville House Price Index change, paid at building permit or final map (14-46.070). FY 2025-26 schedule (effective July 1, 2025, Resolutions 238-01, 72-12 and 136-23): $21,885 per single-family detached unit, $8,419 per multifamily unit for projects of six or fewer units or lots, and $1.75 per square foot for commercial and industrial floor area of 1,001 square feet or more. Income categories use the Watsonville median household income, defined as 70% of the Santa Cruz County median. Federal, state or City-assisted affordable projects meeting the percentages satisfy the chapter in full (14-46.040(c)). Projects with 50% or more affordable units receive priority processing (14-46.080). Release fees for de-restricting units are paid into the affordable housing fund.
- AMI requirement: Rental units 55 years, ownership units 45 years, deed restricted; very low means the lower of 80% of Watsonville median or 50% of county AMI, low up to 100% of Watsonville median or 50% to 80% county AMI, median up to 120% of Watsonville median or 80% county AMI, moderate up to 150% of Watsonville median, above moderate up to 170%; preference for households living or working in Watsonville at least one year; minimum unit sizes and amenity standards in 14-46.060; affordable units built concurrently with market units.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Not applicable; requirement applies at entitlement. No application round as of November 10, 2026. In-lieu fee amounts are in the City's FY 2025-26 affordable housing in-lieu fee schedule; a FY 2026-27 update was not located.)
- Layering notes: The deepest city inclusionary requirement in Santa Cruz County (20% of rental units with half at very low income or voucher holders) and the only city program with a commercial linkage component; it exceeds the County's Measure J (for-sale only) and Capitola's and Scotts Valley's 15% standards. Because 100% affordable projects satisfy the chapter automatically and get priority processing, tax credit developers face no added inclusionary cost, while mixed-income developers can satisfy the very low tier with Housing Authority of the County of Santa Cruz PBV units. Fees flow to the City's Affordable Housing fund (record below). The 2025 code text was read on the zoneomics mirror because codepublishing.com and gocodebook.com returned 403; the City's Affordable Housing page (watsonville.gov/172) was also opened.
- Source: https://www.zoneomics.com/code/watsonville-CA/chapter_35
- Confidence: needs_confirmation (researched 2026-11-08)

**Density Bonus Ordinance (Municipal Code Chapter 14-47, Ordinance 1481-25 effective October 9, 2025) with impact fee deferral concession**
- Agency: City of Watsonville Community Development Department, Planning Division (Director approves ministerial projects; Council approves discretionary projects)
- Type: density bonus
- Typical award: Adopts Government Code 65915 by reference for all housing developments; bonus calculated under 65915(f) for very low, lower, moderate for-sale, senior, foster youth, student and 100% affordable projects, with land donation, child care and condominium conversion bonuses. Local concession menu (14-47.120) adds deferral of development impact fees (park, fire, sanitary sewer, storm drain and traffic fees) until immediately before occupancy, plus other cost-reducing incentives proposed by the applicant or City. Parking capped at 1 space for 0 to 1 bedroom, 1.5 for 2 to 3 bedrooms and 2.5 for 4 or more bedrooms, tandem and uncovered allowed. Density bonus units do not count toward Chapter 14-46 inclusionary units.
- AMI requirement: Rental target units 55 years at affordable rent as defined in Chapter 14-46; for-sale target units 45 years with equity sharing under 65915(c)(2); occupancy as principal residence; density bonus housing agreement recorded.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Submitted with the first project approval as a density bonus housing plan; projects with 30 or more affordable bonus units must identify a monitoring funding mechanism. Processing and monitoring fees are set by Council resolution.)
- Layering notes: The fee deferral concession is the only codified fee relief in Watsonville (no waiver program); 100% affordable projects can also use Chapter 14-46 priority processing. Watsonville's bonus mirrors state law with no local enhancement, unlike the County's enhanced bonus in Chapter 17.12.065. Watsonville was certified for its 2023-2031 Housing Element and offers Downtown Watsonville Specific Plan densities; the Specific Plan (Chapter 14-47 of Part 26 on some mirrors) was not opened. Code read on the zoneomics mirror; codepublishing and gocodebook returned 403.
- Source: https://www.zoneomics.com/code/watsonville-CA/chapter_36
- Confidence: needs_confirmation (researched 2026-11-08)

**Inclusionary Housing in-lieu fee Affordable Housing fund, HOME program income and Successor Agency housing assets**
- Agency: City of Watsonville Community Development Department, Housing Division, and the City as Successor Agency to the Watsonville Redevelopment Agency
- Type: loan
- Typical award: The 2025-2029 Consolidated Plan states that inclusionary in-lieu fees under Chapter 14-46 go to the City's Affordable Housing fund and are used for development, acquisition, rehabilitation and preservation of affordable units, and that PLHA, HOME, CDBG, CalHome and in-lieu fees provide gap financing for the First-Time Homebuyer and Housing Rehabilitation programs. The City has no active state HOME grant (last award $1,546,000 in 2011) and holds over $1,850,000 of HOME program income available for future HOME-eligible activities; it has made over 500 FTHB loans and has 280 inclusionary ownership units. The 2025-2029 plan does not mention Successor Agency property and states the City does not anticipate using publicly owned land for CDBG goals. No in-lieu fund balance, multifamily loan terms or application procedure is published.
- AMI requirement: Affordable to households at or below the Chapter 14-46 income categories (70% of county AMI basis) or HOME limits (80% AMI, 60% AMI for HOME rental units) with recorded affordability covenants of 45 to 55 years.
- Cycle: rolling (next: No open round as of November 10, 2026. No NOFA is published; developers negotiate assistance project by project with the Housing Division ((831) 768-3080). Confirm the in-lieu fund balance and the HOME program income balance with the City.)
- Layering notes: Watsonville's local gap sources are modest and discretionary; the HOME program income (over $1.85 million per the 2025-2029 Consolidated Plan) is the largest identifiable pool and carries federal HOME rules and Davis-Bacon for 12 or more units. Stack with the County of Santa Cruz state HOME tenant-based assistance (which covers Watsonville), Housing Authority of the County of Santa Cruz PBVs, HHAP through the Watsonville/Santa Cruz CoC, and City CDBG (record below). Unlike Santa Cruz city there is no adopted trust fund guideline document. Marked needs_confirmation because no fund balance or program guideline could be opened; the 2025-2029 Consolidated Plan and 2020-2024 Consolidated Plan PDFs on watsonville.gov were read.
- Source: https://www.watsonville.gov/DocumentCenter/View/27152/2025-2029-Consolidated-Plan-and-2025-2026-Action-Plan

### City of West Sacramento

**Affordable Housing, Density Bonuses and Incentives (West Sacramento Municipal Code Chapter 17.23, Ordinance 19-1)**
- Agency: City of West Sacramento Community Development Department, Planning Division
- Type: density bonus
- Typical award: Regulatory. Chapter 17.23 applies in all zones allowing residential use and grants qualifying developments and qualifying land transfers the density bonus, incentives and concessions specified in Government Code 65915 by reference (no local enhancement, no local cap). Requests are processed with the entitlement and approved if state criteria are met; a continued availability agreement is required before approval. Section 17.23.070 restates Housing Accountability Act limits on denying projects with at least 20% low income units. The 2019 zoning code update raised minimum and maximum densities in medium, high density and mixed-use zones (about 2,025 acres), so the Housing Element targets only about 5 density bonus units for the cycle.
- AMI requirement: State density bonus law thresholds (5% very low, 10% low, 10% moderate for-sale, senior, 100% affordable) with covenants per Government Code 65915(c).
- Cycle: rolling (next: None; request in writing to the Planning Division with the project application. The City reviews the chapter in its biannual zoning code update.)
- Layering notes: West Sacramento's leverage is zoning (high base densities in the Bridge District, Washington and Pioneer Bluff specific plan areas, mixed-use and waterfront zones) rather than the bonus itself. SB 35 and now SB 423 streamlining accepted for 10% or more affordable projects. Chapter 15.40 incentives (parking reductions, priority processing, standards waivers) can be combined. The code mirror (zoneomics) matches ecode360's section list; confirm against the official code.

**CDBG entitlement program (2026-2030 Consolidated Plan) and HOME program income**
- Agency: City of West Sacramento Economic Development and Housing Department, Housing Division
- Type: grant
- Typical award: West Sacramento became a CDBG entitlement city in FY 2016/17. HUD formula allocations: FY 2025 CDBG $546,333 and FY 2026 CDBG $517,683, with no HOME allocation (the City is not a HOME participating jurisdiction). A draft 2026-2030 Consolidated Plan and FY 2026-27 Annual Action Plan were reported out for comment in spring 2026 (City notice not opened). Housing uses have been infrastructure for affordable projects ($1,191,428 of CDBG program income for West Gateway Place Phase 1), fair housing services, homeless coordinator staffing, a supportive housing project allocation ($415,862 of CDBG entitlement and program income), first-time homebuyer help and owner rehabilitation. The City holds HOME program income from earlier state HOME awards (a developer fact sheet reports $2,000,000 into West Gateway Place II). State LHTF ($1,000,000) and state CDBG ($551,720) applications were not awarded.

**Inclusionary Housing Ordinance (West Sacramento Municipal Code Chapter 15.40, Ordinance 14-4) with Housing Trust Fund Program in-lieu alternative and Urban Infill Area incentive**
- Agency: City of West Sacramento Economic Development and Housing Department, Housing Division (Housing Manager Raul Huerta, (916) 617-4555)
- Type: regulatory requirement
- Typical award: Requirement, not a subsidy. Residential projects of 5 or more units citywide (adopted April 2014, replacing the redevelopment-area Chapter 15.10): rental projects set aside 10% of units (5% very low income, 5% low income); for-sale projects 10% low income, with rental units substitutable. Units on site, dispersed, at least 90% of the smallest market unit size, concurrent with each 25% of market units. Alternatives at Council discretion: payment into the Housing Trust Fund Program at the amount set in the Book of City Imposts Section VIII-N (a regional comparison in late 2025 listed West Sacramento's in-lieu fee at about $7,699 per dwelling unit, assessed per market-rate unit), acquisition and rehabilitation of market units, off-site construction, or preservation of at-risk units. Projects in the priority Urban Infill Area earn a discount on the in-lieu fee based on adjusted density (dwelling unit equivalents for structured parking, public open space and ground floor commercial). Incentives include reduced parking, priority processing, standards waivers and technical assistance; financial incentives only to the extent City programs exist.
- AMI requirement: Rental: 5% very low (50% AMI) and 5% low income (80% AMI) for 55 years; for-sale: 10% low income with a 45-year goal and recapture on early release.
- Cycle: rolling (next: None (ordinance). The Housing Element (Program HE-PR-1.2) commits to refining Chapter 15.40 to target lower incomes and reduce the burden on market-rate housing; six affordable housing agreements were approved 2018 to 2020. Confirm the current Book of City Imposts fee with the Housing Division.)
- Layering notes: The in-lieu alternative is the main revenue source for the City's Housing Trust Fund (Fund 261-9385), which funds gap loans (separate record). Because the per-unit fee is low relative to Davis ($250,000) and Folsom, most subdivisions in Southport pay the fee rather than build, so West Sacramento's affordable production comes from City-assisted 100% affordable projects in the Bridge District and Washington (West Gateway Place I and II, Landmark Lofts, the Grand Gateway 114-unit project). Overconcentration cap: no more than 40% of a project's units may be inclusionary. No county inclusionary applies inside the city. ecode360 hosts the official West Sacramento code and opened directly; cityofwestsacramento.org (Akamai) returns 403 to scripts and WebFetch, and the Book of City Imposts could not be opened.
- Source: https://ecode360.com/43204558
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)

**Permanent Local Housing Allocation (PLHA) formula funds, Resolution 25-15 five-year plan**
- Agency: City of West Sacramento Economic Development and Housing Department, Housing Division (Housing Manager Raul Huerta)
- Type: grant
- Typical award: HCD's PLHA formula award list shows West Sacramento awarded $763,253 on May 22, 2025 for its 2021, 2022 and 2023 formula allocations ($404,832, $202,903 and $155,518, with $38,163 allowable admin) for eligible activities 1 and 7. Council adopted Resolution 25-15 on February 19, 2025 authorizing the application and five-year plan; press coverage of that meeting reported 55% ($419,789) for the affordable component of the Grand Gateway Master Plan (a proposed 114-unit project at 30%, 50%, 60% and up to 80% AMI) and 40% ($305,301) for owner-occupied rehabilitation grants up to $30,000. HCD's 2024-2028 Formula Allocation NOFA (July 16, 2026) lists West Sacramento at $166,132 for CY 2024 and $177,952 for CY 2025, with an estimated $1,038,325 over five years.
- AMI requirement: Rental component at or below 80% AMI with deeper targeting (30% to 60% AMI) at the Grand Gateway site; owner rehabilitation for low income owners in qualifying neighborhoods.

- Agency: City of Woodland Community Development Department (Housing Analyst Franklin Cui, (530) 661-2019) with the Community Services Department
- Type: regulatory requirement
- Typical award: Requirement, not a subsidy. Citywide outside the Spring Lake Specific Plan: for-sale and multifamily rental projects of 30 or fewer units are exempt; 31 to 80 units provide 5% low income units; 81 or more units provide 10% low income, reduced to 5% if the project is built at 95% or more of maximum allowed density; in Downtown, Corridor Mixed Use and Neighborhood Commercial areas projects of at least 10 units built at maximum density (and at least 10 units per acre) owe 5% for-sale units. - Typical award: Regulatory incentive. Projects of 5 or more units qualify with 10% lower income, 5% very low income, senior housing or 10% moderate income condominiums; base bonus 20% rising 1.5% per 1% of lower income units (2.5% per 1% very low) to a 35% cap under the posted ordinance, and Chapter 15.16 now grants bonuses, concessions, waivers and parking ratios as a matter of right per current Government Code 65915 (up to 50% and unlimited near transit). Listed local incentives include use of local affordable housing funds, waiver or reduction of City building permit, plan check and inspection fees, and waiver or deferral of City impact fees until certificate of occupancy.
- AMI requirement: State density bonus law thresholds (5% very low, 10% low, 10% moderate for-sale, senior or special needs) with covenants of 55 years for rental.
- Cycle: rolling (next: None; request with the planned development, design review or other entitlement application. The Housing Element (Program A.10) commits to keep the ordinance current with state law and to publish a one-page fact sheet.)
- Layering notes: The fee waiver and impact fee deferral incentives are the city's only fee relief for affordable units and are granted project by project with the density bonus agreement (see the fee deferral record). The 2021 Housing Element found the posted ordinance out of date with Government Code 65915; the ecode360 Chapter 15.16 density bonus section (Ordinance 1662, 2020) is the operative text. Woodland's realistic densities already run near maximums (Spring Lake 101-unit project at 80% of RM density), so the bonus matters most on CMU corridor sites such as Tupelo's CMU-A parcel. City fee waivers are public subsidy and can trigger prevailing wage; impact fee deferrals alone generally do not.
- Source: https://www.cityofwoodland.gov/DocumentCenter/View/425/Bonus-Density-Ordinance-PDF
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)

**Development Impact Fee Deferral Program (MPFP fee deferral for multifamily, December 2008 ordinance) and case-by-case deferrals for affordable projects**
- Agency: City of Woodland Community Development Department and Administrative Services (Finance)
- Type: fee waiver
- Typical award: Deferral, not waiver. Under Ordinance No. 1690 (adopted June 21, 2022, no expiration date) residential infill projects (single-family or multifamily on vacant or underutilized parcels in urbanized areas) may defer ten City impact and capacity fees (General City, Library, Police, Water Capacity, Roads, Administration, Storm Drain, Fire, Wastewater, Parks) under a recorded fee deferral agreement and lien; deferred fees are due at the earlier of the final inspection request or 12 months, at the rate in effect at permit issuance. Spring Lake Infrastructure Fees, permit and plan check fees and non-City fees are not deferrable. Approval by the City Manager or Council depending on amount. The Council has also approved case-by-case interest-free deferral to just before certificate of occupancy for affordable projects (Housing Element). The Prohousing application cites Vista Del Robles (72 units, 2024) as a user.
- AMI requirement: None for the general program; affordable projects may also get case-by-case Council deferrals.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Rolling, no deadline as of November 8, 2026. Apply through Community Development, (530) 661-5820.)
- Layering notes: Deferral improves construction-period cash flow but is not a subsidy; combine with the density bonus fee waiver incentive and Fund 1327 loans. Woodland was designated Prohousing by HCD in 2025 (application March 21, 2025), which adds Prohousing points in state programs. Spring Lake has its own financing plan; Spring Lake Infrastructure Fees cannot be deferred.
- Source: https://cityofwoodland.gov/DocumentCenter/View/907/Development-Impact-Fee-Deferral-Program-Guidelines-PDF
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)

**Spring Lake Specific Plan Affordable Housing Plan: inclusionary requirements, Off-Site Affordable Housing Fee and 25% density bonus**
- Agency: City of Woodland Community Development Department (Spring Lake Specific Plan area)
- Type: density bonus
- Typical award: Requirement, not a subsidy. Multifamily projects in Spring Lake must make at least 20% of units affordable to and occupied by very low income households plus 10% low income, or alternatively 25% very low income, with a 25% density bonus for complying projects. For-sale projects owe 10% low income units (exempt under 10 units), with land dedication or, only at City initiative for projects under 50 units, an in-lieu fee equal to the appraised affordability gap per unit plus administration. All single-family market-rate units pay an Off-Site Affordable Housing Fee of $1,100 per unit (Council may reset it, not above $1,300), collected before final map approval and spent anywhere in the City on qualifying affordable units; up to 10% may fund administration.
- AMI requirement: Multifamily: 20% very low plus 10% low, or 25% very low income, permanently affordable; for-sale 10% low income for the longest feasible period.
- Cycle: rolling (next: None (specific plan requirement). The Housing Element (Program A.24) proposes amending the Spring Lake Specific Plan to clarify affordability provisions; several Spring Lake single-family projects have paid in-lieu fees under development agreements.)
- Layering notes: Spring Lake is where most of Woodland's affordable pipeline sits: Mutual Housing at Spring Lake (farmworker, 100 units), a 4.6-acre multifamily site dedicated in 2019 to a nonprofit in place of $900,000 of fees (112 lower income senior units required), and R-20 and R-25 sites intended for 25% very low income projects. A 100% affordable developer can acquire a Spring Lake R-20 or R-25 site and satisfy a market-rate builder's obligation, then draw on Fund 1327 and the off-site fee revenues as gap money. The Plan still names the Redevelopment Agency as fund recipient; the City is housing successor. Chapter 15.16 applies in Spring Lake only where the Specific Plan is silent.
- Source: https://www.cityofwoodland.gov/DocumentCenter/View/422/Spring-Lake-Affordable-Housing-Plan-PDF
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)

**Woodland Housing Successor Agency (former Redevelopment Agency) Low and Moderate Income Housing Asset Fund (SB 341 reporting)**
- Agency: City of Woodland as Housing Successor to the former Woodland Redevelopment Agency (Community Services and Community Development Departments)
- Type: loan
- Typical award: Small. The FY 2021/22 SB 341 report (dated August 1, 2022, the latest posted) shows a Housing Asset Fund ending balance of $51,025 cash (one loan payoff), no real property, five rental loans outstanding totaling $4,123,722 and seven first-time homebuyer loans totaling $674,693 (principal and interest through June 30, 2022). Unencumbered funds were under $1 million, so no excess surplus. Any future money comes only from loan repayments.
- AMI requirement: Health and Safety Code 34176.1 targets: at least 30% of LMIHAF expenditures for rental housing at or below 30% AMI, remainder at or below 60% AMI, with 55-year covenants.
- Cycle: closed/inactive (next: No open round as of November 8, 2026. No later SB 341 report is posted; ask Housing staff for the current balance.)
- Layering notes: Useful negative information: Woodland's post-RDA housing money is the inclusionary Fund 1327, not the successor fund, which held about $51,000 in cash at June 30, 2022. Rental loan repayments could add a small extremely low income layer over time. The SB 341 report is a scanned PDF; it was read page by page as images.
- Source: https://www.cityofwoodland.gov/DocumentCenter/View/9562
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)


### Town of Truckee

**Truckee Deed-Restricted Housing Incentives (Development Code Chapter 18.213, Ordinance 2026-06) and Density Bonus (Chapter 18.212)**
- Agency: Town of Truckee Community Development Department, Planning Division
- Type: density bonus
- Typical award: Non-monetary incentives, not a subsidy. Ordinance 2026-06, adopted April 28, 2026 and effective about May 28, 2026, implements 2040 General Plan Action LU-2.B: a Town-specific workforce and affordable housing bonus with streamlined review and flexible design standards for projects with deed-restricted units, with income criteria set by Council resolution. Chapter 18.212 separately implements state density bonus law, including a Development Bonus for Partnered Commercial Projects (18.212.160).
- AMI requirement: Deed-restricted units meeting the Council-adopted income criteria (workforce levels up to 180% AMI under the companion Homegrown program); state density bonus thresholds for Chapter 18.212.
- Cycle: rolling (next: In effect; requested with the Planning application.)
- Layering notes: Choose one path: projects using State Density Bonus Law cannot take Homegrown payments, while projects using Chapter 18.213 can also draw Homegrown payments, even for their inclusionary units. Draft 7th cycle Program H-3.D adds fee deferrals, land write-downs and incentives beyond state density bonus for acutely and extremely low income, senior and disability housing. The Housing Development Incentives page text says the ordinance was introduced April 7, 2026 with second reading April 28; the Council work plan page reports adoption on April 28, 2026.
- Source: https://www.townoftruckee.gov/677/Housing-Development-Incentives
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)

**Truckee Homegrown Housing Program, Monetary Incentives (formerly Deed Restriction for New Housing Development)**
- Agency: Town of Truckee Housing Division; program operator Sierra Business Council (info@sierrabusiness.org, 530-582-4800)
- Type: grant
- Typical award: Per-unit payment for a 55-year deed restriction on newly built units, paid at certificate of occupancy after recording: studio $100,000, one bedroom $150,000, two bedroom $225,000 for units restricted to 180% AMI; studio $116,000, one bedroom $174,000, two bedroom $261,000 for units restricted to 120% AMI. Guidelines approved June 23, 2026. Town Council has committed $3,600,000 to deed restriction payments, after moving site-acquisition funds into the program in September 2025.
- AMI requirement: Occupants must work within the Tahoe Truckee Unified School District boundary; household income at or below 180% AMI (rent or price capped at 120% AMI affordability) or at or below 120% AMI (capped at 80% AMI affordability); 55-year non-renewing restriction; no short-term rental; one dedicated parking space per unit.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Open; apply after a complete Planning application. Milestones: building permit application within 9 months of entitlement, permit issued within 18 months, first inspection within 24 months, certificate of occupancy within 30 months, or the award is cancelled.)
- Layering notes: Designed for missing-middle workforce units, not tax credit deals: projects entitled under State Density Bonus Law are ineligible, and funds cannot be combined with other assistance that imposes an equivalent 55-year income and workforce restriction. Eligible only in VMT Exemption Areas. Payment at C of O means it works as permanent-loan paydown or equity replacement, not construction financing. A January 27, 2026 BAE valuation analysis informed the revised amounts. Town funds count as public funds under Labor Code 1720.
- Source: https://www.townoftruckee.gov/DocumentCenter/View/2190
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)

**Truckee Inclusionary Housing (Development Code Chapter 18.214) and Affordable Housing In-Lieu Fee (Section 18.210.100; Resolution 2024-65) with dedicated in-lieu fee account**
- Agency: Town of Truckee Community Development Department and Department of Neighborhood Services and Sustainability (Housing)
- Type: regulatory requirement
- Typical award: Requirement, not a subsidy. 15% of all new units in residential projects (and subdivisions of seven or more lots) must be affordable, built no later than the market-rate units; density bonus units are excluded from the base. Alternatives: off-site units in the Truckee region, land dedication, purchase of inclusionary credits, or deed-restricting existing units. In-lieu fee by Council resolution with annual update: $136,851 per required affordable unit under Resolution 2024-65 (up from $115,517 under Resolution 2023-63); projects of six or fewer units or lots pay a scaled fee (Exhibit A1) at the developer's option. Larger projects may pay in lieu only if the review authority finds it furthers affordable housing equally or better. Fees go to a separate interest-bearing account and must be used for Town affordable housing programs that create housing in the Truckee region, not studies (Resolution 2024-65 Exhibit A).
- AMI requirement: Ownership inclusionary units: 100% moderate income, or one-third each low, moderate and above moderate. Rental units: 100% low income, or one-third each very low, low and moderate. Affordability controls under Chapter 18.210 with locals preference; in perpetuity per the Town's Housing Resources page.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Fee is reset annually by resolution; a November 2025 staff report reportedly recommended not adopting an update, so confirm the fee in effect for 2026 with the Town before underwriting.)
- Layering notes: Inclusionary units can receive Homegrown Housing payments only where the project qualifies for the new Chapter 18.213 non-monetary incentives; otherwise required units are ineligible. In-lieu fee revenue supports Town housing programs (Homegrown Housing, THAP, Lease to Locals and similar) rather than a traditional tax credit gap loan NOFA; no Town multifamily NOFA was found. Separate from the Western Nevada County Regional Housing Trust Fund, which Truckee does not belong to (members are the County, Grass Valley and Nevada City). Code text from the October 12, 2023 Article VII PDF on the Town site.
- Source: https://mccmeetingspublic.blob.core.usgovcloudapi.net/truckeeca-meet-8a5450e393694eab8a209bf8d13ee33e/ITEM-Attachment-001-5ec3253d417e438eb7c314a7b15a17aa.pdf
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)

**Truckee Town-owned land public-private partnerships (Edmunds Lofts) and Railyard Master Plan affordable housing obligations**
- Agency: Town of Truckee Planning Division and Town Manager
- Type: land
- Typical award: Edmunds Lofts: Town-owned 0.5-acre site (APN 018-580-052, dedicated by High Altitude Fitness) to be conveyed to Paradigm8 / Sagemodern under a Development and Disposition Agreement for 12 deed-restricted workforce units; entitlements granted in 2025 and building permits under review (75% complete at December 31, 2025). Railyard: Council work plan item 6.3 will move inclusionary and workforce housing obligations from the Railyard Development Agreement into the Railyard Master Plan (late 2026 to early 2027); the Town made a significant financial contribution to the earlier 66-unit Truckee Artist Lofts in the Railyard. Draft 7th cycle Program H-2.H directs annual review of all Town-owned and partner-agency land (TTUSD, Caltrans, Tahoe Forest Hospital, Truckee Donner PUD) for housing.
- AMI requirement: Deed-restricted workforce units per the DDA; Railyard units per the Development Agreement.
- Cycle: closed/inactive (next: No open RFIQ as of 2026-11-08. Council removed the pilot to find another site from the 2025-2027 work plan on September 9, 2025. Watch the Railyard Master Plan amendment (late 2026 to early 2027).)
- Layering notes: Land write-downs of public land are public subsidy for prevailing wage purposes and trigger Surplus Land Act review. Coldstream Commons (48 units at 60% AMI, nine HUD 811 units) is an existing affordable project in the Coldstream Specific Plan area; no new Coldstream affordable commitment was found this pass. Prohousing Designation status for Truckee was not confirmed.
- Source: https://townoftruckee.gov/303/Housing-Our-Workforce
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)

**Truckee Workforce Housing Ordinance for non-residential development (Development Code Chapter 18.216)**
- Agency: Town of Truckee Community Development Department
- Type: regulatory requirement
- Typical award: Requirement, not a subsidy (commercial linkage). Commercial, industrial, institutional, recreational, residential resort and other non-residential projects must build workforce housing for a share of the full-time equivalent employees they generate (Table 7-7; commercial projects of 3,500 square feet or less and industrial of 7,000 square feet or less, or under 7 FTEE, are exempt). Fractions and approved cases may pay the same in-lieu fee ($136,851 per required unit under Resolution 2024-65) or use alternative equivalent actions such as land dedication.
- AMI requirement: Workforce units restricted under Chapter 18.210 affordability controls; occupancy by employees in the Truckee region.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Not applicable. Draft 7th cycle Program H-2.E calls for reviewing the ordinance and an affordable housing credit bank by December 2029.)
- Layering notes: Creates partnering opportunities: commercial developers needing workforce units can buy inclusionary credits from, or dedicate land to, affordable projects. The Edmunds Lofts site came to the Town through a land dedication by High Altitude Fitness under this ordinance. No county equivalent exists.
- Source: https://www.townoftruckee.gov/DocumentCenter/View/1196
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)

**Truckee existing-stock deed restriction programs: Truckee Home Access Program (THAP), Lease to Locals, Rooted Renters and Short-Term Rental Workforce Housing Token pilot**
- Agency: Town of Truckee Housing Division
- Type: grant
- Typical award: THAP pays buyers up to $150,000 (maximum $937,500 purchase price), sellers and local businesses for permanent workforce deed restrictions on homes (cap 245% AMI). Lease to Locals pays owners up to $18,000 to convert homes to long-term local rentals; Rooted Renters pays up to $26,000 to lock in below-market rents. The STR Token pilot gives short-term rental certificates in exchange for 15-year workforce deed restrictions (150% AMI average per adult; applications closed June 20, 2024). Results to date: 871 deed-restricted units (6.2% of stock), 33 THAP homes, 276 Lease to Locals conversions, 76 Rooted Renters units, 37 ADUs created through grants and loans.
- AMI requirement: Occupants must work locally; income caps vary by program (THAP 245% AMI; Token 150% AMI per adult).
- Cycle: rolling (next: Open; THAP parameters under review with revisions targeted for Q4 2026.)
- Layering notes: Not a source for new affordable multifamily, but signals the Town's local revenue priorities: its housing dollars go mainly to deed restrictions of existing stock and middle-income production. The Town's goal is 10% of housing stock deed restricted by 2032. The Council work plan lists a potential housing revenue measure and draft Program H-2.F targets at least $300,000 per year of added local funding (additional TOT, business, sales or transfer tax). Mountain Housing Council of Tahoe Truckee (Tahoe Truckee Community Foundation) is the regional partner for AMI tiers above 120%.
- Source: https://www.townoftruckee.gov/225/Housing
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)


## Private & Philanthropic Sources


### California (Northern California focus)

**Community Vision (formerly Northern California Community Loan Fund) affordable housing loans**
- Agency: Community Vision Capital and Consulting (CDFI), 870 Market Street, San Francisco; lending@communityvisionca.org
- Type: loan
- Typical award: $250,000 to $5 million (larger case by case); terms up to 10 years; loan to value up to 90%; fixed rates generally below market; 1% to 1.5% commitment fee; real estate collateral preferred, subordination to conventional lenders considered; underwriting 4 to 8 weeks after full application.
- AMI requirement: Affordable housing led by mission-aligned developers and other social purpose real estate serving historically underserved communities; borrowers must be California nonprofits or social enterprises.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Rolling; items reviewed as submitted.)
- Layering notes: Borrowers must be California nonprofits or social enterprises (the lending page does not limit lending to nonprofits). Community Vision is a GSAF and Bay Area TOAH originator and an FHLBank San Francisco AHP sponsor partner ($5.95 million awarded with it for 225 Bay Area units). Its Ready to Build program (separate record) provides technical assistance for first-time nonprofit developers. Good fit for community land trusts and service providers moving into housing.
- Source: https://communityvisionca.org/lending/
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)


### California (Orange County headquarters, statewide)

**Clearinghouse CDFI commercial real estate secured loans for multifamily affordable housing**
- Agency: Clearinghouse Community Development Financial Institution, 23861 El Toro Road Suite 401, Lake Forest (Orange County); pre-application at clearinghousecdfi.com/borrowers
- Type: loan
- Typical award: Minimum loan $1,000,000; acquisition, refinance, construction, renovation and gap financing secured by real estate; case-by-case structures; also New Markets Tax Credit allocations ($10 million NMTC plus $4.1 million source loan to Heritage Housing Partners for Napa Redwood Housing, 40 affordable condos, 2026). Clearinghouse secured $100 million through the Treasury CDFI Bond Guarantee Program.
- AMI requirement: Multifamily affordable and special needs housing serving low income households; mixed-use and mobile home parks also eligible.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Rolling pre-application.)
- Layering notes: Orange County based, statewide and multi-state lender with FHLBank San Francisco membership (sponsors AHP grants, including tribal housing awards). Northern California deals opened this pass: Napa Redwood Housing (2026) and a Brilliant Corners enhanced behavioral support home in Vacaville (2022, $741,000). Also a frequent lender in San Diego, Orange and Riverside Counties. Works for for-profit and nonprofit borrowers and public or tribal entities.
- Source: https://www.clearinghousecdfi.com/borrowers/
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)


### California (San Francisco Bay Area core geography)

**Capital Impact Partners (Momentus Capital) acquisition and predevelopment loans**
- Agency: Capital Impact Partners, part of Momentus Capital (CDFI, Oakland office); California contact Eric Relos, erelos@capitalimpact.org, 510-712-9021
- Type: loan
- Typical award: December 2025 term sheet: $500,000 to $15 million for non-operating properties and $500,000 to $20 million for operating properties; term up to 3 years plus two 1-year extensions (operating properties up to 10 years); fixed rate at Treasury plus 4% to 5% or floating 30-day SOFR plus 3.5% to 4.5%, lower with special funding sources; interest only; no prepayment fee for terms of 3 years or less; origination 1% to 1.5% (includes 0.25% underwriting fee), legal typically $30,000 to $35,000; 5% to 10% equity including subordinate debt and grants; 60 to 90 day closings. Also construction, rehabilitation, mini-permanent (up to 90% LTV), bridge and NMTC products.
- AMI requirement: No AMI test stated in Capital Impact term sheets; loans fund mission-aligned acquisition and predevelopment for housing, healthcare, education, commercial and mixed-use projects, with preference for core geographies (California is one).
- Cycle: rolling (next: Rolling.)
- Layering notes: The San Francisco Bay Area is one of Momentus Capital's core geographies and Capital Impact originates for the Partnership for the Bay's Future Bay's Future Fund and Community Housing Fund (lower rates than its standard sheet). Full recourse to sponsors; first lien preferred, second lien case by case. Its CDFI Equitable Recovery award funds a housing developer training and capital access program that expanded into the Bay Area.
- Source: https://www.capitalimpact.org/mission-driven-financing/
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)


### Coachella Valley, Riverside County

**We Lift: The Coachella Valley's Housing Catalyst Fund (revolving loan fund managed by Lift to Rise and LIIF)**
- Agency: Lift to Rise (Palm Desert) with Low Income Investment Fund as fund manager; partners include the County of Riverside, Rural Community Assistance Corporation and about 70 community partners
- Type: loan
- Typical award: More than $44 million available (goal to grow past $80 million); since 2021 more than $26 million committed in low-interest, flexible loans for nearly 900 affordable units including multifamily rentals, homeownership and Polanco (farmworker) parks; the State contributed $15 million. Loan terms are set by LIIF underwriting and are not posted.
- AMI requirement: Community-prioritized affordable housing in the Coachella Valley; projects tracked toward a goal of 10,000 units by 2028.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Rolling through the Lift to Rise pipeline portal and LIIF.)
- Layering notes: Eastern Riverside County only (Coachella Valley cities including Indio, Coachella, Palm Springs, Cathedral City, Desert Hot Springs). Loans repay to the fund at construction or permanent closing. Public contributions (County of Riverside, State of California) may make prevailing wage project-specific. Example: Vista Sunrise on the DAP Health campus in Palm Springs (Coachella Valley Housing Coalition, opened 2024). Layer with Riverside County HWS NOFAs, the City of Indio Local Housing Trust Fund and Palm Springs housing successor loans.
- Source: https://lifttorise.org/we-lift/
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)


### CommonSpirit Health hospital markets in California

**CommonSpirit Health (Dignity Health) Community Investment Program below-market loans**
- Agency: CommonSpirit Health Community Investment Program, San Francisco; cip@commonspirit.org; expression of interest form on the program page; local Dignity Health hospitals act as community liaisons
- Type: loan
- Typical award: Loans up to $10.0 million, tenor up to 10 years, secured or unsecured, concessionary interest benchmarked to inflation, flexible repayment; structures include bridge, line of credit and term. $400 million allocation; $263 million approved across 94 investments as of March 31, 2025; 398 loans and $502.5 million approved since 1990, with affordable housing about 45% of the portfolio. Dignity Health's Homeless Health Initiative has invested nearly $36 million across its California sites since FY2019, including $375,000 in May 2026 for two Yolo County projects ($125,000 Freeman Garden Court, Woodland, 12 units; $250,000 Choice Neighborhoods and Tupelo project, 73 units) and more than $3 million in Yolo and Sacramento Counties to date.
- AMI requirement: Mission-oriented projects addressing social drivers of health, including affordable and supportive housing for low income communities; must show community support and partnership with a CommonSpirit hospital.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Rolling expression of interest.)
- Layering notes: Place-based: investments are tied to CommonSpirit (Dignity Health) hospital markets, which in scope include Sacramento (Mercy General, Mercy San Juan, Methodist, Mercy Folsom, Woodland Memorial in Yolo), Stockton (St. Joseph's, San Joaquin), Merced, Grass Valley (Sierra Nevada Memorial, Nevada County), Redwood City (Sequoia, San Mateo), Santa Cruz (Dominican), San Luis Obispo and Santa Maria, Ventura (St. John's) and the Inland Empire. Loans often go through a CDFI or linked deposit; CommonSpirit also guarantees loans. Dignity Health is a financing partner of the Monterey Bay Housing Trust. Patient, concessionary money that fits predevelopment or gap positions in supportive housing with co-located services.
- Source: https://www.commonspirit.org/impact/community-health-initiatives/community-investment-program
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)


### FHLBank San Francisco district (California, Arizona, Nevada)

**FHLBank San Francisco Affordable Housing Program (AHP) General Fund competitive grants**
- Agency: Federal Home Loan Bank of San Francisco (member-sponsored applications; the project sponsor applies through an FHLBank member bank, credit union, insurer or CDFI)
- Type: grant
- Typical award: 2026 competition: $60.1 million in General Fund grants awarded June 22, 2026 to 39 projects (2,676 units) in California and Arizona from 125 applications; 2026 awards total $66.3 million including the Nevada Targeted Fund, up nearly one-third from 2025. Per the 2026 Implementation Plan, maximum request is the lesser of $2,000,000 or 50% of total project costs, and no more than $65,000 per income-restricted rental unit (scored on a declining scale from $30,000 to $65,000). Four years from award to complete construction and draw funds. Since 1990, $1.48 billion awarded for nearly 160,000 homes.
- AMI requirement: Rental projects must reserve at least 20% of units for households at or below 50% AMI with a 15-year retention period; owner-occupied projects serve households at or below 80% AMI (5-year retention).
- Cycle: annual NOFA (next: No open round as of November 8, 2026. 2026 General Fund awards announced June 22, 2026; FHLBank San Francisco has not posted 2027 competition dates.)
- Layering notes: A grant that flows through a member institution, so line up a member bank or CDFI sponsor (Housing Trust Silicon Valley, Community Vision and Clearinghouse CDFI are members that sponsor awards) early. Scoring favors homelessness and special needs set-asides, ELI units, lower subsidy per unit and donated or discounted property; 2026 awards included $27.9 million for 19 supportive housing developments and more than $20 million for 12 senior developments. Loan pools and revolving funds may not apply to the General Fund. AHP funds are private bank-system money and do not by themselves trigger state prevailing wage, though federal AHP regulations apply. Grants are typically sized at $30,000 to $65,000 per unit and used as gap equity alongside LIHTC and state soft debt.
- Source: https://www.fhlbsf.com/products/community-programs-grants/ahp
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)


### Five Bay Area counties (San Francisco, San Mateo, Santa Clara, Alameda, Contra Costa)

**Partnership for the Bay's Future: Bay's Future Fund (BFF) loans**
- Agency: LISC Bay Area (fund manager and originator) with Corporation for Supportive Housing and Capital Impact Partners as originators; San Francisco Foundation convener; contact Asha Rao, Senior Director of Investments, LISC Bay Area
- Type: loan
- Typical award: $500 million loan fund; structures from predevelopment to mini-permanent; interest typically 4% to 5% set by AMI served, term and originator; loan size up to $7.5 million; loan to value up to 150% for high-impact projects; loans must mature by August 2030.
- AMI requirement: Rental housing serving households at 0% to 120% AMI with deed restrictions.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Rolling through LISC Bay Area, CSH or Capital Impact; all loans must mature by August 2030.)
- Layering notes: Covers San Francisco, San Mateo, Santa Clara, Alameda and Contra Costa Counties. Seeded by Chan Zuckerberg Initiative ($40 million first-loss), Facebook/Meta, Genentech, Kaiser Permanente, the San Francisco Foundation and others; underwriting tolerates more risk, including for emerging developers of color. The August 2030 maturity limit makes this a bridge product; the companion Community Housing Fund provides the long-term 2% money. The deployment goal was $500 million by end of 2025, so confirm remaining availability.
- Source: https://www.lisc.org/bay-area/areas-of-work/affordable-housing/partnership-bays-future/family-of-funds/
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)

**Partnership for the Bay's Future: Community Housing Fund (CHF) 2% long-term loans**
- Agency: LISC Bay Area (fund manager and originator) with Corporation for Supportive Housing and Capital Impact Partners; San Francisco Foundation convener
- Type: loan
- Typical award: $150 million fund; 2% interest; loan size up to $15 million; loan to value up to 150%; term up to 18 years with latest maturity 2038.
- AMI requirement: At least 20% of households housed at or below 30% AMI; Santa Clara County projects must meet the Measure A AMI definition.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Rolling through LISC Bay Area, CSH or Capital Impact.)
- Layering notes: Same five-county footprint as the Bay's Future Fund. The 2% rate and 18-year term make it usable as subordinate permanent debt alongside LIHTC and county soft loans, or as a 16-year loan in lieu of a competitive public gap source (LISC has done this). Check Measure A alignment for Santa Clara County deals.

**Apple Affordable Housing Fund (Housing Trust Silicon Valley), annual Request for Information**
- Agency: Housing Trust Silicon Valley (CDFI; California Finance Lender License 6053356), 75 E. Santa Clara Street Suite 1350, San Jose; lending team Nick Friend (408-703-3837 ext. 223, nick@housingtrustsv.org) and Stephaney Kipple (ext. 244); inquiries applefund@housingtrustsv.org
- Type: loan

Fund is up to $150 million from Apple's 2019 $2.5 billion California housing commitment; 4 to 5 projects selected per round.

### Nine-county San Francisco Bay Area

**Bay Area Preservation Pilot (BAPP) acquisition and mini-permanent loans**
- Agency: Enterprise Community Loan Fund and Low Income Investment Fund (originating CDFIs and fund managers) with the Metropolitan Transportation Commission and Bay Area Housing Finance Authority; MTC contact Somaya Abdelgany, 415-778-5217
- Type: loan
- Typical award: $49 million revolving fund ($10 million MTC plus $39 million CDFI capital). Note A senior up to 85% LTV at lender rate; Note B subordinate (MTC capital) fixed at no more than 2% with a minimum 3:1 leverage; Note C first-loss at 0% with no payments and possible forgiveness if affordability is maintained; maximum program exposure $2,500,000 per borrower outstanding for Notes B and C; maximum 10-year term, no prepayment penalty; origination the greater of $30,000 or 1% of total loans. Two Oakland loans closed preserving 71 homes.
- AMI requirement: Occupied properties of 4 or more units, at least 80% occupied at acquisition, with rents affordable at or below 80% AMI, located in Transit Priority Areas or Priority Development Areas.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Rolling, first come first served through Enterprise or LIIF.)
- Layering notes: Nine-county Bay Area after the 2021 revisions (lower leverage requirement, up to $6 million convertible to forgivable debt, fund term extended to 20 years). Borrowers need 5 years of experience and 4 completed comparable projects (or a qualifying JV partner). Repayment at sale or refinance; pairs with county preservation funds, the City of Oakland and San Francisco small sites programs and BAHFA's separate Housing Preservation Loan Pilot ($17.8 million REAP 2). MTC public capital in Notes B and C, so prevailing wage is marked unclear.

**California Community Reinvestment Corporation (CCRC) bridge and refinance loans for occupied affordable properties**
- Agency: California Community Reinvestment Corporation (bank consortium CDFI), Glendale; contact Jennifer Quevedo, 818-550-9804
- Type: loan
- Typical award: Bridge loans to repay a maturing first mortgage ahead of recapitalization: term up to 5 years with up to 2 years interest only case by case; amortization the lesser of 35 years or 10 years less than remaining economic life; minimum DSCR 1.20; full recourse at CCRC discretion; prepayment greater of yield maintenance or 1%, waived if refinanced by a CCRC loan. Proceeds may fund closing costs, immediate repairs from a property condition assessment and sustainability improvements including an energy audit. Refinance loan terms are posted separately (updated September 2026).

- Agency: California Community Reinvestment Corporation (bank consortium CDFI), 225 W. Broadway Suite 120, Glendale; contact Jennifer Quevedo, jennifer.quevedo@e-ccrc.org, 818-550-9804

Recent regional loans: The Starling, Oakland (Eden Housing, 70 senior units, $6,721,000); Solaire Apartments, San Jose (January 2025, tax-exempt loan with 4% LIHTC); Creekside Trails, San Diego (October 2024 bridge loan).

- Typical award: Cohort program since 2019: technical workshops, a development coach, grant funds for predevelopment activities and a participation stipend for faith-based and community-based landowners; grant amounts not posted.
- AMI requirement: Affordable housing on faith-owned land, typically through a joint venture with an experienced developer.
- Cycle: annual NOFA (next: Next cohort date not posted; join the mailing list on the program page.)
- Layering notes: Useful for developers partnering with congregations under SB 4 (Affordable Housing on Faith and Higher Education Lands Act). Grants cover early feasibility before Housing Trust or CDFI predevelopment loans. Alameda County HCD is a funder, so Alameda projects may have a direct county tie-in.
- Source: https://www.lisc.org/bay-area/areas-of-work/affordable-housing/faithandhousing/
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)


### San Luis Obispo County

**San Luis Obispo County Housing Trust Fund revolving loans (private CDFI)**
- Agency: San Luis Obispo County Housing Trust Fund, 71 Zaca Lane Suite 130, San Luis Obispo, 805-543-5970 (Kathy McClenathen, Deputy Director)
- Type: loan
- Typical award: Notice of Funding Available updated April 1, 2026: up to $3 million available, maximum loan $3 million per project, term generally up to 5 years, 5% to 7% fixed interest, 0.5% to 2% fees plus costs, real estate collateral (may be subordinate), loan-to-value 80% to 100% including senior debt. LIHTC Project Loans (soft, 15-year or longer, from LHTF and PLHA grant funds): up to $40,000 per extremely low income unit and $20,000 per low income unit, $1.5 million per project. Since 2003: 70 loans over $44 million for 1,700 units; $5.9 million closed in 2024 with $20 million outstanding.
- AMI requirement: Extremely low to moderate income (most loans at or below 80% AMI); can finance units to 120% or 160% AMI; priority for housing serving people with disabilities; 40% of HTF resources committed to households with special needs. LHTF Loans: 55-year affordability, LIHTC-like income targeting, and 30% of LHTF funds must serve ELI units.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Rolling; four-step process starting with a phone or email inquiry, then invitation to apply. Maintains a 2026 Multi-Family Readiness List.)
- Layering notes: San Luis Obispo County's Department of Social Services Homeless Services Division (HSD, Devin Drake, Director; George Solis, Principal Administrative Manager; HSDgrants@co.slo.ca.us) runs one combined annual Action Plan NOFA each fall for CDBG, HOME, ESG, HHAP, PLHA, Title 29 and County General Fund Support on the Neighborly portal, and is the Continuum of Care collaborative applicant and administrative entity (CA-614). The Department of Planning and Building runs Title 22 land use incentives and assesses the new Title 31 in-lieu fee; the Behavioral Health Department holds BHSA; the Housing Authority of San Luis Obispo (HASLO) and its San Luis Obispo Nonprofit Housing Corporation, Paso Robles Housing Authority and Peoples' Self-Help Housing are the main developers; and the private nonprofit San Luis Obispo County Housing Trust Fund is the local CDFI gap lender. The Urban County covers the unincorporated area plus Arroyo Grande, Atascadero, Morro Bay, Paso Robles, Pismo Beach and San Luis Obispo (Grover Beach is outside). The County repealed its inclusionary ordinance on June 7, 2022 and replaced it in October 2025 with a voluntary Regional Housing Incentive Program and Regional Housing Fund. slocounty.ca.gov opens directly but rate-limits bursts (HTTP 429); Legistar web API is not enabled for the County. The Housing Trust Fund is the fastest local money in the county and has participated in nearly every recent affordable deal (Cambria Pines, Rolling Hills III, Cleaver and Clark Commons, River Walk Terrace). Use it for predevelopment and acquisition bridges before County and state awards, and ask about the LIHTC soft loan product funded by state LHTF matching grants ($1.5 million LHTF award reported in 2025).
- Source: https://www.slochtf.org/for-borrowers
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)


### San Mateo County and northern Santa Clara County (15 miles from Menlo Park)

**Catalyst Housing Fund (Meta) administered by LISC Bay Area**
- Agency: LISC Bay Area (administrator: underwriting, disbursement, fund and asset management) with Meta (Facebook), the City of East Palo Alto, the City of Menlo Park and Envision Transform Build; contact Lily Berticevich, Director of Community Investment
- Type: loan
- Typical award: $17 million total fund ($9 million-plus initially set aside for East Palo Alto); $75 million LISC leverage goal; 9 deals closed, $16.2 million invested, $6.5 million available; 775 units produced or preserved.
- AMI requirement: At least 60% of financed units affordable to low income households, of which 30% extremely low income and 30% very low income; priority for family housing and no net loss of rent-controlled or deed-restricted units.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Rolling; contact LISC Bay Area.)
- Layering notes: Geography is a 15-mile radius of Meta's Menlo Park campus (roughly SFO to SJC), so it reaches San Mateo County and northern Santa Clara County cities. Projects are defined with community groups and East Palo Alto. Small remaining balance ($6.5 million), so treat as a gap or acquisition source rather than a primary lender.
- Source: https://www.lisc.org/bay-area/areas-of-work/affordable-housing/catalyst-housing-fund/
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)


### Santa Clara County

**Destination: Home Supportive Housing and Innovation Fund (private acquisition and predevelopment financing and developer capacity grants)**
- Agency: Destination: Home (Santa Clara County public-private partnership nonprofit), San Jose; fund seeded by Cisco ($50 million, 2018) and Apple ($50 million, 2019)
- Type: loan
- Typical award: More than $96 million invested since 2018: no-interest or low-interest acquisition and predevelopment financing for 42 extremely low income and supportive housing developments with more than 4,100 units; flexible capacity-building grants to 8 nonprofit developers (1,600 units in pipeline); capacity grants to the Cities of Campbell, Morgan Hill, Mountain View and San Jose. Loan sizes are not posted.
- AMI requirement: Supportive housing and extremely low income (30% AMI) housing for formerly homeless households in Santa Clara County.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Open funding opportunities are posted on the fund page; otherwise rolling by invitation.)
- Layering notes: The private counterpart to the County's Measure A and the Housing Trust Supportive Housing Fund. Zero or low interest acquisition money lets sponsors tie up sites before County Measure A, Homekey+ or NPLH awards. Destination: Home is also a founding partner of the Bay Area Housing Innovation Fund (separate record) and funded a dedicated San Jose planner for supportive housing projects. Santa Clara County only.
- Source: https://destinationhomesv.org/funding-impactful-strategies/supportive-housing-innovation-fund/
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)

**Supportive Housing Fund (Housing Trust Silicon Valley with the County of Santa Clara, Measure A)**
- Agency: Housing Trust Silicon Valley (CDFI; California Finance Lender License 6053356), 75 E. Santa Clara Street Suite 1350, San Jose; lending team Nick Friend (408-703-3837 ext. 223, nick@housingtrustsv.org) and Stephaney Kipple (ext. 244); funded by County of Santa Clara ($16.9 million) with $5 million Housing Trust match
- Type: loan
- Typical award: Maximum $8,000,000 secured by real estate or $800,000 on corporate guaranty; projects with 50% or more eligible units up to 100% of the maximum, otherwise 50%; term up to 3 years; interest 0% to 2% with interest holdback; acquisition up to 100% LTV, construction or rehab 85% LTV. $43 million allocated to date supporting 1,595 permanent supportive housing units started or preserved.
- AMI requirement: Permanent housing with supportive services for extremely low income individuals and families and those with special needs; projects must conform to the County's Measure A NOFA.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Rolling; contact the Housing Trust lending team.)
- Layering notes: Revolving fund created by County MOU June 9, 2015 and amended April 11, 2017 to implement the 2016 Measure A bond pipeline. Repayment is due at the close of County or other public land financing, construction closing or permanent closing. Program guidelines on the site date from 2017; confirm current terms. Prevailing wage is required by the fund guidelines (County Prevailing Wage Requirements), so budget State prevailing wage from the first draw. Pair with the County Office of Supportive Housing Measure A and Affordable Housing Fund records and with Destination: Home's Supportive Housing and Innovation Fund.
- Source: https://housingtrustsv.org/programs/developer-funding/supportive-housing-fund/
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)


### Santa Clara, San Mateo, San Francisco, Alameda and Santa Cruz Counties

**Bay Area Housing Innovation Fund (Housing Accelerator Fund with Apple, Sobrato Philanthropies and Destination: Home)**
- Agency: Housing Accelerator Fund (San Francisco nonprofit lender), with founding partners Apple, Sobrato Philanthropies and Destination: Home; later investors Valhalla Foundation, Harry and Jeanette Weinberg Foundation and individual philanthropists
- Type: loan
- Typical award: $100 million fund (launched July 2024 at $50 million, doubled December 2025). Mezzanine construction-to-permanent loans (September 2025 term sheet): up to $20 million per project, higher on request; construction period interest about 3% to 5% fixed; permanent period subordinate debt repaid from residual receipts and refinance proceeds to a 5% target annualized return; total term up to 20 years; origination up to 1%. Construction-to-permanent first mortgage loans (August 2025 term sheet) with the same $20 million cap, 3% to 5% construction pricing and 20-year maximum. Loans to date: $16 million for 1633 Valencia, San Francisco (Mercy Housing California, 145 PSH units, 19-month build, about $525,000 per unit) and $11 million for Harvey West Studios, Santa Cruz (Housing Matters with MidPen, 120 PSH units).
- AMI requirement: Net new permanently affordable units up to 120% AMI with preference for 50% and 30% AMI; nearly half of pilot homes reserved for formerly homeless or extremely low income households.
- Cycle: rolling (next: Rolling after entitlement; a NOFA is forthcoming (sign up on the fund page). Construction must start within 12 months of commitment and reach certificate of occupancy within 3 years.)
- Layering notes: Eligible counties: Santa Clara, San Mateo, San Francisco, Alameda and Santa Cruz. Intended to let projects skip the LIHTC queue: it funds construction and permanent debt for projects that commit to cost and time targets about 40% below Bay Area averages, with a third-party evaluator documenting the approach. Entitlements must be in hand before commitment. Pairs with county Measure A or local gap funds, Homekey+ and project-based vouchers; residual receipts split must follow local public agency policy where applicable.
- Source: https://www.sfhaf.org/bay-area-housing-innovation-fund/
- Confidence: verified (researched 2026-11-08)
